stories.title: Man sentenced to 15 years for role in killing Naramata woman
stories.summary: More than five years after Kathleen Richardson was killed in her Naramata home, one of the two men responsible for her death has been sentenced to 15 years in prison.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
More than five years after Kathleen Richardson was killed in her Naramata, B.C., home, one of the two men responsible for her death has been sentenced to 15 years in prison.

With 204 days credited for time already served, 27-year-old Ekene Anigbo has 14 years and 161 days remaining on his sentence.

For Julie Robertson, who remembers Richardson as a kind, generous and deeply involved member of the community, the sentencing marks the end of a long and painful chapter.

“She was so kind, she was so giving, she was a huge member of our community,” a tearful Robertson said outside the Kelowna courthouse.

Richardson was 57 when she was killed on June 9, 2021.

Court heard that Anigbo and Jalen Falk broke into her home looking for her son, Wade Cudmore, in gang-related retaliation connected to the killings of brothers Erick and Carlo Fryer the previous month.

Richardson was confronted, restrained and bound with duct tape and zip ties before being shot twice in the face.

In sentencing Anigbo, Justice Allison Beames called Richardson’s killing senseless, describing how both men participated in confronting and confining her before wrapping multiple layers of duct tape around her head and covering her eyes.

The judge said Richardson was in an “obviously extremely vulnerable position” when she was shot twice in the face, killing her instantaneously or near instantaneously.

Anigbo was originally charged with first-degree murder. But following a lengthy trial earlier this year, he was convicted of manslaughter after the judge found the Crown had not proven beyond a reasonable doubt which of the two men fired the fatal shots.

The Crown had sought a life sentence, while the defence argued for a term of 12 to 14 years.

Anigbo’s parole eligibility will be determined by the Parole Board of Canada.

Under federal rules, most offenders become eligible to apply for full parole after serving one-third of their sentence or seven years, whichever is less.

Falk, meanwhile, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and is serving a life sentence, with no possibility of parole for 16 years.

Robertson says she had hoped the sentencing would bring some closure for those who have spent years waiting for answers.

“For me to be here today was like, this is the end. The trials are done,” Roberston said.

Robertson says she often thinks about Richardson, and believes her son, who remains behind bars for the Fryer brothers’ murders, likely does too.

“His actions caused this and that’s something that he has to live with for the rest of his life, and that has got to be heavy.”

stories.title: Two charged in Brockton disturbance
stories.summary: Two people have been charged after a disturbance in Brockton.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Two people have been charged after a disturbance in Brockton.

On Sunday just after 5 a.m., South Bruce OPP were called with a report of a disturbance at a home in the municipality.

Officers found and arrested two people, seizing guns.

A 30-year-old from Huron Kinloss has been charged with:

Uttering threats to cause death or bodily harm

Mischief under $5,000

Operation while prohibited

Unauthorized possession of a firearm

Knowledge of unauthorized possession of a firearm

Breach of firearms regulation – storing firearm or restricted weapon

A 21-year-old from Huron East has been charged with:

Unlawfully in dwelling/house

Failure to comply with a release order other than to attend court

The suspects’ names are not being released in an effort to protect the victim.

stories.title: Nearly a third of Canadians skipping meals due to food insecurity: survey
stories.summary: Results from an annual national poverty survey paint a worsening picture of food affordability in Canada, especially for young people.
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie
stories.content:
Results from an annual national poverty survey paint a worsening picture of food affordability in Canada, especially for young people, as tariffs imposed by the United States continue to shake up the Canadian economy.

The Salvation Army’s 2026 Poverty and Socioeconomic Analysis, released today, polled more than 1,500 Canadians and found that 31 per cent skipped meals or reduced their meal sizes because they couldn’t afford groceries , up from 27 per cent one year ago.

The number of people who reported using community supports such as food banks was also up — 15 per cent of those surveyed this year, compared with 11 per cent last year.

Young people report an even worse situation, according to the research conducted by Edelman Data and Intelligence on behalf of the Salvation Army.

Forty-one per cent of respondents aged 18-34 said they skipped meals, 10 percentage points higher than the average, and 23 per cent said they accessed food supports.

A separate report from Daily Bread Food Bank says the number of children struggling with food insecurity in Toronto has risen, as food bank visits held steady at more than 4.1 million visits for the second year.

The survey also suggests that Canadians are more concerned about U.S. tariffs and their effect on the economy than last year, with nearly nine in 10 saying they were worried the trade war would spike prices for everyday goods.

Three in five surveyed reported their household was already feeling the pinch from U.S. tariffs.

The survey was conducted over several days in September among a nationally representative sample of Canadians, including some current and past users of Salvation Army services, who are members of the online Angus Reid Forum. Residents of Canada’s territories were not included in the survey and a margin of error cannot be calculated for a non-probability sample, the report noted.

On the housing front, half of respondents said they aren’t confident they could find another home in their area that was both affordable and met their household needs, while 24 per cent said they spend at least half their after-tax income on housing costs.

To cover basic needs, 50 per cent of Canadians polled said they dipped into savings while 40 per cent reported taking on debt or using credit.

Glenn van Gulik, a strategic engagement director for the Salvation Army, called the results “deeply concerning.”

“For many families, making ends meet is no longer about cutting back on extras. It’s about making difficult choices between food, housing and other basic necessities,” van Gulik wrote in a statement.

stories.title: Road worker dies after being hit by dump truck in Pickering
stories.summary: A road worker died Monday after being hit by a dump truck near Peter Matthews and Alexander Knox drives in Pickering, Durham Regional Police say.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A road worker died Monday after being hit by a dump truck in Pickering, Durham Regional Police say.

Officers were called around 2:40 p.m. on Nov. 2 for reports of a collision near Peter Matthews and Alexander Knox drives.

“During asphalt repair on Peter Matthews Drive, a dump truck was reversing southbound when it struck a 31-year-old male road worker,” police said in a news release Tuesday.

“The road worker was transported to local-area hospital where he succumbed to his injuries. The driver of the dump truck remained on scene and cooperated with police.”

Roads in the area were closed for several hours while police investigated.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Harper offered Mark Carney government role, new memoir reveals
stories.summary: The book offers Harper's perspective on his tenure in Canadian politics, from uniting the right under the modern Conservative party through a decade in government.
stories.author: Kyle Duggan
stories.content:
Former prime minister Stephen Harper says he offered Mark Carney , then the governor of the Bank of Canada, a role in his Conservative government in 2012 — though not as finance minister. Not right away, at least.

In his new book “Here for Canada: Memoirs of the 22nd Prime Minister,” Harper says he told Carney the finance position was already taken but indicated that he would be next in line for the job when it became vacant.

“Obviously, I did not offer him the post of minister of finance, as it was then not available. However, I indicated that, if he chose to join the government, he would be the leading candidate should the post come open,” Harper writes.

Carney said in an interview on CBC during the 2025 Liberal leadership race that Harper had “asked me if I would be his finance minister in 2012.” He said at the time it wouldn’t be appropriate to go directly from the Bank of Canada governorship to party politics.

In his book, released Tuesday, Harper says while Carney was “highly effective” as bank governor, his finance minister Jim Flaherty was “increasingly” worried in the wake of the 2011 election that Carney was nurturing political ambitions and might wish to seek the Liberal party leadership — something widely rumoured at the time.

“This was a serious concern for us,” Harper writes.

Harper says he brought it up with Nigel Wright, his chief of staff, who suggested a job offer would either secure Carney’s services for the government or force him to rule out a Liberal leadership bid, since he was in the non-partisan role of bank governor.

“Mark took some time to reflect on the opportunity, ultimately declaring that he should stay out of partisan politics,” he said, noting Carney left soon after for the top job at the Bank of England.

The mention of Carney is just a small aside in the nearly 650-page memoir. Harper says he felt he should address the issue since it has “occasionally cropped up in the media.”

The book offers Harper’s perspective on his tenure in Canadian politics from start to finish, from uniting the right under the modern Conservative party through a decade in government.

It also contains a rare first-person account of Harper’s final election campaign and the defeat of his government in 2015.

The former prime minister writes that he debated stepping down from the leadership in the summer of 2014 to rejuvenate the party.

Harper says after deciding to remain at the helm and lead his party into what he knew would be a tough race, he decided he would serve until just after the 150th anniversary of Confederation on July 1, 2017, then call a leadership race.

Harper also says he only learned of one of the most controversial episodes of the 2015 election — his party’s embrace of a “barbaric cultural practices hotline” — during his preparation for the French leaders’ debate in Montreal when the news “flashed across my screen.”

The announcement of the proposed tip line — which frustrated Red Tories and hindered the party’s outreach efforts with multicultural communities years after the fact — was fronted at the time by former cabinet ministers Kellie Leitch and Chris Alexander.

Harper writes he was “furious” upon learning about the policy, which he says he was not consulted on and had to defend on the campaign trail.

The book spans decades of Canadian political history. It includes Harper’s description of face-to-face standoffs with Russian President Vladimir Putin at G8 meetings, his reaction to the 2008 parliamentary crisis — when opposition parties attempted and failed to form a coalition government to oust the Conservatives — and Harper’s personal experience during the 2014 shooting on Parliament Hill, which happened when he was without his normal personal protective detail.

The former prime minister also offers up occasional reflections on current matters. While he attended the World Economic Forum in Davos twice during in his time in office, he now says he opposes it.

If he were prime minister today, Harper writes, he would end the Canadian government’s participation in the WEF, an event he describes as a once-useful forum that has become a club for advancing the “narrow interests of its globalist, elitist attendees.”

stories.title: Carney meeting with Commonwealth leaders in Antigua and Barbuda
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney is in Antigua and Barbuda today for a meeting of Commonwealth heads of government.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is in Antigua and Barbuda today for a meeting of Commonwealth heads of government.

Carney has a full itinerary for his one day in Antigua, which will kick off with a meeting with Antigua and Barbuda’s Prime Minister Gaston Browne.

Carney will then host a working breakfast for Caribbean leaders before the Commonwealth meeting begins.

He will participate in two executive sessions at the meeting and meet one-on-one with the leaders of Australia, Guyana and Ghana.

Carney will also attend a lunch and dinner hosted by King Charles before heading back to Ottawa tonight.

Much of the focus of the Commonwealth meeting will be on trade, though experts say it is also an opportunity to boost diplomatic ties with a variety of countries that belong to the 56-member organization.

stories.title: No one injured after military chopper damaged in landing on Canadian ship
stories.summary: A flight safety report from the Department of National Defence says the incident happened Oct. 6 aboard the Hmcs Ville de Québec in the Norwegian Sea.
stories.author: Aaron Sousa
stories.content:
Defence officials say there were no injuries after a military helicopter was seriously damaged during a night flight landing on a Canadian navy frigate.

A flight safety report from the Department of National Defence says it happened Oct. 6 aboard the Hmcs Ville de Québec in the Norwegian Sea.

The report says as the Cyclone helicopter came in for landing, two main rotor blades clipped its tail boom and severed multiple components, including a tail rotor drive shaft.

It says the four crew members on board performed an emergency engine shutdown and fled the aircraft.

Officials say none of the four were injured, though the helicopter sustained serious damage.

Hmcs Ville de Québec has been at sea since July as part of Operation Reassurance, a Nato mission meant to deter Russian aggression in eastern Europe.

“While no technical issues have been identified to date, the investigation remains ongoing and continues to focus on material & systems, environmental and human factors,” the report issued Thursday says.

stories.title: Three teen boys wanted in London assault investigation
stories.summary: The London police is looking for three teen boys wanted in connection with an assault in the south end of the city late last month.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
The London police is looking for three teen boys wanted in connection with an assault in the south end of the city late last month.

On Oct. 24 just after 10:30 p.m., police said multiple teenagers were seen near Osgoode Drive and Adelaide Street South setting off fireworks towards homes and cars.

Officers added a group of youths assaulted two adults who were outside a home on Osgoode.

Police arrived on scene and arrested three suspects. The victims were taken to hospital with serious, but non-life-threatening injuries.

Three 15-year-old girls have been charged with assault causing bodily harm.

Investigators are now looking for three teenage boys wanted in connection. Anyone who was in the area between 10 p.m. and 11 p.m. and May have seen the assault or has security footage or dash cam footage, is asked to contact the police at 519-661-5670.

stories.title: Judge won’t intervene in case of Winnipeg synagogue vs. congregants opposed to Gaza war
stories.summary: The synagogue says the dismissal was not due to the couple's views, but because of a threatening letter
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
A Winnipeg judge has ruled that a synagogue can revoke the membership of two congregants who became activists against Israel’s war in Gaza.

Congregation Etz Chayim revoked the membership last year of Dr. Emet Eviatar and Dr. David Hoult, a married couple who had been members of the synagogue for more than 30 years.

They took it to court, arguing their membership was revoked due to their criticism of Israel’s response to the October 7 attacks by Hamas. However, the synagogue alleges the pair were banned after one of them wrote a threatening letter.

At the heart of the case was whether the termination was unlawful under the province’s Corporations Act. The decision from Manitoba’s Court of King’s Bench, released on Oct. 23, said that it was not the court’s place to intervene and the synagogue can determine its own membership rules.

A lawyer for the married couple told National Post they were disappointed by the outcome but they are reviewing it with counsel as they decide on future steps.

“Dr. Eviatar and Dr. Hoult do not believe that their family membership was terminated because of a ‘threat’ but because of their political views regarding Israel’s actions in the war in Gaza,” their lawyer Murray Trachtenberg said.

Following the October 7 massacre, when 1,200 people were murdered by Hamas terrorists in Israel, Eviatar co-founded the Manitoba chapter of a group that was critical of Israel’s actions. The group is part of a larger organization of “Israelis and Palestinians opposed to the war in Gaza and Israeli military operations,” according to the courts’ description.

Eviatar also appeared on a CBC radio show in October 2024. She talked about the organization and said the point was to have “hard conversations.” She also said that the group did not use the word “genocide” to describe what’s happening in Gaza, “but it’s a strategic choice and it’s not because they don’t think that’s what’s happening.”

Vandalizing synagogue in Winnipeg with swastikas was a 'cowardly' act meant to 'intimidate,' exec. director says

Israeli group sues Canadian human rights museum over 'Nakba' exhibit

After that appearance, Eviatar said the synagogue’s rabbi called her to say she was no longer allowed to lead a specific service — a role she had maintained for 20 years. A month later, she said the synagogue accused her of “aligning herself with a movement which is mutually exclusive of and contrary to the interests of Jewish people and the state of Israel,” according to the court document.

The conflict between the couple and the synagogue worsened when Hoult was critical of measures being taken to improve security.

In March 2025, the synagogue implemented safety measures, after an assessment by Winnipeg police, that included locked and monitored entrances, a pre-registration requirement for Saturday morning services, and the use of security personnel.

In a letter to the synagogue’s president a few months later, Hoult wrote that “hysteria and paranoia” led to the synagogue “giving Hamas a victory by caving to fear.” He also said the measures were “psychologically stupid.”

The synagogue’s position is that the letter was threatening and “needed to be taken seriously, particularly as it came within weeks of Dr. Hoult’s frustrated attempt” to have the security measures removed. The membership was revoked due to this incident, according to the synagogue.

A lawyer representing Congregation Etz Chayim declined comment to National Post.

Justice Victor Toews wrote in his decision that he did not accept that Hoult’s words “were willfully or otherwise intentionally used to communicate a threat.”

However, Toews noted, in conclusion, that unless there is an underlying legal dispute — which there was not in this case — the law is “clear that religious groups are free to determine their own membership and rules.”

After that appearance, Eviatar said the synagogue’s rabbi called her to say she was no longer allowed to lead a specific service — a role she had maintained for 20 years. A month later, she said the synagogue accused her of “aligning herself with a movement which is mutually exclusive of and contrary to the interests of Jewish people and the state of Israel,” according to the court document.
The conflict between the couple and the synagogue worsened when Hoult was critical of measures being taken to improve security.

In March 2025, the synagogue implemented safety measures, after an assessment by Winnipeg police, that included locked and monitored entrances, a pre-registration requirement for Saturday morning services, and the use of security personnel.

In a letter to the synagogue’s president a few months later, Hoult wrote that “hysteria and paranoia” led to the synagogue “giving Hamas a victory by caving to fear.” He also said the measures were “psychologically stupid.”

The synagogue’s position is that the letter was threatening and “needed to be taken seriously, particularly as it came within weeks of Dr. Hoult’s frustrated attempt” to have the security measures removed. The membership was revoked due to this incident, according to the synagogue.
A lawyer representing Congregation Etz Chayim declined comment to National Post.
Justice Victor Toews wrote in his decision that he did not accept that Hoult’s words “were willfully or otherwise intentionally used to communicate a threat.”

However, Toews noted, in conclusion, that unless there is an underlying legal dispute — which there was not in this case — the law is “clear that religious groups are free to determine their own membership and rules.”

content_blocks.text: A Winnipeg judge has ruled that a synagogue can revoke the membership of two congregants who became activists against Israel’s war in Gaza.
Congregation Etz Chayim revoked the membership last year of Dr. Emet Eviatar and Dr. David Hoult, a married couple who had been members of the synagogue for more than 30 years.

They took it to court, arguing their membership was revoked due to their criticism of Israel’s response to the October 7 attacks by Hamas. However, the synagogue alleges the pair were banned after one of them wrote a threatening letter.

At the heart of the case was whether the termination was unlawful under the province’s Corporations Act. The decision from Manitoba’s Court of King’s Bench, released on Oct. 23, said that it was not the court’s place to intervene and the synagogue can determine its own membership rules.

stories.title: Classes cancelled as SIU investigates death at U of T Mississauga
stories.summary: The University of Toronto cancelled classes at its Mississauga campus Tuesday after a 19-year-old man was found dead in a residence following a police response Monday night.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
The University of Toronto cancelled classes at its Mississauga campus Tuesday after a 19-year-old man was found dead in a student residence following a police response Monday night.

Ontario’s police watchdog is investigating the circumstances because Peel Regional Police officers were at the scene when the man died.

The Special Investigations Unit (SIU) said Peel police received reports that a man had assaulted a woman in Brampton. Officers located a suspect around 9 p.m. at a student residence near Dundas Street West and Mississauga Road.

The university issued a shelter-in-place order for students near McLuhan Court, a residence complex housing hundreds of first-year students, while police responded.

“A gunshot was heard and the man was found inside with a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The man was pronounced deceased early this morning,” the SIU said.

“As Peel Regional Police officers were in and around the scene at the time of the man’s death, the SIU was notified and invoked its mandate.”

No other injuries were reported.

The university said it cancelled classes out of compassion for more than 2,000 students living in residence and others affected by the incident. The shelter-in-place order was also lifted.

“Employees who were likewise required to shelter in place on campus last night will also take the time they need for their wellbeing,” the school said in a notice.

“UTM recognizes that over the coming days there will be many questions from members of our community. Please know that we are here to support you and our community.”

Peel police said in a statement Tuesday officers entered the unit after making multiple unsuccessful attempts to communicate with the man. He was found dead, bringing the incident to an end at approximately 1:30 a.m.

Police said they would hold a news conference later Tuesday but had not announced a time.

The SIU said four investigators and two forensic investigators have been assigned to the case.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the SIU.

stories.summary: Preliminary information suggests the 19-year-old died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The province’s police watchdog says it’s investigating after a 19-year-old man was found dead at the University of Toronto’s Mississauga campus.

The Special Investigations Unit says preliminary information suggests the male died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound after Peel Regional Police officers investigating an assault located the man at the UTM student residence.

News of the person’s death comes after the school issued a shelter-in-place order Monday night for students near McLuhan Court residence, a complex that houses hundreds of first-year students.

Peel police later said the incident, described as a dangerous weapons call, had been resolved and there was no threat to public safety in an update early Tuesday morning.

The SIU alleges the man who died had assaulted a woman in Brampton on Monday afternoon and police located him at a student residence near Dundas Street West and Mississauga Road.

The watchdog says a gunshot was heard and the man was pronounced dead early Tuesday.

The SIU says it has invoked its mandate because Peel Regional Police officers were in and around the scene at the time of the man’s death.

The watchdog says no other injuries were reported and there is no threat to public safety.

UTM says its campus is open today but classes are cancelled.

stories.title: Teddington Park home sells below what sellers paid in 2018
stories.summary: Three-bedroom house close to golf club sells for $2.31-million
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
97 Bocastle Ave., Toronto

Asking price: $2,358,000 (August, 2026)

Previous asking prices: $2,498,000 (June, 2026); $2,698,000 (May, 2026)

Selling price: $2.31-million (September, 2026)

Previous selling prices: $2.5-million (October, 2018); $1,403,250 (August, 2014); $549,000 (August, 2001)

Taxes: $11,839 (2026)

Days on the market: 23

Property days on market: 115

Listing agent: Belinda Lelli, Royal LePage Real Estate Services Ltd.

This three-bedroom house is close to the Rosedale Golf Club, amenities on Yonge Street, and reputable schools, including TFS, the former Toronto French School. The owners, who rented out the house, never had trouble finding tenants. But finding potential buyers was more difficult, especially with tenants limiting access to one-hour open houses each week this spring.

“The sellers purchased in the height of the market in 2018 for $2.5-million, and leased this beautiful home for a great return,” said agent Belinda Lelli.

“I had buyers coming from all over the world, like Korea and China, because we have the top schools [there]. But when people are coming in for a weekend, it was hard to show.”

Once the tenants moved out this summer, the home was painted and professional staged and the 35- by 120-foot lot was landscaped. The asking price was also adjusted, trimming $340,000 from the May sticker price. One guest, drawn to the property’s walkability, negotiated a $2.31-million deal – $190,000 below what the sellers paid eight years previously.

“Once it was all showcased properly, I got the traction I needed,” Ms. Lelli said.

“We sold at nearly 100 per cent of the asking price.”

This two-storey house has separate living and dining rooms, and a family room with a gas fireplace and access to a deck and putting green.

Another deck, accessed through a bedroom, is above the garage and overlooks a double driveway and front courtyard.

There are four bathrooms and a kitchen with granite countertops and stainless-steel appliances.

The basement has a recreation area with a wood-burning fireplace.

“This is in Teddington Park, a small, coveted location that is defined by a few streets, east of Yonge,” said Ms. Lelli.

“What’s very special is it’s a wider lot. You have a garage plus additional four-car parking, which is unheard of.”

stories.title: Buyers seeking two-bedroom condo in North York have plenty of options
stories.summary: Corner unit on Bathurst Street sells for $550,000
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
3830 Bathurst St., No. 404, Toronto

Asking price: $598,000 (August, 2026)

Previous asking price: $669,000 (June, 2026)

Selling price: $550,000 (September, 2026)

Previous selling prices: $665,000 (October, 2021); $515,000 (July, 2019); $345,000 (March, 2017); $335,000 (December, 2012); $311,000 (April, 2010); $260,000 (August, 2006); $217,171 (July, 2006)

Taxes: $2,455 (2026)

Days on the market: 29

Property days on market: 97

Buyer’s agent: Ira Jelinek, Harvey Kalles Real Estate Ltd.

A family seeking a two-bedroom condo in a small building in North York had $650,000 budget this summer, giving them a large selection to choose from. They picked this roughly 870-square-foot unit in an eight-storey building on Bathurst Street, north of Highway 401, paying $115,000 less than what the seller paid in 2021.

“Under $650,000, you can find two-bedroom units in North York, between 800 to 1,000 square feet, quite easily,” said the buyer’s agent Ira Jelinek.

“This one had a good location, layout and size.”

The buyer, who only noticed this two-bedroom unit after its price was reduced to $598,000, used recent sales in the 20-year-old building as a guide in negotiating their $550,000 deal in September.

“There were some sales in 2025 and 2026 of two-bedroom units of similar sizes trading between $525,000 and $575,000,” said Mr. Jelinek.

“We felt $550,000 was the right price, regardless of if they were listed for $669,000 at one time.”

This unit has bedrooms on opposite sides of an open-concept living and dining area with floor-to-ceiling windows and access to a curved balcony facing southwest.

There are stacked laundry machines, two full bathrooms, and a renovated kitchen with quartz countertops and stainless-steel appliances.

stories.title: Toronto’s child hunger rates nearly double as city sees 4.1M food bank visits: report
stories.summary: The Toronto resident is often looking for milk, eggs and vegetables such as potatoes or carrots, to make sure his children get the nutrition they need.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen
stories.content:
When Volodymyr Kravchuk visits the Daily Bread Food Bank, he’s constantly thinking about his two young sons.

The Toronto resident is often looking for milk, eggs and vegetables such as potatoes or carrots, to make sure his children get the nutrition they need.

Kravchuk and his family moved to Canada from Ukraine in September 2023 and he remembers having to start his life over from scratch. While he holds degrees in psychology and marketing, Kravchuk said it’s been difficult finding stable employment and there are essentials that he has to turn to food banks for.

“Sometimes, somebody can lose their job (and) need more money to feed his family,” Kravchuk, who sometimes volunteers at Daily Bread, said. “In one day, everything can change.”

A new report from Daily Bread Food Bank says the number of children struggling with food insecurity in Toronto has risen, as food bank visits held steady at more than 4.1 million visits for the second year.

The non-profit’s latest Who’s Hungry report, released Tuesday, says more than one in eight children living in Toronto rely on food banks, which is nearly double the rate from 2022, when one in 15 children relied on them.

The report says 67 per cent of parents have given up a meal to make sure their children had enough food to eat while 17 per cent had a child in their household go hungry at least once a week in 2026.

Neil Hetherington, CEO of Daily Bread, said this rise in child hunger is “alarming,” as children became the most overrepresented group in food bank clients across the city. He says the roughly 220 food banks his organization services across the city have been feeling the strain.

“The fact that it’s more children than ever before is what’s changing and that it is the working poor,” he said. “It’s a horrific tax on each of the food banks.”

One in 10 Torontonians are still regularly relying on food banks but Hetherington said the city has “risen to the occasion to be able to meet the need.”

However, there are ongoing challenges, especially with the U.S.-Canada tariff war and the cost-of-living crisis.

One in four food bank clients spent all of their income on housing, an increase from one in five clients in 2025.

“We know why they’re coming to food banks and we just have to have the courage and leadership and fortitude to be able to make those policy changes,” Hetherington said.

The report includes several policy recommendations aimed at all three levels of government to address growing food insecurity, such as a provincial establishment of a Shelter Allowance Reserve Fund to help social assistance recipients regain housing and a municipal investment of $100 million to preserve Toronto’s affordable housing.

Kitty Raman Costa, executive director of the Parkdale Community Food Bank, said they’re serving more than 15,000 food clients through delivery and community drop-ins since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Many members of the Parkdale community who are employed still rely on the food bank because of the cost-of-living crisis, Raman Costa said. She’s also seen an influx of families with two working parents come in, who are struggling to balance rent and increasing food costs.

“We need to prioritize items like school lunch supplies, snacks, easy meals that young or older kids can prepare when parents are working,” she said.

stories.summary: Mississauga - The province's police watchdog says it's investigating after a 19-year-old man was found dead at the University of Toronto's Mississauga campus.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Special Investigations Unit says preliminary information suggests the male died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound after Peel Regional Police officers investigating an assault located the man at the UTM student residence.

Peel police later said the incident, described as a dangerous weapons call, had been resolved and there was no threat to public safety in an update early Tuesday morning.

The SIU alleges the man who died had assaulted a woman in Brampton on Monday afternoon and police located him at a student residence near Dundas Street West and Mississauga Road.

The watchdog says a gunshot was heard and the man was pronounced dead early Tuesday.

The SIU says it has invoked its mandate because Peel Regional Police officers were in and around the scene at the time of the man’s death.

UTM says its campus is open today but classes are cancelled.

stories.title: Osap pause hits paramedic students bound to work in underserved areas
stories.summary: Some paramedic students approved to receive funding through a government program aiming to boost health-care staffing have been swept up in the provincewide pause on student aid.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Paramedic students at a career college in northern Ontario who were approved to receive funding through a signature government program aiming to boost health-care staffing have been swept up in the provincewide pause on student aid.

More than 40 affected students have already dropped out, their school says.

Members of Premier Doug Ford’s government have often boasted about their Learn and Stay Grant, which covers the cost of tuition for nursing, paramedic and medical lab technology students who agree to work in underserved areas.

But it is funded through the Ontario Student Assistance Program, which Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn has paused for all career colleges and other private post-secondary institutions.

Quinn has tasked Kpmg with auditing Osap usage in career colleges and said that preliminary findings were of such concern that he enacted the Osap pause sector-wide to protect the integrity of the system until the audit is completed.

Between 2023-24 and 2024-25, the amount of provincial Osap grants to career colleges nearly doubled, to about $1 billion in the latter year, a previous freedom-of-information request by The Canadian Press showed.

A second FOI shows skyrocketing usage at a relatively small number of schools, and the ministry says it now has broad concerns about the integrity of the system.

Only one career college is eligible for the Learn and Stay Grant – CTS Canadian Career College, which offers a paramedic diploma program in North Bay, Sault Ste. Marie and Sudbury.

Some of the career colleges under suspicion saw increases in Osap usage of more than 1,000 per cent over three years. CTS saw a 14 per cent increase over that time, according to the data obtained through FOI.

Aaron Madgett is at the CTS campus in Sault Ste. Marie, trying to become a paramedic after getting laid off from Algoma Steel. He said his stomach dropped when he heard the funding was paused, and wondered if he would have to quit school.

“It kind of ripped away all the goals and aspirations that I had for me and my family, and I was gutted at the time,” he said.

Madgett said the school is helping, such as giving students chapters of textbooks they need, but he is now behind on property tax and electricity payments and has been making use of food bank services. Still, he said he is trying to stay positive.

“I have a positive outlook that things will work out,” he said. “I believe the government — there’s got to be something that they can do. There’s always something. That’s my belief.”

Quinn’s office said in a statement that “work is underway to reassess” Learn and Stay Grant eligibility at CTS Canadian Career College.

“As the Olsg has a separate, rigorous accountability process in place, including in-person instruction and return-of-service commitments, work is underway to reassess Olsg eligibility at this institution,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote.

Quinn touted Monday in the legislature that the Learn and Stay Grant is “supporting students pursuing in-demand health-care careers in communities that need them the most.”

He was speaking to the broader Osap pause in responding to an NDP motion calling on the government to provide a plan within 14 days for relief for affected students.

Quinn said his message to “impacted, legitimate students” is that he is working efficiently to bring forward a stronger Osap for all.

“You deserve an education that is free from fraudulent, abusive, and malicious actors, so that you can get the high-quality, legitimate skills you need to launch successful, fulfilling careers,” he said.

CTS said that 41 students who were supposed to be receiving the Learn and Stay Grant have already dropped out, while 115 grant-funded students are left.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said the government is making students pay for a problem they did not cause.

“The government’s failing,” he said. “It is cutting its nose off to spite its face.”

Fyonna Vanderwerf is in the CTS paramedic program in North Bay. The Learn and Stay Grant was supposed to pay her tuition and other school costs, and she intended to rely on an Osap loan for living expenses while she studied.

“Mortgage, food, gas, money — there’s nothing there, and there won’t be anything there for the foreseeable future,” she said.

“I really want everything investigated. I really do. But I also want accountability for the employment commitment that we signed for.”

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the government should be transparent about the funding streams affected by the Osap pause and the impacts they are having.

“These communities desperately need those students,” she said. “We need those paramedics, and we need those workers out there.”

stories.title: ‘I shared my whole life with this woman’: Canadians awarded $56 million in defamation case against alleged cult leader
stories.summary: In part one of this three-part W5 investigation: “Fake Filtered Cult Leader,” CTV News’ investigative unit examines a self-described spiritual teacher whose online presence helped attract followers around the world.
stories.author: Jack Hauen, Derek Miller
stories.content:
In part one of this three-part W5 investigation: “ Fake Filtered Cult Leader ,” CTV News’ investigative unit examines a self-described spiritual teacher whose online presence helped attract followers around the world. Drawing on interviews and extensive reporting, W5 explores concerns raised by former members and the questions surrounding the organization behind the carefully curated public image.

A Hawaii jury has handed three Canadians one of the largest civil awards in the state’s history after a yearslong battle with an alleged cult leader.

The jury ordered Liane Wilson, who goes by Liana Shanti online, to pay Paula Haygarth and Byron and Stefanie Horvath, all from Saskatchewan, US$40.1 million, or just over C$56 million.

The award is the latest development in a harrowing and bizarre four-year-long legal battle.

Liana Shanti, who claims to be a self-made multimillionaire spiritual teacher with 100,000 online students, originally sued the Canadians, accusing them of online posts that defamed her by saying she was a fraudster and a cult leader who broke up families.

The Canadians counter-sued, accusing Liana Shanti of an online hate campaign accusing them of supporting pedophiles, practising black magic and abusing children.

The cases were filed in Hawaii, where Shanti lives. An eight-person jury there rejected Shanti’s allegations and agreed with the Canadians — that the “spiritual teacher,” as she describes herself as online, defamed them.

‘Paula’s doing witchcraft on your family’

The Canadians were never part of Shanti’s online community, but were targeted online because estranged family members were. Each was associated with an ex-wife who at the time was a student of Shanti’s.

Amanda Brady, of Regina, was one of those ex-wives. She was a follower of Liana Shanti’s for eight years and says the spiritual teacher systematically turned her and her daughters against their stepmother, Paula Haygarth, one of the civil award winners.

“She would message me and say, ‘Oh, your energy came into my awareness today. And so I looked at it, and Paula’s doing witchcraft on your family. You’re in danger. You need to book a session with me,’” Amanda says.

Amanda says she spent more than $750,000 on sessions and courses, partly, she says, because Liana Shanti positioned herself as a psychic.

Liana Shanti’s former students tell W5 that they turned to her for advice about their marriages, children and careers. Many were clustered in and around Regina, Sask.

United Kingdom-based cult expert Kacey Baker has interviewed 30 people who have been affected by Shanti, including ex-followers and family members. She says many of them believe that Shanti runs a cult-like enterprise, making people dependent on her through coercion and control — and vindictive consequences when her authority is challenged.

Students share “deep and vulnerable and extremely personal stories” with Liana Shanti, Kacey says. “It appears that a lot of that content is screenshotted and … then used as smear campaign or intimidation material if a person ever decides to leave the group or to speak out about Liana Shanti.”

The collapse and the fallout

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Liana Shanti warned her followers that Canada was a dangerous place to live, that they needed to get out to protect their children. Two dozen of her Canadian followers fled to Florida, which she pitched as a safe haven.

Almost all of the Canadians eventually left the community and returned to Canada. Liana Shanti lashed out online against them, and their loved ones, calling them demonic, Satanic child abusers.

Everything. She knows everything and all of it was put out,” Amanda says.

Paula Haygarth, who was subjected to years of online abuse, says she “felt an immense amount of relief.”

“It’s just so traumatic to be accused for all of those years for something you never did,” she says.

Liana Shanti says she plans to appeal.

‘Good things happen to good people’

The $56-million jury award, if and when it comes through, will pay for the Canadians’ staggering legal bills, and then some. Paula says hers add up to more than US$600,000. The legal fight has been so costly that Paula and her husband Wade were forced to sell their house in Saskatchewan and move into a trailer.

The couple hasn’t seen a dime so far and they’re not sure they ever will.

“We’re making it work and we’ve always believed that good things happen to good people,” Paula said.

W5 requested an interview with Liana Shanti multiple times, but she declined. In an email, she wrote, “I’m actually not a central character in any story, only a fiction that violent abusive men, child molesters, and the women under their control want so desperately to create. … I sued them. I exposed them. They lashed out.”

Watch the one-hour special presentation of W5’s Avery Haines Investigates Saturday at 7 p.m. ET live on W5’s official YouTube channel and on CTV and Crave

stories.title: Exclusive: They said an online spiritual teacher destroyed their lives. A jury awarded them $56M.
stories.summary: In part one of this three-part W5 investigation: “Fake Filtered Cult Leader,” CTV News’ investigative unit examines a self-described spiritual teacher whose online presence helped attract followers around the world.
stories.author: Jack Hauen, Derek Miller
stories.content:
In part one of this three-part W5 investigation: “ Fake Filtered Cult Leader ,” CTV News’ investigative unit examines a self-described spiritual teacher whose online presence helped attract followers around the world. Drawing on interviews and extensive reporting, W5 explores concerns raised by former members and the questions surrounding the organization behind the carefully curated public image.

A Hawaii jury has handed three Canadians one of the largest civil awards in the state’s history after a yearslong battle with an alleged cult leader.

The jury ordered Liane Wilson, who goes by Liana Shanti online, to pay Paula Haygarth and Byron and Stefanie Horvath, all from Saskatchewan, US$40.1 million, or just over C$56 million.

The award is the latest development in a harrowing and bizarre four-year-long legal battle.

Liana Shanti, who claims to be a self-made multimillionaire spiritual teacher with 100,000 online students, originally sued the Canadians, accusing them of online posts that defamed her by saying she was a fraudster and a cult leader who broke up families.

The Canadians counter-sued, accusing Liana Shanti of an online hate campaign accusing them of supporting pedophiles, practising black magic and abusing children.

The cases were filed in Hawaii, where Shanti lives. An eight-person jury there rejected Shanti’s allegations and agreed with the Canadians — that the “spiritual teacher,” as she describes herself as online, defamed them.

‘Paula’s doing witchcraft on your family’

The Canadians were never part of Shanti’s online community, but were targeted online because estranged family members were. Each was associated with an ex-wife who at the time was a student of Shanti’s.

Amanda Brady, of Regina, was one of those ex-wives. She was a follower of Liana Shanti’s for eight years and says the spiritual teacher systematically turned her and her daughters against their stepmother, Paula Haygarth, one of the civil award winners.

“She would message me and say, ‘Oh, your energy came into my awareness today. And so I looked at it, and Paula’s doing witchcraft on your family. You’re in danger. You need to book a session with me,’” Amanda says.

Amanda says she spent more than $750,000 on sessions and courses, partly, she says, because Liana Shanti positioned herself as a psychic.

Liana Shanti’s former students tell W5 that they turned to her for advice about their marriages, children and careers. Many were clustered in and around Regina, Sask.

United Kingdom-based cult expert Kacey Baker has interviewed 30 people who have been affected by Shanti, including ex-followers and family members. She says many of them believe that Shanti runs a cult-like enterprise, making people dependent on her through coercion and control — and vindictive consequences when her authority is challenged.

Students share “deep and vulnerable and extremely personal stories” with Liana Shanti, Kacey says. “It appears that a lot of that content is screenshotted and … then used as smear campaign or intimidation material if a person ever decides to leave the group or to speak out about Liana Shanti.”

The collapse and the fallout

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Liana Shanti warned her followers that Canada was a dangerous place to live, that they needed to get out to protect their children. Two dozen of her Canadian followers fled to Florida, which she pitched as a safe haven.

Almost all of the Canadians eventually left the community and returned to Canada. Liana Shanti lashed out online against them, and their loved ones, calling them demonic, Satanic child abusers.

“I shared my whole life with this woman. Everything. She knows everything and all of it was put out,” Amanda says.

Paula Haygarth, who was subjected to years of online abuse, says she “felt an immense amount of relief.”

“It’s just so traumatic to be accused for all of those years for something you never did,” she says.

Liana Shanti says she plans to appeal.

‘Good things happen to good people’

The $56-million jury award, if and when it comes through, will pay for the Canadians’ staggering legal bills, and then some. Paula says hers add up to more than US$600,000. The legal fight has been so costly that Paula and her husband Wade were forced to sell their house in Saskatchewan and move into a trailer.

The couple hasn’t seen a dime so far and they’re not sure they ever will.

“We’re making it work and we’ve always believed that good things happen to good people,” Paula said.

W5 requested an interview with Liana Shanti multiple times, but she declined. In an email, she wrote, “I’m actually not a central character in any story, only a fiction that violent abusive men, child molesters, and the women under their control want so desperately to create. … I sued them. I exposed them. They lashed out.”

Watch the one-hour special presentation of W5’s Avery Haines Investigates Saturday at 7 p.m. ET live on W5’s official YouTube channel and on CTV and Crave

stories.title: The plot behind $22M Pearson airport gold heist, as pieced together from court testimony and wiretaps
stories.summary: The story of how one of the world's largest gold thefts went down as pieced together from court testimony, police wiretaps and police records
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
The Toronto airport gold heist plot allegedly began with a secretive introduction of two strangers by a mutual friend who knew each of them had something the other needed if either was to pull off what would be one of the world’s largest gold thefts.

Simran Preet Panesar worked as a supervisor with Air Canada. He was a personable and well-liked man in the airline’s huge cargo warehouse at Pearson international airport. He was 30, married and living in a new-build townhouse in an affluent Brampton neighbourhood.

The man he was allegedly meeting for the first time at this rendezvous was Arsalan Chaudhary, a failed restaurateur known by the nickname Sonny. He was 41, single and living in the penthouse of a high-rise condo in downtown Mississauga.

Their meeting, Chaudhary claimed in court at a trial still underway, was about only one thing: planning an epic heist.

It was “strictly business,” Chaudhary said.

“We were just talking about doing the heist…. Panesar had a great idea and he said it will work.”

Chaudhary admitted he helped plan the heist and has been spilling his side of the story at various court proceedings, including some behind closed doors. One trial is ongoing, others haven’t begun, and not everything he said is proven, but combined with other information, including wiretaps, court testimony and police records, it helps build one picture of the gold heist unfolding and what happened next.

Panesar had been watching cargo come and go at the airport for years. He knew the security of Air Canada’s system and how to defeat it, according to Chaudhary. He knew how cargo moved through the airport and how to manipulate it. He knew the weaknesses of the staff and how to exploit them.

He knew everything about the inside half of a cargo heist. He just needed someone who could do the rest. For that, Panesar was introduced to Chaudhary about six months before the spectacular heist, according to Chaudhary.

“Someone referred him to me,” Chaudhary said, sealing what is still a secret. “They trusted me, and I had certain people that I knew who I could talk to and get the job done.” While that sounds like the introduction to a man of underworld renown, if Chaudhary was a criminal mastermind, he hid it well.

Born in Pakistan, he immigrated to the United States with his family when he was three years old and relocated to Canada a decade later, where he became a citizen. He dropped out of high school and worked for a moving company, as a dump truck driver, and did a stint in the duty-free shop at Pearson airport. He opened a restaurant with his brother just before the pandemic that swept away their business.

Chaudhary had a short criminal record: He was convicted in 2018 of possessing or trafficking in credit card data and possessing property obtained by crime. He received a suspended sentence and never spent a day in jail.

At the meeting, Panesar pitched a high-value heist, Chaudhary claimed. He was skeptical, but Panesar mapped it out and made it sound like it just might work.

“It was COVID. I was out of a job, kind of struggling. This topic came up. We started talking about it. I didn’t take it seriously in the beginning, but eventually, it got serious,” he said. “He knew how to get the gold out, and I told them I’ll take care of the rest…. Meaning, once it’s out, I’ll move it and put it where it’s supposed to go.”

They agreed to split the loot 70-30, with the larger share going to Panesar, Chaudhary said. He settled for that because Panesar said he had to take care of others out of his cut, and Chaudhary realized he needed Panesar more than Panesar needed him.

“Without people working inside, I couldn’t make this happen,” he said. “He was the leading guy.”

Pulling others in along the way, authorities allege, the pair forged the two loose ends of a conspiracy leading to the astonishing theft of a shipping crate shortly after it arrived on an Air Canada flight from Switzerland, carrying 400 kilograms of almost pure gold and foreign currency worth about $2.8 million. Together the contents of the crate were officially valued at more than $22.5 million, but likely worth much more, making it Canada’s largest gold heist.

“I pretty much planned the whole thing with Mr. Panesar,” Chaudhary said. Panesar, however, is not in Canada and has not answered to the allegations in court. His lawyer said Panesar disputes the allegations and intends to fight his charges.

Nobody moves more air cargo into Canada than Air Canada, and nowhere in the country is more air cargo coming and going than at the airline’s main hub in Toronto, Canada’s largest and busiest airport. When an Air Canada jet lands at Pearson it carries passengers in its seats and cargo in its belly.

Evidence at the ongoing trial for a former Air Canada employee who worked underneath Panesar suggests a gold heist was bound to happen sooner or later, or something similar. Security at the cargo warehouse was dreadful. Employee text messages suggest a similar exploit had already been used to steal less noticeable items. So what would happen when someone spotted a load too tempting to resist?

It’s hard to fault the plan.

Someone with knowledge of Air Canada’s procedures, and the credentials to access its computer systems, could easily identify a target shipment that carried something worth stealing and then manipulate the computer-automated sorting system to perform something of a shell game, making a high-value crate that required tight security be treated like a normal box nobody particularly notices.

That would be the inside work of the gold heist, and prosecutors and police allege this was Panesar’s domain.

For the heist to be consummated, however, Chaudhary needed to trigger his side of things, the outside work. Until he did, the gold wouldn’t go anywhere.

“I had to get all my resources together and get everyone together and see who’s going to do what for me,” Chaudhary said. It sounds like a chore, but it wasn’t a long list. He needed a truck. He needed a driver. He needed a place to take the gold after it was stolen. Later, he would need to find a way to melt and sell the gold and launder the cash, but he didn’t work that part out until afterwards.

Chaudhary said he turned first to Archit Grover. Nicknamed Archie or Grove, he was 36, also from Brampton, and Chaudhary’s long-time pal. Grover owned a modest trucking company and Chaudhary asked if he could use one of his trucks. Grover didn’t know it was for a heist, Chaudhary said. “I just told him I had a shipment I have to pick up, if you could help me out with that. I have an air waybill. Everything will be legit. I’ll just let you know when. He goes, ‘yeah, no problem.’”

Chaudhary also asked Grover for a driver. He recommended Durante King-Mclean, a 25-year-old from Brampton, Chaudhary said. Grover had been King-Mclean’s landlord and employer.

“The driver knew least amount of knowledge possible that I could tell him because this was a big job,” Chaudhary said. “Money like that … you don’t know what the person’s going to do.” In other words, he was afraid that if King-Mclean knew the value of the crate he would have in the truck, he might just keep on driving.

Finally, Chaudhary arranged for a quiet spot where the loot could be taken off the truck and divided. He settled on a farm near Acton, Ont., a 50-minute drive west of the airport.

“It was through a friend who I knew that said I could do something over there. It was, like, they had a little shed there that I could pay him to rent.… I just needed a shed to move the gold from one truck to another.… and I paid him, like a hundred bucks.” Prasath Paramalingam, 34, another friend from Brampton, helped him rent it, he said.

By late March Chaudhary had arranged for the truck, the driver and the destination. He just needed to wait until his inside man found an irresistible target.

That came on April 17, 2023, when heavy incoming air freight from a precious metal refinery in Zurich was destined for Toronto. News of that shipment ignited hundreds of phone calls, group chats, texts and encrypted messages firing back and forth.

“Gooooood morning it is,” an early-morning text that day pinged on the phone of Parmpal Sidhu, a 53-year-old Air Canada cargo employee known as Paul who worked under Panesar but was also his friend. The text was from Panesar’s phone, court heard. It was followed by, “We looking good anyways for today.”

On the day of the heist, Chaudhary set up at the Four Points by Sheraton hotel, just four kilometres from the airport.

Phone records show Chaudhary was in contact with King-Mclean 16 times that day, with Panesar eight times, with Grover seven times, with Grover’s trucking business twice, with Sidhu three times, and with Paramalingam once.

As the Air Canada plane was over the Atlantic, from inside the large Air Canada facility a series of computer transactions discreetly changed the instructions for what the airline’s automated cargo sorting system was to do with that crate of gold. The login credentials of an Air Canada manager were used to delete a code flagging the crate as a high-value shipment. That meant that when it arrived, instead of being sent to a locked and guarded storage room it was treated as general cargo.

Under the login credentials for a different Air Canada manager the computer was then told the crate was not to be unpacked by cargo staff and divided for its two customers — TD Bank collecting the gold and a Vancouver foreign exchange picking up the currency — but kept intact instead. That meant no one would open the crate to see its contents, and the gold and the cash would be kept together for the heist.

Court heard that the two managers whose credentials were used were not working that day and were not involved in the heist. At the time, Air Canada’s computer security at the warehouse was poor, with login credentials routinely shared among employees.

The flight touched down in Toronto nine minutes early, shortly before 4 p.m.

Chaudhary said that Panesar gave him a legitimate Air Canada air waybill that had been carefully doctored to allow a customer to collect the targeted crate, and Chaudhary gave it to King-Mclean. Court heard that Sidhu’s log-in credentials were used to print it off.

The cargo automation faultlessly followed its new instructions and the crate of gold moved unnoticed around the warehouse on a device like an enormous baggage carousel, taking it where the new codes told it to and dropping it into a cavernous sorting area known as a pit.

At 6:30 p.m., King-Mclean backed a white truck into loading bay 12 at Air Canada’s cargo warehouse on Brittania Road East. The heist was truly underway.

Wearing a facemask, hat, gloves, work boots and a safety vest, King-Mclean handed the doctored waybill to an Air Canada employee who passed it to cargo handlers to retrieve the crate. The driver paced about waiting before moving into the loading bay to open the back of his truck.

John Iheme, a station attendant at the warehouse, went to help the waiting customer. He said he was unaware of the heist plot and didn’t know of his unwitting role until Peel Regional Police investigators showed him internal security video showing their interaction, he said. Iheme greeted the driver with a fist bump, after which King-Mclean removed the heavy-duty work glove from his right hand.

Iheme found the crate matching the number written on the waybill in the pit. He loaded it onto a forklift, whirled it out to the waiting driver and even helped King-Mclean load it onto the truck. The driver gave Iheme an appreciative fist bump before climbing back behind the wheel and driving off.

Chaudhary had told King-Mclean to head west and then north to get to the farm he had arranged. Chaudhary drove close to the truck all the way.

Not everyone involved in the heist knew exactly what they had stolen.

The shipping manifest said it was high-value goods, provided the weight of the crate and said it contained gold and currency but didn’t specify much else. Some of the heft could have come from bags of pennies.

They didn’t know how successful their heist was until they met up at the farm and opened the crate.

It is hard to imagine there wasn’t a moment of dumbfounded ecstasy.

Inside they saw thousands of small strips or bars of gold — not the brick-sized gold ingots seen in movies. Chaudhary called them biscuits. Each was stamped with the TD logo of the Toronto Dominion Bank and a serial number. Stacks of biscuits were inside hardshell boxes with a lid that pulled off, like old sewing machine cases, he said.

Chaudhary, Panesar and King-Mclean unloaded the boxes of gold and cash and divided it between the two masterminds, Chaudhary alleged. They did a rough split by eyeball rather than counting individual biscuits and bills. Chaudhary said he trusted Panesar to make sure he got a full 30 per cent.

“He trusted me with everything, so I had to trust him with something. Without trust, we couldn’t make this happen,” Chaudhary said. He loaded his cut into his Range Rover.

By 9:30 p.m., when armed Brink’s guards arrived at the Air Canada warehouse expecting to pick up a crate of gold, the crooks were unloading the loot 50 kilometres away.

By 10 p.m., as Air Canada staff were searching for the crate with increasing alarm, the crooks were leaving the farm and going their separate ways. Chaudhary headed to a condo he rented for a stash house so his loot wasn’t stored where he slept.

“The plan was to basically clear the gold out, melt it, get the money, pay everyone out … everyone will be quiet about it because everyone got paid, and that’s it. Normal life, pretty much,” Chaudhary said.

The endgame proved the diciest part of the heist.

“I knew I needed help to melt the gold,” Chaudhary said.

Chaudhary had made many trips back to Pakistan over the years, and he got to know a man there named Ibrahim who had connections. He’d known him for about 12 years. Chaudhary asked Ibrahim if he could get him gold melting machines. Ibrahim, who was in Pakistan, arranged for him to meet with someone in Canada who got him the equipment, Chaudhary said. He started melting gold in his condo after watching how-to videos on YouTube.

“It’s not brain surgery. It’s pretty simple: Put it on, heat it up, put it in there. It melts,” he said. Melting it destroyed the logos and serial numbers. “No one could tell where it came from.”

Chaudhary said he reached out to another friend, this one in Canada, to help him sell the reforged gold. He had been close friends with 39-year-old Amit Jalota for at least 15 years. Jalota was an actuary and made good money.

“He had some contacts,” Chaudhary said. “I made up a story… and asked him if he could get it exchanged for some cash for me. He’s a friend, so I didn’t really have to tell him a lot.”

Chaudhary gave gold to Jalota in increments — about three of his forged bars at a time — and Jalota took the gold to Ali Raza court heard. Raza was the 36-year-old proprietor of Mashallah Jewellers, a store near the airport in a retail hub catering to South Asian and Middle Eastern interest in gold. It was an easy sale.

“They took all of it,” Jalota texted Chaudhary on June 9, 2023. “They get horny when they see it hahahah. They can’t let it go.”

“I didn’t know who Ali Raza was. It was not my person,” Chaudhary said. “Only time I find out who Mr. Raza was when the newspapers came out,” with news of arrests for the heist.

Chaudhary said he got more than a million in cash back.

“I knew the money couldn’t stay in this country,” he said.

He turned again to Ibrahim in Pakistan. Ibrahim helped him transfer the money out of Canada and into Pakistan using underground banking, or, as Chaudhary called the service, “Ibrahim’s guy.” Chaudhary then flew to Pakistan to collect it. “I give the guy money (in) Canada and receive it in Pakistan.”

Chaudhary thought he had found the key to unlocking the cash value trapped in his stolen gold without drawing attention from police in Canada.

“All of a sudden, I was kidnapped,” Chaudhary said. “I was kidnapped by the police over there.… They blindfolded me, and they took me to a place that I don’t know where I was. And they told me they would torture me, do things with me, leave my body where no one will ever find me again, and it’ll be the last time I see anyone.

His kidnappers connected him on FaceTime video calls to their colleagues in Canada; Chaudhary told them where to go to scoop up the rest of his hidden gold, and then to a family member’s home to take his cash.

“They held me until they grabbed everything.” Once his kidnappers’ colleagues in Canada had their hands on the loot they blindfolded him again and drove him into town, told him to lie on the road and count to 30 before looking up. When he took off his blindfold, they were gone.

paragraphs: The Toronto airport gold heist plot allegedly began with a secretive introduction of two strangers by a mutual friend who knew each of them had something the other needed if either was to pull off what would be one of the world’s largest gold thefts.

Simran Preet Panesar worked as a supervisor with Air Canada. He was a personable and well-liked man in the airline’s huge cargo warehouse at Pearson international airport. He was 30, married and living in a new-build townhouse in an affluent Brampton neighbourhood.

The man he was allegedly meeting for the first time at this rendezvous was Arsalan Chaudhary, a failed restaurateur known by the nickname Sonny. He was 41, single and living in the penthouse of a high-rise condo in downtown Mississauga.
Their meeting, Chaudhary claimed in court at a trial still underway, was about only one thing: planning an epic heist.
It was “strictly business,” Chaudhary said.
“We were just talking about doing the heist…. Panesar had a great idea and he said it will work.”

Chaudhary admitted he helped plan the heist and has been spilling his side of the story at various court proceedings, including some behind closed doors. One trial is ongoing, others haven’t begun, and not everything he said is proven, but combined with other information, including wiretaps, court testimony and police records, it helps build one picture of the gold heist unfolding and what happened next.

Panesar had been watching cargo come and go at the airport for years. He knew the security of Air Canada’s system and how to defeat it, according to Chaudhary. He knew how cargo moved through the airport and how to manipulate it. He knew the weaknesses of the staff and how to exploit them.

He knew everything about the inside half of a cargo heist. He just needed someone who could do the rest. For that, Panesar was introduced to Chaudhary about six months before the spectacular heist, according to Chaudhary.

“Someone referred him to me,” Chaudhary said, sealing what is still a secret. “They trusted me, and I had certain people that I knew who I could talk to and get the job done.” While that sounds like the introduction to a man of underworld renown, if Chaudhary was a criminal mastermind, he hid it well.

Born in Pakistan, he immigrated to the United States with his family when he was three years old and relocated to Canada a decade later, where he became a citizen. He dropped out of high school and worked for a moving company, as a dump truck driver, and did a stint in the duty-free shop at Pearson airport. He opened a restaurant with his brother just before the pandemic that swept away their business.

Chaudhary had a short criminal record: He was convicted in 2018 of possessing or trafficking in credit card data and possessing property obtained by crime. He received a suspended sentence and never spent a day in jail.
At the meeting, Panesar pitched a high-value heist, Chaudhary claimed. He was skeptical, but Panesar mapped it out and made it sound like it just might work.

“It was COVID. I was out of a job, kind of struggling. This topic came up. We started talking about it. I didn’t take it seriously in the beginning, but eventually, it got serious,” he said. “He knew how to get the gold out, and I told them I’ll take care of the rest…. Meaning, once it’s out, I’ll move it and put it where it’s supposed to go.”

They agreed to split the loot 70-30, with the larger share going to Panesar, Chaudhary said. He settled for that because Panesar said he had to take care of others out of his cut, and Chaudhary realized he needed Panesar more than Panesar needed him.
“Without people working inside, I couldn’t make this happen,” he said. “He was the leading guy.”

Pulling others in along the way, authorities allege, the pair forged the two loose ends of a conspiracy leading to the astonishing theft of a shipping crate shortly after it arrived on an Air Canada flight from Switzerland, carrying 400 kilograms of almost pure gold and foreign currency worth about $2.8 million. Together the contents of the crate were officially valued at more than $22.5 million, but likely worth much more, making it Canada’s largest gold heist.

“I pretty much planned the whole thing with Mr. Panesar,” Chaudhary said. Panesar, however, is not in Canada and has not answered to the allegations in court. His lawyer said Panesar disputes the allegations and intends to fight his charges.

Nobody moves more air cargo into Canada than Air Canada, and nowhere in the country is more air cargo coming and going than at the airline’s main hub in Toronto, Canada’s largest and busiest airport. When an Air Canada jet lands at Pearson it carries passengers in its seats and cargo in its belly.

Evidence at the ongoing trial for a former Air Canada employee who worked underneath Panesar suggests a gold heist was bound to happen sooner or later, or something similar. Security at the cargo warehouse was dreadful. Employee text messages suggest a similar exploit had already been used to steal less noticeable items. So what would happen when someone spotted a load too tempting to resist?
It’s hard to fault the plan.

Someone with knowledge of Air Canada’s procedures, and the credentials to access its computer systems, could easily identify a target shipment that carried something worth stealing and then manipulate the computer-automated sorting system to perform something of a shell game, making a high-value crate that required tight security be treated like a normal box nobody particularly notices.
That would be the inside work of the gold heist, and prosecutors and police allege this was Panesar’s domain.
For the heist to be consummated, however, Chaudhary needed to trigger his side of things, the outside work. Until he did, the gold wouldn’t go anywhere.

“I had to get all my resources together and get everyone together and see who’s going to do what for me,” Chaudhary said. It sounds like a chore, but it wasn’t a long list. He needed a truck. He needed a driver. He needed a place to take the gold after it was stolen. Later, he would need to find a way to melt and sell the gold and launder the cash, but he didn’t work that part out until afterwards.

Chaudhary said he turned first to Archit Grover. Nicknamed Archie or Grove, he was 36, also from Brampton, and Chaudhary’s long-time pal. Grover owned a modest trucking company and Chaudhary asked if he could use one of his trucks. Grover didn’t know it was for a heist, Chaudhary said. “I just told him I had a shipment I have to pick up, if you could help me out with that. I have an air waybill. Everything will be legit. Chaudhary also asked Grover for a driver. He recommended Durante King-Mclean, a 25-year-old from Brampton, Chaudhary said. Grover had been King-Mclean’s landlord and employer.

“The driver knew least amount of knowledge possible that I could tell him because this was a big job,” Chaudhary said. “Money like that … you don’t know what the person’s going to do.” In other words, he was afraid that if King-Mclean knew the value of the crate he would have in the truck, he might just keep on driving.
Finally, Chaudhary arranged for a quiet spot where the loot could be taken off the truck and divided. He settled on a farm near Acton, Ont., a 50-minute drive west of the airport.

“It was through a friend who I knew that said I could do something over there. It was, like, they had a little shed there that I could pay him to rent.… I just needed a shed to move the gold from one truck to another.… and I paid him, like a hundred bucks.” Prasath Paramalingam, 34, another friend from Brampton, helped him rent it, he said.
By late March Chaudhary had arranged for the truck, the driver and the destination. He just needed to wait until his inside man found an irresistible target.

That came on April 17, 2023, when heavy incoming air freight from a precious metal refinery in Zurich was destined for Toronto. News of that shipment ignited hundreds of phone calls, group chats, texts and encrypted messages firing back and forth.

“Gooooood morning it is,” an early-morning text that day pinged on the phone of Parmpal Sidhu, a 53-year-old Air Canada cargo employee known as Paul who worked under Panesar but was also his friend. The text was from Panesar’s phone, court heard. It was followed by, “We looking good anyways for today.”
On the day of the heist, Chaudhary set up at the Four Points by Sheraton hotel, just four kilometres from the airport.

Phone records show Chaudhary was in contact with King-Mclean 16 times that day, with Panesar eight times, with Grover seven times, with Grover’s trucking business twice, with Sidhu three times, and with Paramalingam once.

As the Air Canada plane was over the Atlantic, from inside the large Air Canada facility a series of computer transactions discreetly changed the instructions for what the airline’s automated cargo sorting system was to do with that crate of gold. The login credentials of an Air Canada manager were used to delete a code flagging the crate as a high-value shipment. That meant that when it arrived, instead of being sent to a locked and guarded storage room it was treated as general cargo.

Under the login credentials for a different Air Canada manager the computer was then told the crate was not to be unpacked by cargo staff and divided for its two customers — TD Bank collecting the gold and a Vancouver foreign exchange picking up the currency — but kept intact instead. That meant no one would open the crate to see its contents, and the gold and the cash would be kept together for the heist.

Court heard that the two managers whose credentials were used were not working that day and were not involved in the heist. At the time, Air Canada’s computer security at the warehouse was poor, with login credentials routinely shared among employees.
The flight touched down in Toronto nine minutes early, shortly before 4 p.m.

Chaudhary said that Panesar gave him a legitimate Air Canada air waybill that had been carefully doctored to allow a customer to collect the targeted crate, and Chaudhary gave it to King-Mclean. Court heard that Sidhu’s log-in credentials were used to print it off.

The cargo automation faultlessly followed its new instructions and the crate of gold moved unnoticed around the warehouse on a device like an enormous baggage carousel, taking it where the new codes told it to and dropping it into a cavernous sorting area known as a pit.
At 6:30 p.m., King-Mclean backed a white truck into loading bay 12 at Air Canada’s cargo warehouse on Brittania Road East. The heist was truly underway.

Chaudhary had told King-Mclean to head west and then north to get to the farm he had arranged. Chaudhary drove close to the truck all the way.
Not everyone involved in the heist knew exactly what they had stolen.

The shipping manifest said it was high-value goods, provided the weight of the crate and said it contained gold and currency but didn’t specify much else. Some of the heft could have come from bags of pennies.
They didn’t know how successful their heist was until they met up at the farm and opened the crate.
It is hard to imagine there wasn’t a moment of dumbfounded ecstasy.

Inside they saw thousands of small strips or bars of gold — not the brick-sized gold ingots seen in movies. Chaudhary called them biscuits.
