stories.title: Next mayor of Niagara Falls calls for community consultations on Ford’s casino plan
stories.summary: The Premier is seeking up to three new casino operators for the region as Ontario aims to spur tourism
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford should consult with Niagara Falls residents about his plan to bring more casinos to the region, the city’s incoming mayor says, citing some community concerns about the viability of expanding the gambling industry.

In an interview with The Globe and Mail, Lori Lococo, who was elected mayor in the Oct. 26 municipal election, said she supports increasing tourism but added that the community should have a chance to give feedback about the province’s plans to spur development in Niagara.

Ms. Lococo, a 56-year-old two-term city councillor who focused her campaign on affordability, beat 16-year incumbent Jim Diodati. She is to be sworn into office on Nov. 16.

Ms. Lococo said voters wanted to see change in the city of about 100,000, known for its spectacular waterfalls and tourist attractions. Niagara Falls currently has two casinos, but the region has also struggled with changing visitor habits in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Mr. Ford has made boosting tourism in the region one of his priorities, releasing a multi-billion dollar “Destination Niagara” strategy last December with the goal of attracting 25 million annual visitors and doubling the region’s tourism to generate an additional $3-billion for Ontario’s GDP each year.

The government said the plan – which includes additional “world-class gaming,” culinary experiences, and arts and culture, as well as an expanded airport – will lead to billions of dollars in growth for the provincial economy, as well as tens of thousands of jobs.

But the focus on gambling, including more Las Vegas-style casinos, has also raised questions about the government’s priorities and added to general concerns around the proliferation of online gambling, as well as the need for community consultation.

Last week, the Ontario government announced it would be slashing the gambling tax rate in Niagara as it issued a call for investors for up to three new casino operators.

Ms. Lococo said the province has heard from the tourism industry, experts and investors on it Destination Niagara strategy.

“Now, I think we need input from our residents. It’s really important that the residents feel heard,” she said, noting that before the first casino opened in Niagara Falls in 1996, there was a local referendum.

“I’m not saying that we need a referendum. But what I’m saying is, that the residents want to be heard, and they’re wondering why they haven’t been asked yet about their feelings and how it’s going to impact them.”

She said she will be reaching out to Mr. Ford’s office to ask how residents can offer feedback, either through open houses, surveys or other means. The province has given casino operators until Dec. 3 to show interest in the region, and will then choose shortlisted proponents who will be able to enter a competitive process to submit detailed proposals for new casino developments.

Ms. Lococo said the Premier called her after her win last week to congratulate her, but they did not discuss substantial issues.

She said among residents’ concerns are falling revenues for traditional casinos and job losses.

“A lot of casino cities are seeing the same decreases,” she said.

“It changes their city when a lot of people lose their jobs. So people are concerned about, if we bring more casinos here, how is that going to work itself out when there’s already a decrease in spending.”

Addictiveness of online gambling is also an issue she wants to see addressed.

“A lot of young people are getting so in debt because of this online gaming, it wrecks their financial future,” she said.

In addition, there are questions about infrastructure needs and traffic if tourism increases substantially, she said.

Scott Clark, a spokesperson for Ontario’s Tourism, Culture and Gaming Minister Zee Hamid, said the government is championing the region as a premier tourist destination, including by making the “gaming environment more competitive.”

“We will continue to engage with municipal leaders, including Mayor-elect Lori Lococo, as well as Indigenous communities, industry partners and community members as we deliver on our plan to double the number of annual visitors to more than 25 million, generate $3 billion annually for Ontario’s GDP and create 46,500 new jobs across the region,” he said in a statement.

Born and raised in Niagara Falls, Ms. Lococo worked for more than 25 years in the legal field as an administrator and clerk before running for council in 2018.

Ms. Lococo said she agrees with the province that the tourism sector is incredibly important. She said plans for the area should strike a balance between attractions, natural beauty, gambling, restaurants and entertainment.

“I don’t think that people really want to be considered a gaming city. It could be part of a bigger picture,” she said. “But it’s also people’s homes.”

stories.title: Paul St-Pierre Plamondon to meet with Mark Carney after Canada-EU summit tension
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has agreed to meet with Prime Minister Mark Carney before the Francophonie Summit in November.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has agreed to meet with Prime Minister Mark Carney before the Francophonie Summit in November.

St-Pierre Plamondon made the announcement in a social media post, and it comes after days of tension between the two leaders.

St-Pierre Plamondon did not attend the Canada-European Union Summit in Montreal last week after Ottawa refused to grant him official speaking rights.

Carney told daily newspaper La Presse in an interview published Saturday that he wanted to meet St-Pierre Plamondon to set common goals and ensure good relations between Ottawa and Quebec.

St-Pierre Plamondon, who became premier after his Parti Québécois won a minority government in last month’s provincial election, thanked Carney for what he called his change of tone.

He said he was accepting the invitation as long as the meeting took place in Quebec City.

Quebec’s separatist movement knows exactly what it’s doing. It won’t pass up a single chance to turn a slight from Ottawa into something that

“Unsurprisingly, I simply ask that this meeting be held in accordance with Quebec law, specifically the Act Respecting the National Capital Commission, which stipulates that meetings of this nature must take place in Quebec City,” wrote St-Pierre Plamondon.

The Canada-EU summit, which took place on Thursday and Friday, brought together Canadian and European leaders including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

The federal government said that St-Pierre Plamondon had been invited to dinner with EU representatives, but had not been given a speaking role at the summit.

St-Pierre Plamondon accused Ottawa of muzzling him.

“The federal government would have us believe that giving the Quebec premier permission to serve shrimp cocktails at a reception constitutes an acceptable and sufficient form of influence in representing Quebec’s interests,” he wrote on social media on Tuesday.

He later announced he would not be attending the summit, sending newly-appointed chief diplomat Pascal Paradis in his place.

“He was invited to the dinner and he refused,” Carney told reporters in Ottawa, also on Tuesday. “It’s his decision to leave the chair empty.”

In his post on Sunday, St-Pierre Plamandon looked back on the summit, writing that Quebec was “relegated to the status of an extra” and that the federal government had not recognized the province’s “existence and right to be at the discussion table.”

St-Pierre Plamondon also did not attend the First Nations-First Ministers meeting in Ottawa early last week, saying he wanted to prioritize a different approach with Indigenous peoples.

The Francophonie Summit, scheduled for Nov. 14–16, will take place in Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia. St-Pierre Plamondon is set to lead the Quebec delegation there.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 1, 2026.

stories.title: Veteran whose daughter died in military training exercise named Silver Cross Mother
stories.summary: The Royal Canadian Legion says Virginia Hicks’ family has a long history of military service and she served in the Canadian Armed Forces for 29 years.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A veteran whose daughter died during a military training exercise in 2002 has been named the 2026 National Silver Cross Mother.

The Royal Canadian Legion says Virginia Hicks will place a wreath at the National War Memorial in Ottawa on Nov. 11, an annual tradition on behalf of Canadian mothers who have lost a child serving in the Canadian military.

Hicks’ daughter Mariebeth Short died on Sept. 23, 2002 during a training exercise in Petawawa, Ont., when the light armoured vehicle she was training in rolled over.

The Royal Canadian Legion says Hicks’ family has a long history of military service and she served in the Canadian Armed Forces for 29 years, working in supply and logistics.

This year’s Remembrance Day ceremony comes just weeks after four Canadian soldiers were killed and dozens more were injured during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright in Alberta.

Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pte. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C., were killed in a grass fire last month.

Strong, sudden winds propelled the nearby fire toward 84 members of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry who were conducting two exercises in the military base’s training area, about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said that the Canadian Forces National Investigation Service is leading a full investigation into the tragedy with support from the RCMP.

Hicks says she has much in common with all mothers who have lost a child serving in the military.

“We all share the same sorrow, we all share the same bravery, and same love and respect for our children as we do for any other child who has passed,” she said in a statement.

stories.title: Amid criticism, Toronto police say they couldn’t arrest Bridle Path suspect at the hospital
stories.summary: Police say evidence to arrest Daijohn Richards came the day after he was discharged
stories.author: National Post staff
stories.content:
Toronto Police are moving to address what they call “confusion” about why a suspect in the violent Bridle Path home invasion that injured a family of four was allowed to leave the hospital after being treated for a gunshot wound himself.

Police are asking the public for help in finding Daijohn Richards, 23, of Toronto. The other two suspects were described as being in their 20s but have not been identified. Richards is believed to have been shot accidentally by one of the attackers.

Toronto police inspector Kristy Smith told reporters Saturday morning that police had spoken to Richards prior to him being discharged from hospital late Thursday morning. She added that police gathered evidence to arrest him by evening on Friday.

Amid social media criticism of the decision not to detain him, Toronto police issued a statement late Saturday afternoon.

“We want to address some confusion surrounding the investigation into the home invasion in the Bridle Path neighbourhood,” police said in the statement.

“Investigators immediately recognized the potential connection between the home invasion and the individual who showed up at hospital with a gunshot wound. But recognizing a potential suspect and having enough evidence to arrest them are two different things.”

“Police need reasonable grounds, supported by evidence, to make an arrest,” it added.

The statement, which was posted on X with replies turned off, was nevertheless flooded with fierce opposition among users.

“There is no realm of the universe in which this is an acceptable thing for law-enforcement to say and do (or more specifically, not do),” wrote @thevivafrei, who identified themselves as a former litigator, in a quote tweet.

“There’s a lot of ground between ‘arrest’ and ‘do nothing,’” wrote user @pdrobertson.

Richards is wanted for four counts of discharge firearm with intent to wound, four counts of robbery with a firearm, three counts of aggravated assault and three other charges. Police have released his image and said he May show signs of a shoulder injury.

“We will continue to gather evidence and will go where the evidence takes us. We are grateful for the professionalism, tenacity and commitment of our investigators who continue this work,” Toronto police said in the Saturday afternoon statement.

“Let’s keep the focus where it belongs: finding the outstanding suspects and holding those responsible for this violent home invasion accountable.”

At 3 a.m. on Thursday, three attackers armed with guns and a hammer broke into a home in Toronto affluent Bridle Path neighbourhood. The suspects, each armed with a gun, located the residents on the second floor and demanded valuables, police said.

The victims, David Morton, a 75-year-old real-estate executive, his wife Doriana Zohil-Morton, 64, and two adult daughters Maggie and Cristina, were all injured. Three family members were shot, and two were struck in the head with a hammer.

“What should have been the safety and security of our own home became a terrifying and life-threatening experience,” Morton said in a statement released Friday.

“While we are focused on recovery and supporting one another as a family, we are also deeply concerned about the increasing violence associated with home invasions and the safety of families throughout Toronto,” he added.

“Police need reasonable grounds, supported by evidence, to make an arrest,” it added.
The statement, which was posted on X with replies turned off, was nevertheless flooded with fierce opposition among users.

“There is no realm of the universe in which this is an acceptable thing for law-enforcement to say and do (or more specifically, not do),” wrote @thevivafrei, who identified themselves as a former litigator, in a quote tweet.
“There’s a lot of ground between ‘arrest’ and ‘do nothing,’” wrote user @pdrobertson.

Richards is wanted for four counts of discharge firearm with intent to wound, four counts of robbery with a firearm, three counts of aggravated assault and three other charges. Police have released his image and said he May show signs of a shoulder injury.

“We will continue to gather evidence and will go where the evidence takes us. We are grateful for the professionalism, tenacity and commitment of our investigators who continue this work,” Toronto police said in the Saturday afternoon statement.
“Let’s keep the focus where it belongs: finding the outstanding suspects and holding those responsible for this violent home invasion accountable.”

At 3 a.m. on Thursday, three attackers armed with guns and a hammer broke into a home in Toronto affluent Bridle Path neighbourhood. The suspects, each armed with a gun, located the residents on the second floor and demanded valuables, police said.

The victims, David Morton, a 75-year-old real-estate executive, his wife Doriana Zohil-Morton, 64, and two adult daughters Maggie and Cristina, were all injured. Three family members were shot, and two were struck in the head with a hammer.
“What should have been the safety and security of our own home became a terrifying and life-threatening experience,” Morton said in a statement released Friday.

“While we are focused on recovery and supporting one another as a family, we are also deeply concerned about the increasing violence associated with home invasions and the safety of families throughout Toronto,” he added.

stories.title: True or false? How fake online reviews are concerning businesses
stories.summary: There are things people can do to take precautions when shopping, including caution when "flawless" ratings are given, and that the best advice is word of mouth.
stories.author: Sean Previl, Touria Izri
stories.content:
Online reviews can help people decide what to buy, but business owners and consumer watchdogs say some are confusing customers because they’re not actually real.

For Charlotte Ashley, owner of Trident Booksellers and Cafe in Halifax, fake reviews have led customers to request items the business doesn’t even carry.

“Maybe they want menu items that we don’t serve,” said Ashley. “People are disappointed and that’s not the kind of visit that we want them to have at our business.”

Ashley pointed to one such review posted on Google that gave the business five stars but also said the supposed customer got a mushroom quesadilla that the cafe doesn’t serve.

She’s unsure what has caused the fake reviews to pop up on her business’s page or the motive behind them.

But fake reviews are far from new, with a report by the Canadian Anti-monopoly Project showing there’s a market for them on Google and Amazon.

The report says fake reviews harm three groups: consumers because they “obscure” the true quality of the service or product; honest sellers because the reviews put them “at a clear disadvantage”; and platforms if consumers lose trust in them.

“There is a substantial market for fake reviews operating kind of in plain sight and it affects customers who are looking at reviews on all sorts of platforms,” said Emily Osborne, a fellow at the project and policy researcher at the Canada Shield Institute.

Osborne said fake reviewers can be recruited in various ways, including through social media groups.

She said a third-party seller could ask reviewers to post a five-star review potentially in exchange for a free product.

Companies such as Amazon have acted to take down fake reviews, Osborne noted.

Osborne told Global News the Canadian government needs could do more to hold the platforms more accountable.

“I think there’s some space for Canadian policymakers to require better enforcement against fraud on platforms,” she said.

There are posts that exist on social media by “professional review providers,” with a list of prices provided with some offering 100 reviews for $180.

Kay Dean, a U.S.-based consumer watchdog, says the marketplace for fake reviews is “immense.”

“It’s just shocking how immense the problem is, I believe it distorts the whole small business economy globally,” said Dean, who started Fake Review Watch, a website and YouTube channel where she posts her investigations and research. Dean is a former federal prosecutor.

She said her investigations have found businesses bartering and trading reviews with each other on social media. She’s also found marketers and search engine optimization companies with “networks of profiles” that post negative reviews.

“So there’s just a variety of ways to procure fake reviews, it’s very, very easy and inexpensive,” she said.

The exact number of fake reviews online is difficult to determine. But a 2023 report by the U.K. government found 11 to 15 per cent of all reviews on e-commerce platforms for three common product categories were likely fake. Product categories typically included consumer electronics, home and kitchen, and sports and outdoors.

It also found well-written fake reviews can distort consumer decision making, with buyers 3.1 per cent more likely to purchase a product.

There are things people can do to take precautions when shopping, including using caution when “flawless” ratings are given. Experts say the best advice comes through word-of-mouth.

stories.title: Brian Mulroney doc takes home $25,000 prize at Windsor film fest
stories.summary: Windsor - A satirical documentary about a former prime minister’s rise to power has claimed a top prize at the Windsor International Film Festival.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The southern Ontario film festival handed the $25,000 WIFF Prize in Canadian Film to “Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney,” directed by Winnipeg-born filmmaker Matthew Rankin.

The documentary, which premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival and was an audience favourite in the Midnight Madness program, splices archival footage of Mulroney before his days in 24 Sussex Drive, while incorporating multi-media collage elements for a highly-stylized, technicolor exploration of political celebrity.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Smart glasses are showing up in Toronto nightclubs. Not everyone’s ok with it

The film beat out other Canadian works, including “Nina Roza” about a Bulgarian-Canadian art consultant who returns to his homeland to investigate a supposed child prodigy and “Haunted” about a teenager who discovers her new countryside home is haunted by a 19th-century woman.

The WIFF jury praised “Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney” for its “uniquely Canadian voice, and intelligence and humour.”

The jury also acknowledged the work of archive producer Marika Lapointe, who sifted through over 80,000 pieces of archival material for the film.

In an interview with The Canadian Press in September, Rankin spoke about how Mulroney wielded charm to climb his way through the ranks of the Progressive Conservatives to the country’s top office.

“It’s not exactly a biopic of the man,” Rankin said. “It’s really about the construction of his image.”

The documentary was somewhat familiar ground for Rankin, who’s known for his debut feature film “The Twentieth Century,” a surreal, fictionalized portrait of William Lyon Mackenzie King, Canada’s 10th Prime Minister.

His follow-up feature “Universal Language” was shortlisted for an Oscar.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 1, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Government relations worker waffles between having fun in his 20s and saving for a home
stories.summary: Grant, 25, has a master’s degree and very little debt thanks to minimizing expenses during his undergrad
stories.author: Saira Peesker
stories.content:
Name, age: Grant, 25

Annual income: $75,000

Debt: $17,477 student loan

Savings: $5,650 in savings account, $22,000 in tax-free savings account

What he does: Government relations for a utility company

Where he lives: Ottawa

Top financial concern: “It’s hard not to say home ownership. It’s this big looming thing that makes me feel if I’m not doing the right things now, it will never happen.”

During his undergraduate degree, Grant delayed having some fun in the first few years to save money and set himself up for the future.

Even though he was keen to get out into the world, he chose to attend the University of Guelph, where his dad worked, granting him free tuition. Grant lived at home for two years before getting an apartment with friends.

“That was one of the first financial sacrifices I think I made – giving up that residence-life experience,” he said. By the time he moved to Toronto for graduate school, he felt he had a handle on his finances.

“I didn’t feel as bad spending $40,000 on a master’s degree, and paying Toronto rent and Toronto living expenses,” he said.

He got an internship in Ottawa after graduating, then landed a full-time job. He and his girlfriend live in a basement apartment downtown.

Now in his mid-20s with a good job, Grant still wrestles with competing ideas of saving versus enjoying life while he is young.

“I am just fearful that in 10 to 15 years, I will look back on my 20s with regret that I didn’t do enough, or the opposite, where I find myself in a difficult financial position when it comes time to think about kids, homeownership and retirement planning,” he says.

Grant says that pressure comes from his peers, social media and news coverage about workers being replaced by artificial intelligence.

“Some people I admire work really hard and have this ‘grindset,’ where they do what they have to do to get ahead,” he says, adding that his generation has been fed “the idea that there are going to be no jobs.”

Grant says having his savings deducted automatically from his paycheque helps him feel better about spending money on fun stuff.

“My partner and I will spend 150 bucks on dinner, three or four nights a year,” as a treat, he says. “We’ll still go out otherwise, getting a drink or an appetizer, but not both.”

Investment and savings: $1,327

$527 to work pension. “Defined benefit.”

$800 to TFSA. “I still have a lot of contribution room, which in part comes from waiting to enter the workforce and choosing to go back to school.”

Servicing debt: $170

$170 to student loan. “Interest-free federal portion. Going low and slow.”

Household and transportation: $1,585

$1,100 to rent. “We pay $2,200 monthly for a two-bed, two-bath basement apartment.”

$27 to renters insurance

$80 to electricity. “My partner pays gas. Water is covered in our lease.”

$200 to gasoline

$42 to car maintenance. “It is my partner’s car. I help her out with the cost.”

$15 to transit. “We are very central and do a lot of walking.”

$25 to Uber. “Ubers are also weirdly cheap in Ottawa.”

$0 to cellphone. “Still on the family plan. Thanks, Mom.”

$96 to internet

Food and drink: $540

$250 to groceries. “$500 for our household.”

$30 to coffee shops

$200 to restaurants

$60 to alcohol. “Beer when heading over to a friend’s place and a cheap bottle of wine with dinner every now and then.”

Miscellaneous: $2,204

$1,246 to payroll deductions

$150 to going out. “By far, the hardest part of my budget to police.”

$55 to streaming services. “Streaming bundle through Bell for TV shows, sharing a Sportsnet account with friends, my partner and I split the cost of DAZN to watch football.”

$30 to other apps. “Spotify, Globe and Mail, Apple storage.”

$25 to electronics

$50 to clothing

$50 to sports. “Summer rugby club and City of Ottawa pickup hockey in the winter.”

$60 on hobbies. “Card game once a week, backpacking gear.”

$40 on haircuts

$15 on cosmetics. “Shampoo, conditioner, face wash.”

$4 on dentist. “I have pretty great coverage through work.”

$4 to prescriptions

$333 to vacations

$13 to donations

$100 to gifts

$16 to credit card fee. “Amex Cobalt.”

$13 to sports betting. “$25 a few times per year on FanDuel and we usually have a $25 buy-in for our fantasy football leagues.”

Some details may be changed to protect the privacy of the person profiled. We want to thank them for sharing their story. Are you a millennial or Gen Z who would like to participate in a Paycheque Project? Send us an e-mail.

stories.title: A Toronto man’s family secret inspires new musical
stories.summary: A DNA test purchased on sale led Toronto performer Noam Tomaschoff to discover he was donor-conceived and had at least 35 half-siblings. He has turned the unexpected family discovery into a new musical, Our Little Secret, running Nov. 3 to 22 in Toronto.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
A DNA test bought on sale led to a discovery that would change one Toronto performer’s understanding of his family and eventually inspire a musical.

At 31, Noam Tomaschoff learned that the man he had grown up calling his father was not his biological father and that he had been conceived using a sperm donor. But that was only the beginning of the surprises.

After taking a consumer DNA test, Tomaschoff discovered he had at least 35 half-siblings around the world, a revelation that has since become the inspiration for Our Little Secret: A True New Musical .

Speaking on CTV’s Your Morning on Wednesday, Tomaschoff said the decision to take the test was not driven by any particular suspicion.

“Absolutely nothing other than the fact that it was on sale.”

A family secret comes to light

Tomaschoff said his parents initially questioned why he wanted to take the test. Realizing they would have to explain the circumstances of his birth before the results arrived, they decided to tell him the truth.

“They sat me down together, and we were on the table, and we all held hands, and this is when I knew something was wrong,” he recalled.

The conversation was an emotional surprise, particularly because his parents had never intended to reveal the secret, Tomaschoff added.

He said his immediate reaction was one of complete disbelief.

“The reaction was total surprise. I was shocked,” he said.

Tomaschoff said his parents had followed the general clinical guidance of the time, which encouraged some families not to disclose donor conception to their children. They were also concerned about preserving his sense of connection to them and the family.

“My first instinct, once I could gather the words, was to tell my friends about it,” he said.

From 35 siblings to the stage

The DNA results initially connected Tomaschoff with 15 close relatives. That number eventually grew as he found more siblings through other platforms.

Although he has not connected with all of them, many are part of a Facebook group, and one lives close enough that they regularly spend time together.

For someone who grew up as an only child, discovering such a large extended family was an unexpected turn.

The revelation left Tomaschoff with a story he felt compelled to share, even if he wasn’t initially sure how to tell it.

“I need to tell somebody. I need to tell this story.”

He eventually began discussing the idea with two of his high school friends, Ryan Peters and Russell Citron, who would become his collaborators on the project.

Rather than simply recounting the experience on stage, the trio decided to turn it into something more theatrical.

“This should be a musical,” Citron told Tomaschoff.

The idea made sense for the longtime friends, who shared a love of musicals and a history of singing together. Their unusual story would eventually become Our Little Secret, A True New Musical.

An opportunity to perform at the Toronto Fringe Festival, secured through a lottery, gave them a deadline to bring the production to life.

They secured a spot through the festival’s lottery, giving them a July 2023 performance date to work toward. What had started as conversations between three longtime friends was now something they had to write, develop and bring to the stage.

Our Little Secret: A True New Musical runs from Nov. 3 to 22 at Toronto’s CAA Theatre.

stories.title: Veteran who lost daughter in military training exercise named Silver Cross Mother
stories.summary: A veteran whose daughter died during a military training exercise in 2002 has been named the 2026 National Silver Cross Mother.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A veteran whose daughter died during a military training exercise in 2002 has been named the 2026 National Silver Cross Mother.

The Royal Canadian Legion says Virginia Hicks will place a wreath at the National War Memorial in Ottawa on Nov. 11, an annual tradition on behalf of Canadian mothers who have lost a child serving in the Canadian military.

stories.title: Liberals out-fundraise Conservatives by almost $1M in third quarter of 2026
stories.summary: The Liberal Party surpassed the Conservatives in fundraising by almost $1 million in the third quarter of 2026, says Elections Canada.
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Liberal Party surpassed the Conservatives in fundraising by almost $1 million in the third quarter of 2026, says Elections Canada.

Records published by Elections Canada show the Conservatives raised $3.9 million, while the Liberals raised $4.9 million.

In the second quarter of the year, the Conservatives raised $5 million, while the Liberals raised $4.3 million.

When asked at a press conference Sunday about being surpassed by the Liberals in fundraising, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre accused Prime Minister Mark Carney of “using the corporate powerbrokers that he’s paying off” with tax dollars.

Poilievre also said Carney was giving an “unprecedented gusher of gifts to his corporate friends through subsidies and handouts.”

On Sunday, Carney called six federal byelections in ridings in Quebec, Ontario and Saskatchewan for Dec. 7.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 1, 2026.

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Build a high-rise by 2027, save 50%; New incentive program passed by St. Thomas City Council
stories.summary: The owners of The Highlands apartments in downtown St. Thomas are getting set to construct their second tower.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The owners of The Highlands apartments in downtown St. Thomas are getting set to construct their second tower.

“We are at the city right now to add a nine or 10 storey building, which will add great housing to the supply in St. Thomas,” said Lee Greenwood, a partner in the property.

If all the permits are in place by the end of 2027, they will be able to take advantage of a new incentive bylaw passed by St. Thomas city council.

In order to meet their housing targets and unlock funding from the federal Housing Accelerator Fund (HAF) agreement, the city is offering a 50 per cent reduction on development charges for high-rise buildings five storey’s or greater.

This reduction will save hundreds of thousands of dollars.

“It’s a huge reason to start a project,” said Greenwood. “It takes a substantial line item out of the budget and allows us to deliver really good quality housing at the best rents we can.”

On Oct. 21, 2026, the governments of Ontario and Canada gave St. Thomas $19.6 million in funding to support housing growth and critical infrastructure .

It will be money used to help offset the reduced charges.

“We’re making it easy for someone to start a project that used to maybe be too expensive,” said Joe Preston, St. Thomas mayor.

There are currently three other proposed high-rise properties who could take advantage of this discount in 2027.

The third building at Alma College, a new multi-residential development by Drewlo Holdings on the brownfield site at Elm Street and Wilson Avenue and the two future towers at Elgin Centre.

“It’s going to take a long time to build those, but they’re going to do it with a bigger smile on their face even than they did last time,” said Preston. “If you’ve got less upfront money or you able to borrow money at a cheaper rate because some of it is already paid by not being a charge, it lets the simplicity of building affordable housing be there for people.”

The City’s original target of 1,183 new housing units between 2025 and 2027 increased to 1,204 as part of the additional funds received early in 2026.

The additional housing targets for affordable units and missing middle have already been achieved.

They have only reached 15 per cent of their target units in buildings five stories or greater.

Ontario Housing Minister Rob Flack says the $19.6 million, along with reducing the HST on purpose building housing rentals is already showing tremendous success.

“We got rid of the HST in 2023, and this year alone, up until September, we’ve seen more than 20,000 units built across the province, up 40 per cent over last year, which was also a record year,” said Flack. “With the increased supply comes increased competition and what are we seeing across the province is rent coming down. We’re bringing affordability back on the menu.”

The new Highlands apartments will be market-rent housing, but they’ll work with the city to determine potential affordable housing units.

The first building is full of young professionals and people moving to the community for work.

This next one will be within the timeline of the incentive program and calls the offer by the city a “game changer.”

“This allows us to put the money back into a building to deliver great units and great amenities,” said Greenwood. “The community we built here at Highlands is fantastic and we want to replicate it again.”

stories.title: Defence giant Lockheed Martin acquires N.S.-based undersea warfare company
stories.summary: Dartmouth - United States defence and aerospace giant Lockheed Martin has acquired Nova Scotia-based undersea defence company Ultra Maritime for $3.45 billion.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Dartmouth - United States defence and aerospace giant Lockheed Martin has acquired Nova Scotia-based undersea defence company Ultra Maritime for $3.45 billion.

Lockheed Martin completed its acquisition of Ultra Maritime last week after the two companies signed a deal in July.

Lockheed Martin says it had been an investor in Ultra Maritime since 2022.

Based in Dartmouth, N.S., and founded in 1947 as Cossar (Canada) Ltd., Ultra Maritime specializes in advanced undersea and anti-submarine warfare.

The company’s website says it manufactures sonar solutions, sonobuoys and torpedo defence systems to detect and track submarine threats for allied navies in more than 30 countries, including Canada and the U.S.

Ultra Maritime says it employs about 2,000 people in five countries, and as of last year, the federal government said the company employed more than 250 people in Dartmouth, N.S.

Lockheed Martin’s president of Rotary and Mission Systems, Stephanie Hill, says the acquisition of Ultra Maritime will allow it to meet the growing demand for undersea warfare capability worldwide.

“By joining forces with Ultra Maritime, we’re accelerating our commitment to deliver the most advanced undersea and anti-submarine warfare capabilities to our U.S. and allied partners across the globe,” said a statement from Hill.

The announcement comes after a recent surge in investment in defence and shipbuilding in Nova Scotia.

After inking the deal with Ultra Maritime, Lockheed Martin Canada also partnered with Invest Nova Scotia in July, committing to adding up to 320 skilled jobs in the province within the next five years.

It says it will add up to $126 million in salaries and benefits to the local economy based on growing demand for its Canadian-made combat management system.

Earlier that month, Prime Minister Mark Carney also announced that German firm Tkms was the preferred bidder to build 12 new submarines for the Royal Canadian Navy.

The deal is expected to increase the number of sailors, maintenance workers and naval suppliers in Halifax, home to Canada’s largest naval base.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 1, 2026.

stories.title: Giving fabric a new life: Quebec business tailors a new role in the circular economy
stories.summary: Montreal - A Quebec-based company is tailoring itself a place in the upcycling industry by breathing new life into discarded fabric — and it has no plans to slow down.
stories.author: Audrey Sanikopoulos The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - A Quebec-based company is tailoring itself a place in the upcycling industry by breathing new life into discarded fabric — and it has no plans to slow down.

Business and life partners Maude Girard and Gabrielle Huppé founded Next Chance six years ago. From their workshop on the south shore of Montreal, the pair and their team use discarded textiles from the fashion industry to make reusable gift wrapping or decorative items.

“According to the Ellen MacArthur Foundation, 12 per cent of all textiles produced worldwide are thrown away without ever being used,” said Girard in an interview.

And the situation is no different in Quebec, where nearly 344,000 metric tons of textiles were disposed of in 2023, according to the latest data from Recyc-Québec. This represents an increase of more than 114 per cent since 2011.

Faced with this reality, Girard and Huppé came up with the innovative idea of collecting fabric scraps, end-of-run lots, or rolls with manufacturing defects to give them a second life.

“We’ll go to designers and manufacturers and partner with them,” said Huppé. “We’ll be able to collect (the fabric) before it ends up either in a landfill or in the recycling stream.”

Since launching their business in 2020, the two women have drawn on their creativity to offer an ever-growing range of products, including reusable gift wrap, tote bags, tablecloths and hair accessories.

“We’re always looking for ways to give a second life to the different types of fabrics we recover,” said Girard.

Next Chance is a Quebec-based company specializing in upcycling textiles to create items like reusable gift packaging.

While the textiles recovered from the fashion industry are of good quality, the entrepreneurs aren’t ruling out the possibility of one day using fabric from discarded clothing, even if that presents more challenges.

Huppé gave the example of a garment made from a blend of cotton and polyester.

“You can’t reprocess the fabric because it’s all mixed together, and there’s no process that allows you to recycle a fabric like that,” she said. “That’s why, right now, it all ends up as waste.”

“We’ve been working on this project for several years now, but it hasn’t been implemented yet. It’ll be rolled out in the coming years,” added her partner.

Since its inception, Next Chance has managed to salvage 56,090 metres of fabric — the equivalent of 20 times the length of the Jacques-Cartier Bridge. The two women aim to reach 90,000 metres of salvaged fabric by next Earth Day, ON April 22, 2027.

“We still have a ways to go, but really, with all the enthusiasm we’ve generated — and even the great partnerships we’ve just signed — we think we’ll be able to reach our goal,” said Huppé.

The holiday season is the time of year when they collect the most fabric, said Girard.

Next Chance currently employs 14 people, both full-time and part-time.

Six years after its founding, customer demand continues to grow, allowing the two women to offer their products to the rest of Canada.

“We source almost exclusively from Quebec right now. Eventually, if we recover everything there is to recover, we’ll be able to branch out a little,” said Girard.

“There’s so much fabric discarded by the fashion industry — the quantities are astronomical. So really, we haven’t reached the point where we can recover everything that’s available in Canada,” she added.

While they already distribute their products to 200 retail locations across the country, the entrepreneurs plan to expand beyond the country’s borders in the coming years, with an eye toward the New York, California and even European markets.

“Eventually, we’ll begin our international expansion in the United States, ... but within the next five to 10 years, we’ll want to officially expand into Europe,” said Huppé, who was on a business trip to Paris this week to explore that market.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 1, 2026.

stories.title: Ahead of budget, Poilievre urges Carney to end diesel taxes and cut spending
stories.summary: The leader of the official opposition also called on Carney to "keep your promised debt anchors," urging the prime minister to reduce the deficit until the budget is balanced.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is reiterating his call for the federal government to end all taxes on diesel and cut wasteful spending as Prime Minister Mark Carney prepares to unveil his budget Thursday.

“Conservatives are demanding that he (Carney) cut wasteful spending to bring down deficits, inflation and taxes so Canadians can afford a good life,” Poilievre said during a news conference Sunday.

He went on to cite data from the Parliamentary Budget Officer, who projected $733 billion in additional debt in the next five years. That includes a $63.3-billion deficit in the 2026-27 fiscal year, down from a forecast $71.8 billion in the Pbo’s June outlook.

In a letter, Poilievre urged Carney to reduce the cost of government. He wrote this should include cutting bureaucracy, wasteful foreign aid, and cancelling the Alto high-speed rail project between Toronto and Quebec City.

The leader of the official opposition also called on Carney to “keep your promised debt anchors,” urging the prime minister to reduce the deficit until the budget is balanced.

The PBO has predicted the government will not meet its fiscal anchor of maintaining a declining deficit-to-GDP ratio; instead, the office expects the measure to rise in 2027-28 and 2029-30.

“This budget should be judged against his promise to Canadians,” Poilievre said.

Poilievre also called for the elimination of federal taxes on diesel until Canada Day and for Ottawa to suspend the GST on fuel until summer and scrap what he called the Fuel Standard Tax.

Earlier this week, the federal government unveiled its title and theme for the upcoming budget, which Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne’s office said reflects a period of “profound change and uncertainty.”

Titled “Masters OF OUR Destiny: Budget 2026,” Champagne’s office said the title was inspired by the 1962 Quebec electoral campaign of then-premier Jean Lesage.

The note from Champagne’s office said the slogan at the time was “a defining expression during a moment of profound change and uncertainty,” as the Lesage government was planning to build up hydroelectric resources and institutions that would support the economy.

Ottawa’s latest budget comes as Carney’s government continues to rework Canada’s economy and trade relationships to reduce reliance on the U.S., amid ongoing tariffs and trade tensions.

As Poilievre outlined his demands Sunday, Carney released a statement saying he had a “good conversation” with President Donald Trump and the teams from both countries were going to work in the coming weeks towards a “mutually beneficial” trade deal.

— with files from Global News’ Ariel Rabinovitch and The Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney had ‘good conversation’ with Trump, trade talks to continue
stories.summary: Deal would create jobs, improve affordability and respect Canada’s sovereignty, Prime Minister says
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Formal trade talks are expected to resume shortly between Canada and the United States after what Prime Minister Mark Carney is calling a “good conversation” with U.S. President Donald Trump.

The Prime Minister said on X Sunday he had a productive call with Mr. Trump on the future of Canada-U.S. trade, one he said built “on our recent constructive discussions” over the outlines of a possible trade deal.

“Our teams will now be working in the coming weeks to deliver that outcome,” Mr. Carney said.

Mr. Trump said on Sunday that his administration has the “concept” of a new trade deal with Canada, but declined to offer details.

A source familiar with the matter said that formal negotiations are expected to begin in a few days.

The source, whom the Globe is not identifying because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the matter, said the conversation between the two leaders took place Saturday.

They said that Mr. Trump ordered his team to resume formal talks as a result of the conversation.

Talks are expected to pick up where they left off in August when Canada and the United States were deadlocked over matters including automobile trade.

Mr. Carney on X said his idea of a good deal is one that would “create jobs for our workers, boost affordability for families, and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture, and sovereignty.”

The U.S. President, speaking to reporters after deplaning in Dubuque, Iowa, said that he had spoken with Mr. Carney on trade in recent days.

“I spoke to him again yesterday, and we have the concept of a deal that’s going to be great for our farmers, great for our country, and we’ll be fine for that,” the President said.

Canada walked away from the trade-deal bargaining table with Washington in August. Mr. Carney at the time said the United States was offering a “bad deal” that “asked too much and offered too little” for this country.

In August, the Prime Minister also said U.S. trade proposals would have curtailed Canadian sovereignty and eroded or destroyed major industries here.

Mr. Carney has given three main reasons for abandoning trade talks in August. He said the U.S. refused to extend tariff relief to medium- and heavy-duty trucks, which would have affected the viability of General Motors and Ford plants in Ontario. He also said the U.S. was pushing for changes around the discoverability of French-language content for online streaming services, and that Washington had suggested language that Ottawa believed could have restricted Canada’s ability to make trade deals with other countries.

With a report from Reuters

stories.title: Carney says he and Trump had ‘good conversation’ on stalled Canada-US trade talks
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says he had a "good conversation" with U.S. President Donald Trump on Canada-U.S. trade.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says he had a “good conversation” with U.S. President Donald Trump on the future of trade between the two countries.

Carney says in a social media post Sunday that the conversation builds on previous ones they have had about what a mutually beneficial trade deal looks like.

He says such a deal would create jobs for workers, improve affordability for families, and respect “Canada’s languages, culture and sovereignty.”

The prime minister says his team and Trump’s are to continue working together in the coming weeks to achieve a deal.

Carney tagged Trump’s social media account in the post.

Diplomatic relations between Canada and the U.S. have been dicey since Carney’s government walked away from formal trade talks in August and the prime minister accused the Americans of making unreasonable last-minute demands.

In response, Washington imposed tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian goods, and Ottawa followed up with retaliatory tariffs on American products.

Trump recently announced he would lift some of the 50 per cent tariffs on Canada at the end of October, while adding tariffs to dozens of new products, including Canadian garbage and sewage.

Last week, Carney described progress on a new trade deal as limited while reiterating that Ottawa is prepared to make a deal but only when it suits Canadians’ interests.

The post comes ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States, where the ongoing Canada-U.S. trade dispute has emerged as a key issue among some candidates. There have been suggestions that a deal might be possible in order to try and boost Republican chances of retaining control of Congress or the Senate.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says the U.S. and Canada will be working in the coming weeks to deliver a “mutually beneficial” trade deal after a conversation with President Donald Trump.

Carney confirmed the chat between the two world leaders in a post on social media Sunday.

“This builds on our recent constructive discussions on the outlines of a mutually beneficial trade deal that would create jobs for our workers, boost affordability for families, and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture, and sovereignty,” Carney said.

“Our teams will now be working in the coming weeks to deliver that outcome.”

While the comments are the latest signal a trade deal could still occur, it also appears to suggest an agreement won’t be reached before the U.S. midterms on Tuesday.

The prime minister’s comments come after he told reporters Wednesday that the federal government was “not at that position right now” in terms of reaching a trade deal.

Asked by reporters Wednesday why he was willing to entertain a deal before the midterms — and whether Canada was being set up to be the “fall guys” by the U.S. administration if it loses — Carney said they’re after the right deal.

Last Monday, Global News reported that the once-stalled talks between the two countries were “moving quickly” at the political level, according to multiple sources with direct knowledge of the negotiations.

Canada walked away from talks with the U.S. in August, with Carney saying the U.S. had made a last-minute push for language that would limit Canada’s ability to enter trade deals with other countries, water down French language requirements, and hurt the country’s struggling auto industry.

The break down in talks led to Trump’s previously threatened 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods to take effect, with Canada responding with dollar-for-dollar retaliatory duties.

Trump previously commented on Canada during a campaign rally on Thursday in South Carolina for the Republican senate candidate. He suggested Canada had been “treating us extremely nicely recently,” adding his tariffs on their northern neighbours had the effect of improving relations.

The president has yet to comment Sunday in relation to Carney’s comments.

Asked about Carney’s statement, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre pushed Carney to “get a great deal.”

“It’s time for Mr. Carney to put the big talk in the past and deliver real results,” Poilievre said Sunday at a news conference.

Talks of a potential trade deal also come days before the federal government is set to announce its latest budget on Thursday.

stories.title: Trump says U.S., Canada have the 'concept of a very good deal'
stories.summary: Speaking to reporters in Iowa on Sunday, Trump said the countries were "very close" to reaching a trade deal.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - U.S. President Donald Trump says Canada and the United States have “the concept of a very good deal.”

Speaking to reporters in Iowa on Sunday, Trump said the countries were “very close” to reaching a trade deal.

“We’ve been losing money for many years with Canada,” he said. “We have the concept of a deal that’s going to be great for our farmers, great for our country and it’ll be fine for Canada too.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney said on social media Sunday that he had a “good conversation” with Trump on the future of trade between the two countries.

A spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office said the conversation between the leaders took place on Saturday.

Carney said the conversation builds on previous ones they have had about what a mutually beneficial trade deal looks like. He said such a deal would create jobs for workers, improve affordability for families, and respect Canada’s languages, culture and sovereignty.

“Our teams will now be working in the coming weeks to deliver that outcome,” he said.

The conversation comes ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States, where the ongoing Canada-U.S. trade dispute has emerged as a key issue among some candidates.

Trump told reporters on Sunday the Keystone XL pipeline project was part of the negotiations, adding that Canada would pay for “all of it.”

“We’re going to give them the route, and it’s largely been determined but they’ll build the Keystone pipeline,” said Trump.

Trump boasted in August about reviving the Keystone XL pipeline project, touting it as a win in trade negotiations with Canada. At the time, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that Canada and the U.S. “have a Deal!”

A subsequent post showed a rendering of the president yanking a pipeline out of the ground beside a tombstone labelled “buried by Biden” and alongside another sign reading “Keystone Pipeline. Completely Free. Energy. Jobs. America First.”

Keystone XL, which could bring more than 800,000 barrels of additional oil from Alberta to the U.S., was proposed almost 20 years ago. But after years of challenges from U.S. landowners, Indigenous leaders in both countries, and environmental groups, former U.S. president Joe Biden killed it by revoking a key U.S. permit in 2021.

Almost a year ago, Carney raised with Trump the prospect of reviving the project, as part of a larger pitch to link energy co-operation and support for Canada’s steel and aluminum sectors. Trump signed an executive order in April to approve a new pipeline which would utilize existing portions of the abandoned Keystone project.

At a press conference Sunday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre encouraged Carney to “get a great deal.” He said everyday Canadians can’t afford to wait for a trade deal with the U.S.

“The prime minister promised in the last election he would get an even better deal than we had before. He’s broken that promise so far,” he said. “It’s time for Mr. Carney to put the big talk in the past and deliver real results.”

Tuesday’s midterm election brings high stakes for both Republicans and Democrats. A Democrat wave could see a Congressional check to Trump’s unprecedented use of executive powers during the remainder of his tenure.

Polling shows Democrats are favoured to take the House, where a net gain of three seats would give them a majority. The future of the Senate is less clear, where some polling shows a Democrat net gain of four seats is within reach.

While Trump’s first term rattled the bilateral relationship between Canada and the U.S., his second term blew it up. Canada was an early target of Trump’s tariffs and Canadians were shocked and appalled by the president’s repeated threats of annexation.

Tensions escalated further in August when trade talks collapsed. Trump slapped an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs, banned imports of other Canadian products and signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America.

The trade war is deeply unpopular in states like Michigan and Maine, where tight Senate races ultimately could decide which party gains congressional control.

But even if Democrats emerge triumphant this week, or win the White House in 2028, it’s not clear that Trump’s tariff wall would suddenly drop.

Carney said last week that Canada was not yet in a position to reach a trade deal with Trump’s administration.

On his way into the weekly Liberal national caucus meeting on Parliament Hill, Carney said on Wednesday that Ottawa was prepared to make a deal only when it suits Canadians’ interests.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 1, 2026.

—With files from Fakiha Baig, Nick Murray and Kelly Geraldine Malone

stories.title: 4 teenagers killed, two injured in single-vehicle crash in Puslinch
stories.summary: During a mid-morning press conference Sunday, Wellington County OPP detachment commander Insp. Karen Medeiros said the vehicle May not have had enough seatbelts for all six occupants.
stories.author: Prabhnoor Kaur
stories.content:
Four teenagers are dead and two others in hospital with serious injuries after a single-vehicle collision in Puslinch early Saturday morning.

Ontario Provincial Police said officers were called to Watson Road South, just north of Wellington Road 34, shortly after 1:35 a.m. Oct. 31.

The six people were travelling in the SUV when it left the narrow rural road, struck a guardrail and entered a ravine on Watson Road South, between Maltby Road East and Wellington Road East.

Police identified the deceased as a 19-year-old male from Mississauga, a 19-year-old male from Brampton, a 17-year-old female from Mississauga and a 15-year-old female from Milton. All four were pronounced dead at scene.

The two survivors, both girls from Mississauga were taken to hospital.

“A 17-year-old female from Mississauga remains in hospital with life-altering injuries, while a 16-year-old female from Mississauga sustained non-life-threatening injuries,” police said Sunday during a police media briefing.

During a mid-morning news conference Sunday, Wellington County OPP detachment commander Insp. Karen Medeiros said the vehicle May not have had enough seatbelts for all six occupants.

“But apparently it’s under investigation to determine whether or not speed or the seatbelts were the causing factors,” she added.

Police have not confirmed who was driving the vehicle or how they occupants knew each other.

Watson Road South remained closed as of Sunday morning to ensure safety of motorists because of damage to the guardrail.

OPP Inspector Karen Medeiros briefs media Sunday, Nov. 1

“Four young people have lost their lives in a matter of moments. Families have been forever changed and an entire community is searching for answers,” said Medeiros.

“Our responsibility is to ensure those answers are based on evidence, facts a thorough investigation. That work will continue in the days and weeks ahead.”

News of the tragedy was also posted on social media sites with some people paying tribute to their friends. One person who knew one of the teens in the car said the friends regularly travelled to Guelph to visit university friends.

stories.title: Prime Minister Mark Carney calls six federal byelections for December
stories.summary: Voters in six federal ridings in Quebec, Ontario and Saskatchewan will be heading to the polls Dec. 7, after Prime Minister Mark Carney called byelections Sunday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Voters in six federal ridings in Quebec, Ontario and Saskatchewan will be heading to the polls Dec. 7, after Prime Minister Mark Carney called byelections Sunday.

A press release from the Prime Minster’s Office says byelections will take place in three Quebec ridings, including Laurier—Sainte-Marie, Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie and Saint-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton, where seats were previously held by the Liberals, the NDP and the Bloc Québécois respectively.

The remaining byelections are for Ontario ridings Brantford—Brant South and Scarborough North, along with Saskatchewan riding Yorkton—Melville.

The Conservatives held seats in Yorkton—Melville and Brantford—Brant South, while the seat in Scarborough North belonged to the Liberals.

Carney’s Liberals currently have a majority government after winning three byelections earlier this year.

In a tweet Sunday, Conservative Leader Pierre Pollievre asked that Canadians choose a different path, saying that his party’s plan will save money, protect jobs and reform the immigration system.

“I think it’s an opportunity for hard-working Canadians who think it’s unacceptable for Mark Carney to drive up their cost of gas, groceries and housing to vote for a for a party that will fight to save you money,” he said at a news conference later Sunday.

The byelections come after members of Parliament quit the House of Commons for diplomatic appointments, provincial politics or retirement.

Since the 2025 election, 13 of 343 members of Parliament have decided to step down.

The prime minister must call an election between 11 and 180 days after a member’s resignation.

A pastor and longtime Conservative is running as an independent candidate in Brantford-Brant South in Ontario after the party chose to bypass a local nomination contest and appoint Brantford Mayor Kevin Davis as its candidate.

Dave Carrol’s decision to run independently adds intrigue to the byelection, as it could draw votes from the Conservatives, who were already expected to face a tough challenge from the Liberals.

“Party leadership chose to appoint another candidate, skipping the process we have valued for decades,” Carrol, who previously sought the Conservative nomination, said on social media. “That decision, while legal, has been received poorly, and rightfully so.”

In the Saskatchewan riding of Yorkton-Melville, the Liberals are running candidate Aaron Kienle, the mayor of Yorkton, against Conservative Nelson Pohl, a farmer who owns a furnace cleaning company.

That riding has been held by the Conservatives and its predecessors, the Reform Party and Canadian Alliance, for more than 30 years. The Liberals have not won there since the riding was first created in 1968.

Cathay Wagantall, who was elected as a Conservative MP in 2015, won Yorkton-Melville with more than 77 per cent of the vote in 2025. She resigned in August.

The Laurier-Sainte-Marie riding was previously held by former environment minister Steven Guilbeault who left in the summer after a public disagreement with Carney over environment policy.

On Sunday, the Liberals announced that Guy Cormier, former president and CEO of Desjardins Group, will be their candidate in the byelection in Laurier–Sainte-Marie.

The Bloc is fielding Zumretay Arkin, the former vice-president of the World Uyghur Congress while the NDP has nominated epidemiologist Nima Machouf.

The St-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton byelection is needed because Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay quit the Bloc caucus in June ahead of a successful run provincially for the separatist Parti Québécois.

The Liberals are running former provincial politician Chantal Soucy, who represented the Coalition Avenir Québec in the National Assembly for eight years before choosing not to run again in the election this fall. The Bloc has nominated Caroline Emond, the former director general of the International Dairy Federation.

Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie was the only riding the NDP won east of Manitoba in the last federal election, and it was opened in August when MP Alexandre Boulerice resigned ahead of his successful provincial run for Québec solidaire.

The Liberals are running human rights advocate Jean-Sébastien Vallée, while the NDP are fielding Pierre Céré, a Quebec activist who made a brief bid for the leadership of the Parti Québécois in 2015.

The sixth byelection is to be held in Scarborough North, which former Liberal Shaun Chen vacated in August citing ongoing medical issues related to a vehicle crash in 2025.

The Liberals are seeking to hold onto the seat with accountant James Li.

Carney has had a string of byelection successes already this year.

Byelections were held in April in the Quebec riding of Terrebonne — a vote the Supreme Court ordered redone after issues with mail-in ballots during the 2025 election — along with the Liberal strongholds of University-Rosedale and Scarborough Southwest in Toronto. The three Liberal wins coming on the heels of five MPs who crossed the floor to the Liberals, cemented Carney’s majority government.

The Liberals swept another three ridings on Aug. 31, flipping a Conservative seat in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord and holding seats in Beaches-East York and North Vancouver-Capilano.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 1, 2026.

With files from Tori Fitzpatrick in Halifax

stories.title: OPP release details of victims, injured in fatal collision near Guelph
stories.summary: OPP said investigators continue to gather and preserve evidence in what she calls a complex investigation, but it is too soon to determine the exact details of what occurred.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
One of the people injured in a fatal early morning single-vehicle crash Saturday has life-altering injuries, with police saying the second received non-life-threatening injuries.

Wellington OPP, fire and paramedic services responded to reports of the collision shortly after 1:30 a.m. Saturday on Watson Road South between Maltby Road East and Wellington Road 34, south of Guelph, Ont.

Six people were in the vehicle, police said. Four were pronounced dead at the scene, while two were transported to hospital.

“Our investigation has determined that six occupants were travelling in the vehicle when it left the roadway, struck a guardrail and entered the ravine,” said Insp. Karen Medeiros, detachment commander for Wellington OPP.

No names were released but OPP said the victims include a 19-year-old man from Mississauga, 19-year-old man from Brampton, a 17-year-old girl from Mississauga and a 15-year-old girl from Milton. A 17-year-old female remains in hospital with life-altering injuries as does a 16-year-old who received non-life-threatening injuries. Both teens in hospital are from Mississauga, according to police.

Medeiros said investigators continue to gather and preserve evidence in what she calls a complex investigation, but said it is too soon to determine exactly what happened. Anyone who May have been travelling in the area early Saturday, or who has surveillance or dashcam footage, is asked to contact OPP.

Asked about seatbelt use, Medeiros cautioned that the investigation is looking into whether speed or seatbelt use were contributing factors. But she said she did not believe there were enough seatbelts for the number of people in the vehicle.

— with files from Global News’ Rachel Morgan

Four teens, including two from Mississauga, one from Brampton and another as young as 15 from Milton, were killed in a single-vehicle crash early Saturday morning in Puslinch, Ont., just south of Guelph, police say.

The Ontario Provincial Police said first responders were called to the site of the crash at Watson Road South, just north of Wellington Road 34, around 1:30 a.m.

stories.title: ‘He’s a leader’: Ben Casselman blossoms as Western Mustangs advance to OUA semifinal vs Windsor
stories.summary: The Western Mustangs picked the perfect time to end a four-game losing streak against their rival Wilfrid Laurier Golden Hawks.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The Western Mustangs picked the perfect time to end a four-game losing streak against their rival Wilfrid Laurier Golden Hawks. Seven different players scored touchdowns as Western beat the Hawks 58-41 in the OUA quarterfinal at Alumni Field in London, Ont. on Saturday, Oct.

31, 2026. IN Photos: Western Mustangs vs. Wilfrid Laurier Western quarterback Ben Casselman threw for 405 yards and two scores and added a rushing touchdown in the win. “I think we really leaned into our running attack a bit more,” said Casselman after a 55-39 defeat to those same Hawks last week.

“It’s safe to say we had the training wheels on him early on,” said Faulds. ”He’s gained the confidence of our coaching staff and of our players. He’s a leader within the group and everyone trusts him.” Western ran for 274 yards, led by Ethan Dolby who had 18 carries for 155 yards and a touchdown.

He also had a big first down run late in regulation to seal the victory. “We’ve got to lean on our offensive line, especially in playoff football, whether it was Dolby, whether it was Jack Kelly,” said Faulds. “It didn’t matter who was touching the ball.

Even Geoff Clubine there at the end and Ben Casselman had a couple big carries. We’re a fully balanced attack, so it keeps them guessing whether it’s through the air or it’s on the ground.” The biggest difference between Saturday’s win and the loss in the final game of the regular season was the play of Western’s defence.

They had key third-down stops and forced turnovers which lead directly to Western scores. “He (Faulds) just he fired us up in the locker room,” said Dylan Tharby, who had a forced fumble and was in on nine tackles for Western.

“He was kind of like, you know, last week was a fluke. It was kind of like now it’s do or die for us. He told us to walk in in a sense and be better.” Western did surrender 41 points, but Faulds says other than a few long scores, he was thrilled with his defence.

“In the first half, our defense only gave up 14 points,” said Faulds. “Laurier in that second half is kind of knowing based on us, we kept scoring that they had to throw the ball around and do all that. So, you call the game a little bit differently that way,” he added.

“We’ve got a lot of trust and confidence in our defense and our defense played so much better. We got pressure on their quarterback and we made it tougher on them. So sure, Laurier scores 41 points versus 55. But the 41 they scored was a lot tougher.

It wasn’t one big play here or one big play there, they scored it was eight, nine or ten play drives.” Western will now face Windsor at Alumni Field next Saturday in the OUA Semifinal. They haven’t faced the Lancers since back in Week 2 when Casselman wasn’t the starting quarterback.

“It should be a physical game and it should be a good one,” said Casselman. “Every time we play them it’s a physical one. We’re going to have to establish the run early and get back to the pass late. You know it’s another game.” Faulds says he didn’t even take part in Halloween because it was right back to the film room with the coaches to prepare for the Lancers.

They’ve got some great running backs and a defense that flies around. We haven’t watched film on them for about eight weeks or seven weeks. So, it’ll be getting acclimated with them in the film room.” Kickoff is scheduled for 1 p.m. on Saturday, Nov.

7, 2026, at Alumni Field. The other semifinal features Ottawa at Queen’s.

stories.title: Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week
stories.summary: Canada
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week:

Earnings and the stock market

The steady stream of third-quarter earnings reports from the biggest names in corporate Canada continues this week. The financial results come after technology stocks sold off on Friday amid worries about the billions being spent on AI and concerns the money being spent on chips and data centres may not be worth it.

Macklem at committee

Senior Deputy Governor Carolyn Rogers looks on as Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem responds to a question during a news conference in Ottawa, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026.

Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem and senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers are at the House of Commons standing committee on finance on Tuesday. The appearance comes after the central bank raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent.

Trade numbers

Truck traffic is shown on the Gordie Howe International Bridge, that connects Windsor, Ont., and Detroit, Michigan, is shown on Monday, Aug. 24, 2026.

Statistics Canada will report September merchandise trade figures on Wednesday. The data comes after trade talks between Canada and the United States fell apart in August and the U.S. imposed a fresh round of tariffs, followed by counter-tariffs by Canada.

Federal budget

Minister of Finance Francois-Philippe Champagne gives remarks at a luncheon ahead of the Canada-EU Summit, in Montreal, on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026.

Federal Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne will deliver his budget on Thursday. Prime Minister Mark Carney has been focused on an aggressive infrastructure agenda to build the economy in the face of U.S. tariffs and geopolitical changes.

The furnace is monitored at Nexans Canada Inc., a copper rod and wire manufacturer in Montreal on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026.

Statistics Canada will offer its latest snapshot of the job market on Friday when it releases its labour force survey for October. The economy lost 68,000 jobs in September as the unemployment rate increased 0.1 percentage points to 6.5 per cent.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 1, 2026.
