Morgan Breitkreutz, the staffer brought into Carney’s office to offer special advice around the referendum, marked his final day in that role on Friday, a position that was always meant to be temporary — something those across the federal Liberal government also hope to be the case for the separation push coming from Alberta.

But as Carney vows further collaboration with Smith, including on immigration — an area where the premier left the referendum armed with a narrow win in her efforts to take more control over the system — Smith also prepares to face her grassroots.

It will be in Calgary in late November where members of her United Conservative Party are expected to vote on a resolution as to whether they want her government to “oppose federally imposed net-zero mandates” as well as “review provincial carbon-pricing and (carbon capture, utilization and storage) policies” to “ensure they protect Alberta’s economy and autonomy,” citing concerns over costs to taxpayers and sector competitiveness.

Carbon capture and storage is the emissions-reducing technology that is set for a massive expansion under the Ottawa-Alberta energy pact that is tied to plans to fast-track a new oil pipeline to the West Coast. More agreements with the companies behind that project, known as Pathways, are expected to be signed by Nov. 15.
So although Alberta and Ottawa are trying to put the referendum behind them, more tests of their relationship — from her base this time — potentially lie ahead.

When asked about that upcoming party vote and Smith’s commitment to the “grand bargain” struck with Carney, a spokesman said the premier remains committed to the deal, “including the Pathways Project.”
Ryan Fournier said the party welcomes internal debates “on a wide range of issues and diverse perspectives.”
“Members can bring forward ideas they believe the government should consider, some will pass, and others won’t. We’re proud of that democratic process and the honest debate it allows,” he wrote.
Since Smith entered into that energy deal last year, Jeffrey Rath, the lawyer and outspoken separation supporter has been calling for her removal.

On Friday, he learned he had been kicked out of the party — a move Smith explained was due to “multiple” breaches to its members’ code of conduct and his declared intention of attending November’s gathering to push the party towards independence.

Speaking to the Star, Rath, a leader affiliated with the Alberta Prosperity Project, the most prominent of the independence groups, accused Smith of wanting to quell dissent and suggested her move would only “inflame” the party’s independence supporters, of which he says there are many.
“It’s going to increase the resolve and people are going to become even more determined to fight for the heart and soul of our party.”
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith arrives to speak to the media in Calgary, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026, after the provincial referendum.

Smith has indeed sought to bring down the hammer, as Rath and others this week circulated an image of a form those looking to join the party’s board would be asked to sign, vowing to honour the referendum results that showed nearly 75 per cent of Albertans voted to remain in Canada, against the 25 per cent who wanted to see a binding vote held on separation.
Chris Scott, an independence advocate whose group, Let’s Talk Alberta, staged events across the province leading up to the Oct.19 vote, is among those looking to run.

Seated in his cafe in Mirror, Alta., last week, with the defeat of the referendum less than 48 hours old, he describes his role as one of wanting to “repair the rift between the federalists and the separatists” within the party, “or at least try.”
“The goal for me is not independence. The goal has always been sovereignty. I just see independence as the only clear path to the sovereignty we need. But I can be convinced.”

For years now, his Whistle Stop Cafe, which Scott bought back in 2019, has served as a hub for those who champion standing up to government, first over COVID-19 mandates — as Scott did when he defied provincial orders to close — and then later for independence.

His highway-side cafe, which also serves as a gas station and convenience store, pays homage to both. Inside, framed prints from scenes of the 2022 “Freedom Convoy” decorate the walls. By one window, a sticker reads, “I stand with Chris + Tamara,” referring to protest’s leaders found guilty of mischief.

Signs that read “Quebec Got to Vote, Why Can’t We,” and a “Our Future Our Choice” are placed just outside. Near the highway, a row of Alberta flags stand planted, as do large signs telling passersby to “Send Ottawa Your Message” by voting “Yes” on Oct. 19, but the signs lie tipped over, toppled much like the push for independence itself.
But while independence leaders have all vowed to keep up their fight, Scott doesn’t mince words about the campaign they mounted.
“It was a complete disaster,” he says from his cafe seat. “Like an absolute steaming pile of s—t. There was no campaign.”

He points to the actions taken by Rath and Mitch Sylvestre, another prominent independence leader whose title as CEO of the Alberta Prosperity Project has since been disputed by Scott and another member of its larger board, who say the pair had been previously removed from their positions.

Both Rath and Sylvestre have rejected that claim, with Sylvestre saying in a statement and also in a recent online call held with project members that the dispute was nothing more than internal drama spilling into public view. Scott and Sylvestre have since met to discuss their issues.

It was also on that call that Sylvestre, a major fundraiser within the United Conservative Party who presides over one of the constituency associations calling for a review of Smith’s leadership, delivered the message to supporters that the fight ahead needed to be a political one.
“Let me be clear about this: If you’re buying a UCP membership, you are not buying it to support the UCP,” he said in the Oct. 22 call.

“You are buying it to support our cause for independence. And if you’re going to the (annual general meeting in Calgary), you’re going to support our cause for independence. There’s no other reason for us to go there.”

stories.title: Michiganders slammed by historic political ad spend ready for midterms to end
stories.summary: Detroit - Gwyneth Love is ready for the United States midterm elections to be over. The 24-year-old Michigander lives in the eye of the political storm.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Detroit - Gwyneth Love is ready for the United States midterm elections to be over. The 24-year-old Michigander lives in the eye of the political storm.

The tight race between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for a key Michigan Senate seat could ultimately decide which party holds power in Congress.

“I feel like this year more than any years we’ve been getting a lot more ads,” Love said Friday in Detroit.

Amelia Cunningham and Gwyneth Love are ready for the midterm elections to be over. Like many Michiganders, they have been inundated with political advertisements from the tight race between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for a key Senate seat. (Oct. 31, 2026)

“It honestly is very insane when you see so many ads telling you who to vote for and you can’t really believe what they tell you.”

Tuesday’s midterm election brings high stakes for both parties. A Democrat wave could see a Congressional check to U.S. President Donald Trump’s unprecedented use of executive powers during the remainder of his tenure.

Polling shows Democrats are favoured to take the House, where a net gain of three seats would give them a majority. The future of the Senate is less clear, where some polling shows a Democrat net gain of four seats is within reach.

Republicans have rolled out record spending in an effort to hold their Senate majority. The party is fighting for votes, even in historically Republican seats, amid Trump’s plummeting favourability over controversial policies, rising gas prices, tariffs and the war in Iran.

Spending on political ads ahead of the midterms is set to be the highest in U.S. history at $11.6 billion, according the AdImpact, an advertising intelligence firm. The Detroit News reported in early October that Michigan’s Senate contest was already the most expensive race in that state’s history.

The United States has become deeply partisan and it’s unclear how much the dollars spent on advertising will equate to ballots cast on election day.

What is evident on the streets of Detroit is frustration and exhaustion from the barrage of campaign messaging in the highly competitive race.

Love said she just can’t escape the political discourse. She was continuously bombarded with political ads on television and social media while getting ready to attend an anime and pop culture convention in downtown Detroit with Amelia Cunningham on Friday.

“It kind of gets to the point where you’re almost uncomfortable watching them,” Cunningham, 24, said.

Both Love and Cunningham said they were motivated to vote because of affordability issues and the high cost of gas. Love added she’d cast a ballot for “anyone other than Mike Rogers.”

“He’s been pushing so many ads being so rude to other people,” she said.

Both candidates have released sharp attack ads criticizing the other. Rogers has gone after his opponent’s background and controversial past remarks. El-Sayed has condemned Rogers for his corporate ties and legislative records.

The Republican candidate distanced himself from Trump’s trade war with Canada in recent weeks. In a campaign ad released last month, Rogers is seen drinking a Labatt’s beer and telling voters “Canada is not our enemy.”

Stacy Riley said she feels awful about the tension between the two countries. But it’s not the top issue for the 54-year-old nurse practitioner.

She works in public health and that’s the motivating factor for why she supports El-Sayed, who also worked in that field as an administrator and is an epidemiologist.

“I’ve never seen it tight like this,” Riley said. “I’ve ever seen so much money spent and probably on both sides.”

Detroit historically leans Democrat, although Trump was able to garner up a decent surge of voters during the 2024 election.

Black voters are potential difference-makers in the race. In the final weeks of the campaign both El-Sayed and Rogers have been trying to shore up support from the Black community.

But the constant political messaging is tiring, said Jerome Watkins.

“I voted yesterday and I’m still getting them. I thought that would stop them,” Watkins said with a laugh outside a Detroit grocery store Friday.

Like many Michiganders, the 67-year-old voted because of the economy and high gas prices. The trade war with Canada wasn’t particularly on his radar and he was hopeful trade between the two countries could return to pre-Trump times.

While Watkins voted for El-Sayed he said it wasn’t because of the Democrat’s policies.

“It was part of the anti-everything going on with Trump and I didn’t ever like Mike Rogers anyway,” Watkins said. “So that was it.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 1, 2026.

stories.title: Overnight traffic detours on Fanshawe Park Road as construction nears completion
stories.summary: Fanshawe Park Road rehabilitation project overnight detours. (Source: City of London)
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
The City of London says the Fanshawe Park Road rehabilitation project is nearing completion, and crews are preparing for final paving before winter.

Overnight road work begins tonight and will take place between North Centre Road and Adelaide Street North from 6 p.m. to 7 a.m. to remove the existing top layer of asphalt.

Eastbound traffic detours: Nov. 1-2 (two nights).

Traffic will be detoured in one direction at a time, while traffic travelling in the opposite direction can continue through the area.

City officials warn that nearby residents May experience overnight noise from asphalt milling and are encouraged to keep windows closed.

Additional traffic detours will be required during final paving, with details to be announced later.

stories.title: Her daughter died in training too. Now Canada’s Silver Cross Mother has a message for Wainwright families
stories.summary: Virginia Hicks has been named Canada’s 2026 National Silver Cross Mother by the Royal Canadian Legion.
stories.author: John Vennavally-Rao
stories.content:
Frankford, Ont. — Virginia Hicks has been named Canada’s 2026 National Silver Cross Mother by the Royal Canadian Legion.

On Remembrance Day, she will lay a wreath at the National War Memorial in Ottawa on behalf of every Canadian mother who has lost a child in military service. Hicks lost her own daughter, 22-year-old Sapper Mariebeth Short, in a training accident in 2002.

“I’m very honoured to be the Silver Cross Mother,” Hicks said. “Surprised, very honoured.”

When she lays the wreath, she knows where her thoughts will be.

“I’ll be thinking about Mariebeth for sure and thinking about all the parents who’ve lost their children, how their heart is feeling that day,” she said. “You just kind of wish… that there’s never going to be another Silver Cross Mother.”

Hicks is herself a veteran, having served in the Royal Canadian Air Force for nearly 30 years working in logistics and supply. “I wanted to do something that made a difference,” she said.

Her daughter had her own reasons for signing up. “Meeting new people and having new adventures, I think was one of her biggest reasons for joining the military,” Hicks said.

Service runs in their family. Hicks’ father was a military firefighter and her grandfather an airman. Her mother’s three uncles served in the Second World War. Hicks’ husband, Brian, also spent three decades in the military as a construction engineer.

Short followed in their footsteps. Born in Comox, B.C., she had initially hoped to become a navigator in the navy, but her math skills fell short. Recruiters offered other options, including combat engineering. She had just turned 20.

Her parents were a bit skeptical. “She was four foot 11 and 95 pounds, soaking wet,” Hicks said.

“We were maybe a little uncertain, but we also knew that she had the attitude that give me a job, and I’m going to prove you wrong.”

She did, hauling pins weighing more than 16 kilograms (35 pounds), two at a time, and fitting them underneath bridges. Coworkers nicknamed her “Shorty,” Hicks says, “but it had nothing to do with her ambition or her strength or her willingness to do any job that they gave her.”

“She had a lot of respect from all the people she worked with.”

In September 2002, Short was looking forward to her first deployment to either Bosnia or Afghanistan. Her unit was taking part in a training exercise involving light armoured vehicles, or LAVs. The Friday before, she called her parents, excited. Her stepfather reminded her to be careful — the LAV was a big piece of equipment, and dangerous. On the morning of the exercise, she told her mother she’d be the first to drive.

Later that day, Short was standing in the gunner’s hatch when the vehicle rolled twice and landed on its side. “Mariebeth was underneath it twice when it rolled,” Hicks says.

A military investigation later found there had been a defect in the wheel assembly from when the vehicle was built.

When a military padre came to Hicks’ door to deliver the news that Short had been killed, she didn’t believe him.

“You’re lying; it’s not possible,” she recalls saying to him. “You never expect that when you’re speaking to your kid in the morning that they’re all excited, and that this is what’s going to happen at the end of your day.”

Short was given a full military funeral in Trenton attended by hundreds of soldiers. She was buried in her uniform.

The only piece of it her mother still has is Short’s beret. Hicks has kept it all these years and showed it to CTV News during an interview at her home.

Hicks received the Memorial Cross — commonly called the Silver Cross — in 2009 and was surprised by that. She had believed it went only to families of those killed overseas.

“I didn’t realize at that time that it was actually given to soldiers who perished in service of their country. Whether it was in a training accident, whether it was in a work-related accident, or whether it was overseas,” she said.

When Short died the Memorial Cross had been limited to deaths on overseas missions. Rule changes in 2007 and 2008 extended it to all service-related deaths since October 2001, including those in training at home.

That is the message Hicks wants to spread this year.

“People think that a person who dies in theatre is more important than someone who dies in training, and that has to be so wrong,” she said. “You are training so hard so that when you go to theatre, this doesn’t happen.”

It hit home again in October, when four soldiers were killed in a fire during training at CFB Wainwright in Alberta.

“It was like a cold shower. Oh my God! Not again,” Hicks said. “And your heart goes out to the parents, the loved ones, girlfriends of these young soldiers.”

Her advice to those families is to be patient while the military investigates. “It will get easier. I can promise them that, but it’ll never go away.”

Hicks still visits Short’s grave several times a month and returns to the site of the rollover in Petawawa every year.

As for what Short would make of her mother being chosen National Silver Cross Mother:

“I’m hoping that she would be proud,” Hicks said, “knowing that we supported her in everything that she endeavoured to do, even when she called me that Monday morning and said, ‘I’m going to drive. I’m going to be the first driver.’ It’s like, ‘yes, go get her, girl.’”

stories.title: Silver Cross Mother keeps daughter’s memory alive after 2002 training exercise accident
stories.summary: 22-year-old Private Mariebeth Short was serving as a sapper in the 2 Combat Engineer Regiment at CFB Petawawa
stories.author: Erin Anderssen
stories.content:
Every year, Virginia Hicks places red roses in the branches of a lonely maple tree growing on the Mattawa Plains at CFB Petawawa in Ontario.

The tree marks the place where her daughter, 22-year-old Private Mariebeth Short, died in 2002 during a training exercise while serving as a sapper in the 2 Combat Engineer Regiment. Mrs. Hicks remembers seeing the little sapling, randomly sprouting in the grass when she visited the site the day after the accident. Now bushy and tall, the maple is waiting there every Sept. 23, when she returns with flowers and memories.

This year, Royal Canadian Legion chose Mrs. Hicks, a veteran herself, to be Canada’s Silver Cross Mother. On Remembrance Day, the retired sergeant from Trenton, Ont., will lay a wreath at the National War Memorial in Ottawa.

She will kneel there for a moment, she says, and think about her daughter and what she might have accomplished. She’ll think about all the military families, past and present, grieving sons and daughters.

This year, the ceremony will happen less than a month after four soldiers died and dozens were critically injured in a devastating fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta, during a training exercise that also went terribly wrong.

Sapper Short was always challenging herself, her mother recalls. In high school, she was a competitive long-distance runner – despite standing under five feet tall and weighing less than 100 pounds. “She was as strong as she was short,” Mrs. Hicks says.

She had just completed a month of training on the light armoured vehicle at her first posting at CFB Petawawa when she called her mother and Brian Hicks, her stepfather, in Halifax. She was excited that she was about to drive the vehicle for the first time.

“You realize this is a very big piece of equipment,” warned Mr. Hicks, at the time a warrant officer in a construction engineering unit. “Yes, yes, Warrant, I’ll be careful,” Sapper Short promised.

She sounded so happy, Mrs. Hicks, 69, recalls. Despite the cautions on their phone call, she was saving her worry for when her daughter soon deployed to either Afghanistan or Bosnia.

Wearing a uniform came with risks, as Mrs. Hicks well knew. She grew up hearing about her three uncles who fought in the Second World War. Her father was a military firefighter, often posted overseas. By the age of 11, Mrs. Hicks had walked among the crosses at Vimy Ridge and stood on the beach at Dieppe. During one posting, her family lived in Lamorteau, a Belgian village near the French border, in a house still pockmarked with bullet holes from the Nazi invasion.

In 1989, she travelled from her home in Moose Jaw, Sask., to sign up at the recruiting office in Regina – a five-foot-tall, 30-year-old mother with four school-aged children. She wanted to serve her country.

“I’m very, very proud to be Canadian,” she says. “When you come home, you realize we take everything for granted. And we shouldn’t.”

At boot camp, the much-younger recruits nicknamed her “Mom.” She helped them sew labels on their uniforms, and traded ironing for boot polishing. When she woke every morning, sore and tired, she’d tell herself: “Shut up. You wanted this. Go to work.”

She was assigned to logistics, co-ordinating supplies. When she was deployed to the Persian Gulf, and her then-husband objected, she arrived for training at CFB Petawawa a single mother. By the time she retired in 2017, she’d also served two missions to Afghanistan.

When Sapper Short announced, a year after graduating high school that she wanted to enlist as well, her mother and stepfather made certain she was serious.

And when she decided to become a combat engineer – a front-line role responsible for building and demolishing roads and bridges to move troops forward and hold the enemy back – they were candid about the difficulties she could face, including resentment from male soldiers who might assume she wasn’t strong enough. Mr. Hicks warned her that, as the smallest person in her crew, she’d likely be sent into the tightest spots and might spend a lot of time standing up to her neck in cold water.

Her mother recalls the defiant reply: “Oh, for God’s sake. I brought the form home for you guys to look at, but this is what I want to do.”

Nothing is guaranteed once you put on the uniform, Mrs. Hicks says. “When you sign on the dotted line, that’s your life for your country.”

Still, you don’t expect a grim-faced padre to arrive at your house when your child is still on Canadian soil. paragraphs: Every year, Virginia Hicks places red roses in the branches of a lonely maple tree growing on the Mattawa Plains at CFB Petawawa in Ontario.

The tree marks the place where her daughter, 22-year-old Private Mariebeth Short, died in 2002 during a training exercise while serving as a sapper in the 2 Combat Engineer Regiment. Mrs. Hicks remembers seeing the little sapling, randomly sprouting in the grass when she visited the site the day after the accident. Now bushy and tall, the maple is waiting there every Sept. 23, when she returns with flowers and memories.

This year, Royal Canadian Legion chose Mrs. Hicks, a veteran herself, to be Canada’s Silver Cross Mother. On Remembrance Day, the retired sergeant from Trenton, Ont., will lay a wreath at the National War Memorial in Ottawa.

She will kneel there for a moment, she says, and think about her daughter and what she might have accomplished. She’ll think about all the military families, past and present, grieving sons and daughters.

This year, the ceremony will happen less than a month after four soldiers died and dozens were critically injured in a devastating fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta, during a training exercise that also went terribly wrong.

Sapper Short was always challenging herself, her mother recalls. In high school, she was a competitive long-distance runner – despite standing under five feet tall and weighing less than 100 pounds. “She was as strong as she was short,” Mrs. Hicks says.

She had just completed a month of training on the light armoured vehicle at her first posting at CFB Petawawa when she called her mother and Brian Hicks, her stepfather, in Halifax. She was excited that she was about to drive the vehicle for the first time.
“You realize this is a very big piece of equipment,” warned Mr. Hicks, at the time a warrant officer in a construction engineering unit. “Yes, yes, Warrant, I’ll be careful,” Sapper Short promised.
She sounded so happy, Mrs. Hicks, 69, recalls. Despite the cautions on their phone call, she was saving her worry for when her daughter soon deployed to either Afghanistan or Bosnia.

Wearing a uniform came with risks, as Mrs. Hicks well knew. She grew up hearing about her three uncles who fought in the Second World War. Her father was a military firefighter, often posted overseas. By the age of 11, Mrs. Hicks had walked among the crosses at Vimy Ridge and stood on the beach at Dieppe. During one posting, her family lived in Lamorteau, a Belgian village near the French border, in a house still pockmarked with bullet holes from the Nazi invasion.

In 1989, she travelled from her home in Moose Jaw, Sask., to sign up at the recruiting office in Regina – a five-foot-tall, 30-year-old mother with four school-aged children. She wanted to serve her country.
“I’m very, very proud to be Canadian,” she says. “When you come home, you realize we take everything for granted. And we shouldn’t.”

At boot camp, the much-younger recruits nicknamed her “Mom.” She helped them sew labels on their uniforms, and traded ironing for boot polishing. When she woke every morning, sore and tired, she’d tell herself: “Shut up. You wanted this. Go to work.”

She was assigned to logistics, co-ordinating supplies. When she was deployed to the Persian Gulf, and her then-husband objected, she arrived for training at CFB Petawawa a single mother. By the time she retired in 2017, she’d also served two missions to Afghanistan.
When Sapper Short announced, a year after graduating high school that she wanted to enlist as well, her mother and stepfather made certain she was serious.

And when she decided to become a combat engineer – a front-line role responsible for building and demolishing roads and bridges to move troops forward and hold the enemy back – they were candid about the difficulties she could face, including resentment from male soldiers who might assume she wasn’t strong enough. Mr. Hicks warned her that, as the smallest person in her crew, she’d likely be sent into the tightest spots and might spend a lot of time standing up to her neck in cold water.
Her mother recalls the defiant reply: “Oh, for God’s sake. I brought the form home for you guys to look at, but this is what I want to do.”
Nothing is guaranteed once you put on the uniform, Mrs. Hicks says. “When you sign on the dotted line, that’s your life for your country.”

Still, you don’t expect a grim-faced padre to arrive at your house when your child is still on Canadian soil. The chaplain delivered the news in the Hicks living room while Mrs. Hicks cursed and screamed and called him a liar. And then he organized plane tickets for the next-day trip to CFB Petawawa.

In the field by the maple sapling, Mrs. Hicks learned that her daughter had passed the wheel of the light armoured vehicle to a crew member. She was standing with her head above the gunner’s hatch when a front tire hit the groove of an old slip trench, Mrs. Hicks says. The wheel assembly broke off, and the vehicle rolled over twice.

In the scramble to pull her back inside, Sapper Short’s gear became tangled. She was declared dead at the scene. The investigation report Mrs. Hicks received 18 months later concluded, she says, that a substandard weld in the new vehicle caused the accident.

This September, Mrs. Hicks and her husband once again made the three-hour drive to Petawawa. The base is part of the couple’s own history: they met here, 35 years ago. Now they come to place the roses – two at the memorial that bears Sapper Short’s name and picture, and 10 in the tree – to make sure her story is remembered.

A few weeks after the accident, Mrs. Hicks received a video in the mail. It was filmed the year before, when Sapper Short was part of a group testing new bomb suits. The video shows her laughing with her fellow soldiers, concentrating on a math task. “You see the life she had,” Mrs. Hicks says. They watch it every year, before they leave for the Petawawa, so the memory of her daughter smiling carries her through the day.

stories.title: Why Stephen Harper refused to take a call from Paul McCartney: from Harper's new book
stories.summary: In excerpts from his new memoir, former prime minister Stephen Harper shares stories of Paul McCartney and Yo-Yo Ma.
stories.author: Stephen J. Harper
stories.content:
From 2006 to 2015, Canada had a prime minister who offered few public insights about his inner life. Not even Stephen Harper’s family (wife Laureen, daughter Rachel and son Ben) were much on display. However, he had his passions. In these excerpts from his new memoir “Here for Canada: Memoirs of the 22nd Prime Minister,” Harper recounts three moments where the piano-playing PM’s interest in music came to the fore.

Sir Paul McCartney

In 2008, when Paul McCartney was touring in North America, he had a concert in Quebec City to celebrate its 400th anniversary. During that time, he had appeared on television with his then-wife Heather Mills attacking the Canadian seal hunt — a fashionable cause for celebrities at that time. But this annual harvest had worked hard to adopt more humane killing mea­sures over the decades, and my Government strongly supported it as a critical industry in parts of Atlantic and Northern Canada, especially among the Inuit. Frankly, I was fed up with affluent celebrities looking to burnish their social activism credentials at the expense of these Canadian workers.

So when Ray Novak came into my office one day saying he had, of all people, Paul McCartney on the line and that he wanted to talk with me, I asked him what it was regarding. “I think it’s about the seal hunt,” Ray said. “Well, then, tell him I won’t take the call,” was my immediate response. Stunned, Ray asked, “Really? Are you serious?” “Yeah, just tell him I’m not taking the call,” I responded.

Ray went back to his office and delivered the message, making me, I suspect, the first person since Decca Records refused to sign the Beatles in 1962 not to take a call from Paul McCartney. I felt terrible about it, not just because I am a huge Beatles fan but also because, as a McCartney watcher, I could see that this out-of-character, abrasive activism was the product of a doomed marriage.

All that said, it was not a hard decision. As prime minister, I took seri­ously my foremost duty to represent the interests of the Canadian people. On this matter, I was defending those interests, and the views of a foreign celebrity were irrelevant. Besides, I have always been careful about my relationships with celebrities. Given the publicity-seeking nature of their careers, such associations can be a dangerous thing.

However, my eventual 2013 meeting with McCartney in Ottawa did have an ulterior motive. It had been facilitated by representatives of the Canadian music industry as part of their efforts to influence the government on copyright policy. As we were, in fact, examining the issue of expiring copyrights on 1960s music, this was pertinent. McCartney’s office had been clear that he wished to raise “issues related to the music business” with me. We had indicated that I would listen but make no commitments.

I met Sir Paul about a half-hour before he went on stage. He was cordial in introducing himself, but instead of bringing up anything about the music business, he started asking me about my trip to Lac-Mégantic and if I could share some of the things I had seen and witnessed on the ground.

From his demeanour, it was clear that the event had shaken him. He paid careful attention as I spoke and at the end asked, “Is there anything I can do?” I responded that I would be going back to Lac-Mégantic, prob­ably several times in the near future for funerals and memorials, and I would certainly pass on his condolences. McCartney never did raise the business issues.

After our meeting, Sir Paul proceeded to put on a magnificent show. He played for three hours. At seventy-one years old, he took no breaks, although his much younger bandmates did … It was wonderful to see McCartney doing what he clearly loved as if he were still a teenager.

Two weeks later, when his tour took him to Quebec City, Sir Paul paid to bring a thousand fans from Lac-Mégantic to the concert. Further, he offered free concert tickets for all those willing to go to Lac-Mégantic to help with the recovery. Only sometime later did I receive a short letter from him on the copyright issues.

As a politician, I have a sufficiently cynical side about the things that people say. However, in this case, Sir Paul showed how genuine his sym­pathies for the people of Lac-Mégantic were. He did not have to do what he did. For me, it was refreshing to meet somebody you admire for some­thing and find them to be worthy of that admiration in other areas of their life as well.

Beatle for a Day

When I was in London in 2009 for the G20 meeting, my family joined me. They did not come on many of these trips, but every so often they would, depending mostly on the school year calendar. The timing of the summit was only four weeks prior to my fiftieth birthday, and it turned out they had set up a surprise for me.

Knowing all too well my lifelong love of the Beatles, Laureen suggested we all go to Abbey Road and take that iconic shot from the album cover of the same name with the four of us crossing the road. “Why not?” I said. “I mean, people are doing that all the time there, so it should not seem too abnormal.” Right? Wrong. Being prime minister meant that security insisted on clearing the intersection. It was a little embarrassing, but it did get us a better photo. Ben took his shoes off, so he really got into the vibe.

With the picture taken, and us standing in front of the studio, Laureen said, “Why don’t you go knock on the door and see if anyone’s there?” “I’m not just going to start knocking on their door for no reason,” I told her. At that, she revealed that she had arranged a full studio tour, and they were expecting me …

Our hosts took us through the facility. They demonstrated the use of the best modern recording equipment. They also shared a few stories. When someone in our group tried to use their cellphone but discovered there was no connection in the place, which seemed a little odd, our host laughed and said, “I can tell you that last week Keith Richards was here recording some­thing. I’m not making this up,” he said. “He was running down the hall yelling, ‘I can’t get no cell reception!’”

As I have said, being PM does come with some very good perks. Well, this was right up there with the best of them. When the official tour was over, they took me to the famous Studio 2, where the Beatles did almost all their recording. Our hosts pulled out all the various pianos and keyboards that the members of the Beatles had used for composing and performing — some of these instruments had the ivory almost worn off the keys — and let me try out the pianos and keyboards. This fanatic was in heaven!

With a Little Help From His Friends

The pressure to take (my) revived interest in playing music to another level came from none other than Laureen. Like many prime ministers’ spouses, she involved herself in a number of charitable and non-profit activi­ties. In this capacity, she had become honorary chair of the annual gala at the National Arts Centre. Five weeks before the event, out of the blue, she said, “I think you should play at the gala.”

I assumed she was joking, or maybe just thinking out loud. “What are you talking about?” I asked, stunned at the suggestion. “You should get up on stage with your band and do a number,” she said. Still rather taken aback, the best I could come up with was, “Are you kidding me?” She was not. “You’re actually pretty decent, and you can do it.” But she was as insistent as I was hesitant, adding the hard to dismiss, “Please do this for me …”

A few days later, I brought the band over and ran the idea by them. Called Herringbone, they were a Celtic-rock group used to playing in front of live audiences in Ottawa and on the road. However, this would be their biggest gig to date, with orders of magnitude greater attention than they were used to. Yet they were keen on the idea.

The next question was, “What would we play?” Naturally, this being me, Beatles tunes came to the fore. The guys suggested relatively easy numbers, to play it safe. They first proposed “Eight Days a Week,” which I could do, although it is not one of my favourite Beatles songs. We ended up settling on, “With a Little Help From My Friends,” which was perfect for all kinds of reasons. In preparation, we worked up to two or three practices a week to tighten up the band, finding time later in the evenings …

On the evening of the performance, October 3, 2009, it would have been an understatement to say that I was nervous. While I was routinely in front of crowds, I had not performed musically before strangers in more than thirty years …

We sneaked into the National Arts Centre early that Saturday for an onstage rehearsal. Besides me, there was Richard Linke on guitar, Andre Van Schyndel on bass, Phil Nolan on drums, and Colin McSweeney, who acted as our “manager.” Colin also sang with us occasionally, but not on that night. When we got there, Colin told us, “We have a surprise for you. Yo-Yo Ma is going to sit in with your group.” Apparently, he had been at our sound check, heard us, and wanted to play.

Having worked to really nail this tune as a group, my first reaction was, “Does he know the song?” McSweeney stopped me short, saying, “Prime Minister, cut it with the artistic temperament. It’s Yo-Yo Ma, for crying out loud. He’ll learn quick.” It did not hurt when later Yo-Yo came run­ning up to me to introduce himself saying, “I’m Yo-Yo Ma. Are you Paul McCartney?”

When I got on the stage that night, there were a range of reactions, but mainly bewilderment. What was the prime minister doing on the National Arts Centre stage? Was he going to give a speech? In the middle of the con­cert? However, as we launched into the song , it became obvious I was there to play, and the crowd got into it too. They did get a laugh at me singing “I just need someone to love,” which, admittedly, did not quite fit my image. In the end, the performance was very well received, with a long-standing ovation to top it off. Yo-Yo stood out in obviously having a lot of fun … A little help from my friends, as the song says.

So when Ray Novak came into my office one day saying he had, of all people, Paul McCartney on the line and that he wanted to talk with me, I asked him what it was regarding. “I think it’s about the seal hunt,” Ray said. “Well, then, tell him I won’t take the call,” was my immediate response. Stunned, Ray asked, “Really? Are you serious?” “Yeah, just tell him I’m not taking the call,” I responded.

Ray went back to his office and delivered the message, making me, I suspect, the first person since Decca Records refused to sign the Beatles in 1962 not to take a call from Paul McCartney. I felt terrible about it, not just because I am a huge Beatles fan but also because, as a McCartney watcher, I could see that this out-of-character, abrasive activism was the product of a doomed marriage.

All that said, it was not a hard decision. As prime minister, I took seri­ously my foremost duty to represent the interests of the Canadian people. On this matter, I was defending those interests, and the views of a foreign celebrity were irrelevant. Besides, I have always been careful about my relationships with celebrities. Given the publicity-seeking nature of their careers, such associations can be a dangerous thing.

However, my eventual 2013 meeting with McCartney in Ottawa did have an ulterior motive. It had been facilitated by representatives of the Canadian music industry as part of their efforts to influence the government on copyright policy. As we were, in fact, examining the issue of expiring copyrights on 1960s music, this was pertinent. McCartney’s office had been clear that he wished to raise “issues related to the music business” with me. We had indicated that I would listen but make no commitments.

I met Sir Paul about a half-hour before he went on stage. He was cordial in introducing himself, but instead of bringing up anything about the music business, he started asking me about my trip to Lac-Mégantic and if I could share some of the things I had seen and witnessed on the ground.

From his demeanour, it was clear that the event had shaken him. He paid careful attention as I spoke and at the end asked, “Is there anything I can do?” I responded that I would be going back to Lac-Mégantic, prob­ably several times in the near future for funerals and memorials, and I would certainly pass on his condolences. McCartney never did raise the business issues.

After our meeting, Sir Paul proceeded to put on a magnificent show. He played for three hours. At seventy-one years old, he took no breaks, although his much younger bandmates did … It was wonderful to see McCartney doing what he clearly loved as if he were still a teenager.

Two weeks later, when his tour took him to Quebec City, Sir Paul paid to bring a thousand fans from Lac-Mégantic to the concert. Further, he offered free concert tickets for all those willing to go to Lac-Mégantic to help with the recovery. Only sometime later did I receive a short letter from him on the copyright issues.

As a politician, I have a sufficiently cynical side about the things that people say. However, in this case, Sir Paul showed how genuine his sym­pathies for the people of Lac-Mégantic were. He did not have to do what he did. For me, it was refreshing to meet somebody you admire for some­thing and find them to be worthy of that admiration in other areas of their life as well.
Beatle for a Day

When I was in London in 2009 for the G20 meeting, my family joined me. They did not come on many of these trips, but every so often they would, depending mostly on the school year calendar. The timing of the summit was only four weeks prior to my fiftieth birthday, and it turned out they had set up a surprise for me.

Knowing all too well my lifelong love of the Beatles, Laureen suggested we all go to Abbey Road and take that iconic shot from the album cover of the same name with the four of us crossing the road. “Why not?” I said. “I mean, people are doing that all the time there, so it should not seem too abnormal.” Right? Wrong. Being prime minister meant that security insisted on clearing the intersection. It was a little embarrassing, but it did get us a better photo. Ben took his shoes off, so he really got into the vibe.

With the picture taken, and us standing in front of the studio, Laureen said, “Why don’t you go knock on the door and see if anyone’s there?” “I’m not just going to start knocking on their door for no reason,” I told her. At that, she revealed that she had arranged a full studio tour, and they were expecting me …

Our hosts took us through the facility. They demonstrated the use of the best modern recording equipment. They also shared a few stories. When someone in our group tried to use their cellphone but discovered there was no connection in the place, which seemed a little odd, our host laughed and said, “I can tell you that last week Keith Richards was here recording some­thing. I’m not making this up,” he said. “He was running down the hall yelling, ‘I can’t get no cell reception!’”

As I have said, being PM does come with some very good perks. Well, this was right up there with the best of them. When the official tour was over, they took me to the famous Studio 2, where the Beatles did almost all their recording. Our hosts pulled out all the various pianos and keyboards that the members of the Beatles had used for composing and performing — some of these instruments had the ivory almost worn off the keys — and let me try out the pianos and keyboards. This fanatic was in heaven!
With a Little Help From His Friends

The pressure to take (my) revived interest in playing music to another level came from none other than Laureen. Like many prime ministers’ spouses, she involved herself in a number of charitable and non-profit activi­ties. In this capacity, she had become honorary chair of the annual gala at the National Arts Centre. Five weeks before the event, out of the blue, she said, “I think you should play at the gala.”

I assumed she was joking, or maybe just thinking out loud. “What are you talking about?” I asked, stunned at the suggestion. “You should get up on stage with your band and do a number,” she said. Still rather taken aback, the best I could come up with was, “Are you kidding me?” She was not. “You’re actually pretty decent, and you can do it.” But she was as insistent as I was hesitant, adding the hard to dismiss, “Please do this for me …”

A few days later, I brought the band over and ran the idea by them. Called Herringbone, they were a Celtic-rock group used to playing in front of live audiences in Ottawa and on the road. However, this would be their biggest gig to date, with orders of magnitude greater attention than they were used to. Yet they were keen on the idea.

The next question was, “What would we play?” Naturally, this being me, Beatles tunes came to the fore. The guys suggested relatively easy numbers, to play it safe. They first proposed “Eight Days a Week,” which I could do, although it is not one of my favourite Beatles songs. We ended up settling on, “With a Little Help From My Friends,” which was perfect for all kinds of reasons. In preparation, we worked up to two or three practices a week to tighten up the band, finding time later in the evenings …

On the evening of the performance, October 3, 2009, it would have been an understatement to say that I was nervous. While I was routinely in front of crowds, I had not performed musically before strangers in more than thirty years …

We sneaked into the National Arts Centre early that Saturday for an onstage rehearsal. Besides me, there was Richard Linke on guitar, Andre Van Schyndel on bass, Phil Nolan on drums, and Colin McSweeney, who acted as our “manager.” Colin also sang with us occasionally, but not on that night. When we got there, Colin told us, “We have a surprise for you. Yo-Yo Ma is going to sit in with your group.” Apparently, he had been at our sound check, heard us, and wanted to play.

Having worked to really nail this tune as a group, my first reaction was, “Does he know the song?” McSweeney stopped me short, saying, “Prime Minister, cut it with the artistic temperament. It’s Yo-Yo Ma, for crying out loud. He’ll learn quick.” It did not hurt when later Yo-Yo came run­ning up to me to introduce himself saying, “I’m Yo-Yo Ma. Are you Paul McCartney?”

When I got on the stage that night, there were a range of reactions, but mainly bewilderment. What was the prime minister doing on the National Arts Centre stage? Was he going to give a speech? In the middle of the con­cert? However, as we launched into the song , it became obvious I was there to play, and the crowd got into it too. They did get a laugh at me singing “I just need someone to love,” which, admittedly, did not quite fit my image. In the end, the performance was very well received, with a long-standing ovation to top it off. Yo-Yo stood out in obviously having a lot of fun … A little help from my friends, as the song says.

content_blocks.text: From 2006 to 2015, Canada had a prime minister who offered few public insights about his inner life. In these excerpts from his new memoir “Here for Canada: Memoirs of the 22nd Prime Minister,” Harper recounts three moments where the piano-playing PM’s interest in music came to the fore.

stories.title: ‘Definitely not fun’: Manitoba farmer wants better mitigation measures, after losing roughly 500 acres to flooding
stories.summary: Heavy rains and severe storms flooded nearly half, around 800 hectares, of his farmland near Clandeboye, Man., approximately 41 kilometres north of Winnipeg.
stories.author: Alex Karpa
stories.content:
Clandeboye, Man. – This year’s farming season has been nothing short of challenging for Curtis McRae.

Heavy rains and severe storms flooded nearly half, around 800 hectares, of his farmland near Clandeboye, Man., approximately 41 kilometres north of Winnipeg.

Although he managed to salvage some of the damaged crops, he still lost approximately 200 hectares, making this one of the most challenging years he’s faced as a farmer.

“It’s right up there, absolutely,” he said. “Definitely not fun.”

A two-day storm in June dumped dozens, and in some areas, hundreds of millimetres of rain.

About 255 millimetres of rain fell in Stonewall, Man., and surrounding communities in just a few hours, flooding fields and causing significant crop losses.

Some of McRae’s fields had nearly a metre of water, which remained there for several weeks.

He says the heavy rains and flooding in June left his farmland completely saturated all season long. With excess moisture still a concern, he worries the effects of this year’s flooding could carry over into next year’s crops.

“I can’t leave acres like this unattended, but they’re still wet from the June 9 storm,” he said.

“The soil is still very, very saturated. Any little precipitation we get doesn’t seem to go anywhere. It just sits.”

McRae isn’t alone. Farmers across Manitoba are facing similar conditions as they try to salvage what they can from a difficult growing season, while hoping to get relief through crop insurance.

“Certainly, a lot of claims probably are in the process right now with some of those hard-hit areas,” said Jill Verwey, who is a producer and president of the Keystone Agricultural Producers (KAP) in Manitoba.

“So, a lot of producers will be struggling with below-average yields.”

The latest crop report from the Manitoba government shows some producers are still working to complete the harvest.

Ninety-four per cent of the harvest is complete province-wide, but with more precipitation in the forecast, Verwey is concerned some producers May not have the conditions needed to prepare their fields for next year.

“We saw that back when we had the flood of 2011 and 2014, and those hangovers lasted two to three years,” she said.

“A lot of guys are just choosing to park their equipment and have a good start for 2027.”

“We’ve had summers where November brings us some really favourable weather, so we still have that to look forward to in the next little while and hoping that producers have the ability to get the work done if they can,” she said.

For McRae, recovering from this season’s damage is only part of the challenge.

He’s calling on local and provincial governments to provide better mitigation measures, including improved culvert maintenance and clearer drainage channels.

He says better drainage and flood mitigation will be key to protecting his land and preventing future losses.

“A lot of work to be done, a lot of repairs on infrastructure that has been broken for years, and hopefully it gets repaired,” he said.

“This is long-term, society making decisions and not knowing what the repercussions are. When you restrict farmers, you restrict your food, and guess what? Your food price goes up.”

stories.title: Union says over half of P.E.I.’s Parks Canada workforce in limbo over potential job losses
stories.summary: More than half of Prince Edward Island’s Parks Canada workers are waiting to find out if they’ll lose their jobs as the agency prepares to slash hundreds of positions across the country.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Brackley Beach, P.E.I. – More than half of Prince Edward Island’s Parks Canada workers are waiting to find out if they’ll lose their jobs as the agency prepares to slash hundreds of positions across the country.

The federal agency told CTV News 53 of its 98 employees on the Island received notices in October their roles might be affected. It’s not clear yet how many will be laid off.

“These are real people with real lives and real concerns about what’s coming for their future,” said Chris Di Liberatore, a regional executive vice-president with the Public Service Alliance of Canada.

The cuts weren’t a complete surprise, he said, given the Liberal government’s comprehensive expenditure review aimed at reducing the size of the federal public service. But the number of employees facing an uncertain future caught the union off guard, as did the timing.

Some members received the news on the last day of their working season, something Di Liberatore called “quite disrespectful”.

Nationally, Parks Canada plans to eliminate the equivalent of around 500 full-time positions and has notified nearly 3,000 employees their jobs are impacted by the adjustment.

In a statement to CTV News, the agency said the positions might no longer be required due to a lack of work, discontinued functions, or they’re being moved somewhere employees don’t want to relocate to.

But their roles have become especially important as Ottawa encourages more people to visit national parks, Di Liberatore said.

Parks Canada visits rise

Amid trade tensions with the U.S., th e federal government introduced the Canada Strong Pass, offering free admission to parks and historic sites to promote domestic tourism and make exploring closer to home more affordable.

It worked. Visits to Parks Canada sites rose 13 per cent in the summer of 2025 compared with the same period in 2023, prompting the government to renew the program this year.

The numbers from 2026 are not yet available, but on P.E.I., the agency anticipated significantly more traffic, warning that parking lots at popular beaches could fill before 11 a.m.

The Canada Strong Pass ended Sept. 7. The employees now in a precarious position are the same people who greeted visitors, maintained trails and campsites, and responded when hikers got lost, Di Liberatore said. Their responsibilities also extend to search and rescue.

“To reduce these members at a time when we’re asking more and more people to come and visit our beautiful parks just makes absolutely no sense,” he said.

He wonders whether artificial intelligence played a role in the decision, and whether Ottawa believes automated kiosks could replace some employees.

Parks Canada’s own 2026–27 departmental plan calls for expanding AI and automation, including virtual assistants, to improve efficiency. But the agency hasn’t linked those initiatives to the workforce reductions.

Di Liberatore urged the government to reconsider the cuts, arguing that an economic downturn is a time to strengthen public services, not reduce them.

stories.title: Can a car cut in front of me at a red light to make a right turn?
stories.summary: If you want to turn right at a red light and you’re stuck behind a stopped car, you’ll have to wait, full stop, experts say
stories.author: Jason Tchir
stories.content:
I was recently stopped at the stop line at a red light waiting to go straight. There were cars behind me wanting to turn right, but it’s a narrow road, and there wasn’t enough room to the right of my car for them to squeeze by. Two drivers passed me on the left in the left-turn lane, drove into the intersection in front of my car, and then made the right turn. Is this legal? – Jeremy, Mississauga

If you want to turn right at a red light and you’re stuck behind a stopped car, you’ll have to wait, full stop.

“If there’s a vehicle legitimately stopped ahead of you, waiting to proceed straight, that doesn’t give you permission to invent another lane to get around it,” Angelo DiCicco, chief executive officer of the Ontario Safety League, a not-for-profit focusing on driver education, said in an email. “Sometimes the safest and most courteous thing you can do is simply wait your turn.”

When a car is stopped at the stop line and you’re waiting behind it to make a right turn, you can’t legally pass it on the left and go into the intersection around it, police said.

That move could break multiple laws. Depending on the circumstances, you could face charges including making an unsafe lane change , making an improper right turn , running a red light and, possibly, careless driving , Constable Amanda Steenson, a spokeswoman for Peel Regional Police, said in an email.

Break every rule?

In Ontario, the law states that you have to turn right from the right-hand lane or far right side of the road – so you can’t turn right from the left lane.

And while you can cross the stop line on a red light to make a legal right turn, you can’t cross it to go straight or, usually , to turn left.

The rules vary by province, but we couldn’t find any that let you swing around a stopped car and cut in front of it to turn right.

“When I hear about manoeuvres like this, I find myself shaking my head,” DiCicco said. “Sometimes I wonder whether drivers have forgotten the rules of the road or whether they’ve simply decided those rules shouldn’t apply when they’re in a hurry.”

The move isn’t only illegal – it’s dangerous, he said.

”The driver waiting at the red light has no reason to anticipate another vehicle suddenly cutting across their path," DiCicco said. “Add a pedestrian or cyclist to that situation and the consequences could be serious.”

Right to turn right?

But when there’s no right-turn lane, can you pass the stopped car on the right to make your right turn?

Generally, you can as long as there’s enough room in the lane to do it safely. But you can’t move into the bike lane or otherwise create a lane “where none exists,” Steenson said.

If the squeeze is so tight that you’re not sure you’ll clear the car you’re passing, stay where you are and wait for the light to turn green, said Sean Shapiro, a road safety consultant and former Toronto traffic cop.

”If you have to make unsafe moves [to get somewhere on time] … you were late when you left the house," Shapiro said.

And if you’re heading straight and are about to stop at a red light, should you be moving as far left as you can to give right-turning cars space to get past you?

Only if you can do it safely, DiCicco said.

“If there’s adequate space within the lane, leaving room for someone to turn right can help traffic flow,” he said. “But there is no general obligation to cross the centre line or compromise your own safety to accommodate an impatient driver [behind you].”

stories.title: $10,000 for rooftop solar? No, thanks. Why homeowners are rejecting an Ontario rebate that ‘doesn’t make any sense’
stories.summary: Ontario’s Home Renovation Savings Program requires homeowners to choose between $10,000 and the ability to sell power back to the grid.
stories.author: Marco Chown Oved
stories.content:
When Peter Leiss decided to get solar panels and a battery installed, he could have put in the paperwork to qualify for a $10,000 rebate from the provincial government.

That’s because Leiss says the rebate comes with a catch that makes it impossible to accept.

“If we had taken the rebate, all the excess power that’s produced goes into the grid and you don’t get any credit for it,” he said. “It doesn’t make any sense.”

Leiss isn’t alone. Despite shelling out tens of thousands of dollars to generate clean electricity, most people installing solar panels and batteries are turning down the government subsidy, the Star has learned.

“For probably 95 percent of our clients, it’s actually not a good option,” said Beau Badore, owner of solar panel installer Heliotechnik. Homeowners, he says, will pay off their system more quickly by turning down the rebate and getting paid for their excess power.

Restricting the rebate in such a way not only discourages folks from installing solar, experts say, it also hampers society from reaping the benefits: cheaper electricity and lower bills.

Ontario is the only province that makes people choose. Other provinces not only allow homeowners to receive a government rebate and sell their solar generation into the grid, many require it in order to capture the full value of the technology.

Solar power has been hailed as the cheapest form of energy in history , is being installed on rooftops around the world and can push power into the grid to alleviate bottlenecks, avoiding costly grid upgrades and keeping power bills down for everyone. In the U.K. and Australia, solar is flooding grids with so much energy, it has led to utilities offering free electricity . But experts say these benefits only work if those with solar panels are incentivized to share their power.

“This is a huge missed opportunity,” said Badore.

Internal Ministry of Energy documents, obtained via access-to-information legislation, show that the province was warned that taking away the ability of solar panel owners to sell their power would “significantly limit the uptake of residential solar PV systems.”

An internal analysis found that payback periods for solar installations would almost double without “net metering,” which pays households for exported energy with credits that offset their power bills.

The payback period for a non-exporting solar system would be between 30 and 40 years or “higher than its economic useful life of 25 years,” the government analysis found. Net metering reduces that payback time to 23-29 years, while allowing system owners to both take the rebate and export energy reduces the payback time to 17-22 years.

Adding a battery makes the rule even worse for homeowners, pushing up the payback period to 73 to 100+ years with the rebate alone. If homeowners could claim both incentives, that would come down to 26 years, the analysis found.

These lengthy payback timelines mean installers might suggest their customers not sign up for the rebate “since (net metering) offers a better business case,” the analysis found.

The ministry still ended up recommending the either/or approach, because it considered allowing both to be “double-dipping of government incentives,” the documents state.

“Our government launched the largest energy efficiency framework in Canadian history, offering rebates of up to $10,000 for households through the Home Renovation Savings Program to lower costs while supporting the adoption of (small scale generation like rooftop solar),” said Noah Mawji, spokesperson for Ontario Energy Minister Stephen Lecce, in an emailed statement.

The province has taken steps to reduce barriers and support smarter planning for these small power producers, “as part of an all-of-the-above approach to meet rising energy demand while keeping electricity affordable,” he wrote.

Combining the rebate and net metering was allowed in Ontario until 2024, when the Home Efficiency Rebate+ program abruptly stopped taking new applications . Since January 2025, when the new Home Renovation Savings Program was launched, only 339 people have received a solar panel and/or battery rebate, said the Independent Electricity System Operator, which helps administer the program. There is no tally of the total number of solar projects installed province-wide during that time, but installers estimate only one in 10 customers opt for the rebate.

The problem with the program

Forcing people to choose transforms a policy that ostensibly encourages rooftop solar into one that limits its adoption and stifles its benefits, experts say.

“If you are not net metered, your system is only useful for you,” said Phil McKay, senior director of member programs at the Canadian Renewable Energy Association. “So you get a smaller system and there’s less power for your neighbours.”

Typically, rooftop solar produces electricity that’s used first to power the home or business it sits upon. Excess power can be fed into a battery and stored for later — when the sun goes down — or exported into the grid for others to use.

This benefits the owner by reducing their power bill, but it also benefits the grid both right away and over the long term.

Because solar panels produce most during midday hours, they reduce the need for expensive natural gas generation at peak times, reducing the cost of electricity for everyone. Over the long term, rooftop solar can save the power system from having to make costly upgrades to transmission lines because it produces power where it is used, replacing the power that would otherwise have to be delivered over long distances.

A recent study by Clean Energy Canada quantified those savings and found that rooftop solar, combined with smart thermostats, home batteries and two-way EV chargers, could save utilities and ratepayers $3.5 billion over the next 20 years.

The case for solar in Ontario

As Canada and the world grapple with a massive increase in electricity demand to power data centres, EVs and heat pumps, “we’re going to need any power we can get,” said McKay.

Ontario projects that electricity demand could increase by 90 per cent over the next 25 years.

“Solar is rock solid. You pay once for the device, and you’ve got a fixed price for the energy it will be producing for 20 plus years,” he said. “And, of course, you’ve got all the climate benefits of displacing fossil fuel generation.”

The City of Toronto has set a goal to get 50 per cent of its power from renewable or low-carbon sources by 2030 and 75 per cent by 2050. “Solar will play a significant role,” the city states in its TransformTO strategy.

Australia and the U.K. have more solar and wind power than their electrical systems know what to

Currently, Ontario’s installed grid capacity is six per cent solar, the vast majority of which is small-scale and rooftop.

This trails many countries around the world, including relatively cold and rainy ones like the U.K., where solar doesn’t work as well, yet makes up 20 per cent of the grid, according to statistics compiled by Ember , a clean energy think tank. World leaders include China, which has 32 per cent solar, Australia, where 40 per cent of homes have rooftop solar, and Hungary, which has a national grid where solar makes up 49 per cent of all generating capacity.

At a time when wars are driving up the costs of fossil fuels, solar provides long-term reliable power at a stable and predictable price — all without making climate change worse, said Bobby MacCannell, owner of solar installer Brightworks Energy.

“What’s more reliable in life than death, taxes and the sun coming up in the morning?” he said. “Solar is the quickest, cheapest route to generation with minimal maintenance and a long lifespan.”

These benefits are hidden from the public by “artificially low power rates,” he said, referring to the $7 billion the province spends each year to subsidize power bills .

Getting panels onto roofs has been a slow process, according to Toronto Hydro statistics. Since a high of 322 installations in 2018, the city has not been able to keep the pace up, with only 82 rooftop systems installed in the first 9 months of this year. In a city of three million people, only 3,014 rooftops have solar.

Berlin, Germany, which is further north than Toronto and receives less sunlight, has more than 53,000 rooftop solar systems, up from only 15,000 in 2023, according to a local government report .

Toronto’s home solar accelerator project , run by the Atmospheric Fund, helps homeowners navigate the bureaucracy, permitting and jargon by providing a one-stop shop and a concierge from the beginning to the end of solar panel installation.

But early results show that while the program has increased interest, that hasn’t converted into actual panels on roofs. More than 600 people have signed up, but only 30 have gotten quotes and 10 have installed panels this year, said Chris Caners, director of clean electrification at TAF, which funds projects in the GTA and Hamilton area.

“This can’t be so hard that people get frustrated and give up,” he said. “Let’s incentivize uptake, not make the economics worse.”

stories.title: Canada's new high-wage immigration rules offer bonus points to applicants, but experts warn the system is easy to game.
stories.summary: Experts say the new rules can help attract highly skilled migrants, but could also open a back door for others.
stories.author: Nicholas Keung
stories.content:
Priti Sangam advises multinational companies on how to restructure workforces and modernize operations. Her skills are in demand. Yet Canada, her home since 2024, has repeatedly passed her over for permanent residence.

In early October, the HR consultant from India faced another hurdle when she turned 30 and automatically lost five points under the age criteria of Canada’s competitive skilled immigration system, which ranks candidates based on attributes such as language proficiency, education and work experience.

Then came a break. On Oct. 16, Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab announced that candidates in the skilled immigration talent pool would receive up to 150 bonus points if they have at least one year of Canadian work experience — or a job offer — in one of 186 designated “high-wage” occupations .

“It was a relief when I heard the news,” said Sangam. “I love Toronto and I can see our future here. What’s more disappointing is there are people around me with less qualification and less education getting permanent residence because of certain rules, while you are not getting it.”

Sangam stands to gain an extra 40 points, hopefully qualifying for permanent residence before her work permit expires in January.

Experts say the new high-wage rules can help Canada attract and retain highly skilled migrants amid a still volatile immigration system . But the new rules that open a door for Sangam could also open a back door for others. They warn that the system is ripe for manipulation — and the gaming has already begun.

“All you need to do is just hop onto Reddit or go to some Facebook groups and read everyone’s posts,” said Kubeir Kamal, a Toronto-based immigration consultant.

“So many of them are asking, can I change my occupational code? What if my employer is giving me this job offer letter? You can see everybody is trying to figure out how they can circumvent this” for the bonus points.

Priti Sangam, who came to Canada in late 2024 from India, is pictured in Toronto’s financial centre.

For years, Ottawa gave candidates in the immigration talent pool extra points for having a job offer validated through an approved labour market impact assessment by Employment and Social Development Canada. That bonus was removed in March 2025 out of fraud concerns.

“This temporary measure will reduce fraud by removing the incentive to illegally buy or sell labour market impact assessments to improve a candidate’s chances of being selected to come to Canada as a permanent resident,” the Immigration Department stated at the time.

As part of the changes announced in October, the government said high-wage job offers will not be scrutinized by Esdc. The Immigration Department will be solely responsible for verifying whether an offer is genuine.

Not long after the announcement, social media posts emerged showing that people are already talking about ways to embellish work experience and inflate job responsibilities to meet the occupational criteria on the high-wage list.

Immigration consultant Kubeir Kamal said he has seen social media posts discussing how to manipulate the new bonus rules.

Kamal said unscrupulous agents and employers had charged more than $60,000 for bogus job offers, and he expects that market to return.

While some occupations that require specialized education and licensing such as nursing and engineering are harder to fake, he said others such as education counsellors, human resources managers and purchasing managers are more prone to fraud because the required qualifications are more general and experience-based.

The Immigration Department said removing the Hsdc assessment “does not reduce rigour” as the new process takes an “integrated” approach where immigration officers will evaluate the genuineness of the job offer alongside the candidate’s qualifications and the employer’s ability and need to hire.

Officials will continue to verify qualifying job offers and take measures to identify and address potential fraud or misrepresentation, and the changes will ensure consistency while maintaining integrity of the process, it said.

Rattandeep Singh, an immigration consultant in Brampton, said he has recently been approached by a couple of foreign workers, whose employers agreed to give them updated employment letters that would reflect a higher job position than what they actually held.

One person wanted to upgrade his job title from bookkeeper to financial controller in his profile in the immigration talent pool.

“The advice I gave to the client is that everything we put in the immigration system online leaves a digital footprint,” said Singh. “It might improve your score on paper, but it could also raise questions about the credibility of your employment history.”

Applicants caught misrepresenting work experience or submitting fraudulent job offers face not only refusal of their application but a ban from Canada, he noted.

In the past, employers, at a minimum, were required to show no Canadian was available for the job when trying to validate a job offer to a foreign national, but now they only need to say they’re hiring for one of the listed jobs, said Conservative MP Brad Redekopp, who sits on the parliamentary immigration committee.

It has been known for years that unscrupulous employers not only sell job offers, but also exploit unsuspecting foreign workers by paying below-market wages or requiring kickbacks, he added.

Targets will be influenced by the stubborn math of a temporary resident population that’s proven

“You can be assured that shady immigration consultants and employers will find many more ways to game this system,” Redekopp told a recent news conference, calling for lower immigration and further reforms to the “broken” system. “The result will be defrauded employees, (and) some consultants and employers getting rich off this scheme.”

Vance Langford, a Calgary-based immigration lawyer, said the big question now is what extra steps immigration officials are going to take to verify if these high-wage work experience and job offers are genuine, especially when the department has made major workforce reductions amid budget constraints.

He said officials could ask candidates for tax slips, pay stubs, job offer letters, employment agreements, and go as far as demanding evidence of business meetings they have convened, reports they’ve issued, business correspondence, as well as hiring and firing decisions they’ve approved as proof of credentials in a supervisory or managerial role.

“What it really comes down to is when you get the invitation to apply for permanent residence and you submit your evidence, what is (the department) doing to verify that evidence is valid?” said Langford. “I think they need to do more than ever before.”

The Immigration Department said it will update officer training and focus on verifying whether job offers are real and whether candidates are qualified for the job they claim. It will continue monitoring for fraud through existing tools, including risk-based checks, document verification, information sharing with other government agencies and referrals to enforcement when needed.

stories.title: Matthews, Nylander lead Leafs to 4-2 win over struggling Canucks
stories.summary: Auston Matthews collected his team-leading 11th goal of the season as the Toronto Maple Leafs defeated the Vancouver Canucks 4-2 Saturday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Auston Matthews collected his team-leading 11th goal of the season as the Toronto Maple Leafs defeated the Vancouver Canucks 4-2 Saturday to snap a two-game NHL skid.

William Nylander and Teddy Blueger both had a goal and an assist, while Zack MacEwen also scored for Toronto (8-6-2), which wrapped up a four-game road trip with two wins and two losses.

Brock Boeser, ON the power play, and Max Sasson scored for the Canucks (3-12-1) who have one win in their last 13 games.

Canucks goaltender Leevi Merilainen made 24 saves.

Leafs goalie Anthony Stolarz stopped 26 shots and also earned an assist on Blueger’s empty net goal.

Sasson made things interesting early in the third, drawing the Canucks to within a goal by scoring off the rebound of a Brendan Gallagher shot.

Matthews gave the Leafs a 2-1 lead at 3:47 of the second period, beating Merilainen on the short side after a pretty back-and-forth pass with defenceman Darren Raddysh.

McEwen put Toronto up two goals during a scramble at 12:34.

The teams exchanged first-period breakaway goals.

Nylander opening the scoring with the game just 83 seconds old. He scooped up a puck that bounced off Canuck defenceman Jamie Oleksiak’s stick, skated in alone and lifted a backhand past Merilainen.

Boeser tied the game about nine minutes later. With the Canucks on a power play he got behind the Toronto defence, he took a long pass on the fly from defenceman Filip Hronek and beat Stolarz.

Canucks: Merilainen robbed rookie Gavin McKenna on a power play in the first period. Parked at the side of the net McKenna took a cross-ice pass from centre Jack Roslovic but Merilainen got a pad on his shot. … Centre Jacob Quillan, acquired Oct. 15 in a trade from Toronto, was inserted into the lineup after being recalled from Abbotsford of the AHL on Friday to replace Filip Chytil who was placed on injured reserve after reaggravating a shoulder injury in a 3-2 loss at the San Jose Sharks on Thursday. … Centre Elias Pettersson saw a six-game point streak end (2G, 5A).

Leafs: Roslovic earned an assist on Matthews goal, extending his points streak to six games (3G, 7A). … Toronto has just 28 wins in 86 games playing in Vancouver. … Former Canuck defenceman Chris Tanev and forward Dakota Joshua returned to the lineup. Joshua was playing his first game of the season after suffering a core injury late last year. Tanev missed nine games with an upper-body injury sustained Oct. 10 at Colorado. … Blueger, who spent three seasons with the Canucks, played in his first game in Vancouver since signing a two-year contract with the Leafs.

McEwan was awarded Toronto’s third goal but replays seemed to show defenceman Morgan Rielly’s shot went off Merilainen’s glove, hit defenceman Luke Schenn on the back, then rolled into the net.

Matthews has points in six of his last seven games (5G, 5A).

Maple Leafs: Host the Utah Mammoth on Tuesday.

Canucks: Host the Anaheim Ducks on Tuesday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 31, 2026.
