stories.title: Endangered North Atlantic right whale entangled in gear spotted in the Gulf of St. Lawrence
stories.summary: If located again, officials plan to tag the gear with a satellite tracker and try to disentangle the animal
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Federal officials say they’ve spotted a critically endangered North Atlantic right whale entangled in gear in the Gulf of St. Lawrence.

Fisheries and Oceans Canada says a surveillance flight spotted the whale on Oct. 21 between New Brunswick’s Acadian Peninsula, P.E.I. and Quebec’s Îles-de-la-Madeleine.

The department says the entanglement in the Bradelle Bank region wasn’t spotted until scientists and experts reviewed footage this week.

If the whale is located again, officials plan to tag the gear with a satellite tracker and try to disentangle the animal.

The department says it has not been able to identify the whale or the type of gear it’s caught in.

The entire North Atlantic right whale population is estimated at just 384 animals.

stories.title: Lions roar back, oust Roughriders from playoffs
stories.summary: Nathan Rourke passed for 366 yards and the B.C. Lions came all the way back to beat the Saskatchewan Roughriders 33-26 in the CFL's West Division semifinal on Saturday.
stories.author: Gemma Karstens-Smith
stories.content:
Vancouver – Nathan Rourke passed for 366 yards and the B.C. Lions came all the way back to beat the Saskatchewan Roughriders 33-26 in the CFL’s West Division semifinal on Saturday.

The Lions fell behind 17-3 midway through the second quarter before rallying in the third and taking over the game in the fourth.

Rourke connected on 21 of his 32 attempts, including a pair of touchdown passes to Jevon Cottoy and another to Stanley Berryhill III.

Kicker Sean Whyte added four field goals — his longest was a 48-yard kick — as B.C. eliminated the reigning Grey Cup champions from the playoffs.

Trevor Harris logged 255 passing yards with one interception for the Riders, who bounced the Lions from the post-season in both 2024 and 2025.

Saskatchewan QB Tommy Stevens rushed for a four-yard major in the second quarter and Brett Lauther made six field goals, including two from 55 yards.

The Lions will travel to face the Edmonton Elks (13-5) in the West Division final on Nov. 7.

The East semifinal earlier on Saturday saw the Winnipeg Blue Bombers stun the Argonauts with a 25-22 comeback victory in Toronto.

The Bombers will take on the host Montreal Alouettes in the East final on Nov. 7. Calgary hosts the Grey Cup on Nov. 15.

The Riders and Lions came in with identical 10-8 regular-season records, but B.C. earned the right to host by winning the season head-to-head series 2-1.

The two sides traded field goals over the first quarter on Saturday, starting with Lauther booting the ball 55 yards through the uprights to open the scoring for Saskatchewan.

Each side followed with a 26-yard field goal to make it 6-3 at the end of the opening frame before Lauther scored on another 55-yard kick early in the second quarter.

A turnover on downs proved costly for the Lions midway through the second.

The Riders got the ball at their own 49-yard line and worked it up the field over six plays, capping the drive with Stevens muscling his way into the end zone. Saskatchewan opted to go for the two-point convert and Harris made good, connecting with Samuel Emilus to give his side a 17-3 advantage.

B.C. replied with Rourke scrambling out of the pocket and lobbing a rainbow up the field to an unmarked Berryhill, who dashed over the goal line for the major. Whyte’s kick for the extra point was good, cutting the Lions’ deficit to 17-10.

The home side’s other chance to put up points came late in the first half after defensive back Robert Carter Jr. made a flying grab to pick off Harris’ pass to Emilus midfield, but B.C. couldn’t turn the interception into points.

Keon Hatcher Sr. had a prime opportunity to add points with just seconds left on the clock, too, but dropped the ball inches from the goal line and the Lions settled for a 48-yard field goal that made it 17-13 for Saskatchewan heading into the locker rooms.

Another field goal from Lauther — this time a 34-yard strike — boosted the Riders’ lead to 20-13 early in the third quarter.

B.C. was quick to answer.

Rourke sent a quick dish to Cottoy, who split the Saskatchewan defence and sprinted up the field for a 70-yard touchdown. Whyte added the extra point to level the score at 20-20.

The Riders added another three points with Lauther’s fifth field goal of the night before Rourke found an open Cottoy steps from the end zone.

The Canadian receiver reeled in the pass and took a few strides in for his second major of the game, putting the Lions up 27-23 at the end of the quarter.

The teams once again traded field goals across the fourth and final frame.

Whyte’s 34-yard kick boosted B.C.’s lead to seven points midway through the quarter and the veteran kicker added another from 24 yards with three minutes left on the game clock.

The Riders clawed three points back in the final two minutes of the game when Lauther made a 44-yard field goal to put the score at 33-26.

Whyte’s 49-yard attempt field goal fell short with 49 seconds to go, giving Saskatchewan’s offence one last chance, but the green and white stalled out at B.C.’s 34-yard line.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 31, 2026.

stories.title: Toronto cyclists protest bike lane removals as province wraps up first phase of effort
stories.summary: Demonstrators showed up on the lawns of Queen’s Park with decorative bikes and signs on their backs, hoping to change Doug Ford’s mind
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen
stories.content:
Dozens of cycling advocates and protesters spent their Halloween decrying Ontario’s contentious decision to continue removing bike lanes across Toronto.

The protest comes at the heels of Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria’s announcement on Friday that bike lanes along Bloor Street West in Etobicoke have been officially removed.

“We heard from communities, and that’s why we moved forward on this first part of removal on Bloor Street West,” Sarkaria told CP24 Breakfast, who cited low usage of the lanes as reason for removing them. “The remainder of which will come subsequent in the next construction cycle.”

The 1.2-kilometre stretch of bike lanes has caused tension between construction crews and cycling advocates who showed up to protest the removal in recent weeks , leading to the arrest of four people largely related to mischief.

That unease between protesters and police has caused a sense of unease among the cycling community, said Michael Longfield, executive director of Cycle Toronto, a member-supported charity. But the mood on Saturday afternoon was full of optimism.

“The premier might have taken one kilometre from us but folks are ready to defend the remaining 18,” he said.

Protesters showed up on the lawns of Queen’s Park with decorative bikes and signs on their backs, such as “Bike Lanes Save Lives.” Others showed up in their Halloween costumes while volunteers passed out candy and chocolates.

A skeleton wore a bright orange shirt while mounted on a bike nearby.

Longfield believes there’s still time to change Ford’s mind about the bike lanes, despite the provincial government’s insistence that removing the lanes around sections of Bloor Street, Yonge Street and Avenue Road and around Queen’s Park would ease traffic congestion.

Al-anizi, a longtime Toronto resident, said bike lanes are an issue for people with disabilities and mobility issues, especially for those who don’t feel seen by drivers on the road or have accessible transit modes.

“Drivers can’t see sometimes. I am pretty low and [they] can get aggressive,” he said. “For me, it’s very important to be in a dedicated space for bike lanes. It makes me feel a lot more safe.”

stories.title: Four dead after single-vehicle crash in Puslinch, Ont., police say
stories.summary: Remaining two people inside the vehicle were brought to hospital with life-threatening injuries
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Provincial police in Ontario say four people have died after a single-vehicle crash in Puslinch, Ont.

They say in a news release that police, firefighters and paramedics were sent to the scene on Watson Road South, between Maltby Road East and Wellington Road 34, around 1:35 a.m. on Saturday.

Police say six people were inside the vehicle and four of them were declared dead at the scene.

They say two others were brought to hospital with life-threatening injures.

Police are asking anyone who May have relevant information, dash-camera footage or surveillance footage from the area around the time of the crash to contact the Wellington County OPP office.

The detachment declined to provide any identifying information about those involved in the crash, including their ages, citing a continuing investigation, but said in a statement that a news conference will be held on Sunday.

stories.title: Canada echoes U.S. ‘mass casualty event’ warning for Moscow
stories.summary: The U.S. Embassy in Moscow has issued an alert regarding a threat of a “mass casualty event” at the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve in Moscow.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
The U.S. Embassy in Moscow has issued an alert regarding a threat of a “mass casualty event” at the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve in Moscow.

In a statement posted to its website, the embassy said the threat is “credible” and advised everyone to avoid the area and avoid crowds.

Global Affairs Canada (GAC) repeated the alert Saturday, warning against all travel to Russia as a result of the conflict with Ukraine and “risk of terrorism.”

“If you are in Russia, you should consider leaving the country by commercial means. If you remain in Russia, maintain a low profile. Canadians holding Russian citizenship May be subject to call-up for mandatory military service,” the GAC said.

The armed conflict with Ukraine has resulted in military activity within Russia’s borders. The GAC said attacks are most common near the Russian-Ukrainian border, notably in Bryansk, Kursk and Belgorod oblasts, and in the Black Sea region including Rostov Oblast and Krasnodar Krai.

Government buildings, schools, cultural venues, places of worship, airports and tourist attractions have also become the target of terrorist activity, they said.

Evacuees from Russia-occupied Oleshky crossed into Ukrainian-held territory Saturday as part of a major rescue operation carried out under a ceasefire in the southern Kherson region began early Tuesday.

stories.title: Protesters stage ‘die-in’ against pesticides in Montreal
stories.summary: Participants lay on the ground in front of the Guy-Favreau complex as others dressed in white coveralls moved through the crowd pretending to spray pesticides.
stories.author: Coralie Laplante
stories.content:
Demonstrators are rallying against pesticides with a “die-in” protest in Montreal.

Attendees, many in costume for Halloween, sought to drive home the message that “pesticides kill” with an event in front of Health Canada’s offices downtown on Saturday.

Participants lay on the ground in front of the Guy-Favreau complex as others dressed in white coveralls moved through the crowd pretending to spray pesticides.

Children were invited to trace chalk outlines of pretend victims, while organizers placed a cardboard coffin and tombstones in front of the building, each bearing the names of various diseases.

Thibault Rehn, executive director of Vigilance OGM, which helped organize the protest, says it was calling out “historic setbacks” by the federal government, particularly legislation passed in June that allows cabinet to override Health Canada and authorize the use of banned pesticides.

Similar protests in the province on Saturday were planned for Quebec City, Sherbrooke, Saguenay, Terrebonne, Blainville and Val-David as well as Ottawa.

stories.title: 4 dead, 2 injured following collision near Guelph, Ont.
stories.summary: Wellington OPP, fire and paramedic services responded to reports of the collision on Watson Road South between Maltby Road East and Wellington Road 34.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Four people are dead and two others are in hospital following a single-vehicle collision early Saturday morning south of Guelph, Ont.

Wellington OPP, fire and paramedic services responded to reports of the collision on Watson Road South between Maltby Road East and Wellington Road 34 shortly after 1:30 a.m. Saturday.

Details of the collision are sparse but police said six people were inside the vehicle at the time.

Four people were pronounced dead at the scene and the other two were transported to hospital with life-threatening injuries, police said.

As the investigation continues, Watson Road South remains closed.

stories.title: ‘Li’l Monster Walk and Roll’: Hundreds attend community Halloween event
stories.summary: Main Street in Belmont, Ont. was packed with kids and adults in costume Saturday morning.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Main Street in Belmont, Ont. was packed with kids and adults in costume Saturday morning.

“This is the annual ‘Li’l Monster Walk and Roll’ and many of the businesses in Belmont participate and hand out candy to the kids,” said Tracy Vink-Taylor, past president of the Belmont Swans. “This started a number of years ago and was run by a different organization called The Hub. When that disbanded, the Belmont Swans took it over. It’s a great way to let the little young ones that maybe can’t go out trick or treating late tonight still get a chance to experience and go out.”

The Swans hand out a map to all the participating businesses for the event which begins at 10 a.m. and runs until noon.

“The Belmont Swans are the ones that put it on and they do an awesome job every year,” said Jared Chestnut, owner of Country Pizza. “We’ve got perfect weather for it, so it’s really cool. It’s great for the local businesses and almost everybody participates in town. We used to get like 50 to 100 kids when we used to participate, now I got enough candy for like 500 [kids] and I’m probably going to run out.”

Among those walking down the street was Jose Pineda, a local resident dressed as Batman.

“It’s a great event that this town runs and we absolutely love it,” said Pineda. “We have some family from outside of town also visiting. It’s a great town and I love this event that they’re able to pull off.”

At the Swans’ information table, they had gone through 200 juice boxes in the first 30 minutes.

“It’s just grows and grows every year,’ said Vink-Taylor. “I think last year we had about 360 participants. I’ve talked to a lot of people where they’re from and we’re drawing from London, Dorchester, Harrietsville, and Belmont. We just we love doing events to support the Belmont community.”

stories.title: Canada’s biggest party cities according to Uber; see where London, Ont. ranks
stories.summary: For the second year in a row, London, Ont. has been named Canada’s biggest party city according to Uber’s Nightlife Index.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
For the second year in a row, London, Ont. has been named Canada’s biggest party city according to Uber’s Nightlife Index.

‘Using aggregated, anonymized insights from Uber and Uber Eats, this year’s Index tracks the past year’s late-night trends, from the cities that party the hardest to Canadians’ favourite morning-after cures,’ Uber said in a statement.

Top 10 Partying Cities in Canada

Kitchener-Waterloo

This news comes at an appropriate time, as Uber also declared Halloween to be the second biggest party night.

Halloween isn’t just one of Canada’s biggest nights out. Canadians also stay out later, with Uber data showing that celebrations extend further into the night than usual.

Biggest Nights Out: Top 5 Partying Nights Across Canada

Holiday Party Season

St. Patrick’s Day Weekend

“Whether it’s Halloween, a holiday party, or a night out with friends, Canadians should be able to enjoy themselves and get home safely,” said Laura Miller, head of Public Policy and Communications at Uber Canada. “Having more transportation options makes it easier to plan ahead and leave the car at home. That’s why Uber is proud to work with Madd Canada to encourage safe choices and help prevent impaired driving.”

stories.title: Family launches renewed search for man who went missing on Quebec ski trip
stories.summary: Montreal - The family of an Ontario man is renewing efforts to find him with a search in Mont-Tremblant this weekend, 21 months after he went missing on a ski trip in Quebec.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - The family of an Ontario man is making a deeper technological dive to fish out clues on what happened to their son, who went missing in Mont-Tremblant, Que., 21 months ago.

Metadata linked to Liam Toman’s phone the night the 22-year-old disappeared from the Laurentian ski resort might offer fresh information on his whereabouts, said his father Chris Toman.

“We’ve been mining that data with a digital forensic expert in conjunction with the SQ,” Chris said, referring to the Sûreté du Québec, the provincial police force.

He said cell tower pings, router data and other signal metrics could further help searchers home in on where in the sprawling mountain resort or beyond to look.

“Those are kernels, or data packs, that we have requested — some production orders through the SQ to retain that from some of the third-party apps — and that allows us to narrow that search area a little tighter,” the father said.

The renewed digital effort comes alongside another ground search for Liam over the weekend by volunteer teams and trained search-and-rescue dog units.

Toman vanished at around 3 a.m. on Feb. 2, 2025, after leaving a bar in the ski village north of Montreal following a night of dinner and drinks with friends on a ski trip in Mont-Tremblant.

Liam’s parents and stepmother have said he was last seen on camera walking back toward his hotel, but there was no footage of him heading inside. A last call and text were sent from his phone at around 3:15 a.m., with no activity on his bank account, social media or phone since.

“If you see the video surveillance, he’s walking with purpose,” said Chris. “He’s not lost ... he’s not stumbling. He’s obviously had something to drink, which they all do, but he’s got his faculties, he’s multitasking ... phoning, texting.”

His disappearance prompted provincial police to carry out searches by land, helicopter and in nearby bodies of water.

After his wallet was found in a nearby parking lot seven weeks later, police dispatched more helicopters, dogs, ATVs and searchers on horseback while volunteer groups combed the surrounding hills.

Authorities have not ruled out criminal activity.

The family has also launched a blue wristband campaign, inviting visitors to wear the bracelets as a sign of support and to help keep attention on Liam’s disappearance.

A $50,000 reward remains in place for information leading to his location, as his parents continue to work with police, forensics analysts and the community to find their son.

This weekend marked the 18th or 19th visit Liam’s parents had made to the resort since February 2025, they said.

Since then, new lighting and upgrades to cameras — more now record footage rather than offering only a livestream, for example — have given a small measure of solace to Chris as well as Kathleen Toman, Liam’s mother, and Lara Toman, his stepmother.

“Now if this happened, he would be on camera,” said Lara. “They’ve really taken those steps,” she said, while noting that a security audit at the resort is ongoing.

“If anything positive comes out of this, it’s that we don’t want another family to go through this,” said Chris, who lives in Whitby, Ont.

The couple described Liam as kind, quick-witted and risk-averse.

“He was an old, sensitive soul. He loved his outdoors. He made friends easily, he was very sociable,” Chris said of his son, who graduated from Niagara College with an electronics technician diploma in 2024.

Chris recalled teaching his boy to swim, skate and grill a good steak, while Lara remembers Liam’s close relationship with her own son.

“His stepbrother, Ryan, they were best buds,” she said. “When they were younger, they were sort of like this little team, whether it was football or dodgeball.

“I was lucky to be a bonus mom,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 31, 2026.

stories.title: Sunny skies on Halloween: Here’s your trick-or-treating forecast
stories.summary: There is nothing spooky about your weather this Halloween.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
There is nothing spooky about your weather this Halloween.

A sunny Saturday with a high of 15 degrees leads the way for near perfect trick-or-treating conditions tonight.

We’ll see a few clouds pop up this evening, but you might need to bundle up before candy gathering as a low of plus 4 degrees is expected.

Kicking off the new month Sunday with mainly sunny conditions again and a high of 17 degrees.

Cloudy but above seasonal temperatures stick around for the following workweek.

Here’s a look at the rest of the forecast

Saturday: Mainly sunny. Fog patches dissipating early this morning. High 15. UV index 3 or moderate.

Saturday night: A few clouds. Fog patches developing after midnight. Low plus 4.

Sunday: Mainly sunny. Fog patches dissipating in the morning. Wind becoming south 20 km/h near noon. High 17. UV index 3 or moderate.

Monday: Cloudy. High 18.

Tuesday: Cloudy. High 19.

Wednesday: Cloudy. High 18.

stories.title: ‘Right off the wall’: Zurich couple fill lawn with huge Halloween display
stories.summary: Martin Isaac and Barb Jeffrey have turned their Zurich, Ont. lawn into a Halloween extravaganza.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Martin Isaac and Barb Jeffrey have turned their Zurich, Ont. lawn into a Halloween extravaganza.

“We’ve been doing it for the past six years. Myself and Barbara, and we collect for the Blessings Food Bank each year. It is a labor of love, for sure. And the kids just love it,” said Isaac.

The displays, that range from creepy clowns to a gigantic Frankenstein, take about two weeks to put up on their property on John Street.

“Just a love of Halloween, I guess. Like I said, the kids just love it. We have tours from the Catholic schools. Even the old age home comes down to see it. It’s a riot,” said Isaac.

The couple adds something new each year, trying to up the ante each Halloween.

“We have about 85 displays set up. We have probably 35 more in the top of the garage. We buy from a couple different stores. And then anything that doesn’t move, I build. It’s just a lot of fun,” he added.

Why do they do it? Well it goes back to a life long love for Oct. 31 st .

“We’ve just always loved Halloween. Always. Always. So when we moved to Zurich, it was all cutesy here, and then we kind of got it right off the wall, I guess,” said Isaac.

stories.title: Toronto police identify one suspect in Bridle Path home invasion
stories.summary: The 23-year-old man was injured by gunfire and remains at large despite police interacting with him in hospital, investigators say
stories.author: Colin Freeze
stories.content:
Toronto police have identified one of the three suspects in Thursday’s Bridle Path home invasion as a 23-year-old suffering from an accidental gunshot wound, who remains at large despite officers interacting with him in hospital in the aftermath of the high-profile attack.

“The suspect was discharged from the hospital early in the afternoon yesterday,” Inspector Kristy Smith of the Toronto Police Hold-Up Squad told reporters Saturday morning.

She said police had approached the man while he was getting treatment for his wounds, apparently accidentally inflicted by a fellow attacker, earlier this week.

But detectives working the case did not initially have evidence to arrest him. Insp. Smith said police developed that evidence Friday evening, hours after the suspect’s release from hospital.

The suspect has been identified as Daijohn Richards, 23, of Toronto. Described as armed and dangerous, he now is wanted by authorities on four counts of discharge firearm with intent to wound, four counts of robbery with a firearm, three counts of aggravated assault and other charges.

The other suspects have not been identified and police would not say whether Mr. Richards has faced prior criminal charges.

The rare home invasion in Toronto’s exclusive Bridle Path neighbourhood left three members of a family of four suffering from gunshot wounds. Some family members remain hospitalized, Insp. Smith said on Saturday.

“Some of them have been released from hospital and some of them are still in hospital,” she said. “What I can say is that, through the grace of God, they are in life-altering condition and not life-threatening condition.”

Toronto police said earlier this week that early Thursday, three masked gunmen stormed into the Hyde Park Circle house through its back entrance while a family of four was sleeping inside. Around 3 a.m., a confrontation erupted as the assailants demanded valuables and fired guns. Authorities have said that each suspect was armed with a handgun.

One of the victims was David Morton, a 75-year-old real-estate executive. He released a statement on Friday thanking the public for its support but said the violence traumatized his family.

“What should have been the safety and security of our own home became a terrifying and life-threatening experience,” Mr. Morton, chief executive of the MAC Group, said in the statement. “It is difficult to put into words the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home.”

The family is asking for privacy. The other victims include his wife, Doriana Zohil-Morton, 64, and the couple’s two adult daughters, Cristina and Maggie Zohil-Morton.

Police also now believe that one of the alleged attackers – Mr. Richards – was accidentally hit by bullets fired by a fellow assailant.

“We have identified one of the suspects involved in this home invasion shooting and we are asking for the public’s collective assistance in locating him,” Insp. Smith told reporters at a police station Saturday morning.

“We believe that he was accidentally shot by one of the other suspects in this home invasion,” she said. “Richards was shot in the right shoulder and as such he May be experiencing pain and discomfort in that area and people May see him favouring that side of his body.”

She said police are accusing him of striking fear into a family inside their home and subjecting them to “an appalling level of violence, all for the purpose of acquiring property.”

Insp. Smith said police in Toronto have protocols for speaking with people who arrive at the city’s emergency rooms seeking treatment for gunshot wounds. However, legal restrictions limit what authorities can do before detaining or questioning anyone.

“The suspect walked in on his own to the hospital. There is an agreement in place that we get notified when gunshot victims show up at a hospital. So acting on that protocol, police were called,” Insp. Smith said.

Officers conducted “a number of interactions” with the suspect prior to him being released from the hospital, she said, but they could not immediately form reasonable grounds for an arrest.

Investigators developed evidence Friday night, with help from forensic scientists and police detective work, she said. But by then, the suspect had left the hospital.

stories.title: Bridle Path home invasion suspect, 23, identified
stories.summary: Daijohn Richards, 23, of Toronto is accused of 'appalling violence' on Toronto family of four
stories.author: Anisha Dhiman
stories.content:
One of three suspects accused of violently attacking a family in Toronto’s posh Bridle Path neighbourhood has been identified as 23-year-old Daijohn Richards of Toronto.

A warrant has been issued for Richards’ arrest, while two other suspects remain unidentified. The police service released an image of Richards and noted that he May show signs of a shoulder injury.

“Investigators believe Daijohn Richards was accidentally shot by one of the other suspects during the struggle inside the victims’ home,” Toronto Police Service said in a press release.

The authorities were notified after Richards was at the hospital for treatment for a gunshot wound. He was released from the hospital on Friday. He wasn’t arrested at the hospital because “we don’t just go off of suspicion,” Toronto Police Service Insp. Kristy Smith told a Saturday morning press conference.

A family asleep in their home on Thursday were subjected to “appalling violence all for the purpose of acquiring property,” Smith said. The attack, at approximately 3:40 a.m., in the Post Road and Hyde Park Circle area, left four members of the family injured: Toronto CEO David Morton, 75, his wife Doriana Zohil-Morton, 64, and two daughters Maggie and Cristina.

Morton, 75, released a statement on Friday confirming traumatic details of the attack and expressing concern about “the increasing violence associated with home invasions and the safety of families throughout Toronto.”

Richards is wanted on Canada Wide Warrant and faces four counts of Discharge Firearm with Intent to Wound, four counts of Robbery with a Firearm, three counts of Aggravated Assault, Break and Enter Commit/Dwelling-House, Possess Prohibited Device, and Disguise with Intent.

No further description is available of the two other suspects. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Hold Up Squad at 416-808-7350 or 33 Division at 416-808-3300.

Here’s David Morton’s full statement following violent home invasion in the Bridle Path

Toronto, Ontario – October 30, 2026 David Morton, CEO of MAC Group, issued the following statement on behalf of his family following the horrific and violent home invasion at their residence on Hyde Park Circle in Toronto’s prestigious Bridle Path neighbourhood during the early morning hours of October 29:

What should have been the safety and security of our own home became a terrifying and life-threatening experience.

Three masked individuals forcibly entered our residence, armed with handguns and a hammer. During the attack, three members of our family were shot and are currently recovering in hospital. All four members of our family were also attacked with a hammer, leaving everyone injured and requiring emergency medical attention.

It is difficult to put into words the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home.

Our family is extremely grateful to the Toronto Police Service, emergency responders, paramedics, doctors, nurses and hospital staff who responded so quickly and have been instrumental in providing care and assistance.

We also want to thank our extended family, friends, neighbours and the many people who have reached out with messages of concern, prayers and support. The outpouring of kindness has meant a great deal to us during this incredibly difficult time.

While we are focused on recovery and supporting one another as a family, we are also deeply concerned about the increasing violence associated with home invasions and the safety of families throughout Toronto.

No family should ever have to experience this. People should be able to sleep peacefully in their homes without fear of armed individuals breaking in and threatening their lives.

We sincerely hope that the individuals responsible will be identified, apprehended and brought to justice. We encourage anyone with information that May assist the Toronto Police investigation to come forward.

At this time, we respectfully ask the media and public to allow our family the privacy and time needed to recover from this traumatic experience.

We are a family, and our priority is getting through this together.

The motive of the incident is still known, but it is 'impossible to ignore the context that we're in, of rising radicalization and rising antisemitism'

stories.title: ‘Associate’ EU membership for Canada not a ‘short-term’ project: expert
stories.summary: Carney said Ottawa and Brussels are working toward the "deepest possible partnership short of accession" that would see Canada become the EU's "first associate member."
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has laid out a timeline that would see Canada sign an agreement on a new partnership with the European Union in the next seven months, if all goes well.

Carney said Friday that Ottawa and Brussels are working toward the “deepest possible partnership short of accession” that would see Canada become “the European Union’s first associate member.”

He said in the coming months, the two sides will meet to “determine the full substance, scale and scope of this new form of membership.”

Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, championed the idea of associate membership in Strasbourg, France, last month. On Friday, she said she believes in building a partnership with Canada that “comes closer to membership than anything we’ve done before.”

Even though top EU officials are enthusiastic about closer ties with Canada, the talks won’t necessarily be a walk in the park. The European Union is far from politically united on the idea.

Achim Hurrelmann, co-director of the Centre for European Studies at Carleton University, said it could prove difficult to negotiate that status, especially in the short term.

“I’m not sure if a status with that name can be established for Canada any time soon,” he said.

“It seems that von der Leyen and Carney have decided to just press ahead with the use of this term and use the momentum that’s there on both sides for Canada-EU relations to make this a reality. But in the EU, that often can be quite difficult because once all of the member states get involved — we saw that in negotiating the summit declaration — then the entity is able to move only very slowly.”

Carney and EU officials met for a summit in Montreal on Thursday and Friday, where they agreed on a joint statement promoting what they called a “Canada-EU Alliance for the Future.”

The joint statement commits the two sides to working to “define by the 2027 EU-Canada Summit the concept of an ever-closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself.”

The 27-member bloc ultimately opted against including the term “associate member” in the joint statement. The phrase has seen some pushback from countries like Germany, which see it as a stepping-stone to permanent membership for countries like Ukraine.

EU debates are always complicated matters. In the coming months, major European countries will go to the polls for elections that could shake up the nature of those talks.

Spain’s general election is set for Nov. 29 and the French presidential elections go ahead in April. Poland will also go to the polls next year for parliamentary elections on Nov. 11.

Hurrelmann said the main challenge remains a lack of clarity on the term “associate membership” in Europe. He noted the language used by Canadian officials this week has been the “strongest embrace of associate membership” he’s seen by the Canadian side.

“It’s very clear that even if it’s associate membership … that it’s not just some kind of occasional political agreement, but something quite fundamental,” he said. “So I think the member states definitely will insist on their right to be heard on that.”

Carney said Friday he will meet with the EU presidents periodically to track progress, and Canada’s federal cabinet will meet in March with European cabinets in Canada.

The prime minister will then attend the European Council meetings in June, where the aim is to conclude negotiations. EU members would have to approve the resulting agreement, which would be put to a vote in the House of Commons as well.

Carney has said he’s not married to the term “associate member” and is more concerned about the outcomes from closer economic and defence ties.

“There is a case for an enhanced partnership status,” said Hurrelmann. “Maybe finding a different label will eventually do the trick, but that remains to be seen.”

The joint statement signed Friday calls for more industrial collaboration and supply chain integration and cites various joint projects. There are plans to create a new Canada-EU business council.

The Prime Minister’s Office said Canada and the European Union will in the coming months take their first steps toward a new transatlantic data cable and study how to increase liquefied natural gas exports to the European market.

— With files from Dylan Robertson
paragraphs: Prime Minister Mark Carney has laid out a timeline that would see Canada sign an agreement on a new partnership with the European Union in the next seven months, if all goes well.
Carney said Friday that Ottawa and Brussels are working toward the “deepest possible partnership short of accession” that would see Canada become “the European Union’s first associate member.”
He said in the coming months, the two sides will meet to “determine the full substance, scale and scope of this new form of membership.”

Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, championed the idea of associate membership in Strasbourg, France, last month. On Friday, she said she believes in building a partnership with Canada that “comes closer to membership than anything we’ve done before.”
Even though top EU officials are enthusiastic about closer ties with Canada, the talks won’t necessarily be a walk in the park. The European Union is far from politically united on the idea.
Achim Hurrelmann, co-director of the Centre for European Studies at Carleton University, said it could prove difficult to negotiate that status, especially in the short term.
“I’m not sure if a status with that name can be established for Canada any time soon,” he said.

“It seems that von der Leyen and Carney have decided to just press ahead with the use of this term and use the momentum that’s there on both sides for Canada-EU relations to make this a reality. But in the EU, that often can be quite difficult because once all of the member states get involved — we saw that in negotiating the summit declaration — then the entity is able to move only very slowly.”
Carney and EU officials met for a summit in Montreal on Thursday and Friday, where they agreed on a joint statement promoting what they called a “Canada-EU Alliance for the Future.”
The joint statement commits the two sides to working to “define by the 2027 EU-Canada Summit the concept of an ever-closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself.”

The 27-member bloc ultimately opted against including the term “associate member” in the joint statement. The phrase has seen some pushback from countries like Germany, which see it as a stepping-stone to permanent membership for countries like Ukraine.
EU debates are always complicated matters. In the coming months, major European countries will go to the polls for elections that could shake up the nature of those talks.
Spain’s general election is set for Nov. 29 and the French presidential elections go ahead in April. Poland will also go to the polls next year for parliamentary elections on Nov. 11.

Hurrelmann said the main challenge remains a lack of clarity on the term “associate membership” in Europe. He noted the language used by Canadian officials this week has been the “strongest embrace of associate membership” he’s seen by the Canadian side.

“It’s very clear that even if it’s associate membership … that it’s not just some kind of occasional political agreement, but something quite fundamental,” he said. “So I think the member states definitely will insist on their right to be heard on that.”
Carney said Friday he will meet with the EU presidents periodically to track progress, and Canada’s federal cabinet will meet in March with European cabinets in Canada.

The prime minister will then attend the European Council meetings in June, where the aim is to conclude negotiations. EU members would have to approve the resulting agreement, which would be put to a vote in the House of Commons as well.
Carney has said he’s not married to the term “associate member” and is more concerned about the outcomes from closer economic and defence ties.
“There is a case for an enhanced partnership status,” said Hurrelmann. “Maybe finding a different label will eventually do the trick, but that remains to be seen.”
The joint statement signed Friday calls for more industrial collaboration and supply chain integration and cites various joint projects. There are plans to create a new Canada-EU business council.

The Prime Minister’s Office said Canada and the European Union will in the coming months take their first steps toward a new transatlantic data cable and study how to increase liquefied natural gas exports to the European market.
— With files from Dylan Robertson

stories.title: Suspect identified by police in violent Toronto home invasion
stories.summary: Toronto - Toronto police have identified one suspect in the home invasion attack in the affluent Bridle Path neighbourhood on Thursday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Toronto police have identified one of three suspects in Thursday’s home invasion attack on a family of four in the affluent Bridle Path neighbourhood.

They say Daijohn Richards, 23, suffered an accidental gunshot wound during the attack by one of the other suspects and May be favouring his right shoulder.

In a news conference Saturday morning, Toronto police Insp. Kristy Smith said officers responded to reports of a person with a gunshot wound at St. Joseph’s Health Centre shortly after the home invasion.

Richards was discharged from the hospital early Thursday morning, but investigators only identified him as a suspect and made the connection later.

Officers did not arrest Richards while he was in the hospital receiving treatment, said Smith.

“What we need to make sure is that we ironclad a conviction and we don’t just go off of suspicion,” she said.

A Canada-wide warrant has been issued for his arrest.

Police say they are still looking for the two other suspects. All suspects are still considered armed and dangerous.

Police first received reports of three people shot inside a residence in the Post Road and Hyde Park Circle at around 3:40 a.m. Thursday.

Investigators say a family of four were attacked when masked intruders forced their way into the home through the rear door, armed with guns and a hammer.

The suspects then fled in a dark-coloured SUV. No other description of the vehicle has been provided.

In a statement released Friday, David Morton, CEO of MAC Group, said his family is focused on recovery and supporting one another following the attack.

“No family should ever have to experience this. People should be able to sleep peacefully in their homes without fear of armed individuals breaking in and threatening their lives,” he wrote in his statement.

Some members of the family have been released from the hospital, said Smith.

“Through the grace of God, they are in life-altering condition and not life-threatening condition.”

Police are asking anyone with information about Richards or the other suspects to come forward.

The two male suspects are described as wearing dark clothing and are estimated to be about 20 years old.

So far this year, 119 home invasions have been reported in Toronto, up more than 32 per cent from the same time last year, police said in an email Friday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 31, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. An earlier version, based on police information at Saturday’s news conference, said Richards was discharged from the hospital early Friday afternoon. Police have corrected that to say he was discharged from hospital late Thursday morning.

stories.title: Suspect wanted in violent home invasion was also shot: Toronto police
stories.summary: In an update Saturday morning, Insp. Kristy Smith said police have issued a Canada-wide arrest warrant for 23-year-old Daijohn Richards.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Toronto police have identified one of three suspects in a violent home invasion that took place Thursday in the city’s affluent Bridle Path neighbourhood.

In an update Saturday morning, Insp. Kristy Smith said police have issued a Canada-wide arrest warrant for 23-year-old Daijohn Richards.

Police were first called to a home on Hyde Park Circle, near Bayview and Lawrence avenues, around 3:45 a.m. Oct. 29.

Three masked men allegedly forced their way into the home and eventually confronted the family inside, police said. The men were armed with handguns and one had a hammer.

Four people were inside the home at the time: a man, his wife and their two adult children.

All four people were taken to hospital. Three of the victims were shot and two were struck in the head with a hammer, police said.

In an update Saturday, Smith said some have since been released from hospital.

Smith confirmed Richards also took himself to the hospital later that same day with a gunshot wound in the right shoulder.

“We believe that he was accidentally shot by one of the other suspects involved in this home invasion,” she said.

Richards is wanted on four counts of discharge of a firearm with intent to wound, four counts of robbery with a firearm, three counts of aggravated assault, break and enter, possession of a prohibited device and disguise with intent.

Smith said police believe the other two suspects to be in their 20s.

Police said they do not think the incident was targeted.

“We talk about affluence and people wanting things and entering into an area of affluence where there are things that are sought after is what we believe the motive to be at this time,” Smith said.

In a statement released Friday afternoon, David Morton, CEO of Toronto-based real estate company MAC Group, said three of his family members were recovering in hospital following the attack.

“What should have been the safety and security of our own home became a terrifying and life-threatening experience,” Morton wrote.

He said the family is focused on recovery but it becoming more and more concerned with increasing violence associated with home invasions in Toronto.

“No family should ever have to experience this. People should be able to sleep peacefully in their homes without fear of armed individuals breaking in and threatening their lives,” he wrote.

All four victims are expected to survive though police said two have life-altering injuries.

stories.title: London Knights lose in OT to Sudbury, salvage one point
stories.summary: The London Knights were in Sudbury Friday night taking on the Wolves.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The London Knights have to find a way to hold a lead late in the third period.

For the second straight game on a northern road trip, they blew a lead in the final minutes of regulation time.

The Sudbury Wolves Mason Walker scored with 1:37 left in the third period to send the game to overtime, where the Wolves beat London 4-3.

Just one night earlier, the North Bay Battalion scored with one second left in the third period to send their game with London to extra time, but London won that one.

Marcus Nordmark, Thomas Zocco, and Jaxon Cover all scored for London, who remain two points behind Guelph for top spot in the Midwest Division.

The Wolves played the game wearing custom blueberry-patterned Sudbury Blueberry Bulldogs jerseys inspired by the hit Crave/Hulu TV series Shoresy . The jerseys were then auctioned off to support local children’s sports and community programs.

London will wrap up a three game in four days road trip with a matinee in Sault Ste. Marie Sunday.

stories.title: Your trick-or-treating forecast calls for clouds but dry conditions
stories.summary: There is nothing spooky about your weather this Halloween.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
There is nothing spooky about your weather this Halloween.

A sunny Saturday with a high of 15 degrees leads the way for near perfect trick-or-treating conditions tonight.

We’ll see a few clouds pop up this evening, but you might need to bundle up before candy gathering as a low of plus 4 degrees is expected.

Kicking off the new month Sunday with mainly sunny conditions again and a high of 17 degrees.

Cloudy but above seasonal temperatures stick around for the following workweek.

Here’s a look at the rest of the forecast

Saturday: Mainly sunny. Fog patches dissipating early this morning. High 15. UV index 3 or moderate.

Saturday night: A few clouds. Fog patches developing after midnight. Low plus 4.

Sunday: Mainly sunny. Fog patches dissipating in the morning. Wind becoming south 20 km/h near noon. High 17. UV index 3 or moderate.

Monday: Cloudy. High 18.

Tuesday: Cloudy. High 19.

Wednesday: Cloudy. High 18.

stories.title: B.C.’s adoption of permanent daylight time could cause calendar chaos Sunday
stories.summary: Organizations that rely on scheduling software warn staff, patients of potential issues as other regions turn back the clock
stories.author: Marissa Birnie
stories.content:
Missed surgeries, late deliveries and muddled meeting times are among the issues that could arise as a result of British Columbia’s decision to stay permanently on daylight saving time, information technology experts have cautioned.

When much of North America turns clocks back one hour on Sunday, most of B.C. will instead adopt Pacific Time, or PCT, leading organizations that rely on scheduling software to warn employees of potential issues as the province adjusts.

The Vancouver Coastal and Island health authorities have said patients should double check their appointments, as they May have shifted by one hour.

The University of Victoria and University of B.C. have said staff meetings scheduled on or after Sunday could show the wrong time, especially if they were booked before updates to calendar systems.

While major technology companies, including Microsoft and Google, have updated their software to account for B.C.’s new time zone, calendar appointments created before the updates May need to be changed manually.

M3 Sweatt, a retired Microsoft executive, said he expects practical and operational challenges, especially for travellers and businesses working between Washington state and B.C.

“They’ll need to account for the time differences when doing something as simple as moving across the border, scheduling a meeting over the phone, more planning day-to-day items on their calendar,” he said in an e-mail.

“International ferry and train passengers will see differences in schedules and tickets: when travelling by train, a four-hour trip will be a three-hour trip southbound but a five-hour trip northbound.”

Teams and Outlook events May not migrate automatically, and people should double check the times of recurring meetings, he added.

Microsoft released Windows updates that account for the shift, but noted some Microsoft 365 services, such as Outlook and Teams, would require manual time changes.

A statement from Google said calendar events created in certain time zones May appear one hour late on and after Sunday.

The tech giant has asked users to enable software updates since some products, such as Android phones and smartwatches, May still fall back by one hour.

Darren Coleman, CEO of B.C.-based IT firm Coleman Technologies, said he expects calendar issues will be widespread even after Sunday.

“I think it’s a much bigger issue than most people recognize,” he said.

Coleman said meetings created in scheduling software will be stored with the time zone in place when they were created.

“Not only do we have to make sure that the patches are out so that the computer realizes that there’s a new time zone, we still can’t do anything about the calendar invites that have the previous time zone hard-coded into them,” he said.

Coleman said one of his employees commutes from Washington state to B.C., putting him in different time zones at the start and end of his work day.

The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, which manages the codes that allow software to automatically calculate local time, has updated its time zone database to reflect the switch to permanent daylight time in B.C., Alberta, Manitoba and the Northwest Territories.

But while modern systems update their clocks and scheduling software through automatic updates, many older ones can’t do the same, Coleman said.

Door access systems, security cameras and some point-of-sale systems May also be affected, he added.

“Your employees May not be able to get into your office building if the clocks don’t update. The security cameras May be off. They May be missing meetings,” he said.

Luke Bell, reactive service manager for Victoria-based IT service provider Smart Dolphins, said it has been chaotic trying to make sure clients are prepared.

“Some businesses have really old services or software that they use and they don’t have the means to update to new time zones,” he said. “So there will be some friction potentially. We won’t know until the change happens.”

stories.title: Daylight saving time ends Sunday, but these parts of Canada won’t change their clocks
stories.summary: Figuring out the time differences between each province and territory is getting more complicated
stories.author: Gabriela Panza-Beltrandi, National Post
stories.content:
Time zones are getting tricky in Canada.

Millions are winding back their clocks, while others are stopping the clock on time changes for the first time.

More and more provinces and territories are moving to permanent daylight saving time, and, for some, it’s the first fall they won’t be falling back.

But it’s a confusing mess of whose clocks are changing Nov. 1, and whose aren’t. And how is this going to affect millions of Canadian’s health?

Let’s spell it out.

For the first time, millions in B.C., Alberta, Manitoba, the Northwest Territories and parts of Northwestern Ontario will not be setting their clocks back.

Map reveals which provinces and territories are changing their clocks this year

Daylight saving time ends Sunday. Why B.C. is right to ditch the clock change

Those jurisdictions are scrapping the seasonal time change and staying on daylight saving time as of the start of November.

They’re joining Yukon and Saskatchewan, who’ve already thrown away the time change.

But much of central and eastern Canada will still be falling back Nov. 1, including most of Ontario, Quebec, Nunavut, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, P.E.I., and Newfoundland and Labrador.

Figuring out the time differences between each province and territory is getting more complicated.

With much of the West not changing the clock, in the winter, B.C. and Yukon will be two hours behind the capital of Canada, Ottawa; Alberta, Saskatchewan, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut will be one hour behind; while Manitoba, Ontario, and much of Quebec will be on the same time; part of Newfoundland and Labrador and much of Nova Scotia, along with New Brunswick and P.E.I. will be an hour ahead of Ottawa; while part of Newfoundland and Labrador will be an hour and a half ahead.

In the summer, much of the west will be even further behind Ottawa.

Yukon and B.C. will be three hours behind; Alberta, Saskatchewan, the Northwest Territories and parts of Nunavut will be two hours behind; while another chunk of Nunavut, Manitoba, and part of Northwestern Ontario will be an hour behind. Most of Ontario, Quebec, and the rest of Nunavut will be on the same time as Ottawa; then New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, P.E.I., and part of Newfoundland and Labrador will be an hour ahead; while, finally, the rest of Newfoundland and Labrador will be an hour-and-a-half ahead.

This could be one of the last times Quebec changes the clock with the seasons.

The province says it’s moving to end seasonal time changes, but hasn’t decided whether to stick with permanent daylight saving or standard time.

And which time they choose could really impact people’s mental and physical health, according to doctors.

“Getting rid of the twice-yearly time changes is good, but we should stick with standard time, not daylight saving time.”

Much of Western Canada is staying on daylight saving time, something doctors warn could be worse for people’s health.

“What you’re going to have, especially in the wintertime, is not very much light, particularly as people wake up and commute to work and school, and it’s going to take that light in the morning and put it into the afternoon or into the evening.”

“It’s sort of the opposite of what we want. Like, having lots of light in the evening makes it hard for us to sleep, and not having light in the morning makes it hard for us to have a good mood and have lower energy.”

Doctors warn staying on permanent daylight saving time could lead to miserable winters and summers.

“People are going to be more tired in the mornings. They might see more seasonal depression in the winter months. In the summertime we anticipate more interrupted sleep, and in the winter months we’re going to see more maybe depression, maybe more fatigue during the daytime.”

For now, Canadians in B.C., Alberta, Manitoba, the Northwest Territories, and parts of Northwestern Ontario will have to adjust to not adjusting their clocks this year.

And with more provinces and territories showing an interest in clocking out from seasonal time changes, even more could be adopting one permanent time in the future.

I’m Gabriela Panza-Beltrandi and this is Spelled Out.

The Vancouver Coastal and Island health authorities have said patients should double check their appointments, as they May have shifted by one hour.

As more provinces and territories move away from twice-yearly clock changes, they face a choice between permanent daylight time and standard time. The University of Victoria and University of B.C. have said staff meetings scheduled on or after Sunday could show the wrong time, especially if they were booked before updates to calendar systems.

While major technology companies, including Microsoft and Google, have updated their software to account for B.C.‘s new time zone, calendar appointments created before the updates May need to be changed manually.
M3 Sweatt, a retired Microsoft executive, said he expects practical and operational challenges, especially for travellers and businesses working between Washington state and B.C.

“They’ll need to account for the time differences when doing something as simple as moving across the border, scheduling a meeting over the phone, more planning day-to-day items on their calendar,” he said in an email.

“International ferry and train passengers will see differences in schedules and tickets: when travelling by train, a four-hour trip will be a three-hour trip southbound but a five-hour trip northbound.”
Teams and Outlook events May not migrate automatically, and people should double check the times of recurring meetings, he added.
Microsoft released Windows updates that account for the shift, but noted some Microsoft 365 services, such as Outlook and Teams, would require manual time changes.
A statement from Google said calendar events created in certain time zones May appear one hour late on and after Sunday.

“Some businesses have really old services or software that they use and they don’t have the means to update to new time zones,” he said. “So there will be some friction potentially. We won’t know until the change happens.”

stories.title: The times aren't a-changin' in Western Canada but there's still adjustments ahead
stories.summary: Winnipeg - The clocks aren’t changing Sunday in the Western half of the country, but that doesn’t mean changes aren’t coming as British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, northwestern Ontario and the Northwest Territories all chose this year to stick with daylight time.
stories.author: Ian Bickis The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Winnipeg - The clocks aren’t changing Sunday in the Western half of the country, but that doesn’t mean changes aren’t coming as British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, northwestern Ontario and the Northwest Territories all chose this year to stick with daylight time.

Kids heading to school, construction workers to the worksite and adrenalin-seekers to the slopes are some of those facing the challenge of darker mornings in the months ahead.

In Winnipeg, the sun isn’t going to rise until almost 9:30 a.m. in late December. In Edmonton, sunrise at that point will be around 9:50 a.m. In Prince Rupert, B.C., it will be after 10 a.m.

As more provinces and territories move away from twice-yearly clock changes, they face a choice between permanent daylight time and standard time. Canadian Press Reporter Sandra Ezekwesili explains how health experts, public opinion and economic considerations are shaping the debate over which one to keep. (Oct. 30, 2026)

In exchange, there will be more light in the evenings. But the decisions to end time changes, stemming from widespread popular support, have raised safety and health concerns, as well as some practical challenges.

Canada Border Services Agency, for example, has shifted its hours at 26 land crossings to align with U.S. states, where the clocks will still fall back an hour on Saturday night. The agency says the move will mean more clarity for travellers as well as ensuring no one who gets turned around at the border will get stuck in no man’s land.

At the International Peace Garden straddling the Manitoba-North Dakota border, it will mean following separate hours for the first time, said CEO Tim Chapman.

To adjust, the garden will have employees from either side coming in at their usual times, which will result in roughly half of staff who are Canadian coming in an hour earlier than the Americans.

“It’s going to be another new wrinkle in a lot of the uniqueness here,” Chapman said.

It also means the garden will effectively be open an hour longer, since it will open on Manitoba’s central daylight time and close on North Dakota’s central standard time, but the effects will be muted since the garden is much quieter in the winter, said Chapman.

As for the garden’s carillon clock, he said earlier this week that he wasn’t sure yet which time it will ring out.

“That would be one thing where for some people, it won’t be accurate.”

But things will get simpler at another boundary.

Residents of Lloydminster, which sits in both Alberta and Saskatchewan, will no longer have to juggle different times this winter as Alberta’s permanent mountain daylight time will align with Saskatchewan’s permanent central standard time.

“We’re excited to see it done,” said Mayor Gerald Aalbers.

While the city has stuck with Alberta’s time changes over the years, it has meant confusion for everything from school sports to doctors appointments when heading elsewhere in Saskatchewan.

“There was a constant fight: which time do we have our game at, or what time is our appointment at ... so it really had effects on a number of people.”

For some ski hill operators farther west in the Rocky Mountains, like Banff Sunshine Village, opening time will be delayed a half-hour to 9:30 a.m. so there’s enough light for safety checks.

Even then, Kendra Scurfield, a spokeswoman for the facility, said the safety work will still need to be compressed.

The slopes will stay open later, to 4:30 p.m., but that isn’t a clear-cut benefit given that visitors generally like to head out before 4 p.m. to get on with dinner and other plans, she said.

Employees will also have to adjust to later closings.

“Our operating hours are forced to change because of the decision to stay on permanent daylight time. But those employees with small children, their schools aren’t changing. Their daycare times aren’t changing.”

Schools are having to adjust in other ways as they prepare to welcome kids in the dark.

The St. James-Assiniboia School Division in Winnipeg is adjusting its light timers, to make sure there’s enough visibility around the school grounds. It’s also been reviewing lighting conditions at all community bus stops and will be monitoring the visibility of the volunteer student crossing guards, said assistant superintendent Jaime Siska.

The division is advising parents to make sure students are wearing bright clothing, and asking drivers to be extra vigilant.

“We’re recognizing that students are coming to school in the dark,” Siska said.

The division also sent out tips on how to offset some of the negative effects of getting going before the sun rises, such as turning on bright lights in the morning.

Construction workers, who generally start at 7 a.m., also face the effects of increased darkness.

“There is a bit of a concern around efficiency, with an extra hour of working in the dark. The largest concern is about working during the coldest part of the day outside,” said Darryl Harrison, CEO of the Winnipeg Construction Association.

A later start would mean dealing with traffic, and the knock-on effects on lives by leaving work later.

“Pushing back your workday by an hour, it can really get in the way of your family plans.”

It’s largely because of the hassle of adjustments that provinces have decided to do away with time changes.

But after debating the issue for so long, Aalbers in Lloydminster is just relieved to have it settled.

“What’s really important is we’re able to move forward, and it’s done, and I hope that this debate goes away; the generation that comes forward will not even know what time change was in the future years.”

But it’s not certain the changes will stick. Other countries that tried to go with permanent daylight time have given up on the effort after a few years, including Russia and Chile a decade ago, and the United States, which tried it in the 1970s.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 31, 2026.

— With files from Brittany Hobson in Winnipeg and Dayne Patterson in Calgary

stories.title: Clocks from coast to coast to coast: A breakdown of time change rules across Canada
stories.summary: Much of the eastern half of Canada switch their clocks back on Sunday, while the Western half will not this year. Here's a look at the breakdown of what it means to residents:
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Much of the eastern half of Canada switch their clocks back on Sunday, while the western half will not this year. Here’s a look at the breakdown of what it means to residents:

British Columbia

Announced in March that it was moving to permanent Pacific daylight time. The change also means that parts of northeastern B.C., which have been on mountain standard time year-round, are now in alignment with the rest of the province. It will be aligned with Washington State in the summer months and one hour ahead in winter.

Located in the mountain time zone, also switched to permanent daylight time this year. The province calls it Alberta time.

As more provinces and territories move away from twice-yearly clock changes, they face a choice between permanent daylight time and standard time. Canadian Press Reporter Sandra Ezekwesili explains how health experts, public opinion and economic considerations are shaping the debate over which one to keep. (Oct. 30, 2026)

Saskatchewan

On permanent central standard time since 1966.

Will be sticking with daylight time in the central time zone, meaning it won’t be aligned with the other Prairie provinces and will stay one hour ahead. The province will be on the same time as Ontario and Quebec in the winter and one hour behind in the summer.

Passed a law in 2020 to end the twice-yearly changing of clocks and make daylight time permanent — but only if Quebec and New York agree to do the same. Earlier this month, the province published a regulation leaving a portion of the northwest on year-round time in alignment with Manitoba.

Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says his government intends to abolish the time change. He said on Oct. 28 that the province hasn’t yet decided whether to keep daylight time or standard time year-round.

Atlantic provinces

In 2022 decided to hold off on any move toward dropping the time change until they saw what neighbouring jurisdictions would do.

Moved to end time changes in 2020. The territory observes mountain standard time.

Northwest Territories

Followed Alberta’s lead earlier this year to end seasonal time changes. The territory is on permanent daylight time.

Spans three time zones; continues to change clocks twice a year except for Southampton Island.

stories.title: Drag artist and influencer Kyne Santos is making math cool
stories.summary: The grad student’s creative approach May be the key to getting more students to embrace the subject
stories.author: Dave McGinn
stories.content:
In his most popular video, viewed nearly 15 million times, Kyne Santos explains how to make a Mobius strip and what happens when you cut it down the middle.

There are many videos online that explain the geometric shape that has only one side and one edge, but this might be the only one in which the person doing the explaining is in drag – sparkling purple dress, dangling gemstone earrings, bright pink eye makeup, long black hair cascading over her shoulder, eyes shining with the excitement of geometry.

The video, and many that have since followed, combine Mr. Santos’ twin passions and led to his book, Math In Drag , published in 2024. (Mr. Santos uses she/her pronouns while in drag.)

“After people get over the confusion, they love it,” said Mr. Santos, a 28-year-old graduate student in the mathematics department at Toronto Metropolitan University. “I’ve been able to reach people who wouldn’t have been interested in math at all.”

Canadian students’ scores on provincial and international standardized math tests have been lacklustre for years. Poor performance in the subject has produced plenty of hand-wringing among teachers, policy-makers and parents. There are no easy answers. But whatever the specifics might be, changing the culture around math is a start. Personalities such as Mr. Santos, who find creative ways on social media to explore the subject, may be the key to getting more students to embrace and learn math.

In Ontario, only 52 per cent of Grade 6 students at English-language schools met the provincial standard in math in the 2025-2026 school year, an increase of one percentage point over the previous school year.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s latest Program for International Student Assessment scores, which measures the performance of 15-year-olds from around the world, found 26 per cent of Canadian students performed below level 2, the baseline proficiency level, while 11.1 per cent performed at levels 5 and 6, the highest levels. Level 2 and above is required to participate fully and productively in society, according to the OECD.

“Math is not viewed as something that people want to be involved with or are scared of. What I’d like to see is the broadening awareness of what mathematics is,” said Anthony Bonato, a professor at Toronto Metropolitan University and Mr. Santos’ thesis adviser.

Communicators such as Mr. Santos, who has 1.6 million followers on TikTok – the biggest social media following for a math influencer in Canada – are key to that effort, Prof. Bonato said.

“Drag queens are not something we normally associate with mathematics,” he said. “It helps make math a little less scary. It makes it a lot more approachable.”

Growing up in Kitchener, Ont., Mr. Santos was a teacher’s pet, he said, and math was his best subject. His father, an engineer at Toyota, encouraged his interest. He began competing in math competitions in high school.

“That’s how I started to see that math was more than just solving problems to get the right answer, but actually there was some creativity to it,” Mr. Santos said.

It was also in high school when he began doing makeup and wig tutorials on YouTube, exploring his gender identity in a way he said was fun and creative.

When he began attending the University of Waterloo, one of the most prestigious math programs in the country, he began performing in drag at the campus pub.

In 2020, he competed on the first season of Canada’s Drag Race.

When the pandemic forced everyone into lockdowns, Mr. Santos, needing a creative outlet, began posting videos about some of his favourite math concepts in drag.

“I started off just telling riddles, and then kind of explaining the solution. And people really responded to it,” he said.

In 2024, he won the National Academies Eric and Wendy Schmidt Award for Excellence in Science Communications, which honours outstanding communicators who help make complex scientific topics accessible to the general public.

His video have explained everything from the etymology of the word “calculus” to why graph theory is a cool branch of mathematics.

There’s also the video of how to get good at math, or playing piano or playing Super Smash Brothers – and it’s not the fact that anyone is a “math person.”

“Practice girl, practice,” Ms. Santos says in the video.

Mr. Santos said he’s not only helping students feel better about doing math, he’s also helping dispel stereotypes.

“I’ve been able to reach people who maybe would have turned up an eyebrow at their kids watching a drag queen online, and then when they look over their kids’ shoulders and see that they’re learning about algebra, I think they can start to detangle some of the stereotypes they have,” he said.

“I also just want math to be cool.”

stories.title: Canadian students would get access to EU schools under new deal. Here's what we know
stories.summary: Students could get access to exchanges, academic opportunities through participation in the Erasmus+ program.
stories.author: Amarachi Amadike
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada is working to become the European Union’s “first associate member,” and the partnership could bring new opportunities for students.

During a news conference with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the Canada–European Union Summit in Montreal, Carney introduced a slew of agreements to further harmonize Canada’s economy with Europe , including the extension to Canada of the EU’s flagship funding program for education, training, youth and sport, Erasmus+.

“Through this program, Canadian students can pursue their studies in Barcelona just as easily as they could in McGill,” Carney said at Friday’s press conference.

Here’s what we know and don’t know about the new arrangement.

Canada’s accession to the Erasmus+ program would mean it gains access to the massive centralized EU funding pool, which supports billions of dollars in grants for international student travel and various academic partnerships.

But entering this program requires the federal government to pay a buy-in cost directly into the EU budget before Canadian institutions can gain access to those funds.

The cost of buying in is yet to be announced.

If the U.K.‘s recent Erasmus+ agreement is any indication of potential costs for non-EU members to join the program, then Canada can expect to cough up over $1 billion to fully participate in 2027.

“We don’t view this as ‘paying for something,’” Carney told reporters about the cost of becoming an associate member of the EU. “We view this as coming together … this is a positive association.”

Under the Erasmus+ program, European universities receive funding to establish partnerships with institutions abroad, and organize student and staff exchanges.

The grants go toward a participant’s travel and living expenses, with money also going to the institutions to administer the exchanges. Students, teachers and other staff members apply for placements through their participating institutions.

Canada already had access to the Erasmus+ program before Carney’s announcement.

Since 2015, the program has allowed universities outside Europe, including Canadian institutions, to participate in certain student and staff exchanges through partnerships with European universities.

Under a system called International Credit Mobility, European universities can receive EU funding to arrange exchanges with partner institutions abroad, allowing students to study overseas and earn academic credits.

However, Canada does not currently have the same access to Erasmus+ as EU member states or countries formally associated with the program. Canadian universities generally participate through partnerships with eligible European institutions, rather than accessing the full range of program funding and opportunities directly.

But that would change once the buy-in is finalized.

The EU commission president, von der Leyen, who described Canada as “the most European country outside Europe,” says Erasmus+ is part of a three-pronged approach to bolstering Canada-EU relations.

“We see the world through the same eyes,” von der Leyen said. “What matters nowadays is not where a country is on the map, but what it is ready to build with us, and what it stands for.”

While Carney touted that an “apprentice welder in Manitoba could now complete their placement with an employer in Italy,” specifics on how Canadians can participate in the program are yet to be clarified.

Experts have so far been restrained in their response to the prime minister’s announcement. The Canadian Association of University Teachers said it would be premature to comment on how this will affect Canadian universities as “none of the program specifics are determined yet.”
