What was conspicuously not in the documents released on Thursday was any kind of plan to reduce the size of the public service — a goal that might have been expected given the party in charge of the government. Instead, the Ford PCs touted their work in “constraining” the number of employees added to public payrolls since 2017. Indeed, they have a point: the headcount has only increased by 1.6 per cent over that period, versus what the Ford government says was a 30 per cent rise in the federal public service over the same time. (And a 63 per cent jump in the number of B.C. government employees: Yowza!)

But still, given all the budget pressures, and President Global Instability, there were suspicions that Bethlenfalvy would be announcing significant belt-tightening measures this week. But, no: the document highlighted ongoing reviews at nine provincial agencies such as the Lcbo, Wsib and Metrolink, that will “focus on efficiency, governance and productivity to ensure value for taxpayer dollars.” There was no mention of cutbacks or buyouts or any such words of restraint. Even Dalton McGuinty once took a harsher line on reducing government spending.

This is the paradox at the centre of the Ford government. He hates government waste with the fire of a thousand suns, he never gets tired of saying. But he also really doesn’t like it when people get angry with him. And so, even when delivering bad news — and the Fall Economic Statement is very much that — there isn’t much in there about tough medicine.

There is, instead, hope that all of the spending will deliver results, eventually. And a wish that a certain president will come to his senses. But that’s not something you could confidently put in your forecasts.

stories.title: It’s scary out there. Live theatre is trying to make the most of it
stories.summary: In a time of great political and social unrest, the horror genre is picking up steam
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
It’s been a historic year for horror. Obsession and Backrooms are among the top 10 highest-grossing films of 2026, while Resident Evil , Scream 7 and Scary Movie are in the top 20. But this country’s renewed interest in the genre hasn’t stopped at the cinema: At live theatres across Canada, audiences are gobbling up all the scary stories they can get, and not just now, at the height of so-called spooky season.

Late last year, The Woman in Black , one of the West End’s longest-running shows, played Mirvish’s CAA Theatre; this summer, the stage version of Paranormal Activity ran down the street at the CAA Ed Mirvish Theatre to rave reviews and packed houses. Evil Dead , the bloody, cult favourite musical, is in full swing at cities across the country. And in January, a theatrical adaptation of Stephen King’s Misery will run at the Royal Manitoba Theatre Centre in Winnipeg before touring to rural communities in Manitoba and Ontario.

“We’re in a time of great political and social unrest, and as always happens in those moments, we’re seeing a renaissance in the genre,” said Eric Woolfe, artistic director of Eldritch Theatre (though he prefers to refer to himself as the company’s director of the uncanny).

Since 1999, Eldritch has specialized in ghoulish performances inspired by the likes of the Grand Guignol Theatre in Paris; most of its original works feature highly stylized puppets and costumes. Although attendance for Eldritch’s work at Toronto’s tiny Red Sandcastle Theatre creeps up around Halloween, the company produces eerie fare year-round.

“Every medium has its own set of conventions to make things work,” Woolfe explained, “and film works really well with the idea of control. We can control the frame, and where the viewer looks … In theatre, we can create those fears in people’s imagination. We don’t literally have to have a monster jump out of a box. We can force the audience to a place where they’re imagining it.” A puppet, he added, can encourage an audience to have a more emotional connection to the story at hand.

“Theatre is an outlet for our societal yearnings, for our values and our desires,” he continued. “When we’re scared, we like to be more scared. We like to share that fear with the people around us.”

Indeed, impactful horror stories have tended to cluster around societal instability. The films Dracula and Frankenstein came in 1931, in the depths of the Great Depression. Get Out , Jordan Peele’s psychological thriller about anti-Black racism in the U.S., landed in 2017, as the #BlackLivesMatter movement was crescendoing to the top of public discourse. Ari Aster’s 2019 Midsommar is largely regarded as an exploration of modern eco-fascism, an idea that’s only become more relevant in the age of climate change and water-guzzling data centres.

But by its very nature, live theatre offers a much more immediate sense of a given story’s stakes. (Troupes such as White Mills Theatre Company, best known for their site-specific Gothic work in Toronto, regularly take advantage of that haunted house-style intimacy.) Unlike in a film, a good horror play doesn’t just look and sound terrifying – it feels it, too.

That idea of experiencing horror live, and with a large group – not on a screen and not at home on the couch – is central to most of the blood-curdling plays that have cropped up across Canada in recent months. The Veil premiered in Crow’s Theatre’s studio space last September, and played a short run for Halloween at the Stratford Festival’s Meighen Forum this month. It’ll head to Calgary’s Vertigo Theatre in January.

The show hinges on proximity between its solo actor and the audience. In the play, written by Keith Barker and Thomas Morgan Jones, a buttoned-up lawyer inherits a curse which, try as he might, he just can’t shake.

In the show’s final moments, the audience, tasked with blowing out a real candle onstage, has to grapple with a choice: Should they break the cycle? Or save themselves from the terrors they’ve just seen unfold?

The first time The Veil played with a live audience was enlightening, said Jones. “People were laughing a lot,” he said. “People were audibly going, ‘Oh, no.’ A bunch of people put their hands on their faces. They were doing all of that just from the words being spoken onstage. These people were so invested in that character’s life and relationships that they had a physical reaction to it … people screamed. The fact that that could happen in a theatre felt really special.”

But what made The Veil stand out in its premiere – and what’s kept it popular enough to tour – isn’t just its intimacy. The play incorporates most of the senses, including smell, in its storytelling. Its sound design features naturalistic noises that lure the audience into a false sense of security that’s then abruptly shattered; visually, there’s far more to its spring-loaded set than meets the eye.

“There’s a huge appetite for that sort of adrenalin and excitement,” said Barker, also the Stratford Festival’s director of new plays, about The Veil ’s sensorial tricks. “I feel like theatre is uniquely positioned to give an experience that can scare the pants off people.”

Vertigo Theatre, where The Veil will play in 2027, just closed its production of The Lodger , a Canadian adaptation of Alfred Hitchcock’s 1927 silent thriller by Susie Moloney and Vern Thiessen. Not unlike Eldritch – though at a much larger scale – the company specializes in genre plays, including horror. (The company even has a specialty kitchen for mixing fake blood.)

Scary stories are a “blueprint for bad times,” mused Moloney. “People need to engage with something to purge their own fears. Fear is an extraordinary opportunity for people to come out and share that jump scare together,” she continued.

What are those fears? Take your pick, said Vertigo’s artistic director Jack Grinhaus. “People are scared of the economy. They’re scared of politics,” he explained. “I think people are feeling really destabilized, and horror is a great way to check the barometer of a society, and to feel connected.”

“Horror has always played that role, particularly for the vulnerable,” said Moloney. “The world is on fire right now. It’s a scary place to be. Watching somebody go through hell and come out the other end, I think, is soothing.”

stories.title: Kenora, Ont., fined for removing election signs during 2025 federal race
stories.summary: Kenora - Kenora, Ont., is facing a $1,000 fine from the Commissioner of Canada Elections after the office said city bylaw officers removed election signs while candidates were still campaigning during the 2025 federal race.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Kenora - Kenora, Ont., is facing a $1,000 fine from the Commissioner of Canada Elections after the office said city bylaw officers removed election signs while candidates were still campaigning during the 2025 federal race.

The office of the commissioner says it confirmed 102 election signs were removed by the City of Kenora without providing notice to the campaigns.

The office of the commissioner says it confirmed 102 election signs were removed by the City of Kenora without providing notice to the campaigns.

stories.title: Woman charged in connection with fake 911 reports
stories.summary: A woman has been charged in connection with fake 911 reports in Hanover.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
A woman has been charged in connection with fake 911 reports in Hanover.

On Oct. 20 just after 2 p.m., police responded to an emergency call near 10th Avenue and 10th Street, which a woman allegedly reported gunshots were fired, and she was struck by a stray bullet.

The Hanover police arrived on scene and found the woman who said she needed an ambulance. Officers investigated and determined there was no evidence of a shooting, any injuries, or an emergency.

The woman has been charged with public mischief, failure to comply with a release order, and two counts of failure to comply with a probation order.

Police are now reminding the public that making false reports is a serious offence and takes away resources from those who need immediate help.

stories.title: Ottawa to invest up to $1.6B in Canadian AI firm Cohere
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday his government will invest up to $1.6 billion in Canadian AI company Cohere.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday his government will invest up to $1.6 billion in Canadian AI company Cohere.

He made the announcement in Montreal as he welcomed European Union leaders to a summit aimed at forging closer ties.

“We are not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don’t know or by whom we don’t trust. We’re building it right here in the right way,” Carney said.

In April, Cohere announced it would merge with Germany’s Aleph Alpha and said the company would be “anchored in” Germany and Canada.

On Thursday, Carney called the partnership a concrete example of what Canada and Europe can build together.

He also said that, under the agreement, Cohere will stay Canadian.

Carney said the government is making the announcement on “a commercial basis, alongside private investors including Nvidia, Bell, and Germany’s Schwarz Group.”

Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez said at the announcement that the company, which was founded seven years ago, is now “one of the very few companies in the world building frontier AI technology at a global scale.”

He added that it’s the largest AI company outside the U.S. and China.

In a press release issued Thursday, the government said the funding would be provided in stages, with regular reporting on commitments made by the company.

Those commitments include creating at least 1,000 “new high-paying Canadian technical jobs” and committing at least $1.7 billion to building more computing infrastructure by 2030.

The government says Cohere will also maintain its Canadian headquarters and incorporation, invest in research partnerships, create opportunities for students and graduates and continue working with the Canadian AI Safety Institute.

“Cohere will now be able to develop far more advanced models and products, scale up its computing infrastructure, and expand its Canadian workforce to serve more businesses and governments in Canada and around the world,” the press release said.

“Building this capability at home ultimately means that Canadian businesses and governments will have more choice in how they adopt AI and greater control over their sensitive information.”

In 2024, the government announced it would provide up to $240 million to Cohere to boost its computing capacity. In 2025, Ottawa signed an agreement with the company to identify areas where AI can enhance public service operations.

Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon has often pointed to Cohere as an element of Canada’s strength in AI, saying Canada is one of only a few countries around the world with a large language model.

stories.title: Nearly three-quarters of Canadians support PM in seeking closer ties with Europe
stories.summary: The survey findings have come just ahead of the Canada–EU Summit in Montréal on October 29 and 30
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Almost 73 per cent of Canadians say Prime Minister Mark Carney is on the right track in seeking a closer economic and security alliance with the European Union, according to a new poll by Canada Pulse Insights , a public opinion research firm in Toronto.

Seventy-three per cent of respondents said they agree that, based on the ongoing unpredictability that has come to define Canada’s trading relationship with the United States, strengthening ties with Europe will protect Canada’s economy.

The remaining 27 per cent of respondents disagree, saying Carney is heading in the wrong direction, because closer EU ties will not be sufficient to offset the negative impact of the trade war with the U.S. That figure includes a majority of Conservative supporters who say Carney is heading in the wrong direction.

The survey findings come as the Canada–EU Summit takes place in Montreal on Oct. 29 and 30, where Carney is hosting European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa. The focus of the discussions is expected to be closer co-operation in trade, defence and security, energy, critical minerals and technology.

The poll also found majority support in every region across Canada for the Prime Minister’s approach. British Columbia leads that view at 81 per cent, followed by Atlantic Canada (79 per cent), Québec (75 per cent), Ontario (72 per cent), Saskatchewan/Manitoba (64 per cent) and Alberta (62 per cent).

Meanwhile, support rises with age and education. Among Canadians 55 and over, 83 per cent support Carney’s efforts, compared with 66 per cent of respondents 18 to 34 and 67 per cent of those aged 35 to 54.

Among university graduates, 82 per cent approve. That compares with 70 per cent of respondents with trades or college education, and 68 per cent of those with a high school diploma or less.

Support is lower among Canadians in households earning less than $50,000, at 62 per cent, compared with 75 per cent or more in higher-income households.

Men (71 per cent) and women (75 per cent) express similar views in supporting Carney.

Among supporters of the federal Liberals, 95 per cent support closer ties with Europe, as well as 86 per cent of NDP supporters and 83 per cent of Bloc Québécois supporters. A majority of undecided voters (79 per cent) also support closer ties with Europe.

However, a majority of present Conservative supporters (58 per cent) say that Carney is heading in the wrong direction, while 42 per cent say he is heading in the right direction.

There is a distinct difference between past Conservative voters and respondents who express present support for the party. Among Canadians who said they voted Conservative in April 2025, there is an even split, with 51 per cent saying Carney is on the right track and 49 per cent disagreeing.

This survey was conducted with 1,531 Canadian adults (18+) as part of a Canada Pulse Insights national omnibus survey, fielded from October 1–8, 2026. The margin of error for a comparable probability-based random sample of the same size is ±2.5 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.

stories.title: European Commission head revives 'associate membership' for Canada on eve of meeting
stories.summary: Von der Leyen extolled the current partnership between allies while calling for even more integration with Canada.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Montreal — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Thursday the EU and Canada can work together on “everything” as she renewed her call for the country to join the bloc as an “associate member.”

In a speech right before the start of a two-day Canada-European Union meeting in Montreal, von der Leyen extolled the current partnership between allies while calling for even more integration with Canada.

She notably began her speech reiterating her call for Canada to become the first ever “associate member” of the EU, pushing for “association without accession”.

Her doubling down on associate membership for Canada raised eyebrows because the term has become controversial in Europe, with some countries — notably Germany and half-dozen other countries — dismissing such a move.

A reference for “associate member” for Canada was removed from a draft joint statement between Canada and the EU circulated Wednesday ahead of the summit.

Instead, the Oct. 28 draft document (which could still be changed) referred to an “ever-closer association” between the EU and Canada that will be fully defined by next year’s bilateral summit.

Thursday, von der Leyen told attendees of a C.D. Howe Institute event that Canada and the EU “can build a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we’ve done before.”

She summarized associate membership as better alignment on policies like AI, climate, energy and security, shared governance work between both parliaments and courts, and more integration in certain EU ventures like student-mobility program Erasmus+ or its supercomputing infrastructure for AI.

“We are once again called upon to work on new frontiers together, because the current moment in history calls for it. We are witnessing a deeper decay in international order,” she said. “We can no longer let ourselves be shackled by the limits of the old world order.”

At a separate press conference, Prime Minister Mark Carney dismissed concerns about the nomenclature used to describe the new budding relationship between Canada and the EU.

“This new alliance is not a marketing exercise. The name doesn’t matter. What matters is that the complementarities of our two jurisdictions strengthen our sovereignty,” he said.

In the past, he has emphasized a joint interest in developing AI and data-storage solutions outside of the U.S. and China as well as joint ventures in space technology and telecommunications.

Carney has repeatedly pointed to Elon Musk’s satellite telecommunications company Starlink as a technology he wants Canada to move away from.

Carney, von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa on Friday are expected to sign a final joint statement at the end of their trilateral summit on Friday.

According to the Oct. 28 draft statement viewed by National Post, Canada and the EU have concluded “substantive negotiations” on a new Digital Trade Agreement (DTA) that will supplement the existing free-trade deal between Canada and the EU. The DTA “will improve legal certainty and predictability, facilitate cross-border data flows, and enhance confidence in the digital economy for businesses and consumers.”

During a background briefing with reporters, senior European officials explained that the deal would harmonize rules on digital commerce and specifics like e-contracts and duties on electronic transmissions.

The Oct. 28 document also promises to look into faster money transfer solutions between Europe and Canada.

“We will also support work toward connecting instant payment systems to facilitate faster, lower cost and more seamless cross-border transactions, making it easier for Canadians and Europeans to conduct business, invest and transfer funds across the two economies.”

Carney, von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa on Friday are expected to sign a final joint statement at the end of their trilateral summit on Friday.

According to the Oct. 28 draft statement viewed by National Post, Canada and the EU have concluded “substantive negotiations” on a new Digital Trade Agreement (DTA) that will supplement the existing free-trade deal between Canada and the EU. The DTA “will improve legal certainty and predictability, facilitate cross-border data flows, and enhance confidence in the digital economy for businesses and consumers.”

During a background briefing with reporters, senior European officials explained that the deal would harmonize rules on digital commerce and specifics like e-contracts and duties on electronic transmissions.
The Oct. 28 document also promises to look into faster money transfer solutions between Europe and Canada.

“We will also support work toward connecting instant payment systems to facilitate faster, lower cost and more seamless cross-border transactions, making it easier for Canadians and Europeans to conduct business, invest and transfer funds across the two economies.”

stories.title: A timeline of key events in the Regis Korchinski-Paquet case
stories.summary: A coroner’s inquest is scheduled to start Tuesday in the case of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a 29-year-old Afro-Indigenous woman who fell from a Toronto highrise balcony while police were in her home in 2020.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto — A coroner’s inquest into the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet has been adjourned until further notice after the presiding coroner said Thursday that an “unanticipated investigation” was required.

The 29-year-old Afro-Indigenous woman fell from a Toronto highrise balcony while police were in her home in 2020.

Here is a timeline of key events in the case:

May 27, 2020 : The Special Investigations Unit says it is investigating the death of a woman who fell from a 24th-floor balcony while police were in the apartment. Korchinski-Paquet’s death sparks questions from her family, local politicians, and on social media about the role of police officers in the incident. In the days that follow, Korchinski-Paquet’s mother says she called police that day hoping they would take her daughter to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health but instead the woman ended up dead.

May 30, 2020 : Thousands of people take to the streets in Toronto to protest against racism and demand answers in Korchinski-Paquet’s case. Several smaller marches follow over the next few weeks.

June 3, 2020 : The SIU urges police to stop speaking on the case after Korchinski-Paquet’s family postpones meeting the watchdog, citing concerns about possible police leaks.

June 8, 2020 : Two Toronto city councillors put forward a motion to defund the city’s police force by 10 per cent and use the money for community resources.

June 10, 2020 : Korchinski-Paquet’s family says it will talk to the SIU.

June 11, 2020 : The family holds a small funeral for her.

June 29, 2020 : Toronto city council votes against defunding the police budget but approves numerous reforms to the service, including anti-racism measures and the implementation of body-worn cameras.

July 25, 2020 : Family, friends and community members gather for a memorial and walk to honour Korchinski-Paquet.

Aug. 26, 2020 : The SIU clears police of wrongdoing in her death, finding the officers tried to de-escalate the situation and “though their efforts were unsuccessful,” none of them broke the law. Korchinski-Paquet’s family rejects the findings.

Feb. 3, 2021 : Toronto announces a pilot project to send crisis-support workers instead of police to certain 911 calls in the city. The pilot, set to begin the following year, comes after widespread calls for police reform, including improvements to how police deal with those experiencing mental-health crises.

May 26, 2021 : A lawyer for Korchinski-Paquet’s family says they recently filed a complaint with the Office of the Independent Police Review Director because they believe the report by the SIU doesn’t make sense. The Oiprd confirms it is investigating but declines to comment further, citing confidentiality.

June 19, 2021 : Korchinski-Paquet’s relatives speak at Juneteenth event in Ottawa aimed at demanding accountability and changes to the justice system. Several Black and Indigenous families whose loved ones were harmed or killed by police also attend the event organized by Black Lives Matter Toronto.

June 2022 : Korchinski-Paquet’s family files a $10-million lawsuit against several police officers and the head of Ontario’s police watchdog, as well as Ontario’s attorney general, the City of Toronto and the Toronto Community Housing Corporation. The lawsuit alleges her relatives suffered severe emotional distress after they were provided with “misleading information” at the time of her death.

April 2, 2026 : Coroner Dr. Richard Wells announces that an inquest into Korchinski-Paquet’s death will be held.

May 27, 2026 : Korchinski-Paquet’s parents join advocates at the provincial legislature to call for reforms, including that the recommendations issued by coroner’s inquests be binding and implemented in a reasonable time frame.

Sept. 15, 2026 : The date of the coroner’s inquest is announced.

Oct. 13, 2026 : The coroner’s inquest begins.

Oct. 29, 2026 : The inquest is adjourned indefinitely just after finishing hearing all the evidence in the case.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

stories.title: Carney says Cleveland-Cliffs making ‘mistake’ by not respecting obligations
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday that Cleveland-Cliffs' would be making a "mistake" by not respecting its obligations and commitments after it began laying off workers.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday that Cleveland-Cliffs would be making a “mistake” by not respecting its obligations and commitments, as the U.S.-based owner of Stelco faces potential legal action from the federal government over their laying off of up to 500 Canadian steelworkers.

The comments came at an event in Ottawa when Carney was asked by a reporter if, given what has transpired in recent weeks, the federal government felt it was a mistake to allow Cleveland-Cliffs to acquire Stelco in 2024.

“The mistake here would be Cleveland-Cliffs not respecting the obligations, the commitments that they made in the acquisition,” Carney said in response.

The agreement from 2024, of which only a summary has been shared publicly, includes several legally binding commitments Cleveland-Cliffs and Stelco must maintain, including for employment to be at or above levels measured at the time the agreement was created until 2029.

When pressed for more on Thursday, Carney declined to comment further because there is now a legal process heading before the courts. He added that he would reserve his comments for “some other time.”

This comes just hours after Global News obtained a letter, dated Oct. 29, from Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and addressed to Stelco’s president, Paul Simon. In the letter, Joly said she expects a “concrete and credible plan for re-engagement with these workers.”

While arguing the company has not broken its agreement with the federal government, Cleveland-Cliffs has also argued they “should not be responsible for impacts of external factors beyond their control,” including U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel.

Speaking to reporters Thursday, Joly reiterated that Cleveland-Cliffs and its CEO, Lourenco Goncalves, have actively supported the U.S. tariffs and must “face the consequences” they have on the Canadian market.

Joly said she reviewed an interim compliance report that was provided by Stelco on Oct. 26 but said the report was “far from satisfactory.”

“It does not alter my belief that Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs are not in compliance with their undertakings under the Investment Canada Act as set out in my October 22 section 39 demand,” she said in the most recent letter.

According to the union representing Stelco’s laid-off workers, about 175 have been let go so far, but an internal memo said that could increase to about 500.

Separately, Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves reportedly told The Canadian Press Wednesday that laid off Stelco workers could be recalled by the holidays provided sales of Canadian steel increase.

“It will depend on Canadian customers buying Canadian steel, made by Stelco,” he said in a statement, adding: “If our plan works, my intention is to call back all the 175 workers before Christmas.”

– with files from Global’s Rachel Morgan, Mackenzie Gray and The Canadian Press

stories.title: Churchill River energy agreement with Quebec not open for renegotiation, says N.L.
stories.summary: ST. John's - Newfoundland and Labrador's premier says an agreement with Quebec to develop energy in Labrador is not open for renegotiation.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s - Newfoundland and Labrador’s premier says an agreement with Quebec to develop energy in Labrador is not open for renegotiation.

Tony Wakeham said Wednesday that the Newfoundland and Labrador government had already voted in favour of the non-binding agreement, which he unveiled in August alongside Prime Minister Mark Carney and former Quebec premier Christine Fréchette in St. John’s, N.L.

“Let me be clear: we will not be renegotiating the deal, and will not entertain an attempt by anyone else wishing to renegotiate the deal,” he said.

He made the remarks as reporters pressed him about whether final agreements would be signed before they were debated in the legislature. But there is also a new Parti Québécois government in Quebec that could ask for changes to the multibillion-dollar agreement.

Wakeham said he has not heard any rumblings about Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon wanting changes.

“I think what I’m trying to do is just outline our position,” Wakeham told reporters in St. John’s.

The proposal — which the government has called a definitive co-operation and implementation agreement — lays out plans for Hydro-Québec and Newfoundland and Labrador Hydro to expand the hydroelectric capacity of the Churchill River, which cuts through traditional Innu territory.

Carney has touted the proposal as “the largest clean energy investment in North American history” and his government has promised $10 billion in financing to help it along.

In a Facebook post Wednesday, the grand chief of the Innu Nation in Labrador said Innu were not included in the energy negotiations despite the agreement proposing projects on Innu land. Jodie Ashini pointed to a social media post by Carney saying he met with Wakeham recently in Ottawa, and a public statement from Wakeham pledging to “keep engaging respectfully with the Innu Nation.”

“How is meeting with the prime minister and discussing our lands and not having us at the table respectful?” she wrote. “There is no respect from the (Newfoundland and Labrador) government right now to the Innu.”

“Come to Sheshatshiu and speak with us,” she added, referring to an Innu community in central Labrador where the Innu Nation has its main office.

Ashini has accused Wakeham and his government of interfering with a cultural exhibit detailing Innu history in Labrador. She says the government believes Innu arrived about 300 years ago, after the Europeans. The position erases thousands of years of Innu history, she has said.

On Wednesday, Wakeham said he would table all final energy agreements in the legislature and propose a special debate about them. He would not answer directly when reporters asked if those agreements would already be signed, but he was clear they would not be open for changes.

The Parti Québécois did not immediately respond to a request for comment. St-Pierre Plamondon and his cabinet were sworn in last week, and Wakeham has not yet met with the new premier in person.

“It’s coming,” Wakeham said. “He wants to come to Newfoundland and Labrador for a meeting. He indicated that to me in our last conversation, and I’m looking forward to that.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

stories.title: Loss of Hockey Night in Canada a major blow to tradition, say majority of fans: poll
stories.summary: Nine-in-10 Angus Reid Institute survey respondents say hockey is an important or defining part of Canadian identity.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Just shy of three-quarters of Canadian hockey fans say the end of Hockey Night in Canada is a major loss for Canadian hockey and its traditions, according to a new Angus Reid Institute survey.

Polling found 74 per cent of Canadians who follow the NHL view the end of the traditional Saturday-night broadcast as a significant loss, following a 74-year run on CBC. The sentiment was strongest in Atlantic Canada, where 83 per cent say the loss is significant.

Just seven per cent see the change as a positive development, while another 12 per cent say they are disappointed but do not consider it a major loss.

Despite the changes, hockey remains deeply rooted in Canada’s national identity. Nine-in-10 (90 per cent) say hockey is an important or defining part of Canadian identity, up slightly from the 88 per cent found in 2015 polling.

The CBC’s Saturday-night broadcasts have long been a fixture for generations of Canadian viewers. Beginning Dec. 5, the national public broadcaster will instead use the Hockey Night brand to air eight Professional Women’s Hockey (Pwhl) games on Saturday nights.

The poll suggests there is uncertainty about how many Canadians will watch, however. Only one in five (20 per cent), say they are likely to watch a Pwhl game this season, while 69 per cent probably or definitely won’t.

That said, there is broad public support for women’s sports receiving increased visibility. Nearly two-thirds of respondents (64 per cent) say women’s pro sports deserve more Canadian television coverage. Still, among those who support more coverage, only 30 per cent say they’re likely to tune in.

The survey also points to widespread dissatisfaction with the growing reliance on streaming subscriptions to get their sports fix.

Among Canadians who follow the NHL, despite more overall games being available, 78 per cent say it’s bad that additional subscriptions are required. Only 10 per cent viewed more availability as a good thing.

Across the country, 70 per cent of Canadians say professional sports are spread across too many channels and platforms. Just six per cent disagreed and 23 per cent were unsure.

Subscription costs are another irritant for respondents.

Among subscribers to individual services, 63 per cent of those paying for Sportsnet+ say the monthly price is too much. That figure rises to 71 per cent for those on Dazn and 52 per cent for TSN+ users.

Amazon Prime Video, “which comes with the attached benefit of Prime delivery services,” is viewed more favourably on price, with 54 per cent of subscribers saying its cost is about right.

After the NHL and Rogers Sports & Media agreed to a 12-year, CA$11 billion broadcast extension last April to keep Sportsnet home for hockey in Canada until the end of the 2037-38 season, Amazon and Rogers signed a 12-year sub-license broadcasting this off-season, granting the streamer exclusive rights to Wednesday night broadcasts in both official languages on Prime Video. It replaces Amazon’s Prime Monday Night Hockey that ran for two years, but only in English.

The Monday night games now belong to Sportsnet, but are only available through its Sportsnet+ package. The upgrade is free for Rogers television subscribers, $12.99 monthly for other television service subscribers and $34.99 for those without.

For the most dedicated fan, the total cost can be especially challenging. Among Angus Reid survey respondents who follow the NHL very closely or just closely, 79 and 77 per cent, respectively, say it has become too expensive to follow their favourite teams. Even 63 per cent who don’t follow very closely say it’s getting too costly.

The online survey of 1,806 Canadian adults was conducted Oct. 19-22. The margin of error for a comparable probability-based random sample of the same size is plus/minus two percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

stories.title: Competition Bureau chief urges limits on non-compete clauses for workers
stories.summary: In a letter dated Oct. 29, Interim Commissioner of Competition Jeanne Pratt said the breadth of use of non-compete clauses in Canada is “concerning.”
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
The Competition Bureau of Canada is calling on provincial and territorial governments to limit the use of non-compete agreements in an effort to “foster more competitive labour markets.”

In a letter dated Oct. 29, Interim Commissioner of Competition Jeanne Pratt said the breadth of use of non-compete clauses in Canada is “concerning.”

Non-compete clauses can restrict workers from joining a rival company or starting a competing business for a set period of time after leaving a job.

According to a survey from the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (Oecd), Canada has one of the highest prevalence rates of non-compete clauses with employers reporting that between 29 and 39 per cent of private-sector employees fall under them.

Non-compete clauses were designed to target high-level executives, Jon Pinkus, an employment lawyer and partner at Samfiru Tumarkin LLP in Toronto, told Global News.

He said ideally the clauses should only be used for employees who have a “real fiduciary duty” and who “can do real damage if they go to a competitor.”

But the data tells a different story. Among Canadian firms that use non-competes, 30 per cent reportedly apply them to every employee regardless of their role or seniority, according to the Oecd.

Pratt argued that widespread use of non-compete clauses can reduce job wages, mobility and entrepreneurship.

According to the Oecd, 23 per cent of Canadian workers who report having a non-compete agreement say it has prevented them from changing jobs. Approximately 12 per cent self reported that the agreement prevented them from starting a business.

Despite the prevalence of non-compete agreements, Pinkus said many of them are not enforceable.

“The courts May determine that they are an unreasonable, what we call restraint of trade, and invalidate them on that basis,” he said, adding that the responsibility is on the employer to prove a non-compete is necessary.

But more than 40 per cent of employees operating under a non-compete said they would turn down a competing job even if the agreement was unlikely to be upheld in court, according to the Oecd.

The Government of Canada committed in its 2025 budget to restricting the use of non-compete agreements which it said will “protect workers’ rights, promote labour mobility, strengthen competition, and empower workers to move to a higher-paying job or start their own business.”

Ontario was the first and only province to enact a statutory ban on the use of non-compete clauses which it did so in 2021.

The province’s Employment Standards Act prohibits most new employment non-competes, with a few limited exceptions including certain agreements associated with the sale of a business and agreements involving senior executives.

stories.title: Inquest into death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet on hold for investigation: coroner
stories.summary: A coroner's inquest into the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet was put on hold indefinitely Thursday just as it reached the final stretch of the proceedings.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio
stories.content:
A coroner’s inquest into the death of a Toronto woman who fell from a 24th-floor balcony while police were in her home was put on hold indefinitely Thursday just as it reached the final stretch of the proceedings.

“I know everyone has been working extremely hard during this inquest. Unfortunately, I will be adjourning the inquest until further notice,” said Dr. David Cameron, the coroner presiding over the inquest into the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet.

“The reason for this is that we have some quite unanticipated investigation that needs to be done before we can continue.”

The coroner gave no details on the nature or focus of the investigation but said jurors and the public would be informed when the inquest was ready to resume.

The inquest finished hearing evidence on Wednesday and was set to reconvene Thursday afternoon so that lawyers for about a dozen parties could make their closing remarks and suggest recommendations to the jury.

Korchinski-Paquet, a 29-year-old woman of Afro-Indigenous and Ukrainian descent, died on May 27, 2020 after police were called to the west-end apartment she shared with relatives.

The inquest was temporarily thrown off course after her mother, Claudette Beals, made a new allegation against police, who were cleared of wrongdoing by a watchdog agency.

Beals alleged officers pushed her daughter toward the balcony, causing the inquest to go on an extended break so that lawyers could figure out a way forward.

Two officers who were in the apartment had previously testified that Korchinski-Paquet was allowed into the apartment to use the bathroom, then introduced to a paramedic. Korchinski-Paquet moved quickly to the balcony, knocking over an air conditioning unit in the process, they said.

The Special Investigations Unit, one of Ontario’s police watchdog organizations, found she died while trying to move from her apartment’s balcony to the one next door. The SIU did not participate in the inquest, and its investigation is outside the scope of the proceedings.

Jurors in coroner’s inquests do not assign blame or legal responsibility, but they May make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths in the future.

The inquest has focused largely on Korchinski-Paquet’s history of seizures from epilepsy as well as education and training around epilepsy and postictal delirium or psychosis, mental states that can occur after seizures and lead to uncharacteristic behaviour.

Korchinski-Paquet had experienced two seizures earlier in the day, hours before police were called over a fight involving knives. Korchinski-Paquet, her mother and her brother each called 911 and mentioned her diagnosis and seizures to the call taker, jurors heard.
paragraphs: A coroner’s inquest into the death of a Toronto woman who fell from a 24th-floor balcony while police were in her home was put on hold indefinitely Thursday just as it reached the final stretch of the proceedings.

“I know everyone has been working extremely hard during this inquest. Unfortunately, I will be adjourning the inquest until further notice,” said Dr. David Cameron, the coroner presiding over the inquest into the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet.
“The reason for this is that we have some quite unanticipated investigation that needs to be done before we can continue.”
The coroner gave no details on the nature or focus of the investigation but said jurors and the public would be informed when the inquest was ready to resume.

The inquest finished hearing evidence on Wednesday and was set to reconvene Thursday afternoon so that lawyers for about a dozen parties could make their closing remarks and suggest recommendations to the jury.
Korchinski-Paquet, a 29-year-old woman of Afro-Indigenous and Ukrainian descent, died on May 27, 2020 after police were called to the west-end apartment she shared with relatives.
The inquest was temporarily thrown off course after her mother, Claudette Beals, made a new allegation against police, who were cleared of wrongdoing by a watchdog agency.
Beals alleged officers pushed her daughter toward the balcony, causing the inquest to go on an extended break so that lawyers could figure out a way forward.

Two officers who were in the apartment had previously testified that Korchinski-Paquet was allowed into the apartment to use the bathroom, then introduced to a paramedic. Korchinski-Paquet moved quickly to the balcony, knocking over an air conditioning unit in the process, they said.

The Special Investigations Unit, one of Ontario’s police watchdog organizations, found she died while trying to move from her apartment’s balcony to the one next door. The SIU did not participate in the inquest, and its investigation is outside the scope of the proceedings.
Jurors in coroner’s inquests do not assign blame or legal responsibility, but they May make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths in the future.

stories.title: Ontario projects bigger deficit, cites U.S. tariffs and higher oil prices
stories.summary: Red ink for 2026-27 now expected to total $16.9-billion, Finance Minister says, as province works to protect economy
stories.author: Jeff Gray, Laura Stone
stories.content:
The Ontario government says its deficit for the current fiscal year is now expected to be $16.9-billion, up from the $13.8-billion it projected in its March budget, as U.S. tariffs and higher oil prices have cut the province’s anticipated economic growth in half.

Releasing his fall economic statement on Thursday, Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy defended the deficit, warning that the spending is needed as the trade war with the U.S. intensifies and President Donald Trump ’s threatened additional tariffs, which could take effect Jan. 1, loom over Ontario.

The province’s new larger shortfall was announced just a week before the federal government is to deliver a full-scale budget next Thursday, as Ottawa grapples with the same slowing economic growth and its own struggle to contain spending while mitigating the impact of U.S. tariffs .

Much of the reason for this year’s Ontario deficit figure is a $3.8-billion boost to the province’s contingency fund, which now sits at a total of $4.9-billion. That account could be used for tariff relief, health care costs or other services, Mr. Bethlenfalvy said, and it could be needed if the trade war further darkens the economic picture.

But the fall economic statement also projects additional red ink in future years. The province says next year’s deficit could be $12.7-billion – more than double the prediction in Mr. Bethlenfalvy’s March budget. And for 2028-29, when he had just months ago forecast a $600-million surplus, he now expects a $6.7-billion deficit.

The province’s books, the fall economic statement says, won’t be balanced until 2029-30 – making Thursday the fourth time the government has put off a planned return to black ink since 2024.

When measured as a percentage of gross domestic product, the shortfall projected Thursday isn’t anywhere near as large as those the province ran up in the recessionary early 1990s, under NDP premier Bob Rae, or the record deficits under Liberal Dalton McGuinty in the wake of the 2008 global financial crisis.

But if this year’s projection proves accurate, it would be the largest deficit ever posted – in raw dollars, not accounting for inflation – by the Progressive Conservative government of Doug Ford , even bigger than the $16.4-billion pandemic-fuelled shortfall in 2020-21.

In a speech to the Ontario Legislature, Mr. Bethlenfalvy called this “perhaps the most consequential time in our country’s recent history,” adding that “we are living in a post free-trade, protectionist world.”

Speaking to reporters after delivering the statement in the House, Mr. Bethlenfalvy said the spending is needed amid the uncertainty caused by U.S. tariffs and high oil prices owing to the U.S.-Iran war. But he said he dislikes deficits and is still dedicated to balancing the budget.

“While I’d like to balance today, I am also a realist of the world we’re in,” he said. “We’re not going to slow down our investments in health care, social services and other programs.”

He also argued that Ontario has the fiscal room it needs to run deficits as it faces the tariff crisis, noting recent credit-rating upgrades, the province’s low borrowing costs relative to other provinces and its net debt-to-GDP ratio. That key metric for government finance shows that Ontario’s net debt is now projected to be 37.4 per cent of the size of its economy, down from 37.7 per cent in the March budget.

However, that figure is expected to rise, along with Ontario’s net debt, which is projected to grow beyond $483.8-billion by the end of this fiscal year. Net debt is now set to clear the half-trillion mark next year at $514.7-billion. And it’s forecast to be $541.8-billion the year after that, which is $200-billion more than Ontario’s debt load was when Mr. Ford took office in 2018, after an election campaign in which he accused the predecessor Liberal government of bankrupting the province.

The fall economic statement lays out the damage U.S. tariffs have already done to Ontario. The levies on steel have seen exports to the U.S. sink more than 50 per cent so far this year compared with the same time period in 2024, the economic statement says. Auto exports are down almost 14 per cent since 2024. Exports of all kinds to the U.S. made up 77 per cent of Ontario’s total in 2024. That number fell to 72 per cent in 2025, and it now sits at 64 per cent in 2026 so far, the government said.

Back in March, the Ontario government had predicted modest 1-per-cent growth in real gross domestic product this year, in the face of U.S. tariffs. But now, with the trade war’s escalation, the province expects just half that, based on its conservative read of projections from private-sector economists. Better growth is projected to return next year, though it is still expected to be slow.

Opposition leaders at Queen’s Park panned the government’s fiscal update.

Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles said instead of offering people relief on the high costs of groceries or rent, or proposing solutions to overcrowding in hospitals or schools, Thursday’s update was full of “tired announcements and broken promises.”

“It is stunning to me that this Premier and this Conservative government cannot see what is right in front of them. The people of Ontario are getting crushed under the pressure of rising costs,” Ms. Stiles said.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said the update showed “the worst fiscal management by any government in the history of Ontario.”

As previously announced, the fall economic statement confirms Ontario’s commitment to match the federal government’s “productivity mega deduction,” a sweeping multibillion-dollar tax move to allow companies to accelerate tax writeoffs for a wide range of expenditures.

stories.title: Canadian received Bell Canada text saying 'Welcome to Palestine' while visiting Jerusalem
stories.summary: Bell Canada told National Post that its "roaming notifications are automated by an external vendor’s platform."
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
A Canadian traveller who received a text from Bell Canada welcoming him to “Palestine” while he was in Israel says he is shocked and disappointed.

The Ottawa resident — who only wanted to be identified by his first name, Charles, out of concerns for his safety amid rising antisemitism — told National Post he decided to take a trip to Israel and landed there last week. He was at the Holocaust memorial and museum Yad Vashem in Jerusalem when a text from the telecommunications company popped up on his phone.

“Welcome to Palestine,” it said, followed by information about his account’s travel plan. He said he was nauseated because he was standing in a place that showed the result of the Nazis’ obsession to eradicate the Jewish people. “And I get, from Bell Canada, a welcome to a non-existent country, whose aspirational goal…is to, again, eliminate the Jewish people,” he said.

Hamas, the terrorist group that murdered 1,200 people in Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, the deadliest day for the Jewish community since the Holocaust, refers to the “struggle against the Jews” as “very great and very serious” in its 1988 charter . It calls Jewish people the enemy and says they should be “vanquished.” While there are Palestinians who have denounced the terror group, it has remained in power since taking over Gaza in 2007.

Several European countries, as well as Canada and Australia, recognized the State of Palestine in 2025. Prime Minister Mark Carney said his recognition was conditional, and would be based on whether Hamas would “fully disarm, and play no role in the future governance of Palestine.” Hamas remains in Gaza, using a decentralized system of governance to maintain and expand influence, according to research published by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. Despite the promise of hosting democratic elections this year, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas said they would be postponed until September 2027. There have been no legislative or presidential elections held since 2006.

Charles said it feels like there is a “concerted effort” around the world to erase Israel from existence. But receiving the text from a Canadian company while travelling abroad was especially “outrageous.”

“For them to say to me, a Canadian citizen and a longtime client, ‘Welcome to Palestine’ — to me, that’s making a political statement and it’s inappropriate,” he said.

A spokesperson from Bell Canada told National Post over email that international roaming welcome messages are “automatically triggered when a mobile device connects to a network tower in a new region.”

“Because of the close proximity of network towers in the region, some customers flying into Israel or traveling nearby have occasionally received notifications for roaming in Palestinian territories,” the statement said. “Like those of other global carriers, Bell’s roaming notifications are automated by an external vendor’s platform. This platform retrieves all location terminology directly from an independent, international industry-standard database, and Bell does not determine the language used.”

paragraphs: A Canadian traveller who received a text from Bell Canada welcoming him to “Palestine” while he was in Israel says he is shocked and disappointed.

The Ottawa resident — who only wanted to be identified by his first name, Charles, out of concerns for his safety amid rising antisemitism — told National Post he decided to take a trip to Israel and landed there last week. He was at the Holocaust memorial and museum Yad Vashem in Jerusalem when a text from the telecommunications company popped up on his phone.

“Welcome to Palestine,” it said, followed by information about his account’s travel plan. He said he was nauseated because he was standing in a place that showed the result of the Nazis’ obsession to eradicate the Jewish people. “And I get, from Bell Canada, a welcome to a non-existent country, whose aspirational goal…is to, again, eliminate the Jewish people,” he said.

Hamas, the terrorist group that murdered 1,200 people in Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, the deadliest day for the Jewish community since the Holocaust, refers to the “struggle against the Jews” as “very great and very serious” in its 1988 charter . It calls Jewish people the enemy and says they should be “vanquished.” While there are Palestinians who have denounced the terror group, it has remained in power since taking over Gaza in 2007.

Several European countries, as well as Canada and Australia, recognized the State of Palestine in 2025. Prime Minister Mark Carney said his recognition was conditional, and would be based on whether Hamas would “fully disarm, and play no role in the future governance of Palestine.” Hamas remains in Gaza, using a decentralized system of governance to maintain and expand influence, according to research published by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. Despite the promise of hosting democratic elections this year, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas said they would be postponed until September 2027. There have been no legislative or presidential elections held since 2006.

Charles said it feels like there is a “concerted effort” around the world to erase Israel from existence. But receiving the text from a Canadian company while travelling abroad was especially “outrageous.”
“For them to say to me, a Canadian citizen and a longtime client, ‘Welcome to Palestine’ — to me, that’s making a political statement and it’s inappropriate,” he said.

A spokesperson from Bell Canada told National Post over email that international roaming welcome messages are “automatically triggered when a mobile device connects to a network tower in a new region.”

“Because of the close proximity of network towers in the region, some customers flying into Israel or traveling nearby have occasionally received notifications for roaming in Palestinian territories,” the statement said. “Like those of other global carriers, Bell’s roaming notifications are automated by an external vendor’s platform. This platform retrieves all location terminology directly from an independent, international industry-standard database, and Bell does not determine the language used.”

stories.title: Former MN-S CEO sues for wrongful termination and breach of contract
stories.summary: Métis Nation - Saskatchewan (MN-S) and former CEO Richard Quintal have entered a legal dispute over the former employee’s claims of wrongful termination and breach of contract.
stories.author: Grace Miller
stories.content:
Métis Nation – Saskatchewan (MN-S) and former CEO Richard Quintal have entered a legal dispute over the former employee’s claims of wrongful termination and breach of contract.

Quintal filed his suit on his belief he was let go after an employment contract extension due to political pressures from the Provincial Métis Council (PMC). He alleges he did not receive the compensation he says he is owed.

“On or about April 23, 2026, and as a result of what appeared to be political pressure, the President verbally notified the Plaintiff that the Defendants were going in a different direction and that the Plaintiffs employment with the Defendants was going to be terminated without cause,” reads Quintal’s claim.

He claims after several extensions, he was contracted to work in his position until July 31, 2030, at the time of the termination notice. His claim states PMC confirmed he would be let go effective as of May 15, 2026.

Quintal says he was invited to give an exit speech to PMC and MN-S President Glen McCallum made a public statement and video announcing Quintal’s termination

“The Plaintiff (Quintal) received notice that an emergency meeting of the PMC would be happening on May 11, 2026. The meeting took the entire day, and the President notified the Plaintiff in the evening that a new resolution had been passed, which rescinded his termination without cause and placed him on Suspension,” states the claim.

Quintal says he thinks he was put on suspension to evade the cost of firing him. He says the contract stipulated after being fired without cause he would receive the remainder of the Annual Base Salary which would have been payable over the term of the Agreement.

On June 11, Quintal says he received a letter from MN-S stating that an investigation was going to be launched to review the extension of his contract. He says as of Aug, 24, the investigation was continuing.

Quintal is seeking severance payment in the amount he says he is contractually allocated as well as damages.

MN-S has responded to the court action with an intention to defend the allegations.

stories.title: Ottawa investing up to $1.6B in Canadian AI company Cohere
stories.summary: Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government will invest up to $1.6 billion in Canadian AI company Cohere.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday his government will invest up to $1.6 billion in Canadian AI company Cohere.

He made the announcement in Montreal as he welcomed European Union leaders to a summit aimed at forging closer ties.

“We are not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don’t know or by whom we don’t trust. We’re building it right here in the right way,” Carney said.

In April, Cohere announced it would merge with Germany’s Aleph Alpha and said the company would be “anchored in” Germany and Canada.

On Thursday, Carney called the partnership a concrete example of what Canada and Europe can build together.

He also said that, under the agreement, Cohere will remain Canadian.

Carney said the government is making the announcement on “a commercial basis, alongside private investors including Nvidia, Bell, and Germany’s Schwarz Group.”

Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez said at Thursday’s announcement the company, which was founded seven years ago, is now “one of the very few companies in the world building frontier AI technology at a global scale.”

He added that it’s the largest AI company outside the U.S. and China.

In a press release issued Thursday, the government said the funding would be provided in stages, with regular reporting on commitments made by the company.

Those commitments include creating at least 1,000 “new high-paying Canadian technical jobs” and committing at least $1.7 billion to building more computing infrastructure by 2030.

The government says Cohere will also maintain its Canadian headquarters and incorporation, invest in research partnerships, create opportunities for students and graduates and continue working with the Canadian AI Safety Institute.

“Cohere will now be able to develop far more advanced models and products, scale up its computing infrastructure, and expand its Canadian workforce to serve more businesses and governments in Canada and around the world,” the press release said.

“Building this capability at home ultimately means that Canadian businesses and governments will have more choice in how they adopt AI and greater control over their sensitive information.”

In 2024, the government announced it would provide up to $240 million to Cohere to boost its computing capacity. In 2025, Ottawa signed an agreement with the company to identify areas where AI can enhance public service operations.

Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon has pointed often to Cohere as an element of Canada’s strength in AI and has said that Canada is one of only a few countries with a large language model.

Solomon didn’t answer directly when asked by The Canadian Press whether there is a risk of Cohere leaving the country.

“Today is about providing access to capital to make sure that Canadian companies are built here, that they don’t go elsewhere, that we don’t plant the seed, water the seeds, grow the plant, and let someone else harvest it,” he said.

He also didn’t answer directly when asked whether Carney’s comments on trust meant he was saying some U.S. giants couldn’t be trusted.

“If we don’t build it, we’ve got to buy it from someone else, and if we don’t innovate here, we rent it from someone else and if we don’t make the rules here, we follow someone else’s,” Solomon said. “This is a unique opportunity for Canadians to get a seat at the table on building the future of AI.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

— With files from David Baxter in Montreal

stories.title: Cause under investigation after large dairy barn fire near Listowel
stories.summary: Firefighters from several Perth County-area departments battled a large barn fire near Listowel on Wednesday night
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Firefighters from several Perth County-area departments battled a large barn fire near Listowel on Wednesday night that affected dozens of cattle.

North Perth Fire Department crews from the Listowel, Atwood and Monkton stations were dispatched to a working structure fire at a dairy barn on Line 88 at about 9:05 p.m.

Mutual aid assistance was provided by fire departments from Minto, Mapleton and Howick as crews worked to contain the blaze.

Heavy equipment was brought to the scene at approximately 11:15 p.m. to assist firefighters.

Officials said 88 cattle were involved in the fire, although it remains unclear how many animals were possibly lost.

No injuries to firefighters or anyone else at the scene were reported.

The cause of the fire has not yet been determined and the investigation remains ongoing.

As of Thursday morning, one Listowel fire crew remained at the scene.

Mutual aid assistance was provided by fire departments from Minto, Mapleton and Howick as crews worked to contain the blaze.
Heavy equipment was brought to the scene at approximately 11:15 p.m. to assist firefighters.
Officials said 88 cattle were involved in the fire, although it remains unclear how many animals were possibly lost.
No injuries to firefighters or anyone else at the scene were reported.
The cause of the fire has not yet been determined and the investigation remains ongoing.
As of Thursday morning, one Listowel fire crew remained at the scene.

stories.title: Toronto traffic agent dead after being hit by a truck in East York
stories.summary: Mayor Olivia Chow said in a statement the agent was on duty at the time of the collision, which happened near Millwood Road and Overlea Boulevard.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A City of Toronto traffic agent is dead after being hit by a truck in East York Thursday morning.

Mayor Olivia Chow said in a statement the agent was on duty at the time of the collision, which happened near Millwood Road and Overlea Boulevard.

Police said officers were called to the area at 9:02 a.m. on Thursday and that the victim was pronounced dead on scene.

The driver of the truck remained at the scene, police added.

Chow said she was “heartbroken” to learn the news.

“Traffic agents do some of the most demanding work in our city. They work in live traffic, in all weather conditions, to keep people moving and protect pedestrians, cyclists and drivers,” she said.

“Every shift, they help us get where we’re going safely. We are deeply thankful for that service, and this loss is a painful reminder of the risks they take on our behalf.”

An investigation is underway.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Belleville - Police in Belleville, Ont., say an officer who was shot on Yom Kippur while protecting a synagogue full of worshippers from an armed attacker has been released from the hospital.

Belleville police say Const. Jeff Smith is at home and making “positive progress” in his recovery, a little over a month after the shooting.

stories.title: Ottawa buys stake in Cohere as AI firm raises money at $35.7-billion valuation
stories.summary: Financing is the largest ever by a Canadian startup and would make Cohere the country’s most valuable privately held tech company
stories.author: Murad Hemmadi, Joe Castaldo
stories.content:
The Canadian government is putting $1.6-billion into Cohere as part of a planned $7-billion financing, an unprecedented move to take a stake in a firm it has crowned a Canadian AI champion.

The Toronto-based AI company announced Thursday that it had secured most of the funding round, which would value it at $35.7-billion. The financing is the largest-ever by a Canadian startup. Once completed, it would make Cohere the country’s most valuable privately held technology company.

The round was led by German retail giant Schwarz Group and includes funding from Bell Canada’s venture arm and Luxembourg-based Bullhound Capital, Cohere said on Thursday.

Returning backers that have committed to the financing include chip giant Nvidia Corp., Montreal’s Inovia Capital, and Prosperity7 Ventures, an arm of Saudi Aramco.

The Canadian government’s direct equity investment is notable both because of its size and the fact that Cohere competes in the capital-intensive AI industry, where profits have been elusive. The deal is part of Ottawa’s strategy to build out and secure the country’s AI strengths and economic sovereignty.

Cohere chief financial officer Francois Chadwick said in an interview that the financing is necessary for the company to invest in compute infrastructure, develop its AI models and expand globally.

“Canada needs to be there at the forefront,” Mr. Chadwick said. “Instead of having two global leaders – China and the U.S. – Canada becomes a global leader in the AI world.”

To secure Ottawa’s investment, Cohere has committed to spend $1.7-billion on the buildout of compute infrastructure in Canada by 2030. It has also promised to remain headquartered in the country.

“Under this agreement, Cohere will stay Canadian,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said at a press conference announcing the investment on Thursday, calling the new round a “vote of confidence” in both Cohere and Canada.

The Globe and Mail first reported last month that Cohere had told investors it was in advanced talks to raise as much as US$3-billion, including financing from the Canadian and German governments, at a valuation of US$20-billion.

“We started with some original figures on what we were looking to raise,” Mr. Chadwick said, adding that investor demand was higher than expected. He added: “Because we were oversubscribed on our original thinking, we’ve kept the investment open, and we will be looking to close soon.”

Cohere announced in September it had agreed on final terms on its proposed merger with Aleph Alpha GmbH, a German AI company backed by Schwarz. Earlier this month, Cohere reached a deal to acquire Aisle, a Prague-based cybersecurity startup. It also launched a new version of its flagship software platform North, which lets workers at its corporate and government clients set up AI agents to automate tasks such as financial analysis and coding.

The financing would significantly boost Cohere’s valuation, from roughly US$7-billion in a round last September.

Cohere, which develops large language models and software systems powered by them, faces stiff competition in its chosen market of AI tools for large private and public sector organizations. OpenAI and Anthropic already generate billions of dollars in revenue from such customers. Meanwhile, many businesses are switching some AI tasks to cheaper models, often from Chinese developers, to contain costs.

Cohere is much smaller than the leaders of the field in Silicon Valley. Annualized revenues were up 165 per cent year-over-year last month, and its customer base has increased 20-fold to 300 clients over the last year, the company has said. In February, Cohere told investors it had reached an annualized revenue rate of US$240-million in 2025. (Mr. Chadwick declined to comment on Cohere’s current revenue.)

The company sells its technology as a sovereign alternative to that of U.S. and Chinese developers. Cohere has made many of its recent AI models open source, meaning that users can download and run them on their own hardware. It also touts the control and privacy features of its technology.

Cohere is developing customized tools for highly regulated and sensitive industries such as financial services, telecommunications, health care and energy. The firm will have over 1,000 staff following the Aleph Alpha merger, and has agreed to double that number as part of its federal deal.

Ottawa has championed Cohere as a strategic asset in its bid to make Canada into a significant AI power.

“This company is absolutely critical,” AI Minister Evan Solomon said in an interview. “In the world of AI, we need to make sure that Canada has a building place at the table.” He added that the federal investment was made on “very favourable commercial terms,” and will be paid out based on Cohere reaching its hiring and infrastructure commitments.

Ottawa’s updated national AI strategy, launched in June, also includes $500-million for a new Canadian Tech Growth Fund, which will back later-stage startups and could take equity stakes in them. Ottawa has committed $1.75-billion to help seed venture-capital funds in a bid to boost the amount of investment available to growing firms.

Thursday’s equity investment is not the first support that Ottawa has provided the company. In 2024, a federal industrial fund awarded Cohere $240-million to help pay for the processing power to train its AI models on Canadian soil. Last year, Ottawa signed a non-binding agreement with the firm to test its technology for use in the public service. Cohere has since landed some small federal pilot contracts.

Ottawa’s equity investment “helps position the company on a global front for sovereignty, across global partnerships with other countries,” according to Chris Arsenault, a partner at Inovia, whose firm has put more than US$100-million into Cohere to date. He said the latest round should also inspire other Canadian entrepreneurs that it’s possible to “to build big” and “to become global” at home rather than selling to a larger U.S. firm.

Canada isn’t the only country making direct investments in domestic champions in strategically-important technology sectors. The Trump administration has taken stakes in chip maker Intel and several quantum computer developers.

Founded in 2019, Cohere is led by chief executive Aidan Gomez, one of the authors on a much-cited research paper that provided a key building block for LLMs. The firm’s other investors include Radical Ventures, the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, the Public Sector Pension Investment Board and the Healthcare of Ontario Pension Plan.

Cohere’s models significantly lag those of OpenAI and Anthropic on key capabilities such as coding and cybersecurity, according to industry technical rankings . Mr. Gomez has acknowledged the gap, and said the firm is racing to secure the compute and financing needed to close it.

stories.title: Toronto dad and two daughters shot in violent Bridle Path home invasion: police
stories.summary: Three of four residents of a house in an affluent Toronto neighbourhood were shot during a violent home invasion early Thursday morning.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
A Toronto father and his adult daughter are fighting for their lives in hospital after being shot during a violent home invasion in their affluent neighbourhood early Thursday morning.

Two other members, the man’s wife and other daughter, are also in hospital with what Toronto Police Service said are non-life-threatening injuries suffered as a result of the incident in the Bridle Path area.

In a Thursday morning news conference, Insp. Kristy Smith, of the TPS investigative unit Hold Up Squad, said officers were dispatched to the home on Bayview Avenue and Lawrence Avenue East around 4 a.m., where three masked suspects armed with handguns forced their way in through a rear door. One also carried a hammer, but Smith said it’s unclear if it was used to break into the home.

“Once inside, they confronted the family,” Smith said.

“A struggle ensued during this altercation, in which the suspects fired their guns multiple times, and one victim was struck with a hammer.”

At this time, police don’t believe the victims returned fire.

Smith said it was too early to determine if the home was targeted or the suspect’s motive, though she did imply it could be another case of a home invasion for the purpose of stealing a high-end vehicle, incidents of which she said are on the rise.

In Canada, some police are 'worse than the burglar' for those defending themselves

Indigenous Toronto man with a criminal record of 101 break-ins gets time served

“Typically in an affluent neighbourhood come nice things, and there’s always people out there that want to acquire nice things. And carjackings used to be a way that criminals would acquire cars. That seems to have transitioned into breaking into a home to steal a vehicle,” she said, noting the homeowner’s vehicle was not stolen.

Smith went on to say citizens “can’t go around always being paranoid about having nice things,” but they should “be ultra aware” of whether they are being followed and contact 911 if they feel like they are.

About 30 minutes after the incident, police also responded to a shooting in the area of The Queensway and Parkside Drive, at the opposite end of the city, where one adult male arrived at a hospital with a non-life-threatening gunshot wound. It’s unknown where the incident took place, and there’s no information about a suspect.

“We are aware of that incident, and I can’t say whether it’s connected or not,” Smith said, “but it’s definitely something that we’re going to investigate so that we can draw that connection if there is one.”

Bridle Path residents can expect an increased police presence in the days ahead as police investigate and step up patrols.

“We recognize how frightening and disturbing an incident like this is not only for the victims, but also for the residents and the entire community, including the loved ones of the extended family. People should be able to feel safe in their homes. I want to assure residents that us as the Toronto Police Service will do everything that we can to identify, locate, and bring these suspects to criminal justice.”

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.
