“Lake Ontario is forever.”
Adams is not the first Canadian act to stand up for the body of water.
In August, Blue Rodeo’s hit Hasn’t Hit Me Yet went viral after thousands of fans at their Toronto concert were captured screaming along to the lyric: “Out in the middle of Lake Ontario.”
Co-frontman Greg Keelor told The Canadian Press he was happy to see the song become a “rallying call.”
“That’s a very powerful body of water,” he said.
“Most Canadians, it wasn’t really something in your brain, it was just Lake Ontario. But now it’s taken on a significance and it’s a bit of a line in the sand.”

stories.title: Decimated B.C. NDP caucus meeting to discuss interim leadership after election loss
stories.summary: Members of the decimated B.C. NDP caucus are set to meet at the legislature Thursday to discuss who will be the interim leader of the party after its weekend election defeat.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Members of the decimated B.C. NDP caucus are set to meet at the legislature Thursday to discuss who will be the interim leader of the party after its weekend election defeat.

The caucus has been reduced to 28 members after going into Saturday’s election numbering 47, while the B.C. Conservatives have a crushing two-thirds majority with 63 seats.

Outgoing Premier David Eby announced his resignation as party leader in his election-night concession speech, and it’s not clear if he’ll be at the caucus meeting.

The outgoing NDP caucus met online on Wednesday.

MLA-elect Niki Sharma is expected to speak to reporters ahead of this morning’s meeting.

Geoff Meggs, who was chief of staff for the late former NDP premier John Horgan, says the next leader faces the “reputational challenge” of proving the party can be trusted with taxpayers’ money.

Horgan left Eby a $5.7-billion surplus when he stepped aside in 2022, but Eby’s government turned that into a record deficit that’s forecast to hit $14 billion this year.

Meggs said in an interview on Wednesday that while voters want services protected, they also want to see some balance in spending.

stories.title: Toronto penthouse seller makes six-figure price cut to find a buyer
stories.summary: Two bedroom, three bathroom penthouse south of St. Lawrence Market sold for $1.5-million
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
1 Market St., Ph 1., Toronto

Asking price: $1,599,900 (June, 2026)

Previous asking prices: $1,699,900 (May 26); $1,775,000 (May 7); $1,849,900 (April, 2026)

Selling price: $1.5-million (August, 2026)

Previous selling price: $791,150 (2013)

Taxes: $6,691 (2026)

Days on the market: 58

Property days on market: 110

Listing and buyer’s agent: Elias Ben Khelifa, Corcoran Horizon Realty

Last year, a two-storey penthouse with a large terrace sold for $ 2.6-million at Market Wharf, a 34-storey building south of St. Lawrence Market. Next door, this 1,290-square-foot penthouse had a smaller, two-storey footprint, but considering its custom additions, including three skylights, a third bathroom and a new staircase, agent Elias Ben Khelifa suggested a list price of $1,849,900 this spring.

“It was really hard to use comparable sales in the building or the area to determine what its value was,” said Mr. Khelifa.

“It’s higher than the average price per square foot downtown, but it’s reflective of the fact this is a premium unit and location, basically right by St. Lawrence Market.”

But three cuts to the asking price – and a stretch of sunny weather that underscored the perks of having a 600-square-foot terrace with a built-in barbecue – were needed before the two-bedroom suite received a $1.5-million purchase offer in August.

“It took a little bit longer to sell than usual with market conditions,” said Mr. Khelifa.

“The unit had a west-facing terrace with no overhang, and it was something people were really drawn to. It has amazing forever views of the city.”

The 13-year-old penthouse has 10-foot ceilings, full-height windows and sliding doors to the terrace from the kitchen and living room.

The bedrooms are on the second floor.

The unit has a storage locker and one parking spot. Monthly fees of $1,102 cover water, heating, concierge, and use of building recreational amenities.

“The owner modified the floor plan with the builder, adding skylights and a third bathroom,” Mr. Khelifa said.

“Another major modification was relocating the stairs, which was originally a spiral staircase.”

This article was updated to include the property’s previous selling price.

stories.title: Ottawa-based AI video-surveillance company Solink raises $100-million in growth capital
stories.summary: The company’s software marries security feeds from its cameras to point-of-sale data for insights that businesses can use to improve operations
stories.author: Sean Silcoff
stories.content:
Solink Corp., an Ottawa company that sells artificial intelligence software to monitor business operations in more than 35,000 restaurants, stores and other locations, has raised US$100-million in growth capital.

Toronto-based private-equity firm Vertu Capital led the financing, backed by Goldman Sachs Asset Management’s GS Growth unit and new investors Golub Growth and Comcast Ventures. About 90 per cent of the amount raised went to Solink; the rest was paid to early investors for their stakes.

“We thought it was important to bring on another Canadian backer,” as the country seeks to assert its economic strength at a time of geopolitical uncertainty, Solink’s chief executive officer Mike Matta said. “As a Canadian founder, I’m very passionate about building a category-defining business that just happens to be in Canada.”

This is the third time a Canadian entity has led a Solink financing: Generation Ventures led a $5-million seed financing in 2017 and Omers Ventures led a $23-million venture financing in 2020. (Laura Lenz was the partner on both deals, first at Generation, then Omers.)

Chicago-based Valor Equity Partners led a $16.3-million financing in 2019 and New York-based GS Growth led a US$60-million round in 2023. Business Development Bank of Canada is also an investor.

Ottawa technology billionaire Terry Matthews was an early investor. Last year, he gave up office space occupied by his Wesley Clover International holding company to accommodate Solink’s expansion. The software company now has 350 employees, up fourfold since 2021.

Solink was founded in 2010 by Mr. Matta, who came up with the idea after he spent time tracking customer-traffic patterns for BCE Inc.’s The Source retail chain. Rather than going store to store to collect data, the University of Waterloo electrical engineering graduate set out to develop software that could remotely tap into existing security cameras used by businesses for insurance and security-monitoring purposes. His software would eventually use AI to mine the videos for insights that managers could use to improve operations.

Solink’s software marries security feeds from its cameras to point-of-sale data. It uses AI to rifle through the combined data to pinpoint specific events, such as when employees key in discounts. It uploads relevant snippets to the cloud so operators can access and search them, sending out updates about anomalies and unusual activity.

Solink’s software expanded in scope as customers used its technology for more than just enhancing security and preventing theft and loss. Those applications included ensuring drive-through traffic moves steadily, shelves and display case items are regularly replenished and safety hazards are addressed.

“You’re seeing the Solink platform permeate more through different departments,” said Ms. Lenz, who heads Omers Ventures. “Marketing, sales and operations use it, as well as loss prevention. That increases contract value, net dollar retention and stickiness and reduces churn.”

Solink “sits at the intersection of the physical and digital world, which is an exciting opportunity to be in,” Vertu partner Eric Kafka said. “We see a huge market opportunity. Solink is well-positioned to take that.”

The company’s first key customer was a Tim Hortons franchisee, leading to adoption by hundreds more stores within the chain. It has been adopted by owners or franchisees of such brands as Gap, Five Guys, Jack in the Box, Pet Valu, Dollar Tree, Chick-fil-A and PGA Tour Superstore, across 65 countries.

Solink uploads more than 750 million hours of data a month – 20 times the amount uploaded to YouTube daily, Mr. Matta said. Solink has been growing its revenues by more than 40 per cent a year and is on track to surpass the US$100-million mark on an annual basis by April, he added.

Mr. Matta said Solink now has an opportunity to expand its deployment of AI agents to automate managers’ directions to staff on improving operations based on data received through its platform.

The financing will largely be used to build out the supporting “intelligence layer” for the agents that Solink offers customers. Mr. Matta expects use of those agents and related intelligence tools to account for more than 40 per cent of Solink revenues within three years, up from less than 10 per cent now.

stories.title: Risen from the ashes of tragedy, the ‘Phoenix House’ was built to be a zero-carbon home
stories.summary: The owners’ ultimate goal was to create the first home in Canada to earn Zero Carbon Certification from the International Living Future Institute
stories.author: Matthew Hague
stories.content:
From a certain angle, the roof of JP Clinging and Ritz Aranyaphong-Clinging’s home in Abbotsford, B.C., resembles a bird taking flight. The house is divided into two wings (no pun intended). One is for the couple, both entrepreneurs, and their teenage son. The other accommodates members of their extended family: Ritz’s mother, sister and nephew. Where the two volumes meet, a folding, jet-black roofline rises high into the air in either direction.

“It’s one reason we call it the Phoenix House,” says Vancouver architect Nick Bray, founder of Nick Bray Architecture. (Bray also points out that the roof’s central spine, as it were, also serves a practical purpose: directing rainwater to a downspout).

There is another, deeper reason for the name. The house has, quite literally, risen from the ashes of a tragedy. In 2022, while JP and Ritz were out, an electrical fire tore through their previous home. “We basically lost everything,” says Ritz.

The couple could have taken their insurance payout and moved elsewhere. But they had lived on the property for more than 20 years and didn’t want to leave. “It’s where we have raised our son,” says JP. “We still had our memories.”

In rebuilding, they focused on long-term durability. “After all the shock, we asked ourselves, how do we build back a better home?” Ritz recalls. “We lived four doors away from a firehall, and still this happened.”

Fire protection was paramount. Many of the cladding materials used on the new house are fire-resistant. These include rugged, cement-based Hardie Board panels on the lower level; cedar planks on the upper level, reclaimed from trees damaged in forest fires; and Enviroshake roofing shingles, made from recycled industrial waste.

“Compared to a typical asphalt shingle, which have to be replaced every 15 to 20 years, Enviroshakes are bulletproof,” says Mr. Bray. “They are more like the slate I saw where I grew up in England – something that will last a long, long time.”

Beyond fire resistance, JP and Ritz wanted the house to be sustainable in other ways. “A modern home that gets quickly slapped together might last 40 years,” says JP. “We wanted a home that would last 150 years or longer. We wanted to build for the future, maybe future generations of our family.”

Their ultimate goal was to create the first home in Canada to earn Zero Carbon Certification from the International Living Future Institute. The demanding designation recognizes homes designed to minimize the carbon emissions associated with construction and produce negligible emissions during operation over their lifespan.

During construction, Phoenix House required significantly less carbon than a comparable home of its size – about 3,500 square feet, with room for six full-time residents. Material choices helped. Although little remained of the previous house, some wall studs were salvaged and repurposed, reducing the need for new lumber. The existing foundation was also sound and was reused in its entirety, avoiding the emissions associated with pouring additional concrete. “That was important as concrete is a major source of carbon emissions,” says Mr. Bray.

To improve energy efficiency, the walls are almost completely airtight, minimizing heat loss in the winter. Triple-pane windows are shaded to prevent the house from overheating in summer. A rainwater collection system also reduces reliance on municipal water, an important consideration in a drought-prone region such as southern B.C.

While the house functions as a high-performance green machine, one of its most striking features is its visual appeal. The aesthetic is Scandinavian and clean-lined, with none of the stereotypical hippie look often associated with ultra-sustainable buildings.

Josephina Serra, an interior designer and co-founder of Vancouver’s Form Collective, worked closely with Bray on the design. “JP and Ritz didn’t necessarily care about a future buyer or have a goal of resale,” says Ms. Serra. “So we were able to be a bit bold, play with interesting colours.”

Off the entryway, a switchback staircase combines steps with built-in benches, creating an effect reminiscent of an amphitheatre. It faces a sculptural fireplace with a vapour-based insert that produces no carbon emissions from burning wood or gas.

Along one side of the stairs, the metal railing is painted a bright avocado green. The hue complements the terracotta tones in the nearby kitchen, including a red range hood clad in Dekton, an engineered, porcelain-based surface.

“JP and Ritz are such warm, vibrant people so it really works for them,” says Ms. Serra.

Throughout the interiors, sustainability informed the couple’s decisions. Dekton, also used for the fireplace hearth and various countertops, is manufactured in Spain by Cosentino. “The material had to travel a long way to get here,” says Ritz. “But it’s one of the lowest carbon surfaces on the market, one that will last a long time. Over its whole life cycle, we hope the energy it took to get here is offset by how much we use it, how long it takes before it needs to be replaced.”

stories.title: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk to perform his first spacewalk
stories.summary: Kutryk, along with Nasa astronaut Anil Menon, will upgrade the International Space Station’s power generation system
stories.author: Erika Morris
stories.content:
Astronaut Joshua Kutryk was some 420 kilometres above the Earth when he stepped into the vacuum of space on Thursday morning, making him the fifth Canadian to perform a spacewalk.

Kutryk and Nasa astronaut Anil Menon placed their suits on battery power at 7:57 a.m. EDT, marking the official beginning of the spacewalk. They are working to install solar panels on part of the International Space Station, using the Canadarm2 robotic arm as a base for Menon to stand on.

The spacewalk was expected to last nearly seven hours. The duo will install seven of eight new solar arrays needed to upgrade the station’s power capacity.

Astronauts inside the station wished Kutryk and Menon luck before they left the airlock.

“From Luke [Delaney] and I on the other side of the hatch, good luck. We’re proud of you and we’ll see you on the other side,” Nasa flight engineer Jessica Watkins told them.

Kutryk is on his first mission in space and his trip outside the space station is expected to be his first of two spacewalks.

Before Kutryk, the last Canadian to perform a spacewalk was David Saint-Jacques in 2019.

Saint-Jacques answered questions from schoolchildren at the Montreal Science Centre as the space agency projected the livestream showing the spacewalk.

He described the feat as “one of the most exciting and one of most dangerous things we do” and said Kutryk was in “very good spirits” when they last spoke ahead of the spacewalk.

“It’s kind of the peak of the career for an astronaut to get a chance to put on your own miniature spacecraft that we call a space suit and go outside to do some maintenance work,” he said.

Saint-Jacques said spacewalkers train for thousands of hours in a giant pool and a full-size replica of the space station in Houston. They learn to operate the space suit and study the procedures and equipment needed for their mission.

They also receive step-by-step instructions in real time.

The crew’s mission is crucial, Saint-Jacques said, as the station is nearly 30 years old and its original solar panels have lost efficiency. According to the Canadian Space Agency, the new panels, paired with previously installed arrays, will help increase power generation capacity on the station by up to 30 per cent. The space station is fully electric, said Saint-Jacques.

While astronauts can face technical challenges, such as a stuck bolt or trouble plugging in a connector, the veteran astronaut does not doubt Kutryk’s abilities.

The advice he gave the spacewalker? To really take in the view.

“Give yourself the chance to look around, let it all sink in, and come back with some emotions as well, because that really is what you bring back for yourself,” he said. “It’s very easy to get focused in the work, to want to do a good job.”

Canadian Space Agency astronaut David Saint-Jacques on the advice he gave Kutryk ahead of his spacewalk. The Canadian Press

Canada is also playing a role in the mission from the ground.

While Watkins and Delaney, also a Nasa flight engineer, assisted the spacewalkers with the Canadarm2 robotic arm, a Canadian Space Agency team were monitoring and supporting activities in real time from Longueuil, Que.

Canadian astronaut Jenni Gibbons was supporting the spacewalkers from Nasa’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. The Canadian Space Agency described her as “the voice bridging two worlds” as she was the main link between experts on Earth and the space crew.

Gibbons was giving the astronauts directions as they carried out the maintenance work. She also served as the capsule communicator during the Artemis II lunar fly-by in April.

“Canada delivers. And so I’m very, very proud of our space sector,” said Saint-Jacques. “It’s a long history of success that we should all be very proud of ... at the forefront of exploration, breaking silos, innovating.”

Kutryk and Menon departed from the Quest airlock module on the space station to install solar panels on the portside truss structure of the orbital outpost.

The truss serves as the station’s structural backbone and supports major systems, including solar wings, radiators, power, data and temperature-control equipment.

The crew’s second spacewalk is scheduled for Nov. 5.

stories.title: The election that left Israel in limbo
stories.summary: The Big Story discusses what kind of coalition calculus could be on the horizon in Israel and the impact of the Arab vote.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
Israelis showed up in historic numbers to have their voice heard in Tuesday’s national election.

It’s been more than a day since polls closed, and although official results remain unclear, neither Benjamin Netanyahu or his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, aren’t projected to form a majority government.

Host Caryn Ceolin speaks with Aurel Braun, an international relations professor at the University of Toronto, to discuss what kind of coalition calculus could be on the horizon, the impact of the Arab vote, and the obstacles in the way of a possible unity government.

stories.title: Montreal police explain why it took a day to dismantle unit accused of misconduct
stories.summary: Montreal police say a 16-member patrol unit rocked by a racism scandal remained armed and active for nearly a full day after investigators secured enough evidence to take action.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux
stories.content:
Montreal police say a 16-member patrol unit rocked by a racism scandal remained armed and active for nearly a full day after investigators secured enough evidence to take action about allegations some officers engaged in criminal misconduct.

Police chief Fady Dagher announced at a late Friday evening news conference in mid-June that he was dismantling the unit, explaining the force was moving as fast as possible to protect the public.

But police confirmed they took a day to prepare their move when asked about internal documents showing that investigators reached a threshold justifying “decisive management actions” on June 11, one day before they intervened.

Police say the officers were on duty from 9 p.m. on June 11 until approximately 6:30 a.m. the following morning, during which they were assigned to respond to emergency calls.

A few hours later, police say they dismantled the unit, between 8:30 p.m. and 9 p.m. on June 12.

“Several logistical issues had to be resolved, including replacing the entire team to avoid any interruption of services to the public,” police told The Canadian Press in an emailed statement.

The police force declined to address questions about whether any members had direct contact with the public between June 11 and June 12.

The internal documents were part of a briefing package prepared for Dagher, prior to an appearance at municipal hearings in August. The Canadian Press obtained the documents through access to information legislation.

Ericka Alneus, Montreal’s official Opposition leader, said Dagher needs to be more transparent about what happened, warning that public trust in the force is low.

“This new information raises questions and concerns, at a time when trust with citizens is already fragile,” Alneus told The Canadian Press in a statement. “It is urgent that Mr. Dagher provide an explanation and work to rebuild the relationship with Montrealers.”

The unit operated in Montréal-Nord, a multicultural borough in the city’s northeast with a history of tensions between residents and police, including allegations of police brutality.

Police began investigating the team in March after receiving internal complaints about alleged racism and criminal misconduct, including reports that officers cut the hair of racialized citizens and kept it as trophies.

All 16 members of the unit were removed from their regular duties, with two initially suspended, three assigned administrative duties and 11 reassigned. By August, four officers had been suspended.

Police also referred evidence involving four officers to public prosecutors, who have not yet announced whether criminal charges will be laid.

Ted Rutland, a Concordia University geography professor who researches policing and racial profiling in Montreal, questioned whether the police acted fast enough.

“Could they not have predicted these logistical challenges and, you know, prepared a better plan of action so that they could act more quickly?” he said.

Rutland said the need to maintain emergency services was understandable but questioned whether the officers could have been temporarily removed from patrol duties while replacements were arranged.

Alain Babineau, a former RCMP staff sergeant who now works on racial profiling issues with the Red Coalition, a Montreal-based anti-racism organization, also noted how it took police three months to dismantle the patrol unit after they started the investigation.

“Your number 1 duty is to protect the public, and they failed, in my opinion,” he said.

Babineau argued that officers facing serious allegations could have been suspended with pay while the investigation continued.

He also questioned whether supervisors had ignored warning signs of misconduct.

“How many commanders over the last 10 years have either turned a blind eye to this kind of misbehaviour or been complicit?” he asked.

Police would only inform the public about what had happened at a news conference that began at 10:30 p.m. on June 12, about an hour after they notified journalists.

Stéphane Prud’homme, a lecturer in strategic communications and public relations at Université de Montréal who specializes in reputation management, said the unusual timing and short notice limited journalists’ ability to prepare questions, verify information and seek outside perspectives.

Prud’homme said the documents suggest the force intended to be transparent but do not explain why the news conference was held so late or whether its timing had been planned.

He said genuine transparency also requires giving journalists an actual opportunity to scrutinize information and properly inform the public.

Jennifer Magnus, a former Calgary police officer who now teaches public safety at Wilfrid Laurier University in Ontario and studies organizational culture in policing, said dismantling an entire patrol team quickly and discreetly can be necessary to protect an investigation.

But Magnus said a late Friday news conference with little notice can create the perception that police are trying to limit public scrutiny, particularly in communities where trust in law enforcement is already strained.

stories.title: Canada welcomes EU leaders to Montreal for talks on next steps in relationship
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to welcome European Commissioner Ursula von der Leyen to Montreal Thursday after months of pursuing closer ties with the EU.
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to welcome European Commissioner Ursula von der Leyen to Montreal Thursday after months of pursuing closer ties with the EU.

While membership in the EU is off the table, officials on both sides say they’re looking at ways to forge closer ties in the business, tech, clean energy and critical minerals fields.

Von der Leyen described the proposed partnership as “associate membership” in the 27 nation bloc, but some European leaders have rejected that term.

European officials repeatedly used the phrase “alliance for the future” to describe the relationship in a press briefing Tuesday — phrasing previously endorsed by Carney.

There’s drama on the Canadian side too, as Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has pressured the federal government to allow him to deliver a speech at the event.

Today’s agenda includes a welcome dinner with elected and business leaders before Canadian and European leaders get down to talks on Friday.

stories.title: Fire at New Brunswick military base not threat to public: defence officials
stories.summary: The Department of National Defence says the blaze in the northeastern part of the Canadian Forces Base Gagetown training area is being monitored.
stories.author: Aaron Sousa
stories.content:
Military officials say a fire burning in an area of a central New Brunswick army base isn’t a threat to public safety.

The Department of National Defence says the blaze in the northeastern part of the Canadian Forces Base Gagetown training area is being monitored.

A notice posted on social media says unauthorized entry onto the training area is prohibited and May pose significant safety risks.

“There is currently no threat to nearby communities,” the notice says.

“Residents May observe smoke in the area. The presence of smoke does not indicate a threat to surrounding communities.”

It says scheduled training activities in the area of the fire have been suspended as a precaution. It also says flying drones over the training area is prohibited.

The department also notes that no military members are in the area of the fire.

The notice comes less than two weeks after a devastating grass fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta that killed four soldiers and sent dozens more to hospital.

CFB Gagetown is roughly 27 kilometres southeast of Fredericton and is the second largest military base in Canada.

In April 2005, three soldiers were injured after a military jeep overturned while pulling a trailer during a training exercise at the base.

The department also notes that no military members are in the area of the fire.
The notice comes less than two weeks after a devastating grass fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta that killed four soldiers and sent dozens more to hospital.
CFB Gagetown is roughly 27 kilometres southeast of Fredericton and is the second largest military base in Canada.
In April 2005, three soldiers were injured after a military jeep overturned while pulling a trailer during a training exercise at the base.

stories.title: Young London runner gives up position in race final to help struggling counterpart
stories.summary: A sudden act of kindness from a young London, Ont. boy during a championship race is spreading through southwestern Ontario.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
A sudden act of kindness from a young London, Ont., boy during a championship race is spreading through southwestern Ontario.

Jackson McClymont and Mathias Oke crossed the finish line together at the Thames Valley District School Board cross-country finals, only after Jackson came to Mathias’ aid halfway through the race.

Jackson had been on pace for a strong finish.

“I thought I could get bragging rights or something, maybe I could get a medal!” recalled Jackson.

But as he prepared to sprint, he noticed Mathias, a student at Turtle Island Public School in Woodstock, was struggling.

“He was breathing really hard,” he noticed.

While Jackson was not aware that Mathias battles asthma, he could see the boy he had never met before needed a friend. It is a moment Mathias won’t soon forget.

“And then as I’m going up the hill, I see a hand push me to go farther ahead,” Mathias recalled.

The pair continued the race side-by-side, with Mathias listening to words of encouragement from Jackson.

“[He kept saying], ‘You got to keep pushing, you’re almost there!’” said Mathias.

At the finish line, Jackson decided to take a step back, “I just said, you know, maybe this guy wanted to finish better than he did, so I’m just going to let him go in front of me.”

The moment was captured by Matthias’ mother, Renee. She contacted Jackson’s school, Ashley Oaks in London. His teacher, Ericka Deakin, was among the staff impressed.

Recognition from the school and Mathias’ family followed.

Jackson’s grandmother, Michelle, said he never told her about his act. She learned about it from his school.

“He just did this, and he didn’t go on about it to anybody, and I’m super proud of him!” she said.

Renee said she is grateful for Jackson’s kindness and her own son’s unprompted appreciation, calling it a moment we can all learn from.

“In this day and age where everything is so dark and so heavy, there are kind people, kind kids, kind adults. The people that raised Jackson should be so proud of themselves.”

During the CTV News interview, the boys learned they share several common interests and told us they intend to become — and stay — friends.

stories.title: Rising costs, trade risks cloud Canada’s construction outlook despite activity uptick
stories.summary: The outlook for Canada's construction sector remains "uneven" heading into 2027 as activity improved last quarter, despite challenges such as higher material costs and slower residential demand.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
The outlook for Canada’s construction sector remains “uneven” heading into 2027 as activity improved last quarter, despite challenges such as higher material costs and slower residential demand.

The Canadian Construction Association’s latest quarterly report shows construction sector GDP rose one per cent in the second quarter, driven by gains in both engineering construction and residential building construction.

That followed two consecutive quarterly declines and brought overall activity back to levels seen around a year earlier, the association said.

But there are risks to sustaining that rebound, including the industry’s rising input costs. Statistics Canada said non-residential building construction costs increased 3.5 per cent year-over-year in the quarter, while construction costs for residential buildings rose 2.3 per cent.

The report said steel-intensive construction divisions are experiencing some of the strongest cost increases at more than eight per cent year-over-year.

Higher fuel prices, tariffs on steel and aluminum products, and additional duties on imported wood cabinets and vanities are also contributing to ongoing pricing pressures throughout the construction supply chain.

The report also noted the broader effect of ongoing trade uncertainty on the sector. Around 40 per cent of the inputs used by Canada’s construction industry are imported, with the U.S. accounting for 25 percentage points of that share, it said.

The association said exposure to trade risks is particularly high in engineering construction. In communications and oil and gas engineering, roughly 40 per cent of inputs are sourced from the United States, while imports from south of the border account for around 21 per cent of inputs for residential construction.

“Many contractors saw the tariff announcements. Far fewer heard of new remissions that came quietly in their wake,” the report said.

“Nation-building ambitions have expanded the long-term project pipeline, but the promise of tomorrow’s megaprojects should not distract from the pressures the industry is currently facing. Geopolitical conflicts also continue to have economic consequences long after they fade from public attention. Their effects can persist across energy markets, trade flows, supply chains, project costs, and construction timelines.”

The report also pointed to a “soft” residential pipeline in some of Canada’s largest markets. It said contractors are facing a lack of growth in the existing project pipeline, particularly for highrise residential properties.

That comes as Canada’s population growth has stagnated and its largest housing market remains “subdued,” as the pace of new condo projects in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area has slowed compared with recent years.

“Our industry remains resilient, but we are increasingly divided between emerging opportunities and near-term challenges,” Nicole Emmett, the association’s vice-president of communications, marketing and members services, said in a news release.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

stories.title: If I could turn back time: B.C. is making a mistake by not changing the clocks
stories.summary: It is frankly alarming that for part of the year, sunrise will now occur during regular business hours
stories.author: Marsha Lederman
stories.content:
I walked to the SkyTrain in the dark this week. It was early, but not so early for it to feel like the middle of the night. The stars twinkled (somewhere, behind the clouds). The coyotes hunted. And the workers of Vancouver moved less-than-visibly through it all in the pitch black. It was unnerving.

Normally, this condition would be remedied by the great falling back of early November. When the broadcasters tell us with a smile that we’ll get an extra hour of sleep over the weekend (and parents of young children throw daggers at the device airing this information because they will experience no such thing). I’m a big fan of falling-back. And even of springing-ahead, when we “lose” that hour of sleep, but no longer have sunlight streaming through the windows at 5 a.m. (see young children, above).

Earlier this year, the B.C. government announced that most of the province would do away with the time change and stick with Daylight Saving Time (DST) year-round, getting a ball rolling that Alberta then picked up. And now Quebec will abolish the time change too.

In its surprise announcement last March, B.C. touted a 2019 survey that showed 93 per cent of British Columbians supported a move to permanent DST. More than 223,000 people (out of a population of more than five million) took the online survey.

The survey only offered two choices: stick with the time changes twice a year, or move to DST year-round. It did not offer as an option staying with Standard Time (ST) year-round. That is a remarkable oversight.

The most common response in the survey’s open-ended questions answered by people against the time change indicated that the respondent would prefer to stick with Standard Time.

“It is not possible to estimate to what extent survey respondents would have selected a year-round ST option, had it been made available on the survey,” the report stated.

Notably, people in the construction industry – you know, the folks who are out there working early, in the dark – were significantly more likely than most other groups to prefer the status quo.

Of the 10 formal submissions from organizations and experts that supported ending the twice-yearly change, four argued for year-round observance of ST.

Two of the submissions worried that year-round DST would increase traffic problems during morning commutes in winter months.

And the submission by Vancouver Island’s Medical Health Officers called for “a health-focused review to assist policy-makers when examining future impacts of time observance on the B.C. population.”

As Zosia Bielski, The Globe and Mail’s Time Use Reporter (best job title anywhere) wrote this week, a new paper in the Canadian Medical Association Journal warns of chronic health effects from this move.

“Permanent DST preserves later evening light that May facilitate commuting, recreation, social participation, and some economic activity,” the study states. “But it also prolongs darkness on winter mornings, with potential adverse effects on circadian alignment, sleep, mood, education, and productivity.”

The study suggests sticking with Standard Time would have been the better option, preserving more morning light.

Yes, time changes are disruptive, but only temporarily. And no, it’s not great going home from work in the dark. But you know what’s worse? Sending your kids to school in the dark. Or driving, bleary-eyed, to the office in the dark because your circadian rhythms are all messed up and your sleep has been disrupted.

Vancouver Police called attention to visibility concerns this week after two pedestrians were struck over the course of a few days, including a seven-year-old girl who was hit at 8:30 a.m. on a Thursday, before the non-change. And instead of shifting to earlier light after this weekend, mornings will only get darker.

“This incident is an important reminder for pedestrians to exercise additional caution and for drivers to stay vigilant, especially during darker morning and evening commutes,” said VPD Constable Megan Lui in a news release. The girl was released from hospital with minor injuries.

The other pedestrian who was hit, a 45-year-old woman, was killed. Granted, it was just after midnight and it was raining heavily. “Police are once again calling for additional caution on the roads this season as visibility becomes more challenging for both pedestrians and drivers,” a VPD release said.

It is frankly alarming that for part of the year, sunrise will now occur during regular business hours. In mid-December ahead of the winter break, sunrise won’t happen until Vancouver students are in their classrooms. This could have an effect on school attendance and even marks.

The U.S. tried this in the 1970s and abandoned the experiment within a year. Perhaps that will ultimately be the case here too, and B.C. will return to the previous system – and return this parting gift from outgoing Premier David Eby.

stories.title: The height of ambition: How tall should we build towers?
stories.summary: Will the first mile-high skyscraper be built because it’s needed, because it’s desired, or simply because some powerful egos decree that it can be?
stories.author: Gerry Flahive
stories.content:
Gerry Flahive is a writer in Toronto.

“Does it look like I’m kidding?”

Seventy years ago this month, at a news conference in Chicago, 89-year-old architect Frank Lloyd Wright presented an ethereal 22-foot-tall rendering for his 528-storey “Mile-High” tower. Its design was “as beautiful as it was unbuildable,” as one critic put it. The world’s greatest architect, by his own accounting and that of much of the general public, Wright said at the time that “no one could afford to build it now, but in the future, no one can afford not to build it.” Today, supertalls (buildings more than 300 metres tall) are nearing the one-kilometre mark. By imperial or metric measure, these things are growing higher.

Fifty years ago this month, Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau hosted the official dedication for the recently opened CN Tower in Toronto. It came to define this city’s aspirations, sometimes cringeworthy, to be world-class , giving Toronto bragging rights to the world’s tallest free-standing structure for three decades. Is it possible, or even wise, for the city to seek to reclaim the trophy?

By the count of the Council on Vertical Urbanism , Toronto now stands eighth among cities building supertalls – the latest being the 106-storey SkyTower at the foot of Yonge St., with several more to come. As Wright’s vision has gone from madcap to aspirational in the decades since, the technology to build that high has come, if not the economics or the political will. Will the first mile-high be built because it’s needed, because it’s desired, or simply because some powerful egos decree that it can be?

Wright’s illustration of the proposed building depicted something seemingly impossible but handcrafted, an immense gold and blue sliver, caressed by wisps of clouds. Its terraced base is like an approach to a cenotaph, to be viewed with awe and reverence. It would make the then-tallest Empire State Building “a mouse by comparison” by Wright’s brag, and its 76 “atomic-powered” elevators would not only defy the existing science but also threaten passengers with ear popping. “It might help if the elevator operators passed out chewing gum on the trip down,” one airline executive said.

The 130,000 occupants would arrive by helicopter (there’d be room for 150 to land), or drive into a 15,000-spot parking garage (Toronto’s Yorkdale Shopping Centre, by comparison, has approximately 8,000 spaces). It would not exactly be pedestrian friendly. As one scholar put it, “managing crowd flow through [the Mile-High’s] just three exits would have required people as numbly obedient as those marching into the subterranean City of Work in Fritz Lang’s film Metropoli s.” As transcendent as his idea was on paper, it wasn’t exactly an advertisement for comfort.

No client had asked for it, and no funding was forthcoming, even though the Mile-High was meant to house all city, county and state government employees on a site on the Chicago waterfront.

It almost enters the realm of parody. One thinks of former Torontonian, the humorist and illustrator Bruce McCall, whose 1974 National Lampoon article celebrated the comically large ocean liner, the R.M.S. Tyrannic , “The Biggest Thing in All the World.” “Steerage passengers who board at Liverpool often fail to reach their quarters before Tyrannic has safely berthed at New York. They are advised to run.”

Sociologist and critic Lewis Mumford, a friend of Wright’s, later wrote that “in that project all of Wright’s egocentric weaknesses were crystallized in an ultimate fantasy ... What a monument of futility … if this is what old age had done to Wright, I had no desire to exalt his mummified remains.”

In a way, it was meant to level – literally – the competition by obviating the need for any other tall buildings. Brigitte Raschke, author of Frank Lloyd Wright – The Mile-High Illinois: Utopia or Architectural Critique? wrote that “Wright was an opponent of large cities – especially those he saw as symbols of capitalism.”

The endlessly confident architect put it this way: “I would … decentralize the entire affair and send the people back to greenery where they belong … and maybe build a Mile-High or two or three and then let them live in the country. All you would have to do would be to sweep New York into the Hudson and build two of them in Central Park and that would be the city.”

Here’s David Pontarini, Founding Partner of Toronto’s Hariri Pontarini Architects, the designers of the Pinnacle SkyTower, parsing the seeming contradiction: “Frank Lloyd Wright admired towers without ever really admiring cities. The tower was a device for emptying the city: one vertical vessel of concentration standing over a dispersed, low-rise landscape. It was conceived as singular. Nothing else was meant to stand near it.”

“The world laughed it off,” Paul Hendrickson, author of Plagued by Fire: The Dreams and Furies of Frank Lloyd Wright, told me. “The thing was then and is now unbuildable. But the idea was right, the spirit was right, the daring was right, the vision was right. But the legacy of inspiration was there. He had planted that flag. No matter that the damn thing still couldn’t be built. But he had the leap of imagination, didn’t he?”

Could Wright’s imagination have fired up Toronto’s? It’s possible to imagine a what-if scenario, fed by the often oddball connections Wright had here in the years he was refining the Mile-High.

Wright was a not infrequent visitor to Toronto in those years. How close Wright came to actually building something in Toronto is lost in the archives, but one piece survives: In 1954, an executive from the Dominion grocery store chain wrote to Wright with a proposition, once they found “a very special location” to design a “Dominion Mammoth Market.” The world’s longest horizontal building? No, just a marketing designation for some large supermarkets. It didn’t happen.

But the master architect had no shortage of opinions about large signature projects in Toronto, weighing in vehemently against the various proposed designs for Toronto’s new City Hall. He wasn’t exactly a fan of the winner, from architect Viljo Revell, describing it as “a piece of categorical sterility,” and predicting that it would “advertise to posterity that Toronto is without a soul.” Even the 19th-century Old City Hall couldn’t escape his wrath: he labelled it a “Romanesque abortion.”

Wright’s radio proclamations inspired one Torontonian to send him this plaintive complaint: “We are trying to do something about our buildings in Canada” and enclosed clippings to “show [you] what we are up against.” But this gentleman was likely in the minority, as many Torontonians liked things just the way they were.

In his book Civic Symbol: Creating Toronto’s New City Hall, 1952-1966 , Christopher Armstrong writes of the apprehension about how an innovative design for it might be received: “fears were expressed that the citizenry would resist a highly radical idea like the embrace of such new dogmas as modern architecture or abstract art.”

When the new City Hall did finally open in 1965, I was a frequent kid participant in its guided tours, especially to its stratospherically high 27th floor outdoor observation deck, soon made redundant by the taller TD Centre building: taller, more cerebral, and feeling even more like the future. But that perch was then itself eclipsed by the CN Tower. In the space of a decade the three structures had changed the city’s skyline, reputation and sense of itself as something finally post-Victorian.

On the optimistic day of July 1, 1967, as Canadians were celebrating the nation’s Centennial, a Globe and Mail writer considered the possible features of the Toronto of the year 2067. “The majority of urban-oriented Torontonians will prefer the inbuilt efficiency of the mile-high apartment building.” It should be noted that the author also predicted that via rockets “Torontonians will be able to visit friends in Australia for lunch” and that by 2067 “the super-mayor of the city-state of Toronto will command far more power than” the Prime Minister. (Strong mayor powers, anyone?).

But Toronto has been a vertical city for a long time. It just wasn’t a very tall one, and most of the growth was residential.

The postwar population boom and a housing shortage led to an explosion in the growth of the city out to its suburbs, and upwards with apartment towers of 12, 20 and 30 storeys in St. James Town, Thorncliffe Park and beyond. By the Skydb building database’s count, Toronto now has more than 4,000 highrises of 10 storeys or more, making it seventh in the world, in the company of New York, Hong Kong and Tokyo.

They’re everywhere in the city, but we just don’t notice them any more, unless, perhaps, when something beloved is torn down for yet another condo.

Despite the mockery and the dismissals, the idea of a mile-high building never really went away after Wright’s death in 1959. It took a while for construction technology to catch up, and for the modern skyscraper, mostly the “glass boxes” he derided, to emerge and recast the skylines of major North American cities.

It was only in this century that the supertall pushed the limits even higher, to megatall (600 metres plus), often simply for national prestige and bragging rights. The Burj Khalifa in Dubai, at 828 metres, is still the undisputed champion, and has been for a decade and a half. Major players China and Saudi Arabia have deep pockets and tall ambitions in this field, with the latter’s Jeddah Tower slated for completion in 2028 as the first building to exceed one kilometre. It’s likely no coincidence that undemocratic countries are in the lead, able to brush past any possible local resistance to having a gargantuan icon nearby.

In North America there’s been admiration but also disdain. Even Architectural Record casts doubt on the utility and ethics of the so-called billionaire supertalls, such as those in New York City, arguing that they “represent what is decadent and unequal in the 21st-century American economy.”

Wright’s “master builder” power trip doesn’t apply here. Architect David Pontarini argues that “Toronto’s supertalls belong to a different logic. SkyTower at Pinnacle One Yonge sits within an evolving field of towers of varying height and density rather than above an emptied plain. That model is consistent with the province’s growth plan – density concentrated at transit and urban centres, stepping down from those zones into the surrounding fabric. So, there is room for supertalls within our city fabric, but I don’t expect them to become a dominant force in how Toronto is built.”

Jason Barr, author of Cities in the Sky: The Quest to Build the World’s Tallest Skyscrapers , states quite plainly: “Will a mile-high structure ever be built? Yes. When Wright released his renderings for his mile-high building … it became part of our collective consciousness … the engineering know-how to create a one-mile structure is here. I think rather than asking why buildings are so tall, we should be asking why they aren’t even taller.”

But for what? For whom?

At the CN Tower’s official opening, Pierre Trudeau said: “We don’t have the philosophy to use our great inventions, in a way which is truly compatible with the human aspect of our society. A hundred years ago I’m told that the highest structure in Toronto was a grain elevator soaring up to some hundred feet. But what we must as Canadians start to do is to make sure that our philosophy, our thinking about our society … how we see the year 2076 … [is] to answer the problems of today. The political problems, the philosophical problems of how we use our machines, so that they don’t destroy us.”

When innovation was in fashion in this city and province (or, at least, pushed its way through) we built the Ontario Science Centre, Ontario Place (both their original architecture now discarded), the CN Tower, City Hall, and, most recently, the already wildly popular Biidaasige Park (part of the $1.4 - billion Port Lands Flood Protection project). Impracticality, ego and ambition, deftly channelled into collaborative approaches, can produce remarkable results. We still need to fill the potholes, but we can look up occasionally too.

The CN Tower May be ugly, but it’s ours. It’s technically not a “building,” but merely a free-standing structure (has a more boring term ever been applied to something that became so beloved?). It allowed people to apprehend the city in its fullness, to see it as an urban fabric and a bountifully treed one, over the course, now, of half a century, for the price of a ticket.

We live mostly in two dimensions, heads down, at street level, but the world around us is in glorious 3-D. Up high, that fullness shouldn’t be accessible only to those who make it to the penthouse or the CEO’s office on the umpteenth floor, atomic elevator or not.

Even though downtown Toronto isn’t going to be swept into Lake Ontario to make way for a mile-high building any time soon, it’s my guess that there’ll be one there sooner than Doug Ford’s $100 - billion tunnel gets dug under Highway 401. Just so long as there’s an observation deck.

content_blocks.html: Seventy years ago this month, at a news conference in Chicago, 89-year-old architect Frank Lloyd Wright presented an ethereal 22-foot-tall rendering for his 528-storey “Mile-High” tower. Its design was “as beautiful as it was unbuildable,” as one critic put it. The world’s greatest architect, by his own accounting and that of much of the general public, Wright said at the time that “no one could afford to build it now, but in the future, no one can afford not to build it.” Today, supertalls (buildings more than 300 metres tall) are nearing the one-kilometre mark. By imperial or metric measure, these things are growing higher.

content_blocks.caption: Architect Frank Lloyd Wright at his Wisconsin home in 1938. The Associated Press

content_blocks.text: Fifty years ago this month, Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau hosted the official dedication for the recently opened CN Tower in Toronto. It came to define this city’s aspirations, sometimes cringeworthy, to be world-class , giving Toronto bragging rights to the world’s tallest free-standing structure for three decades. Is it possible, or even wise, for the city to seek to reclaim the trophy?

content_blocks.text: By the count of the Council on Vertical Urbanism , Toronto now stands eighth among cities building supertalls – the latest being the 106-storey SkyTower at the foot of Yonge St., with several more to come. As Wright’s vision has gone from madcap to aspirational in the decades since, the technology to build that high has come, if not the economics or the political will. Will the first mile-high be built because it’s needed, because it’s desired, or simply because some powerful egos decree that it can be?

content_blocks.text: Wright’s illustration of the proposed building depicted something seemingly impossible but handcrafted, an immense gold and blue sliver, caressed by wisps of clouds. Its terraced base is like an approach to a cenotaph, to be viewed with awe and reverence. It would make the then-tallest Empire State Building “a mouse by comparison” by Wright’s brag, and its 76 “atomic-powered” elevators would not only defy the existing science but also threaten passengers with ear popping. “It might help if the elevator operators passed out chewing gum on the trip down,” one airline executive said.

content_blocks.text: The 130,000 occupants would arrive by helicopter (there’d be room for 150 to land), or drive into a 15,000-spot parking garage (Toronto’s Yorkdale Shopping Centre, by comparison, has approximately 8,000 spaces). It would not exactly be pedestrian friendly. As one scholar put it, “managing crowd flow through [the Mile-High’s] just three exits would have required people as numbly obedient as those marching into the subterranean City of Work in Fritz Lang’s film Metropoli s.” As transcendent as his idea was on paper, it wasn’t exactly an advertisement for comfort.

content_blocks.text: No client had asked for it, and no funding was forthcoming, even though the Mile-High was meant to house all city, county and state government employees on a site on the Chicago waterfront.

content_blocks.text: It almost enters the realm of parody. One thinks of former Torontonian, the humorist and illustrator Bruce McCall, whose 1974 National Lampoon article celebrated the comically large ocean liner, the R.M.S. Tyrannic , “The Biggest Thing in All the World.” “Steerage passengers who board at Liverpool often fail to reach their quarters before Tyrannic has safely berthed at New York. They are advised to run.”

content_blocks.text: Sociologist and critic Lewis Mumford, a friend of Wright’s, later wrote that “in that project all of Wright’s egocentric weaknesses were crystallized in an ultimate fantasy ... What a monument of futility … if this is what old age had done to Wright, I had no desire to exalt his mummified remains.”

What a monument of futility … if this is what old age had done to Wright, I had no desire to exalt his mummified remains.”

content_blocks.text: In a way, it was meant to level – literally – the competition by obviating the need for any other tall buildings. Brigitte Raschke, author of Frank Lloyd Wright – The Mile-High Illinois: Utopia or Architectural Critique? wrote that “Wright was an opponent of large cities – especially those he saw as symbols of capitalism.”

content_blocks.text: The endlessly confident architect put it this way: “I would … decentralize the entire affair and send the people back to greenery where they belong … and maybe build a Mile-High or two or three and then let them live in the country. All you would have to do would be to sweep New York into the Hudson and build two of them in Central Park and that would be the city.”

All you would have to do would be to sweep New York into the Hudson and build two of them in Central Park and that would be the city.”

content_blocks.text: Here’s David Pontarini, Founding Partner of Toronto’s Hariri Pontarini Architects, the designers of the Pinnacle SkyTower, parsing the seeming contradiction: “Frank Lloyd Wright admired towers without ever really admiring cities. The tower was a device for emptying the city: one vertical vessel of concentration standing over a dispersed, low-rise landscape. It was conceived as singular. Nothing else was meant to stand near it.”

content_blocks.text: “The world laughed it off,” Paul Hendrickson, author of Plagued by Fire: The Dreams and Furies of Frank Lloyd Wright, told me. “The thing was then and is now unbuildable. But the idea was right, the spirit was right, the daring was right, the vision was right. But the legacy of inspiration was there. He had planted that flag. No matter that the damn thing still couldn’t be built. But he had the leap of imagination, didn’t he?”

content_blocks.text: Could Wright’s imagination have fired up Toronto’s? It’s possible to imagine a what-if scenario, fed by the often oddball connections Wright had here in the years he was refining the Mile-High.

content_blocks.text: Wright was a not infrequent visitor to Toronto in those years. How close Wright came to actually building something in Toronto is lost in the archives, but one piece survives: In 1954, an executive from the Dominion grocery store chain wrote to Wright with a proposition, once they found “a very special location” to design a “Dominion Mammoth Market.” The world’s longest horizontal building? No, just a marketing designation for some large supermarkets. It didn’t happen.

content_blocks.text: But the master architect had no shortage of opinions about large signature projects in Toronto, weighing in vehemently against the various proposed designs for Toronto’s new City Hall. He wasn’t exactly a fan of the winner, from architect Viljo Revell, describing it as “a piece of categorical sterility,” and predicting that it would “advertise to posterity that Toronto is without a soul.” Even the 19th-century Old City Hall couldn’t escape his wrath: he labelled it a “Romanesque abortion.”

content_blocks.text: Wright’s radio proclamations inspired one Torontonian to send him this plaintive complaint: “We are trying to do something about our buildings in Canada” and enclosed clippings to “show [you] what we are up against.” But this gentleman was likely in the minority, as many Torontonians liked things just the way they were.

content_blocks.text: In his book Civic Symbol: Creating Toronto’s New City Hall, 1952-1966 , Christopher Armstrong writes of the apprehension about how an innovative design for it might be received: “fears were expressed that the citizenry would resist a highly radical idea like the embrace of such new dogmas as modern architecture or abstract art.”

content_blocks.text: When the new City Hall did finally open in 1965, I was a frequent kid participant in its guided tours, especially to its stratospherically high 27th floor outdoor observation deck, soon made redundant by the taller TD Centre building: taller, more cerebral, and feeling even more like the future. But that perch was then itself eclipsed by the CN Tower. In the space of a decade the three structures had changed the city’s skyline, reputation and sense of itself as something finally post-Victorian.

content_blocks.text: On the optimistic day of July 1, 1967, as Canadians were celebrating the nation’s Centennial, a Globe and Mail writer considered the possible features of the Toronto of the year 2067. “The majority of urban-oriented Torontonians will prefer the inbuilt efficiency of the mile-high apartment building.” It should be noted that the author also predicted that via rockets “Torontonians will be able to visit friends in Australia for lunch” and that by 2067 “the super-mayor of the city-state of Toronto will command far more power than” the Prime Minister. (Strong mayor powers, anyone?).

content_blocks.text: But Toronto has been a vertical city for a long time. It just wasn’t a very tall one, and most of the growth was residential.
content_blocks.html: But Toronto has been a vertical city for a long time. It just wasn’t a very tall one, and most of the growth was residential.

content_blocks.text: The postwar population boom and a housing shortage led to an explosion in the growth of the city out to its suburbs, and upwards with apartment towers of 12, 20 and 30 storeys in St. James Town, Thorncliffe Park and beyond. By the Skydb building database’s count, Toronto now has more than 4,000 highrises of 10 storeys or more, making it seventh in the world, in the company of New York, Hong Kong and Tokyo.

content_blocks.text: They’re everywhere in the city, but we just don’t notice them any more, unless, perhaps, when something beloved is torn down for yet another condo.

content_blocks.text: Despite the mockery and the dismissals, the idea of a mile-high building never really went away after Wright’s death in 1959. It took a while for construction technology to catch up, and for the modern skyscraper, mostly the “glass boxes” he derided, to emerge and recast the skylines of major North American cities.

content_blocks.text: It was only in this century that the supertall pushed the limits even higher, to megatall (600 metres plus), often simply for national prestige and bragging rights. The Burj Khalifa in Dubai, at 828 metres, is still the undisputed champion, and has been for a decade and a half. Major players China and Saudi Arabia have deep pockets and tall ambitions in this field, with the latter’s Jeddah Tower slated for completion in 2028 as the first building to exceed one kilometre. It’s likely no coincidence that undemocratic countries are in the lead, able to brush past any possible local resistance to having a gargantuan icon nearby.

content_blocks.text: In North America there’s been admiration but also disdain. Even Architectural Record casts doubt on the utility and ethics of the so-called billionaire supertalls, such as those in New York City, arguing that they “represent what is decadent and unequal in the 21st-century American economy.”

content_blocks.text: Wright’s “master builder” power trip doesn’t apply here. Architect David Pontarini argues that “Toronto’s supertalls belong to a different logic. SkyTower at Pinnacle One Yonge sits within an evolving field of towers of varying height and density rather than above an emptied plain. That model is consistent with the province’s growth plan – density concentrated at transit and urban centres, stepping down from those zones into the surrounding fabric. So, there is room for supertalls within our city fabric, but I don’t expect them to become a dominant force in how Toronto is built.”

content_blocks.text: Jason Barr, author of Cities in the Sky: The Quest to Build the World’s Tallest Skyscrapers , states quite plainly: “Will a mile-high structure ever be built? Yes. When Wright released his renderings for his mile-high building … it became part of our collective consciousness … the engineering know-how to create a one-mile structure is here. I think rather than asking why buildings are so tall, we should be asking why they aren’t even taller.”

content_blocks.text: But for what? For whom?
content_blocks.html: But for what? For whom?

content_blocks.text: At the CN Tower’s official opening, Pierre Trudeau said: “We don’t have the philosophy to use our great inventions, in a way which is truly compatible with the human aspect of our society. A hundred years ago I’m told that the highest structure in Toronto was a grain elevator soaring up to some hundred feet. But what we must as Canadians start to do is to make sure that our philosophy, our thinking about our society … how we see the year 2076 … [is] to answer the problems of today. The political problems, the philosophical problems of how we use our machines, so that they don’t destroy us.”

The political problems, the philosophical problems of how we use our machines, so that they don’t destroy us.”

content_blocks.text: When innovation was in fashion in this city and province (or, at least, pushed its way through) we built the Ontario Science Centre, Ontario Place (both their original architecture now discarded), the CN Tower, City Hall, and, most recently, the already wildly popular Biidaasige Park (part of the $1.4 - billion Port Lands Flood Protection project). Impracticality, ego and ambition, deftly channelled into collaborative approaches, can produce remarkable results. We still need to fill the potholes, but we can look up occasionally too.

content_blocks.text: The CN Tower May be ugly, but it’s ours. It’s technically not a “building,” but merely a free-standing structure (has a more boring term ever been applied to something that became so beloved?). It allowed people to apprehend the city in its fullness, to see it as an urban fabric and a bountifully treed one, over the course, now, of half a century, for the price of a ticket.

content_blocks.text: We live mostly in two dimensions, heads down, at street level, but the world around us is in glorious 3-D. Up high, that fullness shouldn’t be accessible only to those who make it to the penthouse or the CEO’s office on the umpteenth floor, atomic elevator or not.

Just so long as there’s an observation deck.

stories.title: Nearly 60% of Canadians plan to participate in Halloween, according to new poll
stories.summary: Nearly six in 10 Canadian residents say they will participate in Halloween in some way this Saturday night.
stories.author: Meredith Bond
stories.content:
Nearly six in 10 Canadian residents say they will participate in Halloween in some way on Saturday night, but Torontonians seem to be the scaredy-cats of the bunch, according to a new poll.

Only 48 per cent of Toronto residents surveyed said they planned to give out treats or go out on Halloween night; the lowest across the regions surveyed and five per cent less than last year.

The Canada Pulse Insights poll for CityNews found Surrey, B.C. had the most enthusiastic bunch, with 65 per cent of people saying they would partake, followed closely behind by those in Alberta, 63 per cent in Calgary and 62 per cent in Edmonton.

In Vancouver and Metro Vancouver, their taste for treats increased the most with 10 per cent more residents saying they would take part in the spooktacular holiday over last year, up to 56 per cent and 59 per cent, respectively.

Fifty-seven per cent of those in the GTA, not including Toronto, will be dressing up or heading out for trick-or-treating.

Across all regions, parents with children under 18 had the highest Halloween spirit, with between 76 to 85 per cent of residents saying they would participate.

Young adults between 18 to 34 were also likely to head out for Halloween, with 65 per to 79 per cent saying they would be participating.

Those planning for a night out on the town for Halloween will have an extra hour to celebrate with Daylight Saving Time (DST) on Sunday morning.

This release draws on Canada Pulse Insights surveys of adult residents in three markets, each asking this year the same question in the same words: Toronto (n=510) and the GTA outside Toronto, the regional municipalities of Durham, York, Halton and Peel (n=825), between Sept. 14 and 25, 2026, Calgary (n=401) and Edmonton (n=383) between Sept. 30 and Oct. 9, 2026, and three British Columbia regions — Metro Vancouver (n=1,374: the City of Vancouver, Surrey and the rest of Metro Vancouver), Vancouver Island (n=511) and the Okanagan Valley (n=498) — between Sept. 28 and Oct. 14, 2026, through an online panel platform managed by Sago.

The margin of error for comparable probability-based random samples of the same sizes is ±4.3 percentage points for Toronto, ±3.4 for the GTA outside Toronto, ±4.9 for Calgary, ±5.0 for Edmonton, ±2.6 for Metro Vancouver, ±4.3 for Vancouver Island and ±4.4 for the Okanagan Valley, 19 times out of 20 .

stories.title: Chance for some showers Thursday, but Halloween weekend looks dry
stories.summary: Starting the day Thursday with some sunshine, but we have the chance for some showers this afternoon into this evening.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
Starting the day Thursday with some sunshine, but we have the chance for some showers this afternoon into this evening.

“The winds early today will be out of the southwest … The cold front will bring the chance for showers,” explained CTV London Meteorologist Julie Atchison. “They’ll be short lived. We need a little bit of rainfall. It’s been extremely dry.”

Conditions will clear up heading into Friday, with lots more sunshine in the forecast.

Trick-or-treaters should expect perfect candy-gathering conditions this Halloween weekend.

“Saturday looks good for Halloween, and mix of sun and cloud during the day. Cloudy Saturday night but staying dry,” said Atchison.

Here’s a look at the rest of the forecast

Thursday: Mainly sunny. Increasing cloudiness in the morning then 60 per cent chance of showers late in the afternoon. Wind becoming southwest 20 km/h gusting to 40 in the morning. High 20. UV index 3 or moderate.

Thursday night: Mainly cloudy. 60 per cent chance of showers in the evening. Wind becoming northwest 20 km/h near midnight. Low 6.

Friday: Sunny. High 13.

Saturday (Halloween): A mix of sun and cloud. High 15.

Sunday: Cloudy. High 17.

Monday: Cloudy. High 15.

stories.title: At this moment in Canadian politics, ‘normie’ is in
stories.summary: As shown by both our Prime Minister and the new B.C. premier, sometimes bland and boring is what the people want
stories.author: Robyn Urback
stories.content:
Former Alberta premier Ralph Klein would occasionally remark on the prosaic, conventional nature of the work he did as leader of his province. In 1998, Edmonton Sun journalist Neil Waugh wrote about Mr. Klein’s “good news” tour, during which the premier travelled across the province to spread the word about how “Albertans have turned their province into the envy of the nation.” As to what made that happen, in Mr. Waugh’s summation of Mr. Klein’s messaging, was “good, old, boring government.”

Mr. Klein himself was folksy and charismatic, but there wasn’t anything particularly dynamic or unconventional in his prescription for the province’s deficit reduction. “Good governance is never exciting,” he once remarked . Ontario’s second-longest serving premier, Bill Davis, espoused a similar ethos, though unlike Mr. Klein, Mr. Davis was boring both in personal affect and in his policy prescriptions. But that didn’t hold Mr. Davis back politically: “Bland works,” he once said .

Perhaps an addendum to that phrase should be that bland works, sometimes. That’s because the political mood in a province, a city and a country is never stagnant. Sometimes, the electorate will be dazzled by a guy who joyfully photobombs weddings and proms, and who will promise to run a series of deficits because to campaign on such a pledge is a very non-conformist thing to do. And at other times, the electorate yearns for the grey-haired central banker who would never be caught in public with so much as an untied lace, but whom they trust to do the good, hard, boring work of steering the ship during a global riptide.

Canada seems to be ushering in an era of “normie” politics, wherein the ostentatious, outrageous and more fringe elements of policy-making – and even politicians proper – are eschewed for the conventional, the bland and even the boring. B.C.’s next premier, Conservative Lorne Doerkson, appears to embody much of that description, though he does seem to possess a bit of that folksy charm that endeared Albertans to Mr. Klein.

To be sure, the B.C. Conservatives’ majority election win can more credibly be attributed to the electorate’s desire to kick out Premier David Eby – for his party’s hideously cynical early election call, for its fiscal mismanagement, its broken promises and so on. Indeed, although the Conservatives lost some votes compared to the 2024 election results, the NDP lost far more .

But it is noteworthy nonetheless that the Conservatives achieved electoral success with a guy who seems like the type to collect your mail when you’re out of town – the kind of person who might have a favourite pen, or falls asleep in front of the TV at 7 p.m. – rather than the far more animated and polarizing character that was his predecessor, Kerry-Lynne Findlay. What Mr. Doerkson has proposed is classic, normal, rather boring conservatism: an income-tax cut, measures to get tough on crime and clean up B.C.’s streets, further development of the province’s resources and so on. In other words, normal stuff.

Normal also prevailed in the recent municipal election in Mississauga, where Alvin Tedjo, who had previously served just one term on council, beat out incumbent mayor Carolyn Parrish and former mayor Bonnie Crombie. Part of his success was due to his catnip platform, which included freezing residential property taxes for everyone for two years, and permanently freezing property tax increases for seniors and bumping up the rebate for low-income seniors. But voters’ support for Mr. Tedjo also seemed to grow as his opponents became ever more unhinged throughout the campaign, resorting to name calling and personal attacks during debates (for example, in one instance, Ms. Parrish referred to Ms. Crombie as “the blonde bombshell.”) While his opponents were busy pulling each other’s hair, Mr. Tedjo stayed above the fray, and the people of Mississauga rewarded him for it. When asked whether he thought the previous mayors’ juvenile antics sunk their campaigns, he responded, “I’m sure it didn’t help.”

Canadians’ apparent appetite for normie politics and politicians is easily attributed to the obvious instability globally, and the insecurity of life at home. When everything seems so expensive, and adequate housing is hard to come by, and you don’t know whether you’ll have a job next week based almost entirely on a 2 a.m. Truth Social post by the U.S. President, you don’t want the person lobbing cheap shots and crafting silly nicknames leading the country, but the serious, kind-of-boring guy who doesn’t understand what “very online” means, and doesn’t care to. He has work to do. Bland works – sometimes. And that sometimes, in Canada, appears to be right now.

stories.title: Scott Gillingham re-elected as mayor of Winnipeg
stories.summary: Gillingham vows to find solutions to homelessness, addiction and crime in the city
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Scott Gillingham was re-elected as the mayor of Winnipeg on Wednesday after a campaign largely dominated by issues ranging from housing to public safety.

Unofficial results showed Gillingham received 80,206 votes to send him to a second term, while former legislature member and city councillor Kevin Klein drew 41,703 votes.

Software developer Noah Redden came in third place with 39,962 votes, and funeral home director Mike Vogiatzakis received 19,463.

Supporters cheered as Gillingham claimed victory late Wednesday.

“Tonight you have given me the honour of serving as your mayor once again,” he told those gathered at a watch party. “Thank you, Winnipeg. I will never take your trust for granted.”

Gillingham said the city’s best days are still ahead. He’s vowed to find solutions to the multitude of issues plaguing the city, such as homelessness, addictions, mental health and crime.

There are many reasons to be optimistic about Winnipeg, Gillingham said, noting new home builds and infrastructure, and revitalizing the city’s downtown.

He said he wants to build on that momentum over the next four years.

“So whether you voted for me or not, I want you to know that I will be your mayor too. My door will be open, your voice will matter and I’ll work every day to make this city better for your family and my family,” he said.

Klein, who owns newspapers including the Winnipeg Sun, congratulated Gillingham in a concession speech at the Norwood Hotel.

He said he was humbled by the support he received and that there would be a news conference Friday to wrap up his campaign and announce his next steps.

Klein previously had an unsuccessful run at the city’s top job in 2022.

Almost all other Manitoba communities also held elections Wednesday, except for the resort areas of Winnipeg Beach, Dunnottar and Victoria Beach, which held votes in July.
