stories.title: The cars that steered Toyota away from ‘boring’ hit the end of the line
stories.summary: Kunal D’souza drives what he calls two of the best performance cars of the last decade - the Lexus LC500 and Toyota Supra OR Toyota and Lexus retire two automotive legends – the Supra and LC 500 – which proved the company is capable of far more than boring, volume-driven vehicles
stories.author: Kunal D’souza
stories.content:
The Lexus LC 500 and relaunched Toyota Supra brought a new wave of enthusiasts to the Japanese automaker in the late 2010s and early 2020s, as the brands worked to reinvent themselves from makers of so-called “boring” cars to ones that prioritized driving enjoyment ahead of maximizing volume and profits.

However, at the end of this year, both will be discontinued, marking the end of the line for two of the best performance cars of the last decade.

The LC 500 is a cross between Lexus’s stately luxury sedans and a spaceship, nearly unchanged from the LF-LC concept shown at the Detroit auto show in 2012. It’s a car that looks like it costs a million dollars, but retailed for a 10th of that.

Even eight years on, it hasn’t aged a day and its ability to turn heads remains unchanged. Under the hood sits a sonorous five-litre, naturally aspirated V8 that sends 471 horsepower to the rear wheels, complementing an exquisite interior that looks and feels like it was tailored by the finest artisans in the industry.

Instead of pounding rough pavement into oblivion, the LC is engineered to gently waft occupants to their destination. The V8 engine, noted for its complex and glorious acoustic range, burbles quietly during a cruise but barks to life the second you start to get more friendly with the throttle.

In the sportiest setting, the suspension and steering firm up just enough to give you the confidence to flow through a twisty back road, but the LC 500 never forgets its main mission of delivering a luxury experience. There’s a wonderful duality here that’s only enhanced with the convertible version, as the V8 becomes more audible with the roof down and takes centre stage.

The final Inspiration Series is limited to just 550 units for North America. The convertible, which I recently drove for a few days, featured a spectacular white and brown leather interior and sat on gorgeous 21-inch forged wheels. The Mark Levinson sound system was designed to perform beautifully even with the roof down, leading to one of the best open-air experiences I’ve had in a car.

Flagship grand tourers like this Lexus are rare now, with BMW also discontinuing its 8 Series this year, leaving just the Mercedes-Benz SL. There are other options if you’re willing to climb the price ladder, but at about $120,000, the usual suspect for a sports car is the BMW M4 – or the Porsche 911 if the budget can stretch a bit further. But those cars were honed on the Nürburgring and have rock-hard suspensions designed to liquefy your spine if the road is anything less than billiard-smooth.

Sports cars for less than $100,000 are even scarcer, especially two-seaters like the Supra, which gained a cult-like status after it was discontinued in 2002. If it weren’t for a partnership with BMW, the current generation might never have seen the light of day.

BMW builds it on the same production line as the BMW Z4 convertible in Graz, Austria, using the same platform, engine and transmission, with the biggest difference being that the Z4 is a convertible. The Z4 is also officially dead after this model year, with no confirmed plans for a replacement.

You’d never be able to tell they were the same car either, given the Supra’s exaggerated curves, extra-long hood and stubby rear deck topped with a duckbill spoiler, compared with the Z4’s cleaner, more understated design. The matte-black paint of the MkV Final Edition Supra gives off the same vibe I got from Tim Burton’s Batmobile.

It feels nothing like the Z4 either, with sharper steering, a louder, more aggressive exhaust note and suspension tuning that gives it an edgier, more agile driving feel. The MkV Final Edition – limited to just 25 cars across Canada – retains the signature 382-horsepower three-litre inline-six but introduces larger front brakes, revised rear differential control and dampers, and stronger underbody bracing.

The Supra is incredibly fun to drive and can be equipped with a six-speed manual transmission. And, just like the last generation, the tuning crowd has found massive potential in modifying them.

Sporty cars like the LC 500 and Supra represent a tiny fraction of the market but make large contributions to brand image. Even the Sienna minivan – arguably Toyota’s least sporty vehicle – adopted the Supra’s bulging rear fenders, taillights and wide stance to forge its own signature appearance.

Sports cars are risky business for automakers. Though they are expensive to engineer and sell in low volumes, they are vital for attracting new buyers to the brand. Ford axed its cars in North America, opting to sell only trucks and SUVs – save for the Mustang, which is the best-selling sports car globally. Ford even leveraged the iconic Mustang nameplate for its first mass-market electric vehicle, the Mustang Mach-E.

In 2025, Toyota sold 427 Supras and even fewer LC 500s in Canada, versus 25,000 Corollas and more than 75,000 RAV4s – the real moneymakers for the company. But the Supra has quickly become a social media legend, and Toyota has confirmed it’s going to make a new one, this time without BMW.

No such successor is planned for the LC 500, a holdout from a bygone era when big personal luxury coupes were more common. At its price point in today’s world, it makes little sense. But it proved that Toyota could build cars with soul rather than just boring, sensible appliances.

stories.title: Carney budget to focus on taxes, shift from Trudeau era
stories.summary: Many economists say amending Canada's much-maligned tax system should be a key element in the recipe to improve productivity.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — Tax reform designed to spur economic growth will be a key pillar in Prime Minister Mark Carney’s second budget, government sources say, signalling another policy shift in the governing Liberals from the Justin Trudeau era.

National Post has learned that the budget, to be unveiled next Thursday, is expected to prioritize tax measures to spur innovation and improved competitiveness as Carney attempts to boost investment and Canadians’ standard of living. Sources say there will also be measures to reduce the red tape that costs businesses time and money.

“It’s a growth and competition budget,” said a senior government source. “We’re trying to create an investment supercycle in Canada.”

Many economists say amending, perhaps even overhauling, Canada’s much-maligned tax system should be a key element in the recipe to improve productivity and growth, which translates into higher wages and jobs.

As reported last week in National Post, the budget will also focus on improving the landscape for Canada’s small and medium-sized businesses. Many economists and others outside the government also expect that Carney’s 2025 campaign promise for a broad review of corporate tax policy, also with an aim to encourage investment and economic growth, will find its way into the Nov. 5 financial plan.

Another key block of Carney’s economic plan, the new productivity mega-deduction that was announced last month at an international investors’ summit in Toronto, May also be formalized as part of the budget. It’s not yet clear if the Liberals will include that tax measure as a budget item or formalize it through separate legislation.

Carney’s primary aim is to improve the Canadian economy’s performance after years of lagging its G7 counterparts. His government’s action to date on that front are in stark contrast to his Liberal predecessor, Trudeau, who focused more on moves to improve economic equality.

Ottawa’s new tax policy measures to boost growth will be part of a suite of moves on this front, as Canada tries to withstand a wide range of new U.S. tariffs, which have hit key industries such as steel, auto, aluminum and forestry.

Other government priorities aimed at the same goals have included re-establishing stronger trade relations with China, India and others, updating infrastructure for exporters, faster approval times for major projects and boosting internal trade.

“There is an opportunity to rebuild the nation and renew its sense of mission,” said a government source.

Canada’s business community now seems more confident about the country’s direction.

Goldy Hyder, chief executive officer of the Business Council of Canada, which represents many of the country’s largest companies, said the productivity mega-deduction was a major step forward for competitiveness and investment and that he looks forward to more reform in the budget. One possibility, Hyder said, would be further changes to capital cost allowance (CCA) rules that dictate how quickly and broadly companies can write off capital costs for things such as machinery, equipment and buildings.

“They’re trying to do what they can.”

The big question for Carney and his finance minister, François-Philippe Champagne, is whether they take a big swing next week at cutting either personal or corporate income taxes after their first budget was seen as mostly tinkering.

Champagne said week that the government’s first priority in making this budget is Canadians’ cost of living. But the second, he said, is economic growth, with the accent on helping small and medium-sized businesses seize opportunities.

He has indicated in recent months that the government will continue to err on the side of what he calls “investments” in the economy, instead of reducing the deficit. Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7, Champagne has said many times, and that leaves room to spend or cut taxes or other revenue sources.

“I think Canadians can understand that we have a strong fiscal position and we’re investing in the things that will generate growth to the country,” he said in July

Champagne is expected to speak more about the government’s budget priorities on Monday during a speech in Ottawa.

Many economists argue that corporate and personal income tax cuts, along with other tax reform measures, are the key to improving Canada’s productivity and standard of living. The problem is that they’re also expensive for a government that has already made big spending promises on such items as defence and cutting an array of taxes that helped fill its coffers.

“Canada’s sluggish economic growth and federal fiscal excesses have become a vicious cycle,” said the C.D. Howe Institute think tank in a report released last week. “Canadians’ incomes are not growing nearly fast enough.”

And to many economists, including Carney, tax reform is an important part of the solution.

To date, the productivity mega-deduction, which the government estimates will cost the treasury $36.5-billion over the next five years, has been the biggest play. It was designed to use the tax system to spur investment, particularly in capital-intensive industries such as energy, mining, transportation, and technology and May well be included in the budget.

Unveiled last month at an international investors’ summit in Toronto, the changes are expected to cut Canada’s projected tax rate on new investment, a key metric for large investors, by slightly more than half, to about 6.4 per cent from 13 per cent.

The Carney government has also made a number of moves to trim or eliminate taxes: pausing the federal tax on gas and diesel, eliminating the federal portion of inter-provincial trade barriers, cancelling the digital services tax, making a modest cut to personal income taxes and the super mega-deduction.

While economists say each of those moves should help the economy, they also add to the deficit.

The challenge for Carney and Champagne is that cutting taxes of any type costs government revenue at a time when Ottawa is adding piles of red ink. There’s also concern that the government needs every penny it takes in during a trade war with the U.S., which consumes about three-quarters of all Canadian exports.

But revenue has not been the federal government’s problem.

As reported earlier this week in National Post, Ottawa May be on track to take in almost $20-billion more in taxes and other revenue this year than had been expected less than six months ago. The increase is largely a function of higher market prices for oil and other natural resources, increased revenue from personal income taxes and a modest jump in inflation.

While that should leave the government more room to spend, cut taxes or reduce the deficit, economists warn that much of that money has already been accounted for through announcements for such things as increased defence spending.

The C.D. Howe Institute says Ottawa can make the economy more productive and boost Canadians’ standard of living without blowing its budget. In a “shadow budget” released last week, the institute calls for Ottawa to shift the burden away from the most harmful taxes, including personal and corporate income taxes, towards the less harmful consumption taxes.

The document’s authors, which include Don Drummond, a former high-ranking official at the Department of Finance and chief economist at TD Bank, also offer a recipe that includes a comprehensive review of spending, cutting out inefficient corporate subsidies, tighter controls on spending and a clear plan to eliminate the deficit by 2030-31.

“Responsible fiscal policy means paying the bills for spending as they come,” the report said.

The government also needs to start using more realistic growth projections so that it avoids making its fiscal problems worse.

The problem, economists warn, is that Canada May be facing dark clouds on the economic horizon, notably its ongoing trade friction with the U.S., and that governments should be more prudent with revenue.

In the government’s spring update, Champagne said the 2025–26 deficit was projected to be about $66.9 billion, down from the $78.3 billion that had been projected in last fall’s budget. That drop was due largely to a fiscal windfall from higher oil prices.

But Ottawa has been amassing large piles of debt for more than half a century, the problem has grown substantially over the last few years. The federal government has now accumulated more than $1.3 trillion in total debt, almost half of which has been added over the last five years.

The document’s authors, which include Don Drummond, a former high-ranking official at the Department of Finance and chief economist at TD Bank, also offer a recipe that includes a comprehensive review of spending, cutting out inefficient corporate subsidies, tighter controls on spending and a clear plan to eliminate the deficit by 2030-31.
“Responsible fiscal policy means paying the bills for spending as they come,” the report said.
The government also needs to start using more realistic growth projections so that it avoids making its fiscal problems worse.

The problem, economists warn, is that Canada May be facing dark clouds on the economic horizon, notably its ongoing trade friction with the U.S., and that governments should be more prudent with revenue.

In the government’s spring update, Champagne said the 2025–26 deficit was projected to be about $66.9 billion, down from the $78.3 billion that had been projected in last fall’s budget. That drop was due largely to a fiscal windfall from higher oil prices.

But Ottawa has been amassing large piles of debt for more than half a century, the problem has grown substantially over the last few years. The federal government has now accumulated more than $1.3 trillion in total debt, almost half of which has been added over the last five years.

stories.title: Auditor general to release reports on greenhouse gases, coal exports, pesticides
stories.summary: Ottawa — The federal spending watchdog plans to issue report cards today tracking government agencies' progress on reducing greenhouse gas emissions and working toward a ban on the export of thermal coal.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal spending watchdog plans to issue report cards today tracking government agencies’ progress on reducing greenhouse gas emissions and working toward a ban on the export of thermal coal.

The latest batch of reports from Auditor General Karen Hogan will also evaluate efforts to reduce health and environmental risks from pesticides, manage the Canadian Dental Care Plan and oversee the national emergency stockpile.

Other audits will examine the activities of Canada’s anti-money laundering centre, the Canadian Armed Forces’ management of ammunition and the federal border agency’s collection of customs duties and taxes.

Another report will assess whether several agencies managed procurement and contracts of selected call centre systems with regard to economy, efficiency and effectiveness.

Hogan plans to hold a media conference to discuss the reports after they are tabled in the House of Commons.

Liberal cabinet ministers and opposition MPs are also expected to comment on the auditor’s findings.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: The U.S. Congress is in play — here are the midterm races to watch
stories.summary: Tight races between Republicans and Democrats continue to heat up ahead of the U.S. midterm elections next Tuesday, with control of Congress up for grabs.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Tight races between Republicans and Democrats continue to heat up ahead of the U.S. midterm elections next Tuesday, with control of Congress up for grabs.

The stakes are sky-high for both parties. For the Republicans, it’s their narrow majority in Congress and what remains of President Donald Trump’s governing agenda.

For Democrats, it’s an opportunity to restrain Trump’s unprecedented use of presidential powers over the remainder of his term.

Polling shows Democrats are close to taking the House, where a net gain of three seats would give them a narrow majority.

Midterm election results in the U.S. tend to swing against the party of the sitting president — and Trump’s deeply unpopular policies, rising inflation and the war with Iran are putting many Republicans in peril.

“When we look at the polling, the feelings about Trump and the Trump administration are soured. In every poll, the trend has been down over the last two years,” said Marc Trussler, director of data science for the University of Pennsylvania’s program on opinion research and election studies.

Trussler said, at this point, it would be “a big surprise that the Democrats weren’t able to gain control of the House.”

But the fate of congressional pushback against Trump ultimately could be decided by a handful of hotly contested Senate races — some of them in places where the president’s trade war with Canada is a top ballot box issue.

Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win the Senate majority. They need to hold seats like Michigan while also gaining others in states like Maine.

“Both of those races are ones in which things are very tight, within the margin of error,” said Trussler, who is Canadian. “And both are going to have very explicitly involved Canada.”

Trump’s attacks on Canada have become a polarizing election issue — nowhere more than in the state of Michigan.

Michigan’s economy is deeply integrated with that of Canada. The president’s decision to hold up the opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge has been a high-profile issue in the campaign — along with the drop in Canadian visitors driven by Trump’s anti-Canada rhetoric.

The blowback over the trade war has been bad enough to convince Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers to put some distance between himself and Trump. In a campaign ad released earlier this month, Rogers is seen drinking a Labatt’s beer and telling voters “Canada is not our enemy.”

Christopher Sands, director of Johns Hopkins University’s Center for Canadian Studies, said Rogers has been walking on eggshells, trying not to alienate Trump while telling voters he would stand up for Michigan.

If the Democrats can’t hold Michigan, their path to flipping the Senate will be much more difficult. Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed — who has said the trade war with Canada makes no sense — doesn’t have a clear lead in the state’s race.

El-Sayed has been a constant target of Trump and Republicans. Opponents have brought up previous controversial comments and have suggested the Democrat has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood.

“If El-Sayed loses, it won’t be because of his position on Canada,” Sands said. “It’ll be because some of the more controversial things he has said.”

In Maine, longtime Republican Senator Susan Collins’s fate could also hinge on Trump’s trade war. The Trump administration recently changed its 50 per cent tariffs on Canada to lessen the impact on Maine in a bid to help Collins ahead of the election.

Collins, who has held the seat for 30 years, has sold herself as an independent-minded Republican who can work with the Trump administration to the benefit of her state. She has long opposed the president’s tariffs on Canada.

The former president says Trump has upset Canadians through his abuse of the country and talks of making it the 51 state.

While Maine voters are unhappy with Trump policies that have pushed up energy prices and caused Canadian tourism to plummet, Democrats have struggled to get their message across since the party’s initial candidate, Graham Platner, dropped out over allegations of sexual assault.

Platner’s replacement Troy Jackson has made the tariffs on Canada a key issue in his campaign since stepping into the role in July. He has accused Collins of enabling Trump’s chaos and points out that she voted to confirm the people driving the president’s unpopular policies.

Canada might not be top of mind for voters in other tight races but the economic impacts of Trump’s policies are major motivators, Trussler said.

The most likely way for Democrats to take control of the Senate is to also flip seats in Alaska, Iowa, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas — all states with significant trade relationships with Canada.

In Ohio, Republican Sen. Jon Husted is facing former Democrat candidate Sherrod Brown.

Husted was appointed to the seat in 2025 that was previously held by Vice-President JD Vance. Lately, he’s been known for Trump’s repeated comments about his body during campaign events.

While Trump carried the state in the last three presidential elections, Brown, who lost a race for Ohio’s other Senate seat in 2024, has consistently outperformed Democrat presidential candidates in Ohio.

Another closely watched race is the one in Texas between scandal-plagued Republican candidate Ken Paxton and the Democrat nominee, state Rep. James Talarico.

Texas hasn’t elected a Democrat statewide since 1994 but the party is hoping that Paxton’s unpopularity, even among Republicans, will allow Talarico to pull off a win in the Lonestar State.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Kutryk to become fifth Canadian astronaut to perform a spacewalk
stories.summary: Joshua Kutryk is set to become the fifth Canadian astronaut to perform a spacewalk today.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Astronaut Joshua Kutryk spent more than seven hours hovering in the vacuum of space on Thursday, making him the fifth Canadian to perform a spacewalk.

The International Space Station was some 420 kilometres above the Earth when Kutryk and Nasa astronaut Anil Menon stepped out.

The duo placed their suits on battery power at 7:57 a.m. EDT, marking the official beginning of the spacewalk. They were back in the station at 3:08 p.m., after a total of seven hours and 11 minutes.

The astronauts successfully installed seven of eight new solar panel systems needed to upgrade the station’s power capacity.

Following the walk, fellow Crew 13 members Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins helped Kutryk and Menon out of their equipment and checked their biomedical data.

After taking off his helmet, Kutryk wiped his face and Menon smiled. Kutryk is scheduled to speak to media Friday morning.

Nasa mission control in Houston said the spacewalk was “essentially flawless.”

Before the spacewalkers left the airlock, their crewmates wished them luck.

“From Luke and I on the other side of the hatch, good luck. We’re proud of you and we’ll see you on the other side,” Watkins, a Nasa flight engineer, told them.

Kutryk is on his first mission in space and his trip outside the space station is expected to be his first of two spacewalks.

Before Kutryk, the last Canadian to perform a spacewalk was David Saint-Jacques in 2019.

Saint-Jacques answered questions from schoolchildren at the Montreal Science Centre as a livestream showing the spacewalk was projected.

He described the feat as “one of the most exciting and one of most dangerous things we do” and said Kutryk was in “very good spirits” when they last spoke ahead of the spacewalk.

“It’s kind of the peak of the career for an astronaut to get a chance to put on your own miniature spacecraft that we call a space suit and go outside to do some maintenance work,” he said.

Saint-Jacques said spacewalkers train for thousands of hours in a giant pool and a full-size replica of the space station in Houston. They learn to operate the space suit and study the procedures and equipment needed for their mission.

They also receive step-by-step instructions in real time.

The crew’s mission is crucial, Saint-Jacques said, as the station is nearly 30 years old and its original solar panels have lost efficiency. According to the Canadian Space Agency, the new panels, paired with previously installed arrays, will help increase power generation capacity on the station by up to 30 per cent. stories.title: Ontario finance minister to table fall economic update
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy is set to provide an update on the province's finances today by tabling his government's fall economic statement.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Ontario’s fiscal outlook has worsened due to global uncertainty and trade disruptions, leading to a larger deficit this year and a delayed path to balance, the finance minister said Thursday in an economic update.

Peter Bethlenfalvy’s spring budget had projected a $13.8-billion deficit this year, but his fall economic statement now says there will be $16.9 billion in red ink.

“The impact of U.S. tariffs which have hit, among others, our steel, auto and manufacturing sectors, and global conflicts such as the Strait of Hormuz impacting energy prices, has led to the world awash in a sea of instability,” Bethlenfalvy said in a speech in the legislature.

“We need to look no further than the price of gas, rising cost of goods due to tariffs and the impact of uncertainty on investment and employment. As a result, Ontario families and businesses are feeling the impacts. No doubt the world has changed.”

The province also projected in the budget that the books would be balanced in 2028-29, but Bethlenfalvy now says that won’t happen until 2029-30.

This marks the fourth time since 2024 that Premier Doug Ford’s government has pushed its path to balance by a year. Officials say that’s not ideal, but the province’s fiscal health is not in as dire shape as it was during the 2008-09 recession or the COVID-19 pandemic.

The outlook has deteriorated since the spring budget due to new U.S. tariffs, the threat of more tariffs, and the war in Iran, officials said. That instability has prompted Ontario to add $3.8 billion this year to its contingency fund, which will sit at $4.9 billion. Most of that is expected to be used by the end of the year, the officials said.

The province is also trying to focus on reducing fraud, error, waste and abuse of taxpayer dollars through an “enterprise-wide” analysis of its programs, Bethlenfalvy said in the economic update.

“A strategic investment in enterprise integrity capabilities could conservatively prevent $500 million to $1.25 billion in losses annually,” the economic statement said.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said Ford has made life more difficult for the average Ontarian since taking office in 2018.“This is the worst fiscal management by any government in the history of Ontario,” he said. “And Ontarians are paying for it right now, and they’ll be paying for it tomorrow, and it’ll be paid for the foreseeable future.”

The province failed to deliver affordability measures in the economic update, said New Democrat finance critic Jessica Bell.“There are no significant measures in the end to make it easier for people to pay for food at the grocery store or pay for rent,” she said.

Bethlenfalvy said the government has already put a wide array of affordability measures in place.

“We moved early on things like the gas tax,” he said. “We cut the HST for homebuyers of new homes. Minimum wage has just gone up from $17.60 to $17.95.”

Previously announced measures in the fall economic statement include matching the federal government’s recent move to give businesses a tax break on capital investments, and billions of dollars in funding for tariff-hit sectors such as steel and autos.

“These actions are helping businesses adapt, attract investment, create good-paying jobs and strengthen Ontario’s resilience,” Bethlenfalvy said.

The province is changing eligibility rules around its computer animation and special effects tax credits to give more of it to film and television producers.

The fall economic statement also includes housing start projections, and it shows starts decreasing slightly this year to 64,700, down from 65,400 starts in 2025. It projects flat growth for 2027 with increases to 71,700 starts in 2028 and 75,400 starts in 2029.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

stories.title: Proposed changes to Blue Box program mean less waste will get recycled, critics say
stories.summary: The province’s proposals mean soft plastic packagine wouldn’t be recycled and residents could no longer put out overflow bundles.
stories.author: Patty Winsa
stories.content:
Proposed changes to Ontario’s residential Blue Box program could result in less household waste being recycled and run counter to the original goal of privatizing collection, environmental groups say.

If adopted, the Ontario government proposals, outlined in a technical briefing document provided to the Star earlier this week , would see the end of flexible plastic in blue bins.

That means plastic rice and cereal pouches, coffee bags, chip bags, bubble wrap, snack wrappers and other soft plastic packaging could end up in the garbage.

The amendments, since posted online , would also phase out a requirement for waste companies to pick up bundles of cardboard and overflow recycling in clear bags placed outside blue bins.

The province is considering eliminating pickup for flexible plastics and overflow recycling,

The delivery of extra bins would also end, except for residents with accessibility needs or those without access to depot collection.

“Plastic and the increasing use of plastics and disposable products, disposable clothing, disposable packaging is driving waste. And it’s expensive to collect,” said Karen Wirsig of Environmental Defence.

When the Ontario government first announced it was privatizing the Blue Box program, one of the goals was to off-load the cost of recycling onto the companies that produce and sell the packaging in the hopes that they would switch to more environmentally-friendly materials.

But instead of driving companies to change their packaging, Wirsig said the government is now proposing changes that could result in less material being recycled to reduce costs.

“This is the inevitable result if you have a government that’s not committed to the original principles of the Circular Economy Act,” said Wirsig, “and is just here to serve … the consumer goods lobby that is saying let us keep doing what we’re doing and don’t make us pay for it.”

Environment Minister Todd McCarthy now says there won’t be new landfills forced on communities that don’t want them.

The proposed changes to the recycling program coincide with a recent announcement by Ontario’s environment minister that the province hopes to burn more garbage for energy and build more landfills as the province runs out of space to dump its trash.

On Tuesday, the government tabled an omnibus bill, Building Ontario Faster Act , that seeks to speed up the permitting and approval regime across all ministries, including for new landfill sites or incinerators.

Ontario’s landfills will be full within 10 years and the province needs to act quickly , Environment Minister Todd McCarthy said.

Emily Alfred, a senior campaigner with Toronto Environmental Alliance, said if the proposed changes to the recycling program are enacted, consumers will be literally left holding the bag, the final arbiters of deciding whether a myriad of plastic packaging goes in the garbage or recycling bin.

“People really relate to recycling and their blue bin as one way that they can have an impact on the environment,” said Alfred. “But it’s just so frustrating.”

She said she’s concerned that consumers are “getting confusing messaging about how to manage waste” and the changes could ultimately mean more recyclables and plastics ending up in landfills and incinerators.

As Toronto’s landfill space risks running out by 2034, the city faces a controversial debate over turning to incineration.

Since Ontario fully transitioned to a producer-run Blue Box system in January of this year, the companies that now have to pay for the program, including packaged goods producers, supermarkets and other retails, have complained that costs have skyrocketed.

The Retail Council of Canada estimated in 2025 that Ontario’s Blue Box recycling program would cost companies $740 million to operate in 2026, nearly four times what they paid when they shared costs with municipalities prior to the province’s transition to privatized recycling, which began in 2023.

Circular Materials, founded by companies such as Costco, Loblaw, and Procter and Gamble, administers the province’s recycling program, negotiating contracts and setting fees for recycling. It is also a Producer Responsibility Organization, competing with other PROs in Ontario while holding 80 per cent of the market.

Producers have complained that there is not enough transparency about what they are being charged for by Circular Materials or why their fees are increasing.

The government has said it May replace Circular with a new independent administrator.

Gary Sands, senior vice-president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Grocers, said one independent grocery store in Toronto was billed $83,315 by Circular Materials in 2024, a charge that rose to $141,996 the next year and $178,262 in 2026.

“For an independent grocer on a two per cent margin, those continuing escalating costs are not sustainable and are disproportionately more significant,” said Sands. “In the context of acute consumer angst around affordability, these increasing costs should be even more concerning to government.”

Sands said it’s too early to say whether the amendments will help bring down costs, but he said that his membership would welcome more transparency, especially because they don’t have a small business representative on the Circular Materials board.

“If this provides more transparency and sheds more light on the revenue that’s being collected, where that revenue is going, costs, all the things that are outlined in the amendments,” said Sands, “our members would welcome that.

“Because the first step to getting a resolution is having a better understanding and more information about what’s going into these fees.”

Confounding the problem in Ontario is a volatile market for recycled plastic, said Elena Mantagaris, a senior adviser for the Association of Plastic Recyclers. Cheap plastic resin from overseas is being dumped on the Canadian market, she said, undercutting prices here for post-consumer recycled plastic resin.

Although Ontario has instituted Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), Mantagaris said the problem is there is no federal regulation requiring recycled content. “We built the front end of the system, but have done nothing to create the right market conditions for the use of post-consumers resin,” she said.

Circular Materials said in an email that it is reviewing the proposed amendments and will provide a response during the current 30-day period for public comment.

The Environment Ministry said in an email that it is “currently consulting on how these changes May help the industry better plan for the future, so that producers pay their fair share of Blue Box costs without surprise fees or changes that could impact their operations.”

Although Ontario has instituted Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), Mantagaris said the problem is there is no federal regulation requiring recycled content. “We built the front end of the system, but have done nothing to create the right market conditions for the use of post-consumers resin,” she said.
Circular Materials said in an email that it is reviewing the proposed amendments and will provide a response during the current 30-day period for public comment.

The Environment Ministry said in an email that it is “currently consulting on how these changes May help the industry better plan for the future, so that producers pay their fair share of Blue Box costs without surprise fees or changes that could impact their operations.”

Public Service Announcement

[](http://london.ca/newsroom/public-service-announcement/temporary-richmond-street-closure-private-sewer-service)

Thursday, October 29, 2026

Richmond Street will be closed between Dundas Street and Queens Avenue from Tuesday, November 3 to Thursday, November 5 while work is completed on a private sewer connection.

This will have significant impacts for people traveling through the area. Drivers and pedestrians are encouraged to plan ahead, follow signs, and allow extra time for their trips downtown.

A map showing the temporary closure on Richmond Street between Dundas Street and Queens Avenue, with signed detour routes for northbound and southbound traffic.

Detour and access

A signed detour will direct drivers around the closure. Drivers should follow the posted detour signs and follow directions.

Southbound traffic will be detoured on Queens Avenue, Talbot Street and King Street. Northbound traffic will be detoured on King Street, Wellington Street, and Queens Avenue.

The east sidewalk of Richmond Street will be closed during this work.

Some LTC routes will be impacted. Please check theLondon Transit Commission websitefor the most up-to-date information on bus schedules and detours.

For more information about construction projects in London, visit theRenew London map.

stories.title: Using AI to improve care for people experiencing homelessness
stories.summary: A new study at London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (Lhscri) and Ices Western is using artificial intelligence (AI) and community partnerships to advance equitable care for people…
stories.content:
Media Release October 29, 2026

A new study at London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (Lhscri) and Ices Western is using artificial intelligence (AI) and community partnerships to advance equitable care for people experiencing homelessness.

The study led by Stephanie Dixon, a research scientist at Lhscri and Ices Western, and an assistant professor in the Departments of Medicine and Epidemiology and Biostatistics at Western University, will develop a new frailty score that accounts for the health impacts of experiencing homelessness. Frailty scores are tools used to assess a person’s overall health and risk of complications. Through the project, Dixon and collaborators will use anonymous health data from more than 35,000 Ontarians who have a history of homelessness. Working alongside community partners, health-care providers, and individuals with lived experience, the team will identify factors that can help create a more accurate picture of health risks for individuals who have experienced homelessness. “Data can tell us a great deal, but it only captures one part of the story,” says Dixon. “By bringing together data, lived experience, and frontline expertise, we hope to build something that helps people see health needs earlier and connect individuals with the care and support they need.”

The long-term goal is to develop a tool that can help physicians and shelter-based care providers identify people who May be at increased risk of poor health outcomes earlier and to deliver more proactive care. The project will also document important gaps in existing health data collection to help researchers better understand where the experiences of people experiencing homelessness are less visible in health care systems. The study is supported through the AMS Healthcare Leadership in Compassion and Artificial Intelligence Fellowship , a year-long program that brings together health-care leaders, researchers, and innovators to explore how AI can be developed and applied with compassion at its core. Through the fellowship, Dixon is collaborating with an interdisciplinary team, community partners, and individuals with lived experience to develop both the frailty score and a broader framework for compassionate, equity-informed AI in health research.

Existing frailty scores help health-care providers identify people at greater risk of illness, hospitalization, or other serious health complications. However, most were developed for older adults living in stable housing and often fail to capture the cumulative impacts of homelessness, including stressors such as trauma, chronic stress, substance use, mental health concerns, and barriers to accessing care. Research suggests that people experiencing homelessness can experience the effects of frailty years earlier than the general population. This can make it difficult to identify who May benefit from additional supports or interventions. To develop a new frailty score, Dixon is collaborating with community partners and individuals with lived experience to create a model that accounts for the health impacts of experiencing homelessness. The AI-driven tool will incorporate stressors not typically included in existing frailty scores, which often place greater emphasis on a person’s age than their life experiences and health challenges. “We are using a co-designed approach,” says Dixon, who has worked with Ices Western for nearly 15 years. “Together we can identify commonly missed stressors such as the cumulative effects of adverse childhood experiences, substance use, infectious disease history, and mental health concerns.”

stories.title: Tips for a safer, more accessible Halloween
stories.summary: Halloween can be a time for neighbourhoods to come together.
stories.content:
Halloween can be a time for neighbourhoods to come together. Ahead of Halloween this Saturday, the City of London is sharing tips to help make trick-or-treating more accessible, keep people safe on neighbourhood streets, and dispose of pumpkins responsibly.

Slow down and stay alert

More children and families May be out walking and cycling on Halloween. Drivers are reminded to slow down, watch for people crossing the street, and take extra care at intersections.

Make your home more accessible for trick-or-treaters

A few tips for creating a welcoming environment for children and families of all abilities to enjoy Halloween:

Bring treats out and remove obstacles. Keep pathways clear and be willing to setup on your laneway or bring treats down to visitors if your entrance has stairs.

Offer alternative treats. Consider offering non-candy options, such as stickers or small toys.

Respect sensory needs. Be mindful that costumes, loud noises and Halloween effects May be overwhelming for some children.

Be patient and inclusive. Be kind to kids of all ages and give children time to participate, whether or not they communicate verbally.

Download a copy of the City's Accessible Trick or Treating sign for a full list of tips. Consider printing a copy to post at your house to show support for a more accessible Halloween.

Staying safe around construction

Construction work continues in neighbourhoods across London to upgrade roads, sidewalks and underground infrastructure. When traveling near these areas, be aware for signs and follow posted detours. For everyone’s safety, stay out of construction zones.

Dispose of pumpkins responsibly

There are three easy ways you can sustainably dispose of pumpkins. First, remove candles and other accessories, and then:

Set out pumpkins beside your Green Bin or cut into smaller pieces and place inside.

Set out pumpkins beside your yard waste bags/containers or cut into smaller pieces and place inside.

If you miss collection or don’t have access to curbside pickup, drop off your pumpkins at your nearest EnviroDepot for composting.

Painted pumpkins should go into the garbage. Please remember to keep your bags and bins under 20 kg (44 lbs).

For waste collection and other City service inquiries, visit service.London.CA .

Together, these small actions can help make Halloween safer and more welcoming for everyone.

stories.title: Profane language and comments about wanting director of education fired earn punishment for York Catholic board chair
stories.summary: Integrity commissioner rules Iafrate spoke and acted inappropriately. Calandra calls the infighting “so frustrating.”
stories.author: Megan Ogilvie; Kristin Rushowy
stories.content:
The York Catholic school board’s integrity commissioner has imposed penalties on board chair Maria Iafrate after ruling she violated the trustee code of conduct when she used “profane and disparaging language” against the board’s former director of education and that her behaviour “contributed to a toxic environment.”

Launched following complaints by fellow trustees, the investigation examined allegations against Iafrate, including that she overstepped her role, engaged in “operational interference,” questioned staff integrity and made inappropriate public statements to staff, including calling the director of education a “f—-ing piece of s—-” and saying she wanted him fired.

Integrity commissioner Daniela Corapi found three instances, out of nine investigated, where Iafrate had breached conduct rules, penalizing her with mandatory governance training and by docking her pay.

The commissioner had directed the board supervisor to publish the findings and sanctions on the York Catholic board website. The report , issued in August, was only made public Wednesday, in part not to interfere with the election, according to board spokesperson Mark Brosens.

“The sanctions imposed by the Integrity Commission are in the process of being fulfilled,” Brosens said. Iafrate could not be reached for comment Wednesday.

The Ontario government seized control of the York Catholic board in March, just weeks after Education Minister Paul Calandra warned trustees they had to fix board finances and dysfunctional governance. At the time, Calandra said longstanding infighting within the board had cost it hundreds of thousands in legal fees.

The York Catholic school board’s integrity commissioner has imposed penalties on board chair Maria Iafrate.

Calandra said Thursday that the behaviour outlined in the report “is one of the reasons why we took over that board.”

While the board also had financial challenges, “it’s another one of those boards where they were spending so much time (dealing with) trustees fighting each other,” he told reporters at Queen’s Park.

“As you get through that report, it just becomes so evident. It just irritates you; it is just very, very frustrating.”

Trustees“ say ‘we’re in it for the kids’ — no, in some of these boards they’re in it to fight each other,” he added. “It’s so frustrating; it’s not why they’re supposed to be there. And I wish I could say that was the only board where this happened.”

York Catholic trustees Elizabeth Crowe and Theresa McNicol each brought separate complaints against Iafrate, alleging she breached numerous codes of conduct.

Iafrate was acclaimed in her Richmond Hill ward in Monday’s election.

Crowe, a longtime York Catholic board trustee, retired this summer, while McNicol, who has held her position for almost 30 years, was re-elected as a trustee for Newmarket, East Gwillimbury and Georgina. The investigation was launched in January.

Education Minister Paul Calandra says he wants to make sure they’re governed by the code of conduct.

In her 34-page report, Corapi noted that Iafrate and McNicol have “been engaged in a prolonged and serious interpersonal conflict that has repeatedly resulted in formal code proceedings.”

The report also describes a tense relationship between Iafrate and John De Faveri, the board’s former director of education, who had previously lodged a workplace harassment complaint against Iafrate. De Faveri retired from his role in June.

Corapi ruled that in three instances Iafrate had broken code-of-conduct rules, including when she called De Faveri “a f—-ing piece of s—-” to board staff and stated he’s “gotta get out of here.” She also ruled Iafrate had broken the code when she told other trustees she wanted De Faveri fired, and when she overstepped her governance and questioned staff professionalism and integrity.

“Some of her conduct appears to reflect errors in judgment, but other conduct, particularly her treatment of John De Faveri and other staff, amounts to flagrant violations of the Education Act and board policy,” Corapi wrote.

In feedback Iafrate provided on a draft of the findings, and published in the report, she asserted De Faveri’s claims against her were false and rejected that she had said she “hated” him, wanted him “fired” and that she had “a longstanding campaign” against him.

Iafrate also denied making negative comments about De Faveri to staff, said she apologized if her messages to staff had come across as “demanding” and accused Crowe of having “improper motives for filing her complaint,” to which Corapi responded “That is not at issue.”

In her findings, Corapi wrote that while Iafrate, who has been a trustee since 2018, has not previously been in breach of the code, “undermining the board’s senior executive to subordinate staff is egregious enough” to outweigh her clean record and warrants a sanction.

Corapi ruled Iafrate must undergo governance training within six months of the report being issued and docked her trustee pay for 30 days.

“Such conduct contributed to a toxic environment and cannot be minimized as mere error,” Corapi wrote.

stories.title: Éric Blais: Mark Carney said no to Quebec’s premier. That’s exactly what he wanted
stories.summary: Quebec’s separatist movement won’t pass up a single chance to turn a slight from Ottawa into something that revives Quebecers’ old feeling of being diminished.
stories.author: Éric Blais
stories.content:
Last week, Ottawa exhaled when about 75 per cent of Albertans voted to stay in Canada and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith promised there would be no second try . Separatism had been tested and found wanting.

This week, the federal government hosts the Canada-European Union summit in Montreal. It has told Quebec’s premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, that he won’t be speaking, or hosting a reception of his own.

Picture a couple still living under one roof, where there’s been talk of separation and one of them clearly wants out. Important friends are coming from overseas and the one who sent the invitations tells the other: you can come, but no toast and no party of your own.

Told he can’t speak at a summit in his own province, Pspp, as everyone calls the premier, answered with an image every Quebecer understands.

His long post didn’t open with trade figures. It opened with a film: ” Le Temps des bouffons ,” Pierre Falardeau’s scathing short documentary about a Beaver Club banquet in the 1980s, where Montreal’s moneyed establishment dressed up as fur-trade barons. In Falardeau’s telling, French Canadians are the ones carrying water on their own land. Most of English Canada has never heard of the film. Then came the punchline: Ottawa, Pspp wrote, seems to think that permission to serve shrimp cocktail at a reception counts as influence.

Pspp knows what this summons. For generations, the French Canadian at the elite’s dinner was the waiter at the private club, the help at the boss’s party, or the clerk told to speak white. Quebec remembers that picture and considers it long settled.

That is a movement that knows exactly what it’s doing. It won’t pass up a single chance to turn a slight from Ottawa into something that revives Quebecers’ old feeling of being diminished.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says the premier was invited to the dinner and declined and that this is a federal summit. By the time you read this, Ottawa May have relented. I doubt it.

Carney is more likely applying what he learned dealing with Donald Trump. If you give him what he wants, he’ll bully you for more. However, with Trump, saying no denies him what he wants. With Pspp, saying no is what he wants.

It’s worth noting that the request for a Quebec reception wasn’t Pspp’s. It came on Sept. 15 from Christine Fréchette’s CAQ, a party that kept telling Quebecers the federation could work for them. Same request and answer.

Nor does Industry Minister Mélanie Joly help by insisting that geopolitics is federal jurisdiction . The summit is mostly about trade, which reaches deep into provincial territory. Quebec had its own negotiator at the Ceta talks.

Even Quebec’s Liberal leader, Charles Milliard, says the premier should have been given the floor. He also says Pspp is wrong to stay away altogether, since an empty chair doesn’t serve Quebec. Both are fair points. But an empty chair is also a symbol, and symbols are this premier’s specialty.

As it turns out, the chair won’t sit empty. In a denouement better suited to an episode of “The Diplomat” than to real-life foreign relations at a time of great disruption, Pspp announced he’d send his newly appointed “diplomat in chief,” Pascal Paradis, to the summit.

In a letter to the European delegation, the premier repeated that his government had been denied the chance to present its views, and warned that this could create uncertainty about how any agreements reached at the summit would be applied. Translation: Quebec might not go along with what Ottawa signs.

The federalist answer cannot be fear. It has to be the harder, more honest case: that a Quebec

It would be tempting, in Ottawa, to file Quebec next to Alberta. Pspp has pledged no referendum while Trump is in office. He won the election, but nearly three voters in four chose someone else. One would expect him to spend the start of his minority mandate proving he can govern.

He seems determined to show he can govern while also preparing a referendum. Rather than put sovereignty on the back burner, the pledge buys time to keep it on the front one and every slight from Ottawa turns up the heat.

Still, the PQ has a problem. To grow support for sovereignty, it believes it needs Quebecers to feel slighted. But most of them like Carney and a premier who picks fights too early risks being tuned out.

Carney is immensely popular in Quebec right now. But Quebecers’ affection for federal Liberals has always been conditional and it has evaporated before.

Alberta was the easy referendum. Ottawa shouldn’t make the next one easier.

stories.title: Western’s first physician assistant class marks milestone at stethoscope ceremony
stories.summary: Western's first class in its new physician assistant graduate program participated in a stethoscope cereomny to mark the milestone.
stories.author: Emily Leighton
stories.content:
Working in patient management at a busy Ontario hospital, Jack Strong experienced the demands and complexities of delivering patient care.

“You see how many people are waiting for care and the pressure that puts on health-care teams,” he said. “It reinforced my interest in a career where I can work directly with patients and help make a difference.”

Strong is among 28 students in the inaugural class of the master of physician assistant studies (Mpas) program at Western’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry.

The students received their stethoscopes and recited a professional oath at a special ceremony on Oct. 27, reaffirming their commitment to ethical, compassionate care and marking an important step in their training.

This slideshow requires JavaScript.

Launched earlier this year , the two-year professional master’s program aims to strengthen Ontario’s health-care workforce and improve access to patient care.

Physician assistants, or PAs, are medically trained professionals who work alongside supervising physicians, supporting patient assessment, diagnosis and treatment across a range of specialties and clinical settings.

The Mpas program combines medical foundations, clinical skills and professional competencies in the first year, followed by clinical rotations across London and Southwestern Ontario in the second. Students also undertake research and quality-improvement coursework.

Strong, who studied biomedical science and anatomical education at the University of Ottawa, was drawn to the flexibility offered by the program.

“I like that we’re not limited to one specialty,” he said. “As my interests evolve, I’ll have the opportunity to explore different areas of health care, from emergency medicine to cardiology and oncology.”

As part of the inaugural cohort, Strong is also eager to help shape the program as it develops.

“Being part of the first class comes with a responsibility,” he said.

“We have an opportunity to share our experiences and help build something that will benefit future students.” – Jack Strong, graduate student in physician assistant studies

For fellow Mpas student Reet Toor, the appeal of the profession is rooted in the relationships she hopes to build with patients.

Originally from Vancouver, Toor completed her undergraduate studies at the University of British Columbia before pursuing graduate studies at Schulich Medicine & Dentistry. During clinical rotations as part of her master’s program in medical sciences, she witnessed the contributions physician assistants make to patient care.

“Seeing how physician assistants work alongside physicians really opened my eyes to the profession,” she said. “I was struck by the important role they play in caring for patients and supporting the broader health-care team.”

“Coming from an immigrant family, I’ve seen how important it is for patients to understand their care. I want to help build that trust and help people feel informed and supported,” she added.

At the ceremony, Dr. John Yoo, dean of Schulich Medicine & Dentistry, encouraged students to embrace the art of listening.

“The stethoscope is a relatively simple instrument, but I believe it is one of the most powerful symbols in medicine,” he said. “It requires you to listen. Not just to heartbeats or breath sounds, but to the human story behind every patient you care for.”

Learn more about how Western is optimizing health for all.

stories.title: Alberta NDP accuses Smith of gerrymandering as province prepares to unveil new electoral map
stories.summary: Proposed map, produced by an independent panel, remains confidential until it’s tabled in legislature next Monday
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Alberta’s new electoral boundaries are expected to be released next week, setting up a contentious battle over the map that will define the province’s political playing field for the next decade – a process that has been plagued by accusations of gerrymandering.

On Wednesday, a committee of MLAs with the United Conservative Party and Alberta NDP met to discuss next steps for the proposed map and report, which was produced by an independent panel and privately delivered to members last week. That report will remain confidential until it’s tabled in the Alberta legislature next Monday.

But Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi and two fellow New Democrat MLAs detailed extensive concerns about the new proposed map on Wednesday, calling it “illegal” and accusing Premier Danielle Smith of gerrymandering, referring to the U.S.-style tactic of manipulating electoral maps to create an artificial advantage.

“This government, in their effort to dodge accountability, has engineered the single worst case of gerrymandering in Alberta history,” Mr. Nenshi said in the public committee meeting.

The Globe and Mail was not able to verify the Ndp’s claims because the report isn’t public.

Ms. Smith later chastised the NDP leader for discussing the report before it is distributed publicly and accused him of questioning the integrity of the independent panel’s chair, retired Alberta judge Brian O’Ferrall.

“He is already prepositioning another election denialism, trying to pre-frame the results as if it’s going to have an impact on the next election,” Ms. Smith said during Question Period.

Alberta’s political boundaries are redrawn every eight to 10 years by an independent panel. Two years ago, ahead of the scheduled overhaul of Alberta’s electoral map, the UCP government determined two more seats were needed to accommodate the province’s recent population boom – particularly in urban centres. This would bring the total number of MLAs in the provincial legislature to 89, a 2-per-cent increase in seats for a province where the population had grown by 20 per cent since the last redistricting.

Continuing with tradition, the UCP and NDP then tapped a five-person panel to hold public consultations and draw the new electoral map to set the stage for the provincial election in October, 2027.

But last April, Ms. Smith rejected the independent commission’s proposed changes to the electoral map. Her government then formed a UCP-dominated committee that tapped a new independent panel charged with taking a second attempt at drawing the electoral map – this time with four more seats, bringing the total to 91.

Ms. Smith’s decision to force a redraw of the maps has injected a charged partisan atmosphere into what is normally a complex process designed to foster compromise and limit political influence. For decades, provincial legislatures have routinely adopted independent panels’ recommendations without question.

The dispute over the first panel’s work began in the spring when it submitted two maps in its final report, known as the majority and minority reports.

One was supported by the majority of its members: the chair, tapped by the governing UCP, and two panelists selected by the NDP. Their map would eliminate two rural ridings to accommodate a population boom in Calgary and Edmonton, where they proposed two additional seats. (The panelists said they wouldn’t have had to remove the rural seats if the commission was provided with two more seats in total.)

The commission’s other two members, both chosen by the UCP, put forward a competing map and report that proposed more than a dozen merged urban and rural ridings, diluting the power of the urban vote. The majority called this vision “unconstitutional” and “illogical.”

An analysis by The Globe and Mail found that the majority map would reduce the Ucp’s electoral advantage by a handful of seats. The minority map, meanwhile, would reduce the Ndp’s strength in Calgary and Edmonton, where most of its political support resides.

In the end, Ms. Smith picked neither, forming a committee dominated by UCP MLAs that oversaw a new redrawing. The new plan gave her government permission to intervene in the process.

The idea to strike a new panel was proposed by the original commission chair, Court of King’s Bench Justice Dallas Miller, who suggested increasing the number of electoral districts to 91 from 89 to accommodate the loss of two rural seats in the majority’s plan. (He made the recommendation on his own, without the support of the four panelists.)

The Alberta NDP said on Wednesday that the new map violates several of the conditions Ms. Smith’s government previously committed to, such as limiting changes to the majority report’s proposals for most of the province. Alberta NDP House Leader Christina Gray said at the Wednesday committee meeting that she believes there is a “clear partisan tilt” to the report.

The three UCP MLAs sitting on the committee – Ron Wiebe, Chantelle de Jonge and Garth Rowswell – were silent on the report’s contents.

stories.title: ‘Local Governance 101’ Okanagan community’s first-ever council trains ahead of inaugural meeting
stories.summary: The desire for growth is also being echoed by residents, many of whom want to see Okanagan Falls thrive while maintaining its small-town feel.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Okanagan Falls’ first-ever municipal council is learning the ropes ahead of its inaugural meeting as the South Okanagan community prepares to take control of its own affairs.

Mayor-elect Matt Taylor, a former regional director with four years of experience, is helping guide the community’s four newly elected councillors through multi-day training sessions focused on the responsibilities of local government.

“Yeah, it’s local governance 101,” Taylor said.

Taylor said bringing local government to Okanagan Falls was one of the reasons he ran for mayor.

“That’s one of the things I wanted to bring to the community, and one of my reasons for running,” he said.

With incorporation comes a new set of responsibilities for the community of approximately 2,700 people.

Nearly 20 services previously delivered by the regional district, including fire protection, parks, water and sewer, are expected to transfer to the new municipality over time.

Taylor said the new council will need to ensure those services are delivered effectively while establishing the administrative and financial foundations of the municipality.

“We’ve got to operate services, and every municipality has to do that, and we’ve got to do that, and we’ve got to do it just as well as everybody else does,” Taylor said.

The municipality will also need to hire staff, about a dozen of them, and establish a financial plan.

“We’ve got to adopt a budget. The province says every municipality has to have a budget. So, boom! Right away, we’ve got to adopt a budget,” Taylor said.

The move toward municipal government comes after a challenging period for Okanagan Falls.

The closure of the Weyerhaeuser sawmill in 2007 dealt a significant blow to the local economy.

In 2019, the community also lost its only grocery store.

A grocery store eventually reopened, but its owners say continued growth will be important to supporting local businesses and creating economic stability.

Kyle Belich, of Belich’s AG Foods, said the community needs to build on its momentum after several years of economic uncertainty.

“We need this momentum. The last five years have been a roller coaster with the economy, with the uncertainty around here,” Belich said.

He hopes the new council will help create conditions for growth.

“I hope they start to pave the way to start to have some growth here. It’s so important. It’s so essential,” he said.

The desire for growth is also being echoed by residents, many of whom want to see Okanagan Falls thrive while maintaining its small-town feel.

“I just want to see more homes for young people. I would like to see it expand a little bit,” said Okanagan resident Barb Mulrooney.

Another resident expressed hope that incorporation could help move the community forward.

“Progress, I would think, and maybe the town will grow a bit,” said Okanagan resident Steve Zanatta.

For the new council, balancing those expectations with the practical demands of running a municipality will be a key challenge as Okanagan Falls enters a new chapter.

The council is expected to hold its inaugural meeting on November 6, marking the next step in the community’s transition to local municipal government.

stories.title: Family of soldier badly burned at CFB Wainwright speaks about his injuries
stories.summary: Family of a soldier severely burned at CFB Wainwright describe Pte. Liam Ramage's injuries and the long path to recovery.
stories.author: Sarah Ryan
stories.content:
Cheryl Ramage is proud to have two sons in the Canadian Armed Forces. Both were training at CFB Wainwright when a fire ripped through the base earlier this month.

The mother of four was attending dinner theatre when friends sent a text message asking: “Are your boys OK?”

“I had no idea what was happening,” she recalled.

Cheryl immediately texted her sons. She heard back from her son Rowan, who was safe. But her eldest, Liam, did not respond.

She checked in with Liam’s wife, Marisa Ramage, who also hadn’t been able to connect with him.

The women met at Liam and Marisa’s home at the Edmonton Garrison.

They scoured the internet for information, and at 3 a.m., they read that the military was keeping communications to a minimum while they notified next of kin.

It took time for them to learn the full extent of the fast-moving fire on Oct. 17 that killed four soldiers and left 39 others injured during a training exercise at the base located southeast of Edmonton.

“Then the doorbell rang,” Cheryl said, dabbing her eyes with tissue. “That was the hardest moment of my life. They walked in and said they had devastating news.”

Marisa assumed the worst. She said she couldn’t stop shaking, like she was in shock.

“I thought Liam was … I thought he was dead,” she said.

Marisa said the military officers started to explain, but she couldn’t bear waiting.

“I did not let them finish their conversation. I went, ‘He’s not dead, right?’ And they were like, ‘No, he is not dead. But he’s got some major, major injuries.'”

With that, the women rushed to Edmonton’s Royal Alexandra Hospital. They weren’t prepared for what they saw.

“We had to identify him by his feet,” Liam’s mother explained.

“Seeing him in a bed with burns on him, I couldn’t be in the room,” his wife said.

Doctors told them 40 per cent of Pte. Ramage’s body had been burned.

“Mostly to his face, head, neck, his hands are bad, both the tops and his palms, both arms, both legs and some on his back as well,” Cheryl explained.

In a moment alone with her husband of three years, Marisa whispered in his ear.

“You are too stubborn to die and there is no way that you’re not making it through this.”

Since that night, the 27-year-old from Red Deer County has undergone multiple surgeries and skin grafts, but the full extent of his injuries is still unknown.

“He can’t see when he wakes up, he can’t speak and he can’t move very much, so he has really no way of communicating,” his mother explained.

Cheryl said her son’s life has already been saved by blood donors, and she encourages people wanting to help to roll up their sleeves and donate.

She says she was told despite his own severe injuries, Pte. Ramage was still trying to save his fellow soldiers when first responders arrived.

That doesn’t surprise his wife, who says he loves to help people.

Marisa doesn’t know what the couple’s future holds, but she’s grateful for every small step her husband is making.

“It’s nice to see him improve. He can move his arms on his right side and his foot on his right side. He can nod yes or no and he can move his mouth.”

His mom says when Pte. Ramage enlisted in the Canadian Armed Forces in 2024, it had been a long time coming.

“He’s always been passionate about the military. That’s really all he’s ever wanted to do,” Cheryl explained.

She said he got his first taste of the military in cadets, where he advanced to the top as a Regimental Sergeant Major.

Since enlisting in 2024, Pte. Ramage has served in Latvia and at the G7 in Kananaskis, Alta.

His mom never thought her son would be in danger on home soil, calling the fire “a freak accident.”

The disaster remains under investigation.

The family is putting together photo albums to bring to Pte. Ramage’s hospital room.

“His smile lit up the room. He’s infectious. He’s a storyteller. He talks nonstop. And that’s what all of his buddies say too. Liam just never stopped talking.”

When he’s not working, Pte. Ramage loves playing bagpipes, cooking and Canada’s game.

“His passion is hockey. Hockey, hockey, more hockey. A diehard Montreal Canadiens fan,” his mom laughed.

The family brought a radio to the hospital this week, so as Pte. Ramage heals, they can listen to games together.

“We’ve created a GoFundMe for Liam. It’s going to be a long road, months if not years of rehabilitation, surgeries,” Cheryl explained.

They’re grateful for the support of the military, including their designated assistant, and plan to continue to stay with Pte. Ramage every day in the hospital.

“He’s got an amazing support system,” Marisa said.

“His military friends have been also phenomenal. They’ve told us stories and they’ve been visiting him, which I think is really good for his mental state.”

“We had to identify him by his feet,” Liam’s mother explained.
“Seeing him in a bed with burns on him, I couldn’t be in the room,” his wife said.
Doctors told them 40 per cent of Pte. Ramage’s body had been burned.
“Mostly to his face, head, neck, his hands are bad, both the tops and his palms, both arms, both legs and some on his back as well,” Cheryl explained.
In a moment alone with her husband of three years, Marisa whispered in his ear.
“You are too stubborn to die and there is no way that you’re not making it through this.”

content_blocks.alt: Pte. Liam Ramage in uniform.
content_blocks.caption: Pte. Liam Ramage in uniform. Courtesy: Family

content_blocks.text: Since that night, the 27-year-old from Red Deer County has undergone multiple surgeries and skin grafts, but the full extent of his injuries is still unknown.
“He can’t see when he wakes up, he can’t speak and he can’t move very much, so he has really no way of communicating,” his mother explained.
Cheryl said her son’s life has already been saved by blood donors, and she encourages people wanting to help to roll up their sleeves and donate.
She says she was told despite his own severe injuries, Pte. Ramage was still trying to save his fellow soldiers when first responders arrived.
That doesn’t surprise his wife, who says he loves to help people.
Marisa doesn’t know what the couple’s future holds, but she’s grateful for every small step her husband is making.
“It’s nice to see him improve. He can move his arms on his right side and his foot on his right side. He can nod yes or no and he can move his mouth.”
His mom says when Pte. Ramage enlisted in the Canadian Armed Forces in 2024, it had been a long time coming.
“He’s always been passionate about the military. That’s really all he’s ever wanted to do,” Cheryl explained.
She said he got his first taste of the military in cadets, where he advanced to the top as a Regimental Sergeant Major.
Since enlisting in 2024, Pte. Ramage has served in Latvia and at the G7 in Kananaskis, Alta.
His mom never thought her son would be in danger on home soil, calling the fire “a freak accident.”
The disaster remains under investigation.
The family is putting together photo albums to bring to Pte. Ramage’s hospital room.
“His smile lit up the room. He’s infectious. He’s a storyteller. He talks nonstop. And that’s what all of his buddies say too. Liam just never stopped talking.”
When he’s not working, Pte. Ramage loves playing bagpipes, cooking and Canada’s game.
“His passion is hockey. Hockey, hockey, more hockey. A diehard Montreal Canadiens fan,” his mom laughed.
The family brought a radio to the hospital this week, so as Pte. Ramage heals, they can listen to games together.
“We’ve created a GoFundMe for Liam. It’s going to be a long road, months if not years of rehabilitation, surgeries,” Cheryl explained.

content_blocks.text: They’re grateful for the support of the military, including their designated assistant, and plan to continue to stay with Pte. Ramage every day in the hospital.
“He’s got an amazing support system,” Marisa said.
“His military friends have been also phenomenal. They’ve told us stories and they’ve been visiting him, which I think is really good for his mental state.”
