stories.title: ‘90s rock song hits No. 1 on the charts nearly 30 years after its debut
stories.summary: Foo Fighters’ 1997 hit “Everlong” has returned to the top of Billboard’s Hard Rock Streaming chart. Written by Dave Grohl during a difficult period in his life, the song continues to connect with listeners nearly three decades later.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
Nearly three decades after it was written, Foo Fighters’ “ Everlong ” is proving that a rock song can outlast the era that produced it.

The 1997 hit has climbed back to No. 1 on Billboard’s Hard Rock Streaming chart for the week of Oct. 31, bringing renewed attention to one of the band’s most enduring songs.

Released as the second single from the group’s second studio album, The Colour and the Shape , “Everlong” has remained a fixture in Foo Fighters’ catalogue, connecting with longtime fans while continuing to reach new listeners.

A song born during a difficult period

The track’s origins are closely tied to frontman Dave Grohl’s personal life. According to music publication Louder , Grohl began developing the song in late 1996 while staying at a friend’s home in Virginia during the breakdown of his marriage to Jennifer Youngblood.

What began as an acoustic guitar idea reportedly took about 45 minutes to put together. Grohl drew inspiration from his relationship with Louise Post, frontwoman of alternative rock band Veruca Salt, with the song capturing the intensity of romantic connection.

The track’s emotional themes, paired with its driving guitars and distinctive vocals, helped establish it as one of the defining songs in Foo Fighters’ catalogue.

Grohl initially had reservations about the song, reportedly wondering whether its sound resembled the work of Sonic Youth. He played a demo for the band’s Thurston Moore and Kim Gordon, who encouraged him to include it on the album, Louder reported.

That decision helped bring the song to a wider audience and cement its place in the band’s history.

stories.title: Calgary-developed wound treatment used on the battlefield in Ukraine
stories.summary: Calgary-based NanoTess received Health Canada approval for its NanoSALV Catalytic in 2022 and evaluated it by treating unhoused populations in encampments.
stories.author: Bill Graveland
stories.content:
An innovative wound and burn treatment initially funded by Canada’s Department of National Defence is now being delivered by drone to help wounded soldiers and civilians in war-torn Ukraine.

Calgary-based NanoTess received Health Canada approval for its NanoSALV Catalytic in 2022 and evaluated it by treating unhoused populations in encampments. It is now being used for military purposes.

“We actually started this company with a grant from National Defence back in 2020 and then have had it come full circle here in 2026 to now be used in the front lines within Ukraine,” said NanoTess co-founder and CEO Megan Leslie.

The results of its use in Ukraine were presented at the CAN Health Network Annual Conference in Toronto on Wednesday.

Leslie said the NanoSALV catalyst is suspended in a lightweight and non-flammable gel that is directly applied. It can be flown by drone to the front line and used by people with limited medical training to treat a range of wounds.

NanoSALV was made available for use on the Ukrainian front lines in June and so far has been used to treat 6,000 wounded soldiers and civilians. The gel uses nanomaterials to speed up and work with the body’s natural healing process. It lowers the amount of energy required for healing and fights germs and other infection-causing micro-organisms.

Clinical pharmacist Hailie Uren said the treatment is critical for buying time on the battlefield. Uren, with the Ukrainian Ministry of Health, said NanoSALV can be applied and go to work when there’s only one nurse to care for up to 90 patients.

“That wound can heal without consistent nursing intervention,” Uren said.

Uren said the catalytic gel is in demand. “(After) I receive a casualty when they first arrive at the hospital I will go and visit them the next day and will have a look at their wound,” she said. “The other people in the room (then) try and find wounds just so I can use it on them as well.”

Burn treatment for soldiers tragically came home to Canada earlier this month when a wind-whipped wildfire killed four Canadian soldiers and burned dozens more at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright.

“My colleagues were responding to some of the larger burn injuries in Edmonton. There was quite a split in Calgary and Edmonton for the larger burns. I would say in Edmonton we have a little bit more experience with the technology,” said Dr. Eric Fung, an Alberta-based surgeon who has spent time in Ukraine.

He said using the gel in a mass casualty event can reduce strain on the system.

“In a mass casualty event it really overloads our already overtaxed system, and we have to find room for these new patients and to accomplish that we need to get people in and out of hospital,” he said.

stories.title: Canadian diver Erik Brown helped save boys trapped in a flooded Thai cave
stories.summary: Experienced in complicated underwater missions, he was well suited to participate in the dramatic 2018 rescue
stories.author: Monte Stewart
stories.content:
Canadian scuba diver Erik Brown was not about to call himself a hero after risking his life to help rescue 12 boy soccer players and their coach, who became trapped in a cave in Thailand as it flooded during a monsoon in 2018. But many people around the world view him as one.

Going in with a team of rescuers after the monsoon ended and before another torrential rainstorm would strike, Mr. Brown spent 63 hours over nine days and seven missions in the Tham Luang Nang Non cave complex in the country’s northernmost province. In what he described as “zero visibility,” he navigated a treacherous four-kilometre underwater route while laying cables, carrying equipment and fighting rushing currents and other obstacles. Working with a hastily assembled team of international divers and two Australian doctor-divers, he helped relay the boys and their coach, who could not swim and were anesthetized to prevent them from panicking and removing their full face masks and breathing gear. Tethered along an overhead guide rope, all 13 of those who were trapped were transported face-down to safety. Their survival prompted rejoicing among a worldwide audience who had followed the rescue through news stories.

“I won’t lie. In my head, I was [thinking] there [was] very little chance it was going to work. … But it did,” Mr. Brown told CBC.

Mr. Brown died on Sept. 15 at the age of 44, his brother, Kirk Brown, told The Globe and Mail.

For his contribution to the Thai rescue, Mr. Brown received several honours, including Canada’s Medal of Bravery (2019); the Royal Canadian Humane Association’s Bronze Medal for Bravery (2018) and admission to Thailand’s Most Admirable Order of the Direkgunabhorn, First Class (2020). He and the other rescuers were fêted at official celebrations in Thailand. But Mr. Brown, who lived in Thailand at the time and felt obligated to help, took the praise in stride, according to Kirk.

“He didn’t feel what he did was heroic,” Kirk said. “He was really good at what he did. He was probably one of the only people that could do it. … So, he went and did it.”

Erik Richard Brown was born in Vancouver on July 13, 1982, and grew up on a hobby farm in its suburb of Langley, B.C., where his family raised cows and chickens. He was the younger of two sons of Richard Brown and Dorothy Brown (née Butchart). His father, a Vancouver firefighter, died of cancer when Erik was nine. Dorothy Brown, now retired, worked as a flight attendant and took the family on dozens of international trips.

“[Erik] always had that exploration bug,” Kirk said.

While growing up in Langley, Erik developed a love for sports and competed for his high-school volleyball and basketball teams, while also playing minor hockey. He went on to earn a business degree from the University of Victoria and then ventured to Australia, where he worked odd jobs and surfed. During a trip to the Great Barrier Reef in 2004, he completed an entry-level recreational scuba-diving course on a whim and, as he told Diver magazine in 2020, “got hooked.” Three months later, he became a certified divemaster, qualified to lead and guide other divers on tours and assist instructors.

“At the end of that trip, I ended up dislocating my shoulder and having to come back to Canada for surgery,” he told Diver. “Surfing was no longer an option, so I tried to think of ways I could stay travelling and stay in the water, and that led me back into diving. I flew to the Philippines after my surgery and became an instructor.”

Mr. Brown went on to train technical and recreational divers, instructors and their trainers, while co-owning dive centres in Thailand and Egypt. He also explored the waters off Iceland, South Africa and elsewhere, produced and appeared in underwater photos and videos, and promoted Hollis-branded scuba-diving equipment internationally.

“For many years, Erik was literally the face of Hollis,” said fellow diver and instructor Greg DeSatnick, who co-owned an internationally renowned dive centre in Egypt with him.

Before the Thai cave rescue, Mr. Brown had undertaken notable rescue missions and shipwreck explorations. During the 2010s, he saved a client trapped in a narrow section of an underwater canyon off the coast of Egypt by removing the diver’s other equipment while keeping his breathing apparatus in his mouth, Mr. DeSatnick said. The manoeuvre was “essentially unheard of” and Mr. Brown “did it flawlessly,” Mr. DeSatnick added.

In 2013, Mr. Brown joined a team of technical divers who placed a memorial plaque on the wreck of the Second World War U.S. Coast Guard cutter Uscgc Alexander Hamilton off Iceland.

As his career unfolded, Mr. Brown developed a passion for cave diving, taking annual trips to Mexico and Florida.

“Caves are where I find myself most relaxed,” he told Diver. “It is the diving I reserve for myself.”

In 2018, however, he put his skills to work for others, flying from his base on the Thai island of Koh Tao to the flooded cave complex. Initially expecting to play a supporting role in an operation involving 9,000 international volunteers, he soon joined the evacuation effort because of his cave-diving expertise.

Mr. Brown headed a transfer station and administered a ketamine-based general anesthetic to the players and coach. The anesthetic lasted about 45 minutes and had to be readministered periodically along the route, he told Diver in 2020 and attendees at the Diving Equipment Marketing Association conference and trade show in Las Vegas later in 2018.

“We had small medical stations set up and would inject the kids if needed,” Mr. Brown told Diver. He and the other divers involved in the rescue had received a crash course on how to do the injections.

“I don’t think I need to explain that this is outside my normal skill set,” Mr. Brown added, indicating that he had been nervous about administering the anesthetic.

Mr. Brown played himself in the 2019 film The Cave, a Thai drama about the rescue, and he became a public speaker, discussing his role in the complex operation at diving conferences, trade shows and other events in various countries. Publicity surrounding Mr. Brown’s exploits boosted his profile considerably.

But Mr. Brown was already well-known in the global diving community before the Thai rescue as a respected diver, instructor and dive-centre operator, Mr. DeSatnick said. Teaching under the Technical Diving International certification program, he helped develop the next generation of professional divers.

Technical diving extends beyond recreational diving, enabling longer, deeper and more complex dives, Mr. DeSatnick said. It requires specialized training, careful gas management and knowledge of sophisticated equipment such as closed-circuit rebreathers, which recycle breathing gas to extend dive times. These skills allow divers to explore underwater cave systems and deep shipwrecks extensively. Mr. Brown developed and tested innovative techniques, procedures and philosophies before introducing them to his students, Mr. DeSatnick said.

“He was just extremely epic,” Mr. DeSatnick said. “He was a game-changer for the technical-diving world.”

Mr. Brown was also a life-changer according to Kirk Brown, Mr. DeSatnick, other colleagues, friends and family members, who paid tribute to him on Facebook.

“He was pretty much everything to everyone,” said Kirk, who was one of his brother’s technical-diving students. “If he was your friend, he was your best friend. If he was your roommate, he was your favourite roommate with the most stories. If he was your teacher, he’s probably the one that taught you the most.

“For me, he was all of those things.”

Mr. Brown’s family has not disclosed the cause of his death or where he died. He leaves his mother, brother and a godson, Erik Ratchinsky, who was named after him.

These skills allow divers to explore underwater cave systems and deep shipwrecks extensively. Mr. Brown developed and tested innovative techniques, procedures and philosophies before introducing them to his students, Mr. DeSatnick said.
“He was just extremely epic,” Mr. DeSatnick said. “He was a game-changer for the technical-diving world.”
Mr. Brown was also a life-changer according to Kirk Brown, Mr. DeSatnick, other colleagues, friends and family members, who paid tribute to him on Facebook.

“He was pretty much everything to everyone,” said Kirk, who was one of his brother’s technical-diving students. “If he was your friend, he was your best friend. If he was your roommate, he was your favourite roommate with the most stories. If he was your teacher, he’s probably the one that taught you the most.
“For me, he was all of those things.”
Mr. Brown’s family has not disclosed the cause of his death or where he died. He leaves his mother, brother and a godson, Erik Ratchinsky, who was named after him.

content_blocks.text: Canadian scuba diver Erik Brown was not about to call himself a hero after risking his life to help rescue 12 boy soccer players and their coach, who became trapped in a cave in Thailand as it flooded during a monsoon in 2018. But many people around the world view him as one.

content_blocks.text: Going in with a team of rescuers after the monsoon ended and before another torrential rainstorm would strike, Mr. Brown spent 63 hours over nine days and seven missions in the Tham Luang Nang Non cave complex in the country’s northernmost province. In what he described as “zero visibility,” he navigated a treacherous four-kilometre underwater route while laying cables, carrying equipment and fighting rushing currents and other obstacles. Working with a hastily assembled team of international divers and two Australian doctor-divers, he helped relay the boys and their coach, who could not swim and were anesthetized to prevent them from panicking and removing their full face masks and breathing gear. Tethered along an overhead guide rope, all 13 of those who were trapped were transported face-down to safety. Their survival prompted rejoicing among a worldwide audience who had followed the rescue through news stories.

stories.title: Liberals vote to keep B.C. tanker ban in place
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Liberal government has voted to keep the B.C. oil tanker ban place, defeating a Conservative bill that would have repealed it.
stories.author: Nick Murray The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The Liberal government voted to keep the B.C. coastal oil tanker ban in place Wednesday, defeating a Conservative bill that would have repealed it.

MPs voted along party lines during second reading in the House of Commons Wednesday, with only the Conservatives voting to move the bill forward to the committee stage.

As they brought forward the bill, Conservatives pointed to a proposal by Calgary-based Strathcona Resources to ship up to 250,000 barrels of Canadian oil daily on existing railroad tracks through Prince Rupert, B.C., to the coast.

“Conservatives have made it clear that we’re willing to work with the Liberals to bring forward amendments if they have concerns with this piece of legislation to see this proposal move forward,” Conservative natural resources critic Carol Anstey told reporters earlier in the day.

“The prime minister has said he wants to make Canada an energy superpower. This is his opportunity to prove that he is serious about that commitment and vote in favour of Bill C-264.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney — who struck a deal with the B.C. government earlier this summer to keep the ban in place — made a rare appearance after question period Wednesday to vote in person on several bills, including C-264.

Shortly after making the tanker ban deal with B.C., Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced the route for the proposed oil pipeline to the West Coast will go south to respect the tanker ban.

Smith, who originally envisioned the pipeline going north, backed the Conservative bill to repeal the ban.

“Canada cannot become a global energy superpower while federal policies continue to stand in the way of getting our energy to the world. Repealing the tanker ban is an important step toward securing better prices for our resources and building a stronger, more prosperous Canada,” Smith said in a media statement.

The existing law, the Oil Tanker Moratorium Act, prohibits tankers from carrying more than 12,500 metric tonnes of crude oil in areas along the northern coast of British Columbia.

Anstey pointed out that the proposal from Strathcona was entirely a private sector pitch without public subsidies.

“This is what they’re asking for to create Canadian jobs and opportunities, diversify exports, and so we want to support that,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

stories.title: 4 GTA residents charged for allegedly smuggling more than 110K kilograms of tobacco across the border
stories.summary: During the course of a complex investigation, a smuggling operation was uncovered which took advantage of Canada's transportation industry, including the extended railway system.
stories.author: Dilshad Burman
stories.content:
By Dilshad Burman

Posted October 28, 2026 4:30 pm.

Four Greater Toronto Area residents have been charged for their alleged roles in a tobacco smuggling ring following a joint investigation between the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) and Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA).

During the course of a complex investigation, a smuggling operation was uncovered which the CBSA says took advantage of Canada’s transportation industry, including the extended railway system.

The accused allegedly transported nearly 116,000 kilograms of tobacco from the United States into Canada as well as between provinces between Oct. 2020 and April 2024.

On Sep. 21, 2026, the four accused were charged with:

Conspiracy to smuggle into Canada

Conspiracy to transport tobacco

Conspiracy to possess raw leaf tobacco

Conspiracy to evade compliance

Each individual also faces additional charges for their respective role in the smuggling ring.

Johnny Gamboa, 48, from Toronto was charged with:

Keeping, acquiring, disposing of goods illegally imported (raw leaf tobacco)

Transporting of tobacco products and raw leaf tobacco

Falsifying or destroying records

False statements or evasion of duties

Smuggle into Canada

Keeping, acquiring, disposing of goods illegally imported

Possession of property obtained by crime over $5,000

Possession of property obtained from offences

Harminder Grewal, 47, from Brampton was charged with:

Keeping, acquiring, disposing of goods illegally imported (raw leaf tobacco)

Transporting of tobacco products and raw leaf tobacco

Falsifying or destroying records

Smuggle into Canada

Keeping, acquiring, disposing of goods illegally imported

False statements or evasion of duties

Rinnamoon Haddad, 50, from Caledon was charged with:

Keeping, acquiring, disposing of goods illegally imported (raw leaf tobacco)

Transporting of tobacco products and raw leaf tobacco

Falsifying or destroying records

False statements or evasion of duties

Avikesh Sharma, 49, from Mississauga was charged with possession of property obtained by crime over $5,000.

All four are scheduled to appear in court on Oct. 29, 2026

stories.title: ‘You got to keep pushing, you’re almost there!’ Young London runner gives up position in race final to help struggling counterpart
stories.summary: A sudden act of kindness from a young London, Ont. boy during a championship race is spreading through southwestern Ontario.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
A sudden act of kindness from a young London, Ont. boy during a championship race is spreading through southwestern Ontario.

Jackson McClymont and Mathias Oke crossed the finish line together at the Thames Valley District School Board cross-country finals, only after Jackson came to Mathias’ aid halfway through the race.

Jackson had been on pace for a strong finish.

“I thought I could get bragging rights or something, maybe I could get a medal!” recalled Jackson.

But as he prepared to sprint, he noticed Mathias, a student at Turtle Island Public School in Woodstock, was struggling.

“He was breathing really hard,” he noticed.

While Jackson was not aware that Mathias battles asthma, he could see the boy he had never met before needed a friend. It is a moment Mathias won’t soon forget.

“And then as I’m going up the hill, I see a hand push me to go farther ahead,” Mathias recalled.

The pair continued the race side-by-side, with Mathias listening to words of encouragement from Jackson.

“[He kept saying], you got to keep pushing, your almost there!” said Mathias.

At the finish line, Jackson decided to take a step back, “I just said, you know, maybe this guy wanted to finish better than he did, so I’m just going to let him go in front of me.”

The moment was captured by Matthias’ mother, Renee. She contacted Jackson’s school, Ashley Oaks in London. His teacher, Ericka Deakin, was among the staff impressed.

Recognition from the school and Mathias’ family followed.

Jackson’s grandmother, Michelle, said he never told her about his act. She learned about it from his school.

“He just did this, and he didn’t go on about it to anybody, and I’m super proud of him!” she said.

Renee said she is grateful for Jackson’s kindness and her own son’s unprompted appreciation, calling it a moment we can all learn from.

“In this day and age where everything is so dark and so heavy, there are kind people, kind kids, kind adults. The people that raised Jackson should be so proud of themselves.”

During the CTV News interview, the boys learned they share several common interests and told us they intend to become – and stay – friends.

stories.title: Ottawa introduces new fines for bogus, unlicensed immigration and citizenship advice
stories.summary: Ottawa — The Immigration Department has announced new fines ranging from $5,000 to $1.5 million for people who give false immigration advice or provide advice without proper authorization.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Immigration Department has announced new fines ranging from $5,000 to $1.5 million for people who give false immigration advice or provide advice without proper authorization.

The new fine policy, which takes effect today, sets a minimum fine of $5,000 for giving immigration advice or acting as a representative on an immigration application without being authorized to do so.

People who are authorized to give immigration advice include lawyers and members of the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants.

The new minimum fine for knowingly giving false or misleading immigration advice is $15,000.

The department says these fines will be higher in cases where an application was approved based on false advice, and for repeat offences.

A registry of those fined under this new program is set to be established in 2027.

stories.title: Former senator Pamela Wallin says Maid committee was ‘chaotic and exclusionary’
stories.summary: criticized the co-chair of a special joint committee on Maid while testifying at an inquiry into a leaked confidential report, calling him “dismissive" and describing the process as “chaotic and exclusionary.”
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Hannah Alberga, The Canadian Press

Posted October 28, 2026 4:15 pm.

Last Updated October 28, 2026 5:27 pm.

Former senator Pamela Wallin criticized the co-chair of a special joint committee on MAID while testifying at an inquiry into a leaked confidential report, calling him “dismissive” and describing the process as “chaotic and exclusionary.”

“It was the worst that I’ve seen it,” Wallin said, testifying from Saskatchewan on Tuesday about the committee and its leadership. Wallin resigned from the Senate earlier this month after 17 years.

The reason for her virtual appearance at a rules and procedures committee hearing was to voice her concerns about information leaked to the media in June, before a report recommending the government “indefinitely” pause the expansion of MAID for mental illness was finalized, or published.

The government has since said it reached the same conclusion as the committee, and on Tuesday introduced a bill to stop the expansion. If passed, the legislation would ban people who suffer from mental illness alone from accessing MAID.

The report at the centre of Wallin’s concerns has been enveloped in controversy, as has the special joint committee of Senate and House of Commons members assembled to study MAID.

Wallin recounted reading an article published in the media in June about the committee’s recommendation before it had been made public.

“It was very troubling,” she said.

She does not name the co-chair of the committee she takes issue with in her testimony, but clarifies that she is not referring to Senator Yonah Martin, whom she described as “fair and balanced.” The other co-chair was Liberal member of Parliament Dr. Marcus Powlowski.

“The chair was very dismissive of any questions that we were asking about the process in there. I’m not going to repeat conversations or what I heard because these are in-camera meetings, but it was chaotic and exclusionary are the two words I will use,” Wallin said.

This was the second meeting in as many weeks for the rules, procedures and rights of parliament committee, which has been tasked with examining and reporting on the leak.

Powlowski did not attend Tuesday’s meeting, and a member of the rules committee said he “refused” to come.

In a phone interview, he told The Canadian Press he was unavailable.

“I do not think it would be appropriate for me, as an elected member of Parliament, working as an elected member of Parliament, to answer to a committee, which is obviously in this inquiry being motivated by the actions of a couple of senators who obviously have an axe to grind because they’re unhappy with the results of the of the process,” he added.

Powlowski, MP for Thunder Bay—Rainy River, also said the inquiry was “a fairly brazen attempt by certain members of the Senate to undermine the democratic process.”

When the MAID report was released in June, a dissenting opinion penned by Wallin and two other senators, told the government not to accept the recommendation.

They also called the committee’s process “highly irregular and flawed,” saying two-thirds of the witnesses invited to testify were openly opposed to MAID for mental illness.

Wallin said she read a newspaper article on June 16, the day before the report was released, citing anonymous sources disclosing the MAID committee’s recommendation not to allow the end of life procedure on the basis of a mental illness. At least three news organizations published similar stories.

That same day, she raised the issue of the leak with the Speaker of the Senate, who ruled on June 18 that it constituted a prima facie case of privilege. Wallin then moved a motion requesting that the committee examine the issue.

“It breaks trust. It’s disrespectful,” Wallin said Tuesday to the committee.

Responding to Wallin’s testimony, Powlowski said, “I was not the source of any leak. As to the way the committee was run, we were quite careful to do everything exactly according to the rules,” he said.

Powlowski said, as far as he is concerned, “It’s over. It’s done.”

“Certain senators don’t want to admit it’s done, they say, how about we make it next goal wins? How about we make it two out of three?” Powlowski said, with a laugh.

Chair of the rules committee, Senator Peter Harder, said discussions will resume at the next meeting, and touch on the idea of asking IT to trace the origin of the leak, or focus on crafting recommendations for future joint committees to avoid similar issues.

stories.title: Jewish community hopes to put $1M fundraiser for hero Belleville cop over the top
stories.summary: Const. Jeff Smith saved the lives of 25 Jewish congregants during gunman's attack on synagogue.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
The Jewish community has come close to meeting a $1 million fundraising goal for the injured Belleville hero cop who put his life on the line to prevent a massacre at a synagogue in Belleville, Ont.

The man behind the campaign is now asking donors to take it over the line.

“We are now $45,744 away from our $1 million goal,” GoFundMe page organizer Derek Kreindler wrote on the page on Tuesday. “Thousands of people from across Canada and beyond have chosen to honour (police officer Jeff Smith) who suffered catastrophic injuries while protecting approximately 25 Jewish worshippers on Kol Nidre. That response has been extraordinary.”

Kreindler adds that a million dollars is neither a milestone, nor a measure of the Jewish community’s gratitude. Having already demonstrated that Canadians laud responders who put themselves in harm’s way to protect the rest of us, he says the $1-million goal “would provide the Smith family with further support as they face a recovery whose length and full consequences remain uncertain.”

“Public attention has understandably moved elsewhere (but) Constable Smith’s recovery has not,” writes Kriendler. “More than $954,000 has brought us within sight of the finish line. Please help us carry the campaign through the final $45,744. We remember. We give thanks. And we stand by those who stood for us.”

On, September 20, members of Belleville’s Jewish community had gathered at Sons of Jacob Synagogue for Yom Kippur services, with Smith providing protection outside. A gunman, former Canadian Armed Forces soldier Sean Ward, attacked the shul, firing at Smith.

Smith was caught on video shouting, “You are going to die for the Jews,” at Smith and another Belleville constable, Michael McCurdy.

Smith remains in hospital in critical but stable condition. Ward was killed in the firefight. McCurdy was unhurt.

A separate GoFundMe page has been set up by the Jewish community for McCurdy, which has raised $55,943 raised of a $60K goal. It notes that McCurdy arrived outside the synagogue to find his fellow officer suffering from multiple gunshot wounds to his head and torso, and continued the battle with Ward, thereby helping to bring the violent attack to an end and saving the Jewish congregants inside.

Inside the synagogue, the Jewish community had heard the gunfire exchange and took shelter together as bullets hit the building.

“In Judaism, pikuach nefesh, the preservation of human life, is among our highest obligations,” writes Kriendler on the page. “Const. Smith fulfilled that obligation not through words, but through courage and action. When members of a vulnerable community needed protection, he put himself in harm’s way.”

Kreindler notes that a beneficiary for the funds has been established. He says the proceeds will transfer directly through GoFundMe to the beneficiary designated by Smith’s family.

He is asking potential donors not to donate again, but instead to share the campaign with one person, family, business or organization. Forwarding the campaign “could carry us through this final stretch,” he says.

In late September, Smith wife, Ashley released an emotional thank you to the supporters and “every scared soul” who was inside the building that night.

In a message on her Facebook page , she posted a photo of her holding her husband’s hand as he laid in critical but stable condition in hospital.

In her statement, Ashley said: “From the deepest part of my heart and soul, thank you … The life-saving hands of paramedics and police. The hands of an angel neurosurgeon. The steady, capable hands of trauma teams, doctors, nurses, RTs, PSWs … The helping hands of neighbours, friends, community members and volunteers. And then there are the hands that held me and my sweet girls when we were living through the scariest and darkest day of our lives …

“I also want to send my love and prayers to the Jewish community, and to every scared soul who was there on Sunday night. Please know that your love, your prayers and your support have reached us. We are deeply grateful. We love you, we see you, we pray for you.”

stories.title: St. Thomas Curling Club completes $1M dollar renovation in time to host national event
stories.summary: A $1M renovation at the St. Thomas Curling Club was completed in time to host the Canadian Curling Club Championship in November.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The 15th time was the charm for members of the St. Thomas Curling Club (Stcc). A $1million renovation to the lobby was approved, and after work started in the spring, it is finally complete. “Nothing had been done since 1955,” said Peter Inch, past president of the Stcc.

“With brown paneling, really not very much light and no windows to allow light to come in. We have tried 14 times to do a renovation and never got approval. This one was number 15 and finally membership said, ‘Yeah, go ahead and do it.’” Money was raised from the Brier, the Scotties Tournament of Hearts, and a capital fund – which is charged to members – helped raise the money over time to do the renovation.

They’ve even added new cameras which show both ends of the rink from the lobby. “We modernized the club to bring it up to date from a number of perspectives,” said Ray Parkes, a member of Stcc since 1974. “When curling is going on, people sitting at tables can glance up and see what’s going on in an end.

Even if you’re at the glass, it makes it easier to see what’s going on at the far end, you can see where the rocks are positioned, and it just allows a little more audience participation in the game.” The club has added a wheelchair accessible lift inside the front door, added an accessible washroom, and upgraded the kitchen.

It is now available for events all year round with air conditioning added to the building. Those changes come just in time to host a national tournament in November. “It is the Canadian Club Curling Championship,” said Inch.

“It is the best club curlers from across Canada, from every province and territory that we’re bringing to St. Thomas. Thank you to the Holiday Inn as we filled it and that’s one of the reasons why we’re able to bring that event here.” After hosting the Grand Slam event last year and a newly renovated club, they have big dreams about what is next.

“We can even try to get a Scotties here at Joe Thornton Centre and we can do that now that we have the hotel rooms here to do it,” said Inch. “You never know what’s coming next year, and we will keep the bidding process going.

This is their national championship and we’re proud to have it.”

stories.title: ‘Godzilla’ El Nino set to bring warmer, drier temperatures to Canada
stories.summary: Water temperatures in the Pacific Ocean where El NIno forms would typically be at least 0.5 C above normal, but this year it's at 3.5 C.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
One of the strongest El Ninos on record could bring a much warmer than normal winter, but the “Godzilla” warming event meteorologists are forecasting could affect parts of Canada in different ways for months.

An El Nino ocean warming event typically occurs every three to seven years and shifts what is normally seen in the Pacific Ocean.

Phillips says trade winds that typically push warm water towards places like Indonesia reverse and weaken. As a result, warm water is pushed towards the coast of North America.

What makes this year’s El Nino a record breaker is the temperature. Water surface temperature in the Pacific hit at least 0.5 C above average in El Nino years but this year, the temperature has hit 3.5 C above average.

“We’ve never seen the water as warm as it is right now in that part of the Pacific, of the tropical Pacific on the east side of the ocean,” said Phillips. “We’ve never seen an El Nino this strong and it’s still growing, it’s still strong.”

Now, Canadians May be wondering why something in the Pacific Ocean could affect people on the East Coast and the answer is the jet stream.

In non-El Nino years, the polar jet stream is settled over Canada and brings us colder weather.

But in El Nino, Global News chief meteorologist Anthony Farnell said the subtropical jet stream moves north.

“It brings a lot of of Pacific air, a lot of mild temperatures, and that travels not just close to the source in B.C., but it’ll travel all the way around the planet, impact the weather in Europe, in Asia, everything is related in the weather world,” Farnell said.

Even though the system will mean warmer temperatures for the most part, it will still vary from coast to coast.

North America is still further away from where El Nino forms in the Pacific, so while places like Peru or Ecuador could see more rain, that likely won’t be the case here.

B.C., Alberta and other parts of the Prairies are likely to see fewer storms and milder temperatures, but Farnell says it could also be drier which could hurt both ski season and next year’s wildfire season.

East of Manitoba, places like Ontario, Quebec and the Maritimes will see above seasonal conditions amounting to less snow.

“That’s kind of a misnomer is people think winter’s cancelled, that’s not the case,” Farnell said. “We’re still going to have those bouts of extreme cold, they May not last as long. The snow that does fall, it could be heavy, but it also doesn’t last as well.”

Snow will also likely melt faster because of the up and down temperatures.

That fast melt could impact people who use snow a lot like ski hills and other winter recreation users, Phillips said.

“You’re going to have warm temperatures come, and when you get that big snowpack and you’ve got a good snow base, all of a sudden the mild air comes or the rain comes and not more snow,” Phillips said.

He added though it began earlier this year, it likely won’t peak for a few more weeks likely in early December.

Even after it peaks, Farnell said its effects are typically delayed.

“So I think over the next six months to a year is when we’re really going to see the extremes,” he said. “It is just going to bring the temperature of the planet up another step and that is something that with climate change combined is going to have some definitely long-lasting impacts.

“With climate change you end with more extremes, so the combo of the two I would say I would bet that they’re going to be big storms, ice storms, droughts, fires, floods, all of that in the months ahead.”

An El Nino ocean warming event typically occurs every three to seven years and shifts what is normally seen in the Pacific Ocean.
Phillips says trade winds that typically push warm water towards places like Indonesia reverse and weaken. As a result, warm water is pushed towards the coast of North America.

What makes this year’s El Nino a record breaker is the temperature. Water surface temperature in the Pacific hit at least 0.5 C above average in El Nino years but this year, the temperature has hit 3.5 C above average.

“We’ve never seen the water as warm as it is right now in that part of the Pacific, of the tropical Pacific on the east side of the ocean,” said Phillips. “We’ve never seen an El Nino this strong and it’s still growing, it’s still strong.”
Now, Canadians May be wondering why something in the Pacific Ocean could affect people on the East Coast and the answer is the jet stream.
In non-El Nino years, the polar jet stream is settled over Canada and brings us colder weather.
But in El Nino, Global News chief meteorologist Anthony Farnell said the subtropical jet stream moves north.

“It brings a lot of of Pacific air, a lot of mild temperatures, and that travels not just close to the source in B.C., but it’ll travel all the way around the planet, impact the weather in Europe, in Asia, everything is related in the weather world,” Farnell said.
Even though the system will mean warmer temperatures for the most part, it will still vary from coast to coast.
North America is still further away from where El Nino forms in the Pacific, so while places like Peru or Ecuador could see more rain, that likely won’t be the case here.

B.C., Alberta and other parts of the Prairies are likely to see fewer storms and milder temperatures, but Farnell says it could also be drier which could hurt both ski season and next year’s wildfire season.
East of Manitoba, places like Ontario, Quebec and the Maritimes will see above seasonal conditions amounting to less snow.

“That’s kind of a misnomer is people think winter’s cancelled, that’s not the case,” Farnell said. “We’re still going to have those bouts of extreme cold, they May not last as long. The snow that does fall, it could be heavy, but it also doesn’t last as well.”
Snow will also likely melt faster because of the up and down temperatures.
That fast melt could impact people who use snow a lot like ski hills and other winter recreation users, Phillips said.

“You’re going to have warm temperatures come, and when you get that big snowpack and you’ve got a good snow base, all of a sudden the mild air comes or the rain comes and not more snow,” Phillips said.
He added though it began earlier this year, it likely won’t peak for a few more weeks likely in early December.
Even after it peaks, Farnell said its effects are typically delayed.

“So I think over the next six months to a year is when we’re really going to see the extremes,” he said. “It is just going to bring the temperature of the planet up another step and that is something that with climate change combined is going to have some definitely long-lasting impacts.

“With climate change you end with more extremes, so the combo of the two I would say I would bet that they’re going to be big storms, ice storms, droughts, fires, floods, all of that in the months ahead.”

stories.title: Trump celebrates Quebec separatist, B.C. Conservative election wins in social media posts
stories.summary: Both St-Pierre Plamondon and Lorne Doerkson have previously criticized Trump’s tariffs
stories.author: Rob Gillies
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump drew criticism Wednesday for celebrating election victories by a Quebec separatist and a British Columbia Conservative, days after his administration accused Canadian politicians of interfering in U.S. elections.

With U.S. midterm elections approaching, Trump shared an article portraying the Quebec victory as a setback for Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and hailed the Conservative win in British Columbia as evidence of the party’s growing strength.

But neither election was a referendum on Carney, whose federal Liberal Party is separate from British Columbia’s provincial Conservatives. Analysts say both results reflected provincial politics, not declining support for the prime minister.

“Congratulations to Paul St-Pierre Plamondon on his WIN!” Trump wrote Tuesday on Truth Social, more than three weeks after the Quebec separatist leader’s Oct. 5 election victory. Trump linked to an article headlined “Separatists win Quebec provincial election in blow to Mark Carney.”

Trump also congratulated British Columbia’s premier-designate, Lorne Doerkson, ON his “Big Victory,” adding: “Conservatives are moving strong in Canada!” The post came one minute before his congratulations to Quebec’s separatist leader.

The posts come amid Trump’s trade war and repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state. St-Pierre Plamondon has criticized Trump’s tariffs and ruled out holding a Quebec independence referendum while Trump remains president.

Trump’s trade war with Canada has become an issue in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, particularly in Michigan and Maine, where Republican candidates have faced pressure over tariffs hurting local businesses. Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers has called for an end to the tariff war.

“It is highly unusual for a U.S. President to comment on Canadian provincial politics or to congratulate provincial election winners,” said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal.

Béland said neither result should be interpreted as a rejection of Carney, whose popularity has been bolstered by his response to Trump.

Nelson Wiseman, a University of Toronto political scientist, said Trump misunderstands Canada’s Conservatives, noting that Doerkson has criticized Trump’s tariffs and called him a bully.

Doerkson spoke with Carney on Tuesday, with both leaders emphasizing co-operation on economic growth and investment.

“Carney’s popularity is at a stratospheric level,” Wiseman said. “The more Trump attacks Canada and Carney, the more popular Carney becomes.”

The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa last week accused Canadian politicians of seeking to influence the Nov. 3 midterms. It cited Industry Minister Mélanie Joly’s comments about targeting Republican states with retaliatory tariffs and Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s U.S. advertisement featuring former President Ronald Reagan criticizing tariffs.

The embassy also cited 11 Canadians charged with illegally voting in U.S. elections between 2012 and 2026, without linking the cases to the Canadian government.

Carney rejected the allegations, saying they had “no merit,” and expressed disappointment with U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra.

Asked Wednesday whether the Trump administration was setting up Canada to be the fall guy if Republicans suffer heavy losses in the U.S. midterms, Carney laughed.

“That’s an interesting way of framing it,” Carney said, before adding that Canada would pursue a trade deal with Washington only when it served Canadian interests.

Béland warned that the accusations could foreshadow a “Blame Canada” narrative if Republicans suffer losses in the midterms.

“It is absurd for President Trump to comment on Canadian provincial politics while the U.S. embassy in Canada is falsely claiming that country is interfering in the U.S. midterms,” Béland said.

stories.title: Calgary city councillors propose temporary pause on data centres
stories.summary: A motion to be discussed next week proposes a temporary moratorium on new rezoning applications related to large-scale data centres within the City of Calgary.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
A group of city councillors and Calgary’s mayor are seeking a pause on new data centre projects to allow the city to develop regulations and do a deep dive on the potential impacts to municipal infrastructure.

A motion on the matter from Ward 2 Coun. Jennifer Wyness, co-signed by Couns. Raj Dhaliwal, Andrew Yule, John Pantazopoulos and Mayor Jeromy Farkas, is set to undergo a technical review at the city’s executive committee next week.

The motion aims to place a temporary moratorium on any new rezoning applications related to large-scale data centres, pending the outcome of a city study into the impacts on municipal infrastructure and the creation of new land-use regulations.

According to the motion, data centres are not specifically defined in the city’s zoning rules and any proposals “must be evaluated and approved in accordance with the current applicable requirements” of the city’s land-use bylaw.

It asks city administration to create a new zoning district that defines data centres, and takes into consideration the varying scales of data centre proposals by March.

“We feel we need to put proper processes in place. We need to put proper guardrails in place, but we need to start with a proper land-use district in our land-use bylaw,” Dhaliwal told Global News.

The move comes months after Rocky View County put a temporary freeze on data centre projects to establish regulations for future proposed projects.

The motion noted other municipalities like Oakville, Ont., Mississauga, Ont., Cumberland, N.S. and Saskatoon, Sask. have done the same.

According to the motion, the term “data centre” encompasses a broad scale of technology infrastructure.

“Small and medium-scale data centres have energy, water and land needs comparable to other commercial and industrial businesses and are an important part of our business ecosystem in Calgary,” the motion reads. “Hyperscale or mega-scale data centers for AI and cloud computing are massive, resource-intensive campuses that have significant impacts to the community and the region.”

If city council approves the motion, city administration would also be directed to study “the risks, implications and opportunities of data centres,” including environmental and economic impacts as well as potential effects on regional water servicing and municipal water infrastructure.

“That’s a challenge that council will need to get ahead of and a pause will allow us to do the research and create an equitable playing ground,” Wyness told Global News.

It remains unclear what a temporary pause could mean for a data centre proposal underway in the city’s northeast.

A rezoning application has been submitted to city administration by Stantec and property management company Walton Global for a large undeveloped parcel of land east of 52 Street NE and north of the community of Redstone.

The application is currently under review, and would allow for large industrial buildings and power generation to make way for a data centre, as well as natural areas and stormwater retention ponds.

Dhaliwal, who represents Ward 5 where the data centre is proposed, said he’s been fielding questions from residents about the project.

“They’re asking for what kind of environmental assessments will be done, what kind of technical studies will be done from noise and heat generation,” he said. “We don’t have those answers and I want to provide those answers to them.”

Walton Global did not respond to Global News’ request for comment in time for publication.

stories.title: Journalist Andrea Warner ‘changed the way we write about music’
stories.summary: She challenged how people think about pop culture, while examining misogyny and exploring why some artists were celebrated and others dismissed
stories.author: Hannah Alper
stories.content:
While Andrea Warner was waiting for her first appointment to see an oncologist after her cancer diagnosis in March, 2024, the first song she and her husband, Carlos Hernandez Fisher, heard was Michael Bolton’s How Am I Supposed To Live Without You . While she felt it should be “illegal” to play that song in the cancer agency waiting room, she also found it very funny.

It was the beginning of her waiting room playlists, which she shared on Instagram alongside updates about her treatment for endometrial cancer. The posts reflected the music journalist’s honesty, gratitude and what she would describe to her editor, Jen Sookfong Lee, as “pathological optimism.”

“Yesterday’s waiting room playlist was as aggressively mid as this news. At least there’s always the music. Long live this wild, cursed hilarious algo,” Ms. Warner wrote on April 23, after learning that some of her tumours had spread.

On Oct. 2, her husband announced that Ms. Warner died on Sept. 27 from the cancer she had fought for nearly three years. She was 47. Surrounded by family, friends and some of her favourite music in her final days, she left behind one last waiting room playlist.

Ms. Warner was a feminist music journalist, author and social justice advocate who championed overlooked artists and challenged how people thought about pop culture. She examined misogyny and questioned why some artists were celebrated while others were dismissed.

“I think she really honestly shows us how ethical, generous, but still entertaining and funny that cultural criticism can be,” Ms. Lee said. “She fundamentally changed the way we write about music in this country.”

Ms. Warner wrote four books, We Oughta Know: How Four Women Ruled the ’90s and Changed Canadian Music ; Buffy Sainte-Marie: The Authorized Biography ; Rise Up And Sing! Power, Protest, and Activism in Music ; and The Time of My Life: Dirty Dancing . Alongside Susan Aglukark, she also co-authored Kihiani: A Memoir of Healing . Ms. Warner was with CBC Music since 2012, eventually becoming an associate producer and a co-host of the weekly podcast Pop This! for a decade.

Andrea Warner was born on Jan. 25, 1979, in East Vancouver to Bob Warner and Elsie Marie Warner (née Allen). Her father was 21 and her mother was 18 when they walked down the aisle, a month before Andrea’s birth. They later had another daughter, whom they named Jennifer.

While growing up, Andrea spent many Sundays in her father’s secondhand shop. When she was in Grade 5, her parents separated shortly before Christmas. Living in a two-bedroom apartment in East Vancouver above a drugstore with her sister, father and grandmother, she received a precious electronic keyboard, a big-ticket item considering the humbleness of the family’s circumstances.

The first time she can remember writing, it was a poem in the shape of a keyboard, letting the keys give voice to the breakup.

By Grade 6, Andrea was writing long novels by hand every night, and poetry when, she joked, she should have been paying attention in class. Her love of reading started in her early teens, with the Babysitters Club series and books by Judy Blume. Eventually, she devoured Shakespeare and cracked open the works of Maya Angelou and bell hooks.

One of the first places she was published was her high school newspaper although the first issue she contributed to was banned, partly because of an editorial Andrea wrote criticizing a new provincewide mandatory career-preparation curriculum that overlooked students who already had jobs.

Ms. Warner worked part-time after school, and with her earnings she would buy Soap Opera Weekly, Soap Opera Digest, and when she was really flush, Entertainment Weekly. It was how she learned about people; the magazines took TV, film and music criticism seriously.

After her father died suddenly when she was in Grade 12, she became the first person in her immediate family to attend university. At the University of Victoria, she accidentally enrolled in professional writing courses instead of the creative writing ones she had intended; she eventually left to pursue journalism studies at Langara College.

When she secured an internship at Soap Opera Weekly between her first and second year, her professors weren’t impressed. They didn’t care that she was living in New York, or living at the same place Leonard Cohen stayed, or that she was getting bylines. Ms. Warner admired soap operas for tackling taboo topics like abortion, racism, homophobia and mental health, and believed the fans – who were predominantly female – deserved respect.

After briefly running her own magazine devoted to arts, culture, politics and feminism, she eventually found herself back at the university she once left, taking the creative writing classes she always meant to take.

It was around then that she met Mr. Hernandez Fisher, whom she married in 2009. Together, they went to Seattle’s Bumbershoot arts and music festival, where Ms. Warner heard Miranda July speak about equity and injustice, power and risk.

The experience inspired her to quit her job and move to Vancouver to pursue writing full-time.

Holly Gordon, a digital producer at CBC Music who worked with Ms. Warner for 14 years, remembers her arriving at pitch meetings overflowing with ideas. She wrote about the greats she admired, from Leonard Cohen to the Tragically Hip, without being starstruck.

“She was really good at bringing a lot of love to a project, even if she was fully examining something,” Ms. Gordon said. “It’s so easy to be judgmental or a bit cutting about something, but it’s a lot harder to be kinder, but still be very to the point.”

She made conscious decisions to focus on the stories of women, women-identifying people and gender-nonconforming people.

“I prioritize telling their stories, asking about their art, celebrating and reassessing their historical contribution to our culture, framing their brilliance with purpose and intention because all too often, a woman’s work goes unnoticed, undervalued or dismissed entirely,” Ms. Warner said in a public talk .

At one point in her career, she started looking closely at everything she loved and everything she thought she hated. As a teenager, she believed Alanis Morissette and Sarah McLachlan were the best, and Celine Dion and Shania Twain were the worst. Confronting her internalized misogyny became the basis of her first book, We Oughta Know .

That thoughtfulness shaped Ms. Warner’s relationships with the people she worked with.

At one point after Ms. Warner’s cancer diagnosis in 2024, Ms. Aglukark travelled to Vancouver to ensure that Ms. Warner wasn’t pushing herself too hard to finish the book. She says in the three days they spent together, she saw her commitment to relationships and writing first-hand.

“I left Vancouver having a deeper respect for the humanity of industry. We forget that because we have deadlines, we have stories. But she was the job. She was a professional writer to the core, and respected the story so much that there was a humanness and a deeper connection,” Ms. Aglukark said.

At the end of an interview with Buffy Sainte-Marie in 2018, while Ms. Warner was working on her authorized biography of the singer, the two women shared that they wished they didn’t have to get off the phone. In her research for the interview, Ms. Warner was “struck” by the lack of a historical record about Ms. Sainte-Marie, she later said, compared with her musical peers.

Ms. Warner wrote the book, which involved about 60 hours of interviews, with the musician based in Hawaii and Ms. Warner in Vancouver. Five years after its publication, Ms. Sainte-Marie came under fire after an investigation by the CBC’s The Fifth Estate into her claims of Indigenous identity. The show’s investigation found evidence that contradicted the account of Ms. Sainte-Marie’s family background that is published in the biography. Ms. Warner never spoke publicly to address those revelations.

Whether it was a collaborator on a book or a stranger at a party, Ms. Lee says she “walked into a room expecting to love everybody.”

Mr. Hernandez Fisher says Ms. Warner was constantly introducing people she thought should know one another and finding ways to support those around her.

Looking back on his time with her, he remembers “a series of adventures.” In the past few years alone, they travelled to San Luis Obispo, Calif., to stay at the Madonna Inn, visited Mr. Hernandez Fisher’s family outside Madrid, often renting a car to explore different areas, and went to London.

He also thinks about their quieter moments, like lying in bed together or watching British crime shows with her grandmother.

Mr. Hernandez Fisher says that through her illness, Ms. Warner never stopped wanting to keep writing – even when she couldn’t. Until the end, she was going through her notes and e-mails for different book ideas, such as a young adult fiction and a memoir filled with her waiting room playlists, he says.

By the early summer of 2026, her latest chemotherapy had stopped working and the cancer had spread. While she never felt well, her husband says, she felt better than she had in a long time.

Mr. Hernandez Fisher remembers her final weeks at home and days at Vancouver General Hospital, as a time that was both sad and joyful. As Ms. Warner’s community streamed in to say their goodbyes, he says, they turned the 10th floor of the hospital “into a real party zone.” That’s what he is holding on to.

Her sense of care for her direct community was inseparable from the one for the larger world, which she was always striving to change.

“She showed us by example how you can be a good person and still be critical of the culture. I don’t think anyone else did it before, and I’m sure many of us will try to emulate [it] going forward,” Ms. Lee said.

In April, 2025, Ms. Warner posted that while she was in the waiting room at BC Cancer, the Carole King song It’s Too Late came on the sound system. The song’s lyrics took on a new, unintended meaning. Even during one of the most difficult periods of her life, she found herself inspired to collect and reflect on the songs she was “subjected to” while waiting for her appointments.

It was another way for Ms. Warner to let people into her life and make them laugh a little more, and think a little deeper.

“It is hard and laughter helps,” Ms. Warner wrote on Instagram, “but so does thinking of ways I can turn toward small acts of kindness, love, resistance and advocacy.”

Ms. Warner leaves her husband, Mr. Hernandez Fisher; mother, Elsie Warner; sister, Jennifer Warner; nephew, Alex Warner-Smith; cousin, Kamiko Allen; and grandmothers, Lena Warner and Donna Allen.

stories.title: AI agents banned by several of Canada’s biggest banks as fears grow
stories.summary: Some of Canada's biggest banks say they are now banning AI agents, like Meta's Muse, while others are taking initial steps to limit them.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Some of Canada’s biggest banks say they are now banning AI agents, like Meta’s Muse, while others are taking initial steps to limit them as the broader financial industry becomes increasingly concerned about potential harms to institutions and people’s wealth.

AI agents, or agentic AI, are software that acts as a personal assistant for accomplishing given tasks. A human user might give an AI agent parameters and prompts from organizing a calendar to drafting emails and making a shopping list.

However, an Axios report on Oct. 22 said some AI agents attempted to take actions that appeared to be independent of user instructions, citing people familiar with the matter.

In some cases, bank customers have shared their login ID and password with agents, with banks typically flagging and blocking those transactions, a person in the banking industry said in that reporting. Still, such transactions cannot be deemed unauthorized if credentials were shared by the customer.

That’s given rise to growing questions about whether Canadian banks are prepared for the trend.

Global News asked Canada’s five largest commercial banks on Oct. 22 if they planned to ban AI agents, as banks in the U.S. are doing, amid these reports. All banks that responded initially deferred to the Canada Bankers’ Association, which said it cannot comment on the operational matters of its members.

TD and RBC later told Global News this week that they have moved to block all third-party AI agents.

“TD has made the decision to block all third-party personal AI agents from direct access to banking information, where authentication is required, while we ensure the appropriate safeguards, authorization mechanisms and oversight are in place,” a spokesperson for TD said Wednesday in a statement.

Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) confirmed to Global News that it sent out a company memo alerting employees on Tuesday.

“RBC has decided to block third-party personal AI agents from direct access to authenticated RBC digital properties including online banking,” a spokesperson from RBC said in a statement.

The Bank of Montreal (BMO) also told Global News on Tuesday that it has taken steps to ban AI agents from accessing some of its systems.

“To protect our clients, BMO does not permit AI agents to access our digital properties or execute transactions,” a BMO spokesperson said in a statement.

BMO also referenced its security guidelines for protecting personal information, saying it will never make an unsolicited attempt to contact someone and ask for “sensitive information,” including passwords, PINs or verification codes.

It adds: “Never share this sensitive information with any unauthorized BMO channels, including through AI agents.”

A spokesperson for Cibc also responded to a Global News request Wednesday.

“We are following developments in personal AI agents closely as these technologies evolve,” a spokesperson for Cibc said in a statement.

“We do not support personal AI agents directly opening or accessing accounts. Clients should not share their banking credentials with an AI agent and should carefully consider what personal or financial information they provide to any AI service.”

Scotiabank said Wednesday that it will “limit” AI agents.

“To protect our clients and their financial information, Scotiabank will limit third-party AI agents from accessing its banking platforms as we closely monitor evolving concerns,” a spokesperson for Scotiabank said in a statement.

As the Canadian financial world takes note of the risks posed by AI agents, the federal government told Global News it’s aware of the reports stemming from the U.S.

“Our government is monitoring this issue closely, and so are banks,” a spokesperson for Canada’s minister of AI and digital innovation, Evan Solomon, said in statement on Oct. 22.

“Canadians should be extremely cautious about sharing their banking passwords with anyone, whether that’s an AI agent, an individual or a company.”

One example of an AI agent is Muse by Meta, which can take banking and payments information and make purchases on behalf of human users.

When Global News asked Meta for a statement regarding the concerns among the banking industry, a spokesperson referred to a blog post from September.

“Muse runs on its own dedicated computer in the cloud, contained so no one else’s agent can reach it. That is where Muse lives and where the data and credentials for any service a person connects are securely stored. A separate Sentinel agent runs on that same machine, kept apart from Muse at the system level. Nothing Muse does reaches the internet unless the Sentinel approves it, and it asks the person for permission when needed,” the blog from Meta said.

Amazon told Global News on Oct. 23 that it has requested Meta remove Muse from accessing its e-commerce platform on behalf of customers.

“We think it’s fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate,” said an Amazon spokesperson in a statement.

“This helps ensure a safe, secure, and reliable customer experience, and it is how others operate including food delivery apps and the restaurants they take orders for, delivery services apps and the stores they shop from, and online travel agencies and the airlines they book tickets with for customers.

Amazon added: “Agentic third-party applications such as Muse have the same obligations, and we’ve requested that Meta remove Amazon from the experience.”

– with files from Reuters and Global’s Jacqueline Hansen

stories.title: Two charged as police seek additional victims in exploitation probe
stories.summary: London police say they're looking for more potential victims through a financial exploitation investigation.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
London police say they’re looking for more potential victims through a financial exploitation investigation.

Police say charges were laid after a complex investigation with many victims.

They say one victim experienced sexual violence and forcible confinement.

According to police, they were investigating threats, coercive control, and suspected human trafficking. Additionally, they were looking into reports of unauthorized bank account access, fraudulent purchases, and theft.

Abdulla Walid Kaddoura, 34, faces the following charges:

Criminal harassment

Procuring/recruiting a person to provide sexual services for consideration

Forcible confinement

Withhold/destroy travel or identity documents for trafficking

Uttering threats to cause property damage

Two counts of theft under $5,000

Two counts of assault

Three counts of sexual assault

Causing unnecessary suffering to an animal

Fail to comply with release order

Ali Ismail, 38, faces the following charges:

Both of the accused remain in custody and are expected to appear in London court in relation to the charges.

Anyone who has had similar interactions with the two accused is encouraged to contact the London Police Service at 519-661-5670. Investigators are also asking anyone with information that May assist the investigation to come forward.

stories.title: One charge against Frank Stronach dropped ahead of second trial, lawyer says
stories.summary: Billionaire businessman will still face other charges related to five remaining complainants in the sexual assault trial
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Frank Stronach’s lawyer says one charge of sexual assault against her client in an upcoming Newmarket, Ont., trial has been dropped.

Leora Shemesh says the prosecution involving one complainant in the trial set for next year has been withdrawn.

Documents filed in court showed that complainant had alleged a sexual assault took place in York Region in 2024.

The billionaire businessman, who has denied all allegations against him, will still face other charges related to five remaining complainants in the sexual assault trial.

Stronach is currently awaiting sentencing after a judge in a separate Toronto trial found him guilty of indecent assault in an encounter that took place nearly 50 years ago.

Ontario Superior Court Justice Anne Molloy has said that the 94-year-old auto parts mogul would not face a jail term.

Stronach was initially found guilty in June on two charges related to separate allegations brought by two of the women in the Toronto trial.

Weeks later, Molloy declared a rare post-verdict mistrial on the sexual assault conviction after Stronach’s lawyer argued that emails from the complainant’s lawyer in a separate civil case told a story that was inconsistent with the woman’s testimony in the criminal trial.

Prosecutors have appealed the mistrial decision.

Weeks later, Molloy declared a rare post-verdict mistrial on the sexual assault conviction after Stronach’s lawyer argued that emails from the complainant’s lawyer in a separate civil case told a story that was inconsistent with the woman’s testimony in the criminal trial.
Prosecutors have appealed the mistrial decision.

stories.title: Empty WestJet plane, catering truck collide at Toronto Pearson airport
stories.summary: No flight crew or passengers were on board when the collision occurred, and the Transportation Safety Board said there was 'no intention of flight.'
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
A WestJet plane collided with a catering truck as it was being towed from a gate at Toronto Pearson International Airport on Tuesday, though officials say no one was on board.

The Transportation Safety Board said in an email that the incident occurred during pushback from the gate just before 8:15 p.m.

“The WestJet Boeing 737 was being repositioned under tow when it came into contact with a catering truck,” a spokesperson for the TSB said.

No flight crew or passengers were on board when the collision occurred, and the TSB said there was “no intention of flight.”

WestJet confirmed in an email that an “aircraft winglet” made contact with a parked catering truck while it was being towed to an overnight parking pad.

No one was injured, the TSB added.

The TSB said it was gathering information at this time, but no investigators were being deployed.

stories.title: Stelco owner hopes to recall laid-off steelworkers before Christmas
stories.summary: Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. CEO Lourenco Goncalves says he hopes to bring back laid-off Stelco workers before Christmas if a plan to increase Canadian sales succeeds.
stories.author: Brett Bundale
stories.content:
Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. CEO Lourenco Goncalves says he hopes to bring back laid-off Stelco workers before Christmas if a plan to increase Canadian sales succeeds.

In a written statement to The Canadian Press, Goncalves says the company is now counting on increased purchases of Canadian-made steel rather than tighter import restrictions to restore jobs at its Ontario operations.

Goncalves says the number of layoffs “was never 500” but is rather 175, despite an internal Stelco letter to employees on Sept. 28 warning that up to 500 workers at Hamilton Works and Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, Ont., could be affected.

He also says Stelco is not for sale for at least the next calendar year, and criticizes Industry Minister Mélanie Joly for publicly discussing the possibility of a sale.

Goncalves says Joly is discouraging foreign investment in Canada by publicly discussing potential buyers for Stelco and criticizing the company’s business decisions.

He says Cleveland-Cliffs had expected to sell more cold-rolled and galvanized steel in Canada when it acquired Stelco in 2024, but that demand has not materialized.

stories.title: Deaths from wildfire smoke up 275% over recent years, new report says
stories.summary: A new Lancet report found there were an average of approximately 4,000 annual deaths associated with wildfire smoke between 2021-25, compared to 1,050 annually in 2003-12.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Deaths from wildfire smoke have jumped approximately 275 per cent in Canada since the early 2000s, according to a major global report, a number public health experts say solidifies the need for more serious climate action.

“Climate change and the impacts on health are not some abstract environmental issue that will affect us some at some point in decades from now. We can measure its effect on health in Canada today,” Ian Culbert, executive director of the Canadian Public Health Association, told Global News.

The report, published in The Lancet on Tuesday, found there were an average of 4,000 annual deaths associated with wildfire smoke between 2021-25, compared to an average of 1,050 annually in 2003-12.

The data comes as Canada has experienced repeated intense wildfire seasons – the past three of which are among the 10 worst on record. As fires scorched across much of the country, with particularly hot spots in B.C., Alberta, the Northwest Territories and northern Ontario, smoke continued to billow into major urban centres creating hazardous air quality conditions.

“You don’t have to live beside a forest fire to experience its health effects,” Culbert said. “Smoke travels enormous distances, so wildfire increasingly becomes a population health issue for communities far removed from the fires themselves.”

Scott Weichenthal, a professor in the department of epidemiology and biostatistics at McGill University, told Global News the casualties of wildfire smoke are far greater than the death toll numbers suggest.

PM 2.5, or fine particulate matter, is commonly the metric quantified as it is a primary pollutant that can travel deep into the lungs and enter the blood stream.

“When wildfires happen, PM 2.5 goes up and we know that PM 2.5 is a cause of premature death – I think that’s where those numbers are coming from,” he said. “But in addition to PM 2.5 fires release a whole range of harmful things, many of which we know cause cancer.”

“Mortality is not the sort of total, it doesn’t reflect totally the impacts of these events on people’s exposures or health effects,” he added.

During intense wildfire seasons, many people look to various Air Quality Indexes, but Weichenthal said these measures of PM 2.5, ozone and nitrogen dioxide are representative of the acute and immediate health effects.

“If you have an existing heart or lung condition, you’re going to be more sensitive to any kind of short-term spikes in pollutant concentrations, which is why we see increases in hospitalizations for heart and lung problems during these wildfire smoke events,” he said.

In terms of long term consequences , Weichenthal said people who live in more polluted areas are at greater risk of dying from cardio respiratory effects, but more research is needed on how prevalent air quality-induced cancers and other ailments are.

According to the report, Canada lost 5.2 million hectares of tree cover in 2024, which is 148 per cent more than in 2016. Wildfires accounted for 86 per cent of this loss. The loss of essential tree cover also makes heat an even more pressing issue.

In 2025, 80 per cent of the heatwave days experienced across Canada were directly attributable to climate change, the report found.

Further, people in Canada were exposed to approximately 36 more hours annually during which heat posed a moderate or higher risk of heat stress during moderate outdoor activity.

Vulnerable groups, including older adults, young children, pregnant women, and those with pre-existing conditions, face the greatest risks.

“This isn’t just, it was a hot summer,” Culbert said. “This is directly the effect of the rising temperature of the planet.”

The ongoing El Niño event, which is expected to peak around December and weaken through early 2027, is setting next summer up for hot and dry conditions. While El Niño typically creates uncharacteristically hot weather, on top of climbing temperatures, the effects on the population could be exacerbated.

“The data that we’re seeing is really serious, and the trends are moving in the wrong direction,” Culbert said.

The Canadian Public Health Association said all levels of government need to take further action to protect communities as the consequences of climate change continue to pile up.

One of the association’s recommendations is to create a permanent climate and health adaptation fund as current Health Canada funding ends in 2027-28.

“Public health really needs predictable, sustained capacity to prepare for heat, wildfire smoke and other climate related threats,” Culbert said. “These aren’t one-off emergencies anymore and so public health really needs the capacity to be in response.”

stories.title: Canadian War Museum acquires type of armoured vehicle used on battlefield in Ukraine
stories.summary: Ottawa - Brampton-based defence manufacturer Roshel has donated to the Canadian War Museum in Ottawa one of its mine-resistant armoured transport vehicles — the same kind being used by Ukraine in the war with Russia.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Brampton-based defence manufacturer Roshel has donated to the Canadian War Museum in Ottawa one of its mine-resistant armoured transport vehicles — the same kind being used by Ukraine in the war with Russia.

Jim Whitham, the museum’s director general, says the museum wanted to acquire a piece of military equipment that had a service history in Ukraine, given Canada’s history of supplying the war-torn nation with equipment.
