stories.title: Liberals, NDP and Bloc defeat bid to scrap B.C. tanker ban
stories.summary: The Conservative private member's bill to allow tanker traffic on the B.C. coast went down to defeat Wednesday.
stories.author: Ryan Tumilty
stories.content:
Ottawa — Liberal MPs voted against a proposed repeal of the west coast tanker ban Wednesday, effectively ending a new proposal to ship oil from B.C.‘s northern coast.

Joined by NDP and Bloc Québécois MPs, Liberals in the house voted down a Conservative private member’s bill that would have repealed the ban, which prevents large oil tankers from transiting the waters north of Vancouver Island along the B.C. coast, or from docking at any port along that section of the coast.

The Trudeau government first introduced the tanker ban in 2019, formalizing a voluntary ban on ships in those waters that had been in place for decades. Prime Minister Mark Carney reaffirmed the ban this summer when he announced the new Pacific Link pipeline would take a route from Alberta to a port near Delta B.C., ON the southern part of the coast.

That part of the coastline is not covered by the ban and oil tankers currently go in and out of the Port of Vancouver to carry oil from the existing Trans Mountain Pipeline.

In return for the pipeline avoiding a northern route and the tanker ban remaining in place, outgoing NDP B.C. Premier David Eby agreed not to challenge the new pipeline in court. Eby lost last week’s election and his replacement, B.C. stories.author: Eli Ridder The Canadian Press
stories.content:
FREDERICTON - The New Brunswick government is bidding to purchase 178 square kilometres of land that supplies an aging pulp mill scheduled to close next month.

Oct. 28, 2026

By Eli Ridder The Canadian Press

Natural Resources Minister John Herron says the purchase is vital to ensure there is sufficient wood supply for any future forestry industry in that region.

He says the bid is under a commercial non-disclosure agreement and so he couldn’t share any details about how much the province was willing to spend.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Donna Skelly home

AV Group NB Inc., an affiliate of the India-based Aditya Birla Group, announced last month it would idle its AV Nackawic mill west of Fredericton, putting more than 300 employees out of work as of Nov. 4.

Herron says the potential land purchase does not include the mill itself, which is still scheduled to close.

Meanwhile, Herron says the government has hired management consulting firm AFRY to analyze what options the province has for the mill, such as potential buyers.

Officials at various levels of government have warned the mill’s closure will have a negative ripple effect on a forestry sector long crucial for New Brunswick’s economy.

AV Group NB did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: EU nations balk at 'associate member' label for Canada ahead of summit: reports
stories.summary: A divide over how far the EU should go in formalizing its relationship with Canada has emerged ahead of a summit in Montreal this week.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
When a joint Canada-European Union statement is issued at their summit kicking off in Montreal on Thursday, there’ll be no mention of “associate membership,” according to reports.

“The main concern is that this is unknown terminology, it might bring up legal uncertainty and expectations from other third countries,” an unnamed diplomat said.

Last month, during a State of the Union address in Strasbourg, France, where Carney was the guest of honour, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed that Canada become an “associated member” of the EU, a term that doesn’t legally exist within the enclave. The idea was presented as a way to build a deeper partnership with a country that shares Europe’s democratic values and strategic concerns but has no intention of outright bloc membership.

Other EU diplomats warned that introducing a class of membership without a clear definition could create legal uncertainty, raise expectations among other countries seeking closer ties with Europe and complicate the EU’s existing arrangements with potential member nations.

Matthias Lüttenberg, Germany’s ambassador to Canada, told CTV his country has used “associate membership” to describe the EU’s relationship with Ukraine and Moldova, two countries striving for full membership.

What is an 'associate member' of the EU? Nobody in Europe seems to have a clue

Carney welcomes EU's 'associate member' plan, while Trump lashes out

“What we have in front of us is something which is not clearly understood by all member states,” Lüttenberg said, suggesting all 27 member nations need “some time to reflect.”

“I think we have been a little surprised by the announcement, which doesn’t mean that we cannot agree on it.”

During a media briefing Tuesday, European officials said member nations are united in the ambition of Canada as an “associate member,” but admitted there is some division over the terminology, per Bloomberg .

Outside of “associate membership,” which is being explored only with Canada in mind, the officials also said talks could result in an “alliance of the future” — a broader framework the EU could extend to other countries that want closer ties without full membership.

The goal is to present a concept at next year’s summit.

Speaking to reporters on his way to the House of Commons on Tuesday, Carney said, “the good news is, it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature.”

“What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians, young Canadians, in terms of opportunities to study, work, and travel; our Canadian businesses in terms of new opportunities; Canadian researchers in terms of depth of opportunity; and Canada as a whole, becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation, so we can live our lives as we choose,” he said, as seen on Cpac .

The summit takes place on the 10th anniversary of the Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta), a deal still not ratified by 10 of the bloc’s members, including France and Greece.

“The agenda of the summit will cover a wide range of topics, including trade, digital, critical raw materials, defence and security, cooperation in education, research and innovation, and youth,” the council wrote.

Meanwhile, a pair of recent surveys indicate Canadians remain open to increased partnership with the EU.

Nearly three-quarters of respondents to a Canada Pulse Insights national poll said Carney was “on the right track in seeking a closer economic and security alliance” with the EU.

“Current Conservative supporters stand apart: 58 per cent say wrong direction, while Canadians who report voting Conservative in April 2025 are almost evenly divided,” the pollster wrote.

On the question of full membership, initial support came in at 58 per cent, but fell to 50 per cent when presented with a list of things that could change.

The Canada Pulse Insights online poll of 1,532 adults was conducted Oct. 1-8. While a non-probability sample panel survey such as this doesn’t have a margin of error, a similar probability sample of that many respondents would have a margin of error of plus/minus 2.5 per cent, 19 times out of 20.

Pollara’s Sept. 10-18 online survey of 2,604 respondents. A probability sample of this size carries a margin of error of plus/minus 1.9 per cent, 19 times out of 20.

stories.title: Fate of private member’s bill to amend Divorce Act still not clear
stories.summary: Bill C-223, introduced by Liberal MP Lisa Hepfner, would amend the Divorce Act to curb parental alienation claims, among other changes.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Justice Minister Sean Fraser indicated Wednesday the government is open to supporting elements of a private member’s bill to amend the Divorce Act, though it’s not clear what the bill will ultimately look like.

Women’s groups warned last week that it appeared the Liberal government had changed its mind and the bill, currently before a House of Commons committee, could be killed.

Bill C-223, introduced by Liberal MP Lisa Hepfner, would amend the Divorce Act to curb parental alienation claims, among other changes.

It would also impose new requirements on lawyers to screen for signs of family violence during divorce cases, give judges new tools to identify the existence and impact of coercive control on children, and ensure that — in some circumstances — children can express their preferences to a judge in a custody dispute.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser said the government wants to see the committee make some amendments.

“We want to ensure that we protect the discretion of the court to consider all evidence that’s in the best interest of the child, but I’m optimistic that we can work with the sponsor to ensure we deliver important protections, but at the same time protect against the concerns that we had around judicial discretion,” Fraser said.

Hepfner told reporters there are elements of the bill that are more controversial than others, but declined to say which elements could be removed.

“If we can pass a version of the bill that everyone agrees, including the (Canadian) Bar Association … would make the family court system safer for kids, then I think we should go ahead,” she said.

Hepfner has said she proposed the legislation after hearing horrifying stories from Suzanne Zaccour, director of legal affairs at the National Association of Women and the Law.

Zaccour said in an interview Wednesday it’s important to know what amendments Fraser has in mind.

“There’s some things that I think everyone should be able to agree on, and I hope that the minister will be prepared to support,” she said.

She said there should be nothing controversial about changing the law to ensure that, in cases where there is “a finding of family violence, that the parent who was abusive should not be able to blame the other parent for their strained relationship with the child.”

A report from the National Association of Women and the Law released in September that looked into the deaths of eight children said the concept of parental alienation is frequently invoked in Canada’s courts.

The report said it’s used by parties in child custody cases to explain why a child resists seeing a parent, and to cast doubt on allegations of domestic violence.

Hepfner said in an interview she can’t say with certainty what the bill will look like at the end of the process.

“But I’m working my hardest to try and just get some substantial changes moving now, and then some certainty or some assurances that the government will continue to look at this issue and address some of the problems that have been raised with my bill,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: N.S. premier’s office scolds professor over comments on AI data centre
stories.summary: The office of Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston has complained to a professor in Toronto for weighing in with comments about a proposed artificial intelligence data centre.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston is doubling down on a complaint his office sent to a university professor in Toronto who commented on a proposed artificial intelligence data centre.

A staffer from Houston’s office sent the complaint last week, emailing a copy of the message to a CBC News reporter and the chair of the professor’s department.

Speaking to reporters Wednesday, Premier Tim Houston said he’s glad his communication adviser sent the critical email.

“I’m happy he sent that message to provide some additional information to somebody who was clearly lacking in information but yet speaking as an expert,” Houston said.

The feedback came after Sibo Chen, an associate professor of communication at Toronto Metropolitan University, gave a media interview to CBC saying that public concerns about the data centre project over water usage and electricity rate hikes were valid.

William Burns, a communications adviser with the premier’s office, said Chen’s “slanted comments” were irresponsible and not backed by research on the local community.

“Nova Scotians deserve facts, not speculation presented in a way that creates unnecessary anxiety,” said Burns’ email, which Chen shared with The Canadian Press.

Members of the public and opposition parties in the province have expressed concerns about Everwind Fuels’ proposed $10-billion data centre, which would be leased to U.S. AI company Anthropic for 20 years.

A petition to stop the development of AI data centres in Nova Scotia on Change.org had over 24,000 signatures as of Wednesday afternoon.

Chen suggested that copying the department chair implies the government was trying to intimidate him.

“I actually study how scholars get harassed when they go to do knowledge mobilization … I’m becoming the subject of my own study,” he said.

Chen says he has studied environmental controversies in Canada for 10 years and this is the first time he has received a complaint from a premier’s office.

“I’m very critical about the oilsands, but I never received a complaint from the premier’s office in Alberta,” he said in a video interview Wednesday. His comments, he said, were about the general implications of AI data centre development and backed by peer-reviewed research.

The premier said he doesn’t know how often his team reaches out to academics to criticize the comments they make to the media.

“I’m not sure how often we are communicating with people who are presenting in the media, but I hope it’s a lot,” Houston said.

“If somebody is presenting themselves as an expert and speaking definitively on something that they’re wrong on, I think it’s incumbent on all of us … (to) say there’s some information you’re missing,” he added.

Nova Scotia NDP leader Claudia Chender called Houston’s comments disturbing.

“The comments that we heard just now from the premier, that he hopes that his staff are reaching out to people in the media regularly to correct them on their professional point of view, that should actually send a chill down peoples’ spines,” Chender told reporters Wednesday.

Chender said the premier’s comments lead her to believe that his staff are “bullying” independent experts who criticize his government’s projects.

The 18,600-square-metre data centre would draw 95 megawatts of electricity in its first phase and 420 megawatts after an expected expansion in mid-2028. Everwind says it will cover the cost of all electricity infrastructure so that project will not increase power rates.

Everwind estimates that the facility will use an average of 100,000 litres of water per day in its first phase and 500,000 litres per day after the expansion is completed.

In his email to Chen, Burns said the government will not support a project that increases power rates to customers.

He also highlighted another CBC interview, where Lois Landry, the warden of Richmond County explained there are provisions in place to protect residents and limit the amount of water the data centre would draw from nearby Lake Landrie.

Burns also suggested that as a professor from a Toronto university, Chen could not understand the impact of data centre in Nova Scotia.

Chen said the response from Burns suggests the government is sending the message that citizens don’t need to be concerned about the project.

However, he said the province hasn’t provided enough information to the public about the proposed data centre and he understands why Nova Scotians are worried.

Chen said local university professors May not feel comfortable expressing their concerns about the data centre after seeing the pushback he received from the Nova Scotia government.

“I think that’s precisely why people don’t want to comment on this,” he said.

— With files from Lyndsay Armstrong

stories.title: Canada continues to oppose American embargo on Cuba at UN
stories.summary: Ottawa - Canada has again voted at the United Nations to oppose the U.S. embargo on Cuba as Havana accuses Washington of running a campaign of coercion to sway the vote.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Canada has again voted at the United Nations to oppose the U.S. embargo on Cuba as Havana accuses Washington of running a campaign of coercion to sway the vote.

In a vote of 130-17 with 25 abstentions, the UN General Assembly today condemned the economic embargo for the 34th year in a row.

stories.title: Bryan Adams releases new 'Lake Ontario' song taking aim at Trump: 'Not an executive order'
stories.summary: Canadian singer-songwriter Bryan Adams has released a new track criticizing Trump's executive order that changesdthe name of Lake Ontario.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Canadian singer-songwriter Bryan Adams released a new track on Wednesday criticizing U.S. President Donald Trump’s August executive order that changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America.

Adams, best known for his successful party-rock anthems and love ballads, released the song titled “Lake Ontario” as part of his new album, How’s It Goin,’ which will be released on Nov. 6.

“The ‘lake of shining waters’ is what the Iroquois called her; It’s a First Nations name, not an executive order,” Adams sings in the new track.

“But things weren’t going his way in Iran; So like a baby tossing the toys from the pram,” the song continues, “But it feels like another distraction; While the Epstein files were getting traction; One day they’ll come out and we’ll say ‘there you go’; And then we’ll all dive into Lake Ontario.”

Trump’s name appears thousands of times in the Epstein files, but he has not been charged with any misconduct and has consistently denied any wrongdoing or knowledge of Epstein’s illegal activities.

The music video combines sweeping shots of Lake Ontario with clips of Adams singing from a rocky outcrop and rowing a boat on the water.

Trump signed an executive order changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” in U.S. government records and maps on Aug. 27, following a breakdown in trade negotiations with Canada .

Asked what message he was trying to send Canada with the executive order at the time, Trump said: “No message…Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade, very sadly.”

Politicians on both sides of the border condemned the name change , with Prime Minister Mark Carney writing on X : “We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.”

Meanwhile, it’s not the first time Adams has used his music to express his frustration with the Trump administration.

On Canada Day, the singer-songwriter released a track called “51st State,” in which he both celebrated the shared history and friendship of Canada and the U.S., and vowed to fight for his country if need be.

“Maybe you’ve forgotten; Maybe you just don’t care; But we always stood beside you; For that liberty we share,” he sings. “You can push us to the brink; But where the open road divides; You’ll find a wall of maple; With us on the other side.”

It also mentions tariffs: “So let me give you some advice, mister; You might have too much on your plate; Go and load us up with tariffs; But we’ll never be the 51st State.”

Both “51st State” and “Lake Ontario” are tracks on Adams’ new album.

“The idea was simply to make a record about Canada,” Adams said of the record in its description on his website . “It started with writing the song for the documentary Canada’s Wild Eastern Edge, and after doing so much research I was inspired to start writing more songs about Canada. Musically, it took me somewhere a little different too, which made the whole thing exciting.”

Other song titles among the album’s 12 tracks include “The Battle of Lundy’s Lane,” “The Ballad of Terry Fox,” and “When Canada Joined Newfoundland.”

“Lake Ontario” full lyrics:

From glacial erosion – to indigenous care From European exploration – to industrial wear and tear The “lake of shining waters” is what the Iroquois called her It’s a First Nations name – not an executive order

But things weren’t going his way in Iran So like a baby tossing the toys from the pram He May have thought it best to throw a low blow And create a real dog and pony show But it feels like another distraction While the Epstein files were getting traction One day they’ll come out and we’ll say “there you go” And then we’ll all dive into Lake Ontario

After centuries of trade and war People settled down on the banks and shores All rivalries and conflicts – had all but ceased But it just took one dude to break that peace

stories.title: Former top Mountie David Teboul quits post, admits assaulting teen lacrosse player
stories.summary: Abbotsford, British Columbia, Canada — Former RCMP Assistant Commissioner David Teboul has resigned from his post and has pleaded guilty to assaulting a teenager who he grabbed by the throat after a lacrosse game involving the officer's son in Abbotsford, B.C., in July 2025.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Abbotsford, British Columbia, Canada — Former RCMP Assistant Commissioner David Teboul has resigned from the force and has pleaded guilty to assaulting a teenager who he grabbed by the throat after a lacrosse game involving the officer’s son in Abbotsford, B.C., in July 2025.

An agreed statement of facts read out in a court at a sentencing hearing in Abbotsford on Wednesday said Teboul held the 16-year-old victim by the neck with enough force to lift the youth off the floor, in what special prosecutor Andi MacKay called an unprovoked attack.

“There was zero provocation in this case – zero,” MacKay said. “I say that Mr. Teboul’s acts were gratuitous and opportunistic violence … he applied the force to (the victim’s) neck not once, but twice. He had obvious less risky alternatives available to him, although frankly there was zero necessity of engaging physically with (the victim) at all.”

Teboul is seeking a conditional discharge, while MacKay said that was “wholly inappropriate” and is seeking a suspended sentence with an 18-month probation period. Sentencing is scheduled for Nov. 19.

The court heard that Teboul quit the RCMP on July 1 this year.

Dawn Roberts, director of communications for the B.C. RCMP, confirmed that Teboul had voluntarily submitted his discharge document over the summer.

“It was accepted and he has retired from the RCMP with 29 years service,” Roberts said in an email.

The statement of facts said Teboul’s teenage son got into a verbal altercation with the victim after their match at the Abbotsford Recreation Centre on July 2, 2025.

Teboul’s wife then got involved before Teboul intervened, holding the victim by the neck twice. The first occasion was brief but Teboul lifted the youth off the floor, while the second lasted 15 seconds as he bent the victim over a low wall.

MacKay said aggravating factors included Teboul making a statement to police that was “irreconcilable” with security camera footage of the altercation.

Teboul told Abbotsford police the victim was “coming at” him with his chest “pumped” and teeth clenched. He said the teenager got in his face before he took action to create distance between them.

But the video played in court showed Teboul moving forward to grab the teen by the neck and pushing him against the wall, arching the victim backwards over the structure.

MacKay told the court there was no way to tell if the discrepancies resulted from Teboul’s “best efforts to recount his experience” or if there was a “more sinister purpose to facilitate some other result.”

But the discrepancies should be noteworthy, she said.

“The Crown submits that these statements are a further abusive and aggravating use of his status as a police officer,” MacKay said.

The statement of facts said Teboul declared he was a police officer during the assault, which May have led to the youth not fighting back.

The plea on the single charge comes more than a year after Teboul was charged with two counts of assault and one count of assault causing bodily harm by choking, suffocating or strangling.

His lawyer, Brock Martland, told the court that a conditional discharge was an appropriate sentence for a father who acted on “protective instinct” when his son faced what he viewed as a threat of violence.

Martland said Teboul had no intention of intimidating the youth when he said he was a police officer, since he “has a duty” to do so during an altercation.

The lawyer said the guilty plea reflected Teboul’s recognition of wrongdoing.

He said his client had lost his career, livelihood, and “his previously outstanding reputation” as a result of the assault that lasted less than a minute.

“He is also a human being,” Martland said of Teboul. “And human beings make mistakes. Even the best and the brightest will have lapses in judgments. He made a mistake. He stepped up and (has) taken responsibility for what he did.”

According to the RCMP’s website, Teboul joined the Mounties in 1997 and served in detachments along the west coast of Canada.

It said his career included more than a decade of homicide investigative work and several years in charge of the RCMP’s Anti-Corruption Unit, before he joined British Columbia’s National Security Counter-Terrorism Program, where he served for eight years and was in charge for nearly three years.

In March 2024, Teboul was appointed assistant commissioner in the position of federal policing regional commander for the Pacific region, which includes B.C. and Yukon. It said he led all federal programs in that role, including national security, drugs and organized crime, border integrity, financial integrity and protective services.

The website said he had also been granted several RCMP service awards and commendations, and he received the King Charles III Coronation Medal in June 2025, about two weeks before the alleged offences.

Martland called Teboul a mentor and trusted colleague for others in law enforcement, and he had worked on some of the largest investigations in Canada during his policing career.

Teboul, dressed in a black suit, mostly sat straight and motionless but leaned forward and wiped his face with a tissue when Martland recounted his family and police relationships.

In an impact statement read by MacKay, the victim said the attack resulted in minor soft-tissue injuries on this neck but worse was the “humiliating” and “degrading” nature of the assault in front of his teammates and others.

“The fact that the individual involved was an assistant commissioner of the RCMP and was off-duty makes this experience particularly difficult for me to understand,” the victim’s statement said.

“Someone in a position of authority and responsibility should be expected to exercise judgment and restraint, especially in a disagreement involving words.”

The victim, whose identity is protected because he is a minor, said he quit lacrosse after the assault because it affected his ability to enjoy the sport.

Teboul’s trial had been set to begin on Tuesday, but the dates were vacated pending Wednesday’s guilty plea.

paragraphs: Abbotsford, British Columbia, Canada — Former RCMP Assistant Commissioner David Teboul has resigned from the force and has pleaded guilty to assaulting a teenager who he grabbed by the throat after a lacrosse game involving the officer’s son in Abbotsford, B.C., in July 2025.

An agreed statement of facts read out in a court at a sentencing hearing in Abbotsford on Wednesday said Teboul held the 16-year-old victim by the neck with enough force to lift the youth off the floor, in what special prosecutor Andi MacKay called an unprovoked attack.

“There was zero provocation in this case – zero,” MacKay said. “I say that Mr. Teboul’s acts were gratuitous and opportunistic violence … he applied the force to (the victim’s) neck not once, but twice. He had obvious less risky alternatives available to him, although frankly there was zero necessity of engaging physically with (the victim) at all.”

Teboul is seeking a conditional discharge, while MacKay said that was “wholly inappropriate” and is seeking a suspended sentence with an 18-month probation period. Sentencing is scheduled for Nov. 19.
The court heard that Teboul quit the RCMP on July 1 this year.
Dawn Roberts, director of communications for the B.C. RCMP, confirmed that Teboul had voluntarily submitted his discharge document over the summer.
“It was accepted and he has retired from the RCMP with 29 years service,” Roberts said in an email.
The statement of facts said Teboul’s teenage son got into a verbal altercation with the victim after their match at the Abbotsford Recreation Centre on July 2, 2025.

Teboul’s wife then got involved before Teboul intervened, holding the victim by the neck twice. The first occasion was brief but Teboul lifted the youth off the floor, while the second lasted 15 seconds as he bent the victim over a low wall.
MacKay said aggravating factors included Teboul making a statement to police that was “irreconcilable” with security camera footage of the altercation.
Teboul told Abbotsford police the victim was “coming at” him with his chest “pumped” and teeth clenched. He said the teenager got in his face before he took action to create distance between them.
But the video played in court showed Teboul moving forward to grab the teen by the neck and pushing him against the wall, arching the victim backwards over the structure.

MacKay told the court there was no way to tell if the discrepancies resulted from Teboul’s “best efforts to recount his experience” or if there was a “more sinister purpose to facilitate some other result.”
But the discrepancies should be noteworthy, she said.
“The Crown submits that these statements are a further abusive and aggravating use of his status as a police officer,” MacKay said.
The statement of facts said Teboul declared he was a police officer during the assault, which May have led to the youth not fighting back.
The plea on the single charge comes more than a year after Teboul was charged with two counts of assault and one count of assault causing bodily harm by choking, suffocating or strangling.

His lawyer, Brock Martland, told the court that a conditional discharge was an appropriate sentence for a father who acted on “protective instinct” when his son faced what he viewed as a threat of violence.
Martland said Teboul had no intention of intimidating the youth when he said he was a police officer, since he “has a duty” to do so during an altercation.
The lawyer said the guilty plea reflected Teboul’s recognition of wrongdoing.
He said his client had lost his career, livelihood, and “his previously outstanding reputation” as a result of the assault that lasted less than a minute.

“He is also a human being,” Martland said of Teboul. “And human beings make mistakes. Even the best and the brightest will have lapses in judgments. He made a mistake. He stepped up and (has) taken responsibility for what he did.”
According to the RCMP’s website, Teboul joined the Mounties in 1997 and served in detachments along the west coast of Canada.

It said his career included more than a decade of homicide investigative work and several years in charge of the RCMP’s Anti-Corruption Unit, before he joined British Columbia’s National Security Counter-Terrorism Program, where he served for eight years and was in charge for nearly three years.

In March 2024, Teboul was appointed assistant commissioner in the position of federal policing regional commander for the Pacific region, which includes B.C. and Yukon. It said he led all federal programs in that role, including national security, drugs and organized crime, border integrity, financial integrity and protective services.

The website said he had also been granted several RCMP service awards and commendations, and he received the King Charles III Coronation Medal in June 2025, about two weeks before the alleged offences.
Martland called Teboul a mentor and trusted colleague for others in law enforcement, and he had worked on some of the largest investigations in Canada during his policing career.
Teboul, dressed in a black suit, mostly sat straight and motionless but leaned forward and wiped his face with a tissue when Martland recounted his family and police relationships.

In an impact statement read by MacKay, the victim said the attack resulted in minor soft-tissue injuries on this neck but worse was the “humiliating” and “degrading” nature of the assault in front of his teammates and others.
“The fact that the individual involved was an assistant commissioner of the RCMP and was off-duty makes this experience particularly difficult for me to understand,” the victim’s statement said.
“Someone in a position of authority and responsibility should be expected to exercise judgment and restraint, especially in a disagreement involving words.”
The victim, whose identity is protected because he is a minor, said he quit lacrosse after the assault because it affected his ability to enjoy the sport.
Teboul’s trial had been set to begin on Tuesday, but the dates were vacated pending Wednesday’s guilty plea.

“There was zero provocation in this case – zero,” MacKay said. “I say that Mr. Teboul’s acts were gratuitous and opportunistic violence … he applied the force to (the victim’s) neck not once, but twice. He had obvious less risky alternatives available to him, although frankly there was zero necessity of engaging physically with (the victim) at all.”

Teboul is seeking a conditional discharge, while MacKay said that was “wholly inappropriate” and is seeking a suspended sentence with an 18-month probation period. Sentencing is scheduled for Nov. 19.

The court heard that Teboul quit the RCMP on July 1 this year.

Dawn Roberts, director of communications for the B.C. RCMP, confirmed that Teboul had voluntarily submitted his discharge document over the summer.

“It was accepted and he has retired from the RCMP with 29 years service,” Roberts said in an email.

The statement of facts said Teboul’s teenage son got into a verbal altercation with the victim after their match at the Abbotsford Recreation Centre on July 2, 2025.

Teboul’s wife then got involved before Teboul intervened, holding the victim by the neck twice. The first occasion was brief but Teboul lifted the youth off the floor, while the second lasted 15 seconds as he bent the victim over a low wall.

MacKay said aggravating factors included Teboul making a statement to police that was “irreconcilable” with security camera footage of the altercation.

Teboul told Abbotsford police the victim was “coming at” him with his chest “pumped” and teeth clenched. He said the teenager got in his face before he took action to create distance between them.

But the video played in court showed Teboul moving forward to grab the teen by the neck and pushing him against the wall, arching the victim backwards over the structure.

MacKay told the court there was no way to tell if the discrepancies resulted from Teboul’s “best efforts to recount his experience” or if there was a “more sinister purpose to facilitate some other result.”

But the discrepancies should be noteworthy, she said.

“The Crown submits that these statements are a further abusive and aggravating use of his status as a police officer,” MacKay said.

The statement of facts said Teboul declared he was a police officer during the assault, which May have led to the youth not fighting back.

The plea on the single charge comes more than a year after Teboul was charged with two counts of assault and one count of assault causing bodily harm by choking, suffocating or strangling.

His lawyer, Brock Martland, told the court that a conditional discharge was an appropriate sentence for a father who acted on “protective instinct” when his son faced what he viewed as a threat of violence.

Martland said Teboul had no intention of intimidating the youth when he said he was a police officer, since he “has a duty” to do so during an altercation.

The lawyer said the guilty plea reflected Teboul’s recognition of wrongdoing.

He said his client had lost his career, livelihood, and “his previously outstanding reputation” as a result of the assault that lasted less than a minute.

“He is also a human being,” Martland said of Teboul. “And human beings make mistakes. Even the best and the brightest will have lapses in judgments. He made a mistake. He stepped up and (has) taken responsibility for what he did.”

According to the RCMP’s website, Teboul joined the Mounties in 1997 and served in detachments along the west coast of Canada.

It said his career included more than a decade of homicide investigative work and several years in charge of the RCMP’s Anti-Corruption Unit, before he joined British Columbia’s National Security Counter-Terrorism Program, where he served for eight years and was in charge for nearly three years.

In March 2024, Teboul was appointed assistant commissioner in the position of federal policing regional commander for the Pacific region, which includes B.C. and Yukon. It said he led all federal programs in that role, including national security, drugs and organized crime, border integrity, financial integrity and protective services.

The website said he had also been granted several RCMP service awards and commendations, and he received the King Charles III Coronation Medal in June 2025, about two weeks before the alleged offences.

Martland called Teboul a mentor and trusted colleague for others in law enforcement, and he had worked on some of the largest investigations in Canada during his policing career.

Teboul, dressed in a black suit, mostly sat straight and motionless but leaned forward and wiped his face with a tissue when Martland recounted his family and police relationships.

In an impact statement read by MacKay, the victim said the attack resulted in minor soft-tissue injuries on this neck but worse was the “humiliating” and “degrading” nature of the assault in front of his teammates and others.

“The fact that the individual involved was an assistant commissioner of the RCMP and was off-duty makes this experience particularly difficult for me to understand,” the victim’s statement said.

Teboul’s trial had been set to begin on Tuesday, but the dates were vacated pending Wednesday’s guilty plea.

stories.title: Canada and EU drop idea of ‘associate member’ from summit declaration
stories.summary: Canada’s efforts to draw closer to the EU also risk angering Trump as trade talks between Canada and the U.S. continue
stories.author: Maria Cheng and Andrew Gray
stories.content:
The European Union has dropped the idea of designating Canada an “associate member” of the 27-member economic bloc after objections from major players, including Germany and France, two sources familiar with deliberations say.

Instead, a new draft of a joint statement, to be issued during a two-day Canada-EU summit that starts Thursday in Montreal, talks of “ever closer association” between Ottawa and Brussels, according to the sources.

This doesn’t change the thrust of efforts to deepen economic and security ties but shelves a term that commanded attention even as it prompted friction between EU members.

The Globe and Mail is not identifying the sources, who Wednesday detailed plans for the summit, because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the matter. One source called the new language a compromise.

A second source said the term “associate member” had become a distraction that threatened to overshadow a summit aimed at deepening economic and defence ties. They said EU states that objected are not opposed to closer association but felt it would be a confusing term for a country that has no intention of becoming a member.

The label was proposed by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in September, but it has no legal basis in the EU treaties that bind the member states together.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz floated the idea of designating Ukraine, which is seeking EU membership, as an “associate member” earlier this year in a letter to EU leaders, the second source noted. His proposal would let Ukrainian officials take part in EU summits and ministerial meetings but not vote in them. There’s no indication this idea gained traction.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said that Canada has no intention of formally joining the EU, which would require this country to bring its laws and regulations into alignment with those of the economic bloc.

The EU and Canada are trying to boost two-way trade and investment in order to reduce economic and strategic reliance on the increasingly protectionist and unpredictable United States under President Donald Trump .

The EU bought about $43-billion of Canadian goods in 2025, roughly 1 per cent of what it imports, according to a new report from TD Economics. Exports to the EU amount to 5 to 6 per cent of Canada’s merchandise exports, roughly the same share as shipments to Britain or China, the bank said.

Canada’s exports of $22-billion in services to the EU in 2025 are “barely a blip considering the EU’s more than $2-trillion in services imports from non-EU countries,” TD Economics said in the report .

The bank’s economists screened trade data across nearly 5,000 product categories, matching goods where Canada has a proven edge with products that the European Union relies on imports to supply.

“The EU imported more than $700-billion of these goods in 2025, suggesting considerable room for competitive Canadian exporters to expand,” TD Economics said, while noting barriers including lack of infrastructure remain.

“European demand increasingly overlaps with Canadian capabilities and the two sides’ strategic interest in diversifying economic ties,” the bank said.

“The largest long-term opportunities span defence, energy, critical minerals, digital markets, as well as financial and other professional services,” TD Economics said. “The biggest gains will need to be unlocked through expanded infrastructure and deeper co-operation to expand investment, improve market access, and build new supply chains in critical areas.”

Mr. Carney this week played down the question of whether Canada is designated “associate member,” saying the title is irrelevant.

“What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians, young Canadians in terms of opportunities to study, work and travel, our Canadian businesses in terms of new opportunities, Canadian researchers in terms of depths of opportunity, and Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation, so we can live our lives as we choose,” he said Tuesday.

The Prime Minister said the Montreal summit is only a beginning and will “launch further formal discussions, negotiations, over the course of the next year.”

EU officials told journalists earlier this week that Ottawa and Brussels are working toward a digital trade agreement that will cement rules for online trade, including e-signatures and e-contracts, paperless trade, secure cross-border data flows, duties on electronic transmissions and e-commerce.

This agreement would effectively expand the existing Canada-EU trade deal into digital trade, the officials said.

This new partnership will include opening Europe’s supercomputing infrastructure to Canada, giving researchers and businesses more opportunities to use the quantum power from these machines to further research into areas such as artificial intelligence and Alzheimer’s, EU officials have said.

Canada is also looking at greater reliance on EU satellite systems to reduce dependence on the U.S.

Mr. Carney recently told The New York Times that he plans to “diversify away from” billionaire Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite-internet network, indirectly citing instances where Ukraine’s access to Starlink services was “turned on and off in a way that was not sovereign to the actors in the conflict,” without naming the country.

Canada and the EU are talking about deepening co-operation on secure satellite connections, including Galileo, the EU’s satellite navigation system, which is the equivalent of GPS, as well as Iris2, the EU’s planned secure satellite network, the officials said. This could give governments and businesses a communication option that doesn’t depend on U.S. or Chinese systems.

And Ottawa and Brussels are discussing Canada participating in GovSatCom, which pools satellite communications capacity from member states for government and military use, they said.

A recent version of the joint statement for this summit also said that deepening ties will mean “connecting instant payment systems to facilitate faster, lower-cost and more seamless cross-border transactions,” making it easier for Canadians and Europeans to conduct business, invest and transfer funds internationally.

In addition, it said, Canada and the EU will co-operate on building telecommunications cables connecting them to Asia as well, as Ottawa and Brussels grow concerned about sending digital traffic through the United States.

“We will launch joint initiatives to improve secure international connectivity between Europe, Canada and Asia through new subsea cable infrastructure,” the draft joint statement said.

“As part of these efforts, we will assess cable routes, points of interconnection, and engage with industry. Our goal is to develop new infrastructure to enhance economic growth, route diversity and resiliency.”

stories.title: A Canadian woman jumped off an iceberg in Newfoundland and made history
stories.summary: Molly Carlson, a 28-year-old Montreal-based diver, talks about the unpredictable iceberg that started breaking after she dove off it.
stories.author: National Post
stories.content:
Molly Carlson admits she had concerns of her own as she leapt off a massive iceberg in Newfoundland and plunged 50-foot in the North Atlantic Ocean.

The 28-year-old from Montreal told National Post on Tuesday that she was more worried about the unpredictability of the iceberg itself, than the temperature of the water.

“After I jumped off, it started breaking on the backside. So the timing was insane. If we were on there for five more minutes, who knows what this story could have been like,” she told Global News on Monday.

Among other risks, the iceberg could have flipped, and its stability could not be guaranteed, according to an iceberg specialist who accompanied the crew at the time of the dive.

Carlson made history being the first known woman to pull off this kind of dive. Videos of the dive, which Carlson completed in June off the coast of Newfoundland and Labrador, were posted online on Oct. 22 by Red Bull and Red Bull Canada. The energy drink company has become known for teaming up with athletes who perform extreme stunts around the world.

Despite some of the concerns shared online, mostly about nearly freezing water temperatures and the safety risks involved, many have shown support for the diver and called her inspiring.

Carlson was accompanied by Canadian ice climber, Will Gadd, who helped her with the journey to the edge of the free-standing iceberg. When recounting the route to the top, Carlson stated that Gadd was a tremendous help.

“Having him climb the berg with me, truly helped me stay as calm as I could before the dive,” Carlson told National Post.

Despite her worries, Carlson said her team flagged any issues well in advance.

“My team went above and beyond with extra safety checks, had emergency crews on site, and brought in an iceberg specialist.”

The support, Carlson said, is what made the experience that much more incredible.

She said she has received immense support, especially from women, who have told her that the accomplishment has inspired them to “try something new, blaze their own trail, and create their own story.”

Becoming the first known woman to complete the dive means more than she can explain, Carlson said. “It makes me proud of my journey and of how I’ve shown up for little Molly,” she said, adding that the moment represents the many chapters of her life and career.

Carlson expressed gratitude for not only her female supporters but also the high-diving community. She said they stand by one another no matter what.

After completing the dive, Carlson said she kept returning to one analogy: “Just like icebergs, there’s so much more to us than what’s visible above the surface.”

She dedicated this project to “everyone who has ever been scared to show what’s underneath,” adding that hearing how many people resonate with that message has been incredible.

stories.title: Manitobans vote in municipal elections across province
stories.summary: In Winnipeg, Scott Gillingham is hoping to keep his job as mayor for a second term
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canada’s run of October voting continues with municipal elections today across Manitoba.

In Winnipeg, home to more than half the province’s population, Scott Gillingham is hoping to keep his job as mayor for a second term.

Polls have shown Gillingham ahead of the 11 other candidates in the race, although his support has recently slipped.

Other mayoral contenders include Kevin Klein, a former legislature member and city councillor, funeral home director Mike Vogiatzakis and software developer Noah Redden.

Key issues in the Winnipeg campaign have been housing, public safety and transit.

Almost all other Manitoba communities are holding elections, except for the resort areas of Winnipeg Beach, Dunnottar and Victoria Beach, which had votes in July.

So far this month, there have been provincial elections in Quebec and British Columbia, a referendum in Alberta, and municipal votes in Ontario, B.C. and Yellowknife.

stories.title: Federal government has paid out $83.2 billion to First Nations over lawsuits since 2007: report
stories.summary: Fraser Institute looks at payouts by Canadian government dating back to 1974, but finds most of the $110 billion came since 2017.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
A new report from the Fraser Institute calculates that the federal government has paid out more than $110 billion to First Nations for lawsuit and class action settlements since 1974, with the vast majority of that amount coming from recent class action lawsuits.

Class action payments since 2007 have cost the government an estimated $83.2 billion, the report found. That’s 73.5 per cent of all payouts since 1974.

This is outside of what Canada already spends on Indigenous issues. Last year, the budget included $25.3 billion for the Department of Indigenous Services, and $16.5 billion for the Department of Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs. That was more than the country spent on its defence budget of $33.9 billion.

The report, Compensation for Past Treatment of Indigenous People , focuses on federal Indigenous spending based on rectifying past grievances and offering compensation through treaty negotiations, lawsuits and settlements, with an emphasis on British Columbia. It was released this month.

In B.C. alone, treaty settlements from 2000 to 2016 amounted to $587 million in payouts, and specific claims settlements, of which there were 270, came to $3 billion. But a small number of class action lawsuits settled between 2007 and 2025 added a further $13.4 billion to the total.

Numbers from the rest of Canada tell a similar story. In the past 52 years, the federal government has given an estimated $113.2 billion (adjusted for inflation) to First Nations in Canada as payouts for lawsuits and class action settlements.

“Most Canadians are not aware of the enormous payments Ottawa has made to First Nations to settle legal claims and class action lawsuits,” said Tom Flanagan, Fraser Institute senior fellow and co-author of the report.

Federal Indigenous spending quadrupled to $40.8B under Trudeau, with 'negligible' improvement to communities: report

Warren Mirko: Wildfires shouldn't be used as a reconciliation morality play

Of this, some $29.4 billion or about a quarter of the total amount was to settle specific claims — essentially cases where a court ruled the federal government had violated treaty rights or the Indian Act in the past.

There has been a distinct increase in the number and value of those claims settlements by Canada for violations of the Indian Act or of historic treaties, the report found.

The Indian Act, first introduced in 1876, is the primary law the federal government uses to deal with First Nations governments and the management of reserve land. It also outlines governmental obligations to First Nations peoples.

“I don’t know how many folks in Canada have seen one of these before, but this is a status card, and it says your friend Wab Kinew is an Indian, within the meaning of the Indian Act,” he said. “I’m not sure if that lines up with your vision of Canada, that we still have a race-based form of identification in this country. But this is a reality.”

In 1974, there were two settlements valued at $1.8 million. But the numbers started to rise significantly beginning in 2017. By 2024, the peak year for payouts so far, there were 69 settlements valued at $7.3 billion. The following year saw a decrease to 30 settlements valued at $2.7 billion.

However, specific claims are only one form of legal compensation for First Nations. Increasingly, class actions and other litigation based on claims of mistreatment or rights violations have been brought against the federal government, including for residential schools, the “sixties scoop” and safe drinking water. Settling class action suits has cost Canada an estimated $83.2 billion since 2007.

Since that year, nine class actions or their legal equivalent have been settled by the federal government. The total value of $83.2 billion includes payments to individual Indigenous people ($49.4 billion) and payments to First Nations and other organizations ($33.8 billion).

“Because Ottawa’s compensatory payments are for historical wrongs, the number of claims — and the amount taxpayers need to pay — should be going down, not up, but that is not the case,” Flanagan noted.

“The significant amount of money that the federal government has paid out, particularly in recent years, acts as an incentive to attract even more legal claims and class action lawsuits to be filed,” he added. “This all begs the question of whether or not these efforts are improving the wellbeing of Indigenous populations in Canada.”

The report found that, as of Aug. 11, 10 claims had been settled for a total of $250 million in fiscal 2026–27. “It is too early to tell whether this decline in the pace of settlement is a harbinger of the future,” it noted.

The report combed through data from various government agencies, and includes more than three pages of references.

“As of September 8, 2026, there were still 694 claims being considered in the administrative process of the Specific Claims Branch, plus another 99 in active litigation, either before the Specific Claims Tribunal or ordinary Canadian courts,” it added. “With so many unsettled claims, the future will depend on how much resistance subsequent federal governments wish to display in the courts or at the negotiating table.”

Data specific to British Columbia found that eight treaties were finalized by the federal government with B.C. First Nations between 2000 and 2016, representing $587.3 million. This represented an average payment of $68,318 for the 8,596 Indigenous People covered.

stories.title: Unclear whether Quebec premier will attend EU summit in Montreal
stories.summary: QUÉBEC - Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has refused to confirm whether he will attend the Canada-European Union summit organized by the federal government after accusing Ottawa of muzzling him.
stories.author: Patrice Bergeron The Canadian Press
stories.content:
QUÉBEC - Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has refused to confirm whether he will attend the Canada-European Union summit organized by the federal government after accusing Ottawa of muzzling him.

By Patrice Bergeron The Canadian Press

The summit, which aims to strengthen political partnership between Canada and the EU, will be held in Montreal on Thursday and Friday.

Prime Minister Mark Carney reiterated on Wednesday that St-Pierre Plamondon was invited to dinner at the head table, alongside European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Donna Skelly home

But the premier is demanding an official opportunity to speak.

He called on Ottawa today to reverse its decision, while remaining vague about whether he would attend the summit.

On Tuesday, the PQ premier accused the federal government of trying to silence him at the important international meeting.

Carney stated that the premier had been invited to the dinner but that St-Pierre Plamondon had decided to leave “an empty chair.”

“It’s a good opportunity to have serious conversations and establish relationships with the president of the European Union. I hope he will reconsider,” Carney told reporters in Ottawa Wednesday morning.

St-Pierre Plamondon maintains that it’s “disrespectful” not to give the premier of Quebec a voice at an event taking place in Quebec where Quebec’s economic interests are being negotiated.

“It’s never too late to do the right thing,” he said in Quebec City.

He cites the Gérin-Lajoie doctrine, which is a Quebec policy stating the province can defend its own areas of jurisdiction and interests on the international stage.

Ruba Ghazal, spokesperson for Québec solidaire, called on all party leaders to demand that Carney allow St-Pierre Plamondon to take the floor at the summit.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published October 28, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canadian Blood Services says donor death not linked to plasma donation a day earlier
stories.summary: Halifax - Canadian Blood Services has confirmed a donor died a day after giving plasma at one of its centres this fall, but the organization says the death was not linked to the donation.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax - Canadian Blood Services has confirmed a longtime donor died a day after giving plasma at one of its centres this fall, but the organization says the death was not linked to the donation.

The non-profit organization declined to say where and exactly when the person died, citing privacy concerns for their family, but they confirmed the donor was a volunteer at a centre where he had donated more than 200 times.

The Ottawa-based organization issued a statement Tuesday saying its medical professionals reviewed the person’s donation records, assessed their last donation and spoke with immediate family members. The family told the organization that medical providers had determined the death was the result of natural causes.

As well, Canadian Blood Services said its review of the case was shared with Health Canada, which advised that no followup was required.

Health Canada said it received word of the death on Sept. 25.

All blood collection services in Canada, including Canadian Blood Services and private businesses, are required by law to report to Health Canada any time a donor dies within 72 hours of making a donation.

In this case, “CBS holds responsibility for conducting a thorough investigation,” Health Canada said in an emailed statement Wednesday, adding the department can call for corrective actions or conduct inspections.

“The information provided by CBS demonstrates that they followed their authorized protocols and procedures .... (T)here is no indication or suggestion of any equipment failures, malfunction, misuse or deviation from established procedures during the donation process.”

Plasma donations in Canada have faced intense scrutiny since March, when Health Canada confirmed it was investigating the deaths of two people in Winnipeg who donated plasma at collection centres run by Grifols, a Barcelona-based company that pays donors.

Health Canada has said those deaths occurred in October 2025 and January of this year.

The department’s investigation found no link between the deaths and the collection process, and Grifols said that at no point was the safety of donors and patients compromised.

Kat Lanteigne, former executive director of the now-defunct advocacy group BloodWatch, said all three deaths should be subjected to a scientific review.

“There is a knowledge gap that we have in Canada in understanding the deleterious impact that the plasma (donation) process can have,” Lanteigne said in an interview Wednesday.

“It doesn’t mean that it did (cause the death), but it’s important to rule it out because it informs regulatory policy in order to strengthen plasma donation rules …. The concern that I have as an advocate is not to assign blame, it’s how to improve the system to protect donors.”

BloodWatch was founded by survivors of Canada’s tainted blood scandal, as well as their relatives and advocates. In the 1970s and 1980s, thousands of Canadians were infected with HIV and hepatitis C after receiving contaminated blood or blood products, prompting a public inquiry, criminal charges and an overhaul of the blood system that led to the creation of Canadian Blood Services.

Lanteigne is now a patient advocate for one of the people who died after donating plasma at a Grifols donation centre in Winnipeg.

“We have this big gap within our system that just simply needs to be fixed,” she said. “We need a better understanding so we can make sure that our regulations are strong.”

Ron Vezina, the organization’s vice-president of corporate reputation, issued an emailed statement challenging the suggestion of a knowledge gap, saying Lanteigne’s comments could create unnecessary doubt about a highly regulated system.

“Canadian Blood Services regularly publishes evidence on donor safety and operates within one of the most rigorously regulated blood systems in the world,” Vezina said.

“Our practices are continually informed by scientific evidence, independent oversight, and benchmarking against leading international blood operators. We … have substantial data demonstrating the safety of donation for eligible donors.”

Grifols entered into a partnership Canadian Blood Services last year.

Last month, Health Canada suspended collections at one of the Grifols donation centres in Winnipeg that had been part of Health Canada’s investigation into the two earlier deaths.

Health Canada found compliance problems at Grifols’ Taylor Avenue location, saying the centre had failed to shore up clinic practices as directed.

And on Oct. 21, the company started accepting limited donations after receiving approval from Health Canada.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

stories.title: Ontario to match Ottawa’s ‘mega’ tax deduction
stories.summary: Measure will boost economy and encourage investment, Finance Minister says
stories.author: Jeff Gray
stories.content:
Ontario will match Prime Minister Mark Carney ’s planned “productivity mega deduction” business tax break meant to boost investment as the country faces the economic drag of U.S. tariffs , the province’s Finance Minister says.

Peter Bethlenfalvy had already said the matching measure was imminent in a speech last week , but told reporters on Wednesday that it would be included in the fall economic statement, set to be unveiled Thursday.

The proposed changes expand recent moves to allow companies to immediately deduct the cost of a range of capital expenses, such as those for new machinery or software, instead of doing so gradually over time.

These accelerated write-off rules will mean substantially lower tax bills in the short term, something both provincial and federal governments say will encourage more companies to invest and expand in Canada.

But the changes come with a price tag in reduced tax revenue. Ontario’s latest measures, to match those proposed federally by Mr. Carney last month, are expected to cost the province’s treasury $8-billion over the next five years. Combined with the previously announced deduction rules, that bill for Ontario would be $12-billion.

The news was meant to act as a preview for Thursday’s fall economic statement, which Mr. Bethlenfalvy said will contain more details. The statement will also provide an update on the province’s finances.

In the budget earlier this year, Mr. Bethlenfalvy projected a $13.8-billion deficit for 2026-27, up from last year. He warned last week that the red ink is needed as the province stares down economic uncertainty. But he said the new tax breaks will not worsen the province’s books.

“It’s absolutely additive. It’ll boost our economy,” Mr. Bethlenfalvy told reporters. “Investors are looking to grow with Canada and Ontario. This is an added feature that gives them the signal that this is the place and time to invest.”

The government estimates that the tax changes will attract an estimated $11-billion in new investment to Ontario and create 30,000 jobs – even as U.S. tariffs target Ontario’s auto, steel and manufacturing sectors.

At the federal level, the Prime Minister used a global investment summit last month to unveil a proposed “productivity mega deduction” to woo investors from around the world to Canada, building on the breaks included in a similar “super deduction” announced last year.

Ottawa estimates that the new federal deduction would cost it $36-billion in the first five years. It is expected to be included in the federal budget, which Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne is set to deliver on Nov. 5.

Giles Gherson, president and CEO of the Toronto Region Board of Trade, stood alongside Mr. Bethlenfalvy as he addressed reporters on Wednesday at the MaRS Discovery District, a hub for startups in downtown Toronto.

Mr. Gherson said the province’s move is “turbocharging” the federal mega deduction, and that the board has advocated for these changes.

“It’s a double boost for businesses answering the call to invest in this province’s growth,” Mr. Gherson said.

He noted the impact of the U.S. tariffs on Ontario’s manufacturing sector but added that even before President Donald Trump , Canada struggled to attract investors, suffering a $1-trillion net outflow of investment from 2015 to 2024.

“The mega deduction would be a game changer to help bring the trillion dollars back home over the next decade,” he said.

Editor’s note: This story was edited to remove a reference to factories, which are already covered by previous tax deduction acceleration measures announced by both Ontario and the federal government.

stories.title: Bryan Adams stands up for ‘Lake Ontario’ in new song referencing Epstein files
stories.summary: Bryan Adams is raging against geographical renamings.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Bryan Adams is raging against geographical renamings.

The Kingston, Ont.-born rocker has released a new single called “Lake Ontario,” which appears to take shots at U.S. president Donald Trump.

In August, Trump signed an executive order directing U.S. federal agencies to refer to Lake Ontario as “Lake America.”

Adams said in a statement his new song is for “all the sane people on both shores who know that the current madness will pass, and that Lake Ontario will always be Lake Ontario.”

In the mid-drive rock tune, the 66-year-old calls out “a baby tossing the toys from the pram” due to things not “going his way in Iran.” Elsewhere in the song, he refers to the ordeal as “another distraction” as “the Epstein files were getting traction.”

Adams is readying a new album, “How’s It Goin’,” described in a release as “his musical love letter to Canada.” It also includes the protest track “51st State.”

“Empires and regimes, dictators and kings, they all come and go,” Adams said in his statement.

“Lake Ontario is forever.”

Adams is not the first Canadian act to stand up for the body of water.

In August, Blue Rodeo’s hit “Hasn’t Hit Me Yet” went viral after thousands of fans at their Toronto concert were captured screaming along to the lyric: “Out in the middle of Lake Ontario.”

Co-frontman Greg Keelor told The Canadian Press he was happy to see the song become a “rallying call.”

“That’s a very powerful body of water,” he said.

“Most Canadians, it wasn’t really something in your brain, it was just Lake Ontario. But now it’s taken on a significance and it’s a bit of a line in the sand.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

Alex Nino Gheciu, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canada-EU Summit set to launch additional talks on a deeper partnership
stories.summary: Ottawa - A stronger alliance between Canada and the European Union would only include a financial commitment if either side joins specific programs in either jurisdiction, a senior government official says.
stories.author: David Baxter The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - A stronger alliance between Canada and the European Union would only include a financial commitment if either side joins specific programs in either jurisdiction, a senior government official said Wednesday.

The next steps in that alliance are expected to be finalized and announced Thursday and Friday, during the Canada-EU Summit in Montreal, and it seems it will not include making Canada an “associate member” of the European Union.

Several European news agencies have reported that idea is off the table, and EU members are looking at terminology around a closer association between the 27-member bloc and Canada.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has repeatedly said the substance of the agreement is more important than the language to describe the evolving relationship. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen first floated the “associate membership” status invite during her state of the union address to European Parliament last month. Canadian officials, including EU Ambassador Jonathan Wilkinson, immediately played down the use of that term, and said a description for the new partnership had not been decided.

This week, several EU member nations rejected the term as proposed language was floated in documents ahead of the summit. European officials repeatedly used the phrase “alliance for the future” to describe the partnership in a media briefing Tuesday — a phrase embraced by Prime Minister Carney.

A Canadian official briefing reporters on Wednesday, ahead of the summit, said the language being used to describe the partnership is more symbolic than significant.

In that briefing, Canadian officials said the summit will focus on deepening ties in areas like business, technology, defence, critical minerals and energy.

They said the government would only be tied to a financial commitment through the alliance only if it joins a program like Erasmus+, the EU’s student exchange program.

The officials did not say specifically which EU programs Canada might join. Carney has publicly indicated a desire for Canada to join Erasmus+.

That program has a budget of roughly $41 billion for its 2021-2027 funding cycle.

The program includes an official welcoming ceremony Thursday followed by a business dinner hosted by Carney. The dinner will gather leaders from various sectors in Canada and Europe alongside top elected officials.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon was invited but has said he will not attend because he is not invited to speak at the formal summit.

Several Canadian cabinet ministers are expected to attend: Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand, Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne, Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, Culture Minister Marc Miller, International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu and AI Minister Evan Solomon.

European officials said this week’s summit is meant to advance conversations on deeper ties that can be finalized at the 2027 Canada-EU Summit, a timeline Carney supported in a comment before the weekly cabinet meeting Tuesday.

Canadian officials were less specific when asked about the likely timeline for securing a more formal deal.

Carney has said any deal with the EU would be brought to Parliament for debate and a vote.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

stories.title: Ontario matches feds’ tax perk for businesses on capital investments
stories.summary: Bethlenfalvy says Ontario's measures would provide about $8 billion in relief that will be a boon to the country over the long term by attracting more businesses to the province.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Ontario is matching the federal government’s recent move to give businesses a tax break on capital investments.

Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy made the announcement ahead of Thursday’s fall economic statement.

Last year, Prime Minister Mark Carney and the federal government allowed businesses to immediately deduct 100 per cent of the cost of some investments, such as machinery, equipment and technology, which applied to about 15 per cent of the investment in capital costs.

Last month, Carney updated the measure, allowing two thirds of assets to qualify.

Bethlenfalvy says Ontario’s measures would provide about $8 billion in relief that will be a boon to the country over the long term by attracting more businesses to the province.

He says this brings Ontario’s marginal effective tax rate to 3.6 per cent.

stories.title: Assault charges against Sault Ste. Marie MPP Chris Scott dropped
stories.summary: Domestic violence charges of assault and assault with a weapon against the member of provincial parliament for Sault Ste. Marie have been withdrawn.
stories.author: Maan Alhmidi The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ontario member of provincial parliament Chris Scott said the withdrawal of domestic violence charges against him was based on evidence and “fairness,” as he maintained his innocence.

Crown prosecutors told Ontario Court Justice Martin Lambert on Wednesday that they are dropping the charges of assault and assault with a weapon against Scott, who represents Sault Ste. Marie.

Scott was charged for an alleged incident on Sept. 19, 2025, prompting his removal from the Progressive Conservative caucus. Court documents specified the charges were being treated as alleged intimate partner violence and the weapon allegedly used was a high chair.

“These charges were not withdrawn because of a legal technicality, an expired time limit, or because evidence was excluded,” Scott said in a statement Wednesday.

“I did not accept a deal or agree to anything that would compromise my position. I maintained my innocence throughout, and I am grateful that I can finally put this matter behind me.”

Prosecutors said in court that Scott has finished counselling in anger management and did not have a past criminal record or any additional charges since last year. They said a charge against Scott’s wife, who was accused of assaulting him in another incident, was also dropped.

Premier Doug Ford’s office said Scott will not return to the PC caucus after the withdrawal of his charges.

Government house leader Steve Clark reiterated that at Queen’s Park.

“We hold our members to a higher standard,” Clark told reporters on Wednesday.

“When he was charged, we made a decision. I wrote to the clerk to say that he’s no longer a member. He can take a seat as an independent. He can ask questions. He can function as an MPP just like everyone else.”

Scott said he’s glad the conclusion of his court case was “guided by evidence, fairness, and due process.”

He said he recognizes the seriousness of domestic violence allegations and victims of abuse should be heard and supported, but evidence must support the allegations and accused individuals should be treated fairly.

“This matter arose during an extremely difficult and deeply personal period in my life, following the breakdown of my marriage in the summer of 2025,” he said. “Like many families navigating separation and divorce, there have been difficult circumstances and ongoing family law proceedings.”

Scott asked for privacy for his family, saying he wants to protect his children.

“I accept public accountability, and I understand that comes with serving in public office. But public accountability does not mean that every intimate detail of a family’s separation, divorce or private circumstances should become public discussion,” he said.

Scott was elected in February 2025 and continues to sit as an independent member in the provincial parliament.

The NDP, whose candidate finished a very close second to Scott in the election, had called for Scott to resign.

Scott said Wednesday he is committed to serving his constituents in Sault Ste. Marie and will focus on moving forward.

—- With files from Allison Jones

stories.title: New Brunswick introduces legislation to crack down on copper wire theft
stories.summary: Proposed changes to the province's Salvage Dealers Licensing Act would only allow people lawfully entitled to possess and dispose of the wire to sell it.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
New Brunswick is planning to crack down on copper wire theft.

The Liberal government says it is moving to restrict the sale of copper wire to licensed salvage dealers.

Proposed changes to the province’s Salvage Dealers Licensing Act would only allow people lawfully entitled to possess and dispose of the wire to sell it.

Sellers would have to provide photo identification and there would be a 48-hour buffer on payments.

The government says telecommunications and electricity companies are reporting increased incidents of theft that can lead to phone, internet and electricity outages.

The province’s public safety minister Robert Gauvin says New Brunswickers should be able to count on their connections.

“Making it harder for people to sell stolen copper is one way we can protect the infrastructure we rely on and keep working toward more reliable cell coverage across the province,” Gauvin said in a statement.

The copper theft legislation was among six bills tabled by Premier Susan Holt’s Liberal government on Tuesday.

Another bill proposes new rules the Liberals say will address the potential misuse of non-disclosure agreements.

Provincial Justice Minister Robert McKee said in a statement that NDAs are being used more frequently and are often used to hide harmful behaviour.

The government says changes would ensure people signing NDAs understand their rights.

Another bill would allow the government to regulate online casinos. A news release says the idea was proposed by the Atlantic Lottery Corporation.

Finance Minister René Legacy says the proposed updates to the Gaming Control Act would allow the province to keep up with how gaming is changing.

“These updates will ensure that new gaming options are developed responsibly and continue to meet the needs of players in a safe and regulated way,” he said in a statement.
