stories.title: Cleveland-Cliffs boss criticizes Joly for saying companies interested in buying Stelco
stories.summary: Industry Minister maintains steelmaker could be forced to divest Stelco because of alleged violations of job commitments
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
Laid-off Ontario steel workers at Stelco Inc. could be back on the job by Christmas, depending on sufficient domestic procurements of steel, Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. chief executive Lourenco Goncalves says.

In an e-mail to The Globe and Mail on Wednesday, he said that increased demand could result in Cliffs recalling 175 people who have lost their jobs.

“It will depend on Canadian customers buying Canadian steel, made by Stelco,” the U.S. company’s CEO said. “If our plan works, my intention is to call back all the 175 workers before Christmas.”

Stelco late last month said it was cutting up to 500 jobs in Canada. But Mr. Goncalves on Wednesday said 175 is the maximum number that will be affected.

It is unclear how Stelco can generate sufficient demand for its domestic steel by Christmas to justify bringing back its workers.

Mr. Goncalves over the past few weeks has said Stelco is unable to make money in its Canadian galvanized-steel business. He has contended that the Canadian market is overrun by cheap imports from overseas.

He has also turned down an offer of financial aid from Ottawa, saying that new capital investment won’t solve the problem of an unprofitable business.

When Cliffs acquired the Canadian steelmaker in 2024, it promised to maintain employment at about the same level for a period of five years.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has said multiple times that Ohio-based Cliffs could be forced to divest Stelco because of alleged violations of its Investment Canada Act commitments, including those concerning employment levels.

Last Thursday, she said she knew of potential buyers interested in acquiring Stelco, a statement that has raised the ire of Mr. Goncalves.

On Wednesday, he dismissed the notion of her conducting a public auction of the company.

“Stelco is not for sale,” he wrote in his e-mail.

“I do not believe that what Minister Joly is doing – when she openly solicits buyers for a company the government does not own – is a good course of action.”

Speaking to reporters in Ottawa on Wednesday morning, Ms. Joly added more fuel to the fire. When asked who was interested in buying Stelco, she declined to name names, citing confidentiality provisions, but said that “publicly traded companies” could be in the mix.

Mr. Goncalves, however, expressed doubt about the existence of buyers for Stelco, and added that even if there are suitors, talks won’t be taking place at this time.

“I will not talk to any buyers, real or imaginary, now or within the next calendar year,” he said.

He added that after Stelco delivers on a year of higher production, and after all of the laid-off workers have been brought back, “I will be glad to sell the company, and only if I decide to do so.”

The fracas between Cliffs and Ottawa has been dragging on for a month. After the layoffs were announced Sept. 28 at plants in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont., Prime Minister Mark Carney said Cliffs had “betrayed” its work force. Ms. Joly has repeatedly demanded that it comply with its promises or face court action, which could result in financial penalties or a sale of Stelco.

Cliffs is adamant that it is complying with its undertakings – the legally binding promises it made to Ottawa in 2024. In a release on Monday, the U.S. steelmaker said it expects to report to Ottawa that Stelco’s annual employment numbers for both its unionized and non-unionized work force will be well above the minimum levels required.

Mr. Goncalves has repeatedly characterized the layoffs at Stelco as “temporary.” He has vowed to recall workers if Ottawa can reach a new deal with the U.S. that would either eliminate or significantly reduce the 50-per-cent tariffs imposed by Washington. He has blamed the closing of Stelco’s galvanized-steel business on those tariffs, which he maintains have made it impossible for the company to compete in the U.S.

Mr. Goncalves also has said that workers will be recalled in Canada if Ottawa does more to stop cheap galvanized-steel imports coming into the country. The federal government last year already erected significant trade barriers against countries suspected of dumping steel into Canada. (Dumping is selling a product below the market price to gain a competitive advantage.)

In an interview, Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, said that Ottawa is unlikely to bend to his demands because it could set a dangerous precedent.

“The government, they’re not going to cave,” he said. “It’s really almost like terrorism because [Cliffs] is holding laid-off people ransom, basically, to get their way.”

stories.title: Canada not yet in position to reach trade deal with U.S.: Carney
stories.summary: Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada is not yet in a position to reach a trade deal with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration, even with the congressional midterms just days away.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada is not yet in a position to reach a trade deal with U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration, even with the congressional midterms just days away.

On his way into the weekly Liberal national caucus meeting on Parliament Hill today, Carney said Ottawa is prepared to make a deal only when it suits Canadians’ interests.

stories.title: Regis Korchinski-Paquet’s brother says police had time to see she wasn’t dangerous
stories.summary: Reece Korchinski previously testified the five police officers called to the family's home \ treated his sister like a suspect and took an "aggressive" tone toward her.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Regis Korchinski-Paquet’s brother told a coroner’s inquest into her death Wednesday that the police officers who responded to reports of a fight involving knives had time to see that neither she nor her family members were a threat once they arrived at the scene.

Reece Korchinski previously testified that the five police officers called to the family’s west-end Toronto home in the late afternoon of May 27, 2020, treated his sister like a suspect and took an “aggressive” tone toward her.

Korchinski said today that while he understood that police had received information about a fight and knives and some injuries, the officers had the opportunity to assess the situation directly and see that neither he, his sister or their mother posed a risk.

Under questioning from a lawyer representing the police union, he said the officers would have seen that the dispute was over by the time they arrived and should have let his sister go into the apartment alone instead of going in with her.

Korchinski-Paquet fell to her death from the apartment’s 24th-floor balcony while police were in the unit.

The inquest has heard that she had a history of seizures from epilepsy, often followed by confusion and aggressive behaviour, and had experienced two seizures that day.

Korchinski-Paquet, her brother and their mother all called 911 to report a fight that day, and each mentioned her diagnosis and seizures on the calls.

Korchinski-Paquet’s mother, Claudette Beals, testified that she called 911 hoping that police would take her daughter to Toronto’s Centre for Addiction and Mental Health.

On Tuesday, Beals said she now feels police should not be involved in incidents involving people experiencing a crisis.

stories.title: 44 arrested, 187 charges laid in Toronto gun and drug probe
stories.summary: The investigation, dubbed “Project Matrix,” began on March 1 in a bid to stop illegal firearms, drug trafficking and other criminal activity within the city’s east end.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Forty-four people are facing 187 charges in connection with a drug and firearms investigation, Toronto police say.

The investigation, dubbed “Project Matrix,” began on March 1 in a bid to stop illegal firearms, drug trafficking and other criminal activity within the city’s east end.

Police said the most frequent charges involved probation breaches, unsafe firearm handling or storage, possession of a Schedule I substance for the purpose of trafficking and possession of property obtained by crime over $5,000.

Investigators also seized eight illegal firearms, 792 rounds of ammunition and a significant quantity of drugs including cocaine, methamphetamine, fentanyl, Mdma, cannabis, psilocybin, and LSD.

“Public safety is our priority, and that means taking decisive action against the criminal activity that impacts our communities,” said 55 Division Det.-Sgt. Andy Johnstone in a news release.

“This initiative will continue, with investigators focused on identifying, disrupting, and holding accountable those involved in illegal firearms and drug trafficking. We will remain relentless in these efforts.”

stories.title: Canada not near trade deal with U.S. before midterms, Carney says
stories.summary: The tariffs have also been a sticking point for the U.S. heading into the midterms, with some Republican candidates who previously applauded them changing their stance.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says the government is “not at that position right now” in terms of reaching a trade deal with the U.S. before the midterm elections next week.

Asked by reporters Wednesday why he was willing to entertain a deal before the midterms — and whether Canada was being set up to be the “fall guys” by the U.S. administration if it loses — Carney said they’re after the right deal.

“We’re prepared to have a good deal for Canadians, the right deal for Canadians,” Carney said ahead of a Liberal caucus meeting.

“We think there’s deals that are in the best interest of Canada, first and foremost, but also are in the interest of the United States. That’s always been the case. We’ve been consistent. If those deals present themselves, we will pursue them, but we’re not at that position right now.”

Carney’s comments come days after Global News reported the once-stalled talks between the two countries were “moving quickly” at the political level, multiple sources with direct knowledge of the negotiations said.

Talks broke down in August, when Canada walked away from negotiations. Carney said after the talks collapsed that the U.S. had made a last-minute push for language that would limit Canada’s ability to enter trade deals with other countries, water down French language requirements, and hurt the country’s struggling auto industry.

U.S. President Donald Trump responded by putting his previously threatened 50 per cent tariffs on a number of Canadian products into effect, and Ottawa responded with dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs.

The most recent discussions have remained at the political level, meaning Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc has been leading the Canadian side, the sources said. Formal negotiations between trade representatives have not taken place yet, according to Canada’s lead negotiator Janice Charette.

Sources told Global News that the Canadian side views this as a window to reach a deal with Trump’s administration ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which polls show could lead to a party shift in at least one half of Congress.

But though talks appear to have restarted, sources still expressed skepticism a deal could get done before Nov. 3, when the midterms are held.

Global News granted the sources anonymity to speak openly about the politically sensitive negotiations.

Meanwhile Reuters, citing four Canadian and two U.S. sources, said the two countries are working on a deal to ease Trump’s tariffs on Canadian steel and autos ahead of those elections.

Whether a deal could be reached is also tentative as there have been deals made in the past by Trump that were only blown up days or weeks later.

The tariffs have also been a sticking point for the U.S. heading into the midterms, with some Republican candidates who previously applauded Trump’s duties against Canada doing an about-face. The Republican candidate in Michigan, Mike Rogers, released an ad early this month asking Trump to end the trade war with Canada which has impacted border states like his.

— with files from Global News’ Mackenzie Gray and Alex Boutillier

stories.title: BoC warns of ‘subdued’ outlook for housing market as rate hike raises borrowing costs
stories.summary: The Bank of Canada's rate hike Wednesday is set to translate to higher borrowing costs for homebuyers, adding further pressure as the real estate sector also copes with rising prices for construction materials.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
The Bank of Canada’s rate hike Wednesday is set to translate to higher borrowing costs for homebuyers, adding further pressure as the real estate sector also copes with rising prices for construction materials.

The central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-point to 2.5 per cent, the first increase in more than three years, as it warned that inflation driven by the war in the Middle East is likely to spread.

“There’s a number of things weighing on housing right now,” the bank’s senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers told reporters, as she described a “subdued” outlook for the sector.

“Certainly, borrowing rates are currently weighing a bit on the housing market. An increase will add to that a bit on the margin, so I think the outlook we’ve got for housing in the forecast here takes all of that into account.”

The big question is whether the central bank’s move is a one-time adjustment or the start of a sustained tightening cycle, said Phil Soper, president and CEO of real estate firm Royal LePage.

He said the sector’s “prolonged weakness is already weighing on economic growth, and higher borrowing costs will only deepen that challenge.”

Shawn Zigelstein, a broker for Royal LePage Signature Realty, said he believes the rate hike won’t have a major effect on consumer confidence just yet.

“It’s not like we are in a market like we were back in 2022 where the prices are increasing substantially on a regular basis,” he said in an interview.

“A quarter-point adjustment really shouldn’t make too much of a difference on someone’s mortgage payments at this point.”

The central bank’s key policy rate had held steady for nearly a year following a series of cuts. Inflation ticked up to 3.1 per cent in September due to high gas prices, and the bank said an increase to the rate is necessary to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices spill over to other goods and services.

Zigelstein said clients he speaks with are more concerned about other day-to-day costs and whether the overall inflation environment makes it the right time to buy a home.

“They have been worried about other factors, including tariffs and such. Are they going to have the jobs that they had? Are their investments going to do what they’ve been doing? So they’ve got bigger concerns than worrying about interest rates,” he said.

“Now, of course, if the rates start to change a little bit, then we will start to see potentially a little bit of a pullback on what people are spending because borrowing costs will be higher.”

While Canada “is not facing a broad mortgage crisis,” there are signs of financial pressure concentrated in specific regions such as the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area and southwestern Ontario, said Aled ab Iorwerth, deputy chief economist for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp., earlier this week.

He said trade tensions are weighing on key manufacturing sectors such as the automotive industry in those areas, leading to labour-market uncertainty and softer housing market conditions.

Cmhc said Ontario’s mortgage arrears rate reached 0.32 per cent in the second quarter, which is still below historical peaks but expected to continue rising through mid-2027. British Columbia and Atlantic Canada are expected to see a more moderate rise in mortgage arrears over the same period.

“The mortgage system is adjusting, but these early warning signs, particularly in parts of Ontario, need to be monitored closely,” ab Iorwerth said in a news release.

Don Kottick, president of Re/Max Canada, said that while an interest-rate increase “May give some buyers pause,” more balanced market conditions in many regions are creating opportunities for buyers, including greater choice and room to negotiate.

In September, the national average sale price fell 1.6 per cent year-over-year to $666,538, according to the Canadian Real Estate Association. National home sales were down 7.7 per cent from the same month last year, as the association cited higher fixed mortgage rates and the Bank of Canada’s “notably more hawkish tone.”

Fixed rates are largely unaffected by the Bank of Canada’s decision, having already moved higher in recent months in line with the bond market. But further movement in the bond market into 2027 could prompt mortgage costs to jump, which “would have a dampening impact on home purchases,” said Michael Waters, CEO of Minto Group, a real estate developer.

“Higher rates, everything else held equal, will reduce levels of purchaser activity for anything durable of size — cars and houses, certainly,” Waters said in an interview.

“The housing sector is very slow right now and so that obviously would be a concern for anyone in that sector.”

Meanwhile, the central bank said Wednesday that higher energy and import costs are expected to raise the costs of housing construction and maintenance through higher prices for materials and equipment.

Any increase to the cost of credit will also have an effect on the ability to build new projects, particularly new housing and supporting infrastructure, said Nicole Emmett, vice-president of communications, marketing and member services for the Canadian Construction Association.

“A home isn’t a home without the roads, sewers and watermains that support it, and higher borrowing costs put pressure on the margins of the contractors building them, which are already stretched by global supply chain disruptions and material costs,” she said in a statement.

“Many contractors also rely on financing for equipment, materials and day-to-day operations.”

Waters said higher interest — construction loans are based on a floating rate — along with rising input costs “will squeeze margins” and potentially lead to fewer large-scale project completions in the coming years.

“Certainly projects are far more challenged today than they would have been six months ago, pre-Iran war,” he said.

“The impact would be fewer projects meeting economic feasibility tests and more projects probably sitting idle until market conditions improve, so that could have a negative impact on the creation of new housing supply.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

stories.title: CTV London takes part in modernized version of glamour shots
stories.summary: M4LL Ph0t0, a mobile portrait booth, is going viral for recreating the nostalgic, unintentionally funny 90’s style glamour shots’.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
M4LL Ph0t0, a mobile portrait booth, is going viral for recreating the nostalgic, unintentionally funny 90’s style glamour shots’. , a mobile portrait booth, is going viral for recreating the nostalgic, unintentionally funny 90’s style glamour shots’.

“We’ve both been in photography for quite some time,” said co-founder Aaron DiGruccio. “This idea came to Leanna’s mind in a fit of boredom.”

Co-founder Leanna DiGruccio said she used to work at Sears and loved the style of department store portraits.

“It’s an entire experience,” she said. “They will be like hey can you do this and we’re like ya we can totally do that.”

The DiGruccio’s said their creations are light-hearted, fun, and designed entirely without the use of A.I. (artificial intelligence).

“We have lost jobs or lost opportunities due to A.I. and there’s this huge push online right now to feed your personal images to an A.I. company or chatbot and it churns out some representation of what you look like in the 80’s,” said DiGruccio. “When you do that, it isn’t actually you, this is an image that’s a combination of everything software has ever been fed.”

Glamour shots were popular during the 1980s and 1990s, offering an old Hollywood style including professional hairstyling and a full makeover.

stories.title: Ontario environment minister hopes to burn more garbage, build more landfills
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario's environment minister says he hopes to burn more garbage for energy and build more landfills following U.S. President Donald Trump's tariff on Canadian trash.
stories.author: Liam Casey The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Ontario’s environment minister hopes to burn more garbage for energy and build more landfills as the province runs out of space to dump its trash, framing it as a way to fight U.S. President Donald Trump’s recent tariff on Canadian waste.

Ontario’s landfills will be full within 10 years and the province needs to act quickly, Environment Minister Todd McCarthy said.

On Tuesday, the government tabled an omnibus bill, Building Ontario Faster Act, that seeks to speed up the permitting and approval regime across all ministries, including for new landfill sites or incinerators.

“We want to have proponents come forward if they have proposals for either a landfill or an energy-from-waste site and then we have ... municipalities that would be willing, able and supportive of being a host community,” McCarthy said Wednesday.

He said communities can say no to a landfill or garbage incinerator.

“Municipalities will hold the pen on whether or not they want a landfill site, but there are benefits, obviously, economic benefits, to having a landfill site, an expansion to a landfill, or energy from waste site in a community,” he said.

At a news conference the day before, however, McCarthy left the door open to imposing landfills on communities if none volunteer to be hosts.

Details in the bill that still has to pass show the province will repeal a section of the Environmental Assessment Act that requires municipal support for landfill sites.

Last year, the province made moves to force the reopening of a landfill site a community in southwestern Ontario did not want.

In 2025, Ontario passed Bill 5, a controversial omnibus bill that sought to speed up approvals for large projects, particularly mines. But that bill also contained a section that exempted the former landfill in Dresden, Ont., from a full environmental assessment as the province looked to reopen it despite opposition from the municipality.

Trump signed an executive order last week that lifted some tariffs on Canadian goods, but added a 50 per cent tariff on Canadian trash, with the measures set to go into force in a few days.

McCarthy said that decision could mean Ontario’s landfills will be full within five years if the tariff stays, but he did not say how many landfills or incinerators the province needs.

A 2024 report from the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy said Canada shipped more than three million tonnes of garbage to the state in 2024.

“Energy from waste is something we can and should embrace,” McCarthy said. “Europe, Great Britain have embraced it because they don’t have landfill capacity. We do, but we do need to improve our landfill capacity because in 10 years we won’t have it. We haven’t built a new landfill site in Ontario for 20 years.”

He said the incinerators produce clean energy, which Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner took issue with.

“I think the minister needs to go talk to the scientists who show, one, that incineration leads to toxic air emissions, and two, the ash from incinerations is quite toxic as well and still has to go to landfill.”

McCarthy pointed to two waste-to-energy incinerators in the province as success stories: Emerald Energy from Waste in Brampton, Ont., and the Durham-York Energy Centre in Clarington, Ont., in the minister’s riding of Durham.

Schreiner said one major stumbling block to building landfills and incinerators is that many residents oppose them in their neighbourhoods.

“People do not want toxic air pollution in their backyard,” he said. “They instead want a government that’s not going to dismantle our blue box program and are actually going to look at ways in which we can reduce the amount of garbage actually going into landfill instead of accelerating and increasing the amount going into landfills.”

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said the government needs to sell the idea to Ontarians.

“You can’t just keep invoking tariffs and Donald Trump as an excuse to do everything or anything that you want to do without any explanation, and that’s exactly what’s happening here,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

“We want to have proponents come forward if they have proposals for either a landfill or an energy-from-waste site and then we have ... municipalities that would be willing, able and supportive of being a host community,” McCarthy said Wednesday.
He said communities can say no to a landfill or garbage incinerator.

“Municipalities will hold the pen on whether or not they want a landfill site, but there are benefits, obviously, economic benefits, to having a landfill site, an expansion to a landfill, or energy from waste site in a community,” he said.
At a news conference the day before, however, McCarthy left the door open to imposing landfills on communities if none volunteer to be hosts.
Details in the bill that still has to pass show the province will repeal a section of the Environmental Assessment Act that requires municipal support for landfill sites.
Last year, the province made moves to force the reopening of a landfill site a community in southwestern Ontario did not want.

In 2025, Ontario passed Bill 5, a controversial omnibus bill that sought to speed up approvals for large projects, particularly mines. But that bill also contained a section that exempted the former landfill in Dresden, Ont., from a full environmental assessment as the province looked to reopen it despite opposition from the municipality.
Trump signed an executive order last week that lifted some tariffs on Canadian goods, but added a 50 per cent tariff on Canadian trash, with the measures set to go into force in a few days.
McCarthy said that decision could mean Ontario’s landfills will be full within five years if the tariff stays, but he did not say how many landfills or incinerators the province needs.
A 2024 report from the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy said Canada shipped more than three million tonnes of garbage to the state in 2024.

“Energy from waste is something we can and should embrace,” McCarthy said. “Europe, Great Britain have embraced it because they don’t have landfill capacity. We do, but we do need to improve our landfill capacity because in 10 years we won’t have it. We haven’t built a new landfill site in Ontario for 20 years.”
He said the incinerators produce clean energy, which Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner took issue with.

“I think the minister needs to go talk to the scientists who show, one, that incineration leads to toxic air emissions, and two, the ash from incinerations is quite toxic as well and still has to go to landfill.”

McCarthy pointed to two waste-to-energy incinerators in the province as success stories: Emerald Energy from Waste in Brampton, Ont., and the Durham-York Energy Centre in Clarington, Ont., in the minister’s riding of Durham.
Schreiner said one major stumbling block to building landfills and incinerators is that many residents oppose them in their neighbourhoods.

“People do not want toxic air pollution in their backyard,” he said. “They instead want a government that’s not going to dismantle our blue box program and are actually going to look at ways in which we can reduce the amount of garbage actually going into landfill instead of accelerating and increasing the amount going into landfills.”
Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said the government needs to sell the idea to Ontarians.
“You can’t just keep invoking tariffs and Donald Trump as an excuse to do everything or anything that you want to do without any explanation, and that’s exactly what’s happening here,” he said.

stories.title: Privacy commissioner investigating provider behind Crime Stoppers data breach
stories.summary: Canada’s privacy commissioner has launched an investigation into a cybersecurity breach involving anonymous tips shared with Crime Stoppers programs across the country.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Canada’s privacy commissioner has launched an investigation into a cybersecurity breach involving anonymous tips shared with Crime Stoppers programs across the country.

The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (OPC) said Wednesday that Commissioner Philippe Dufresne initiated the investigation into Navigate360, the commercial provider that manages the P3 tip platform used by Crime Stoppers.

The probe will examine security safeguards Navigate360 had in place at the time of the breach to determine the organization’s compliance with Canada’s federal private-sector privacy law, the OPC said.

The U.S.-based company said in a statement Friday it first became aware of a breach on March 18. It has now learned a third party accessed one of its systems, obtaining copies of some data between Nov. 21, 2025, and March 5, 2026.

Navigate360 acknowledged names, addresses, dates of birth, social security numbers and other sensitive information May have been affected, though it said the information involved varies by person.

The company, which also provides software to some schools in the U.S., said phone numbers and email addresses were also exposed.

However, it said it has found no evidence the personal information exposed has been used for fraud or identity theft.

The OPC has contacted Crime Stoppers and Navigate360, it said.

“The Opc’s engagement with both organizations is focused on ensuring that the necessary steps are being taken to address the breach and protect Canadians’ personal information,” the OPC said in a statement.

“This includes breach containment and measures to reduce risks to those affected, as well as actions to prevent future breaches.”

The OPC added it would not provide further details while the investigation is active.

Several Canadian police forces have suspended their use of Crime Stoppers as concerns grow over the breach.

Sean Sportun, chair of Toronto Crime Stoppers, said last week 176,859 tips submitted to the P3 software between January 2022 and November 2025 were affected, including 12,392 that May contain personal information. Navigate360 later supplied a separate list containing 14,973 names.

However, Sportun said the list “lacks detail necessary to measure the risk involved” because it did not identify who the names belonged to.

“We never ask for your name, and we don’t want it. But people sometimes include details to explain what they saw,” Sportun said.

“Before a tip goes to investigators, our practice is to remove those details. It has come to light that some of those original tips containing potentially identifying information were stolen from P3.”

Toronto Crime Stoppers continues to press Navigate360 for details, he added.

The company said in its statement it remains dedicated to ensuring the privacy and security of the information under its control.

“Upon discovery of this incident, Navigate360 immediately instituted mitigation measures. Navigate360 promptly implemented additional and enhanced safeguards and enlisted the support of a leading cybersecurity firm to enhance the security of our network, systems, and data,” it said.

“Navigate360 also launched a comprehensive investigation, identified individuals who May have been affected, reported the incident to law enforcement, and notified regulatory bodies.”

Sean Sparling, a former deputy chief of the Sault Ste. Marie Police Service, previously told Global News officers across Canada use Crime Stoppers “on a daily basis.”

He said he relied on Crime Stoppers for many of his own investigations.

“Knowing Crime Stoppers and how well it’s organized, how well it works and its importance to the law enforcement community and the safety of our communities, I fully expect they’re going to recover from this,” Sparling said.

Police services that have suspended their use of Crime Stoppers said members of the public can submit information through regular police-reporting channels, although those methods are not anonymous.

Anyone facing an immediate emergency should call 911.

“Until we have a safer way to protect you, please do not send us tips by phone, online or through the app,” Sportun said.

“Pausing our program means that option isn’t available now, and we did not make this decision lightly. We are pausing because those people deserve a system we can fully stand behind.”

stories.title: Quebec government says it plans to end the time change
stories.summary: Paul St-Pierre Plamondon wrote on social media on Wednesday that Quebecers will most likely set their clocks back one hour for the final time this weekend.
stories.author: Mathieu Paquette
stories.content:
Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says his government intends to abolish the time change.

He says the province hasn’t yet decided whether to keep daylight time or standard time year-round.

St-Pierre Plamondon wrote on social media on Wednesday that Quebecers will most likely set their clocks back one hour for the final time this weekend.

He said studies have found the time change is counterproductive to health and is hard for children to adjust to.

St-Pierre Plamondon said he plans to consult with experts during a series of hearings in the coming months before making a final decision on whether to stay on permanent summer or winter time. He said there will be a short parliamentary commission on the topic.

“Dear parents who have to spend several weeks managing your children’s reaction to this time change, this is likely the last year we’ll be imposing such unnecessary constraints on ourselves. We invite the public to follow our work closely,” he wrote on social media.

The previous Coalition Avenir Québec held an online consultation in 2024 that found 91 per cent of the approximately 214,000 respondents said they wanted to end the time change, and 72 per cent wanted to keep daylight time year-round.

But then-justice minister Simon Jolin-Barrette noted that the consultation had highlighted several issues, including expert opinions and alignment with neighbouring jurisdictions.

He said in 2025 that further deliberation and consultation were necessary.

By keeping daylight time year-round, Quebecers would enjoy a later sunset during the winter. But this would mean the sun would rise an hour later during the short winter days, which could have negative consequences, according to several experts.

The analysis published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal a few weeks ago examined multiple studies and concluded that health evidence favours moving to permanent standard time — not daylight time — in part because it better aligns with the body’s rhythm.

If Quebec were to move forward with abolishing the time change, it would follow in the footsteps of several Canadian provinces. Those include British Columbia, Alberta, and Manitoba, which ended the practice this year.

These three provinces have chosen to keep daylight time year-round, as has the Northwest Territories.

In Ontario, certain regions in the northwestern part of the province will also maintain daylight time year-round to align with Manitoba.

In 2020, Ontario passed a law to make daylight time permanent, but it has not yet taken effect. The province noted that coordination with its neighbours, such as Quebec and New York, was essential.

Saskatchewan has not changed its time since 1966, while the Yukon ended the practice in 2020.

The analysis published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal a few weeks ago examined multiple studies and concluded that health evidence favours moving to permanent standard time — not daylight time — in part because it better aligns with the body’s rhythm.

If Quebec were to move forward with abolishing the time change, it would follow in the footsteps of several Canadian provinces. Those include British Columbia, Alberta, and Manitoba, which ended the practice this year.
These three provinces have chosen to keep daylight time year-round, as has the Northwest Territories.
In Ontario, certain regions in the northwestern part of the province will also maintain daylight time year-round to align with Manitoba.
In 2020, Ontario passed a law to make daylight time permanent, but it has not yet taken effect. The province noted that coordination with its neighbours, such as Quebec and New York, was essential.
Saskatchewan has not changed its time since 1966, while the Yukon ended the practice in 2020.

stories.title: Trump cheers Canadian provincial election wins, but analysts say they’re no rebuke of Carney
stories.summary: Toronto (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump drew criticism Wednesday for celebrating election victories by a Quebec separatist and a British Columbia Conservative, days after his administration accused Canadian politicians of interfering in U.S. elections.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Rob Gillies, The Associated Press,

Posted October 28, 2026 10:35 am.

Last Updated October 28, 2026 11:24 am.

Toronto (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump drew criticism Wednesday for celebrating election victories by a Quebec separatist and a British Columbia Conservative, days after his administration accused Canadian politicians of interfering in U.S. elections.

With U.S. midterm elections approaching, Trump shared an article portraying the Quebec victory as a setback for Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and hailed the Conservative win in British Columbia as evidence of the party’s growing strength.

But neither election was a referendum on Carney, whose federal Liberal Party is separate from British Columbia’s provincial Conservatives. Analysts say both results reflected provincial politics, not declining support for the prime minister.

“Congratulations to Paul St-Pierre Plamondon on his WIN!” Trump wrote Tuesday on Truth Social, more than three weeks after the Quebec separatist leader’s Oct. 5 election victory. Trump linked to an article headlined “Separatists win Quebec provincial election in blow to Mark Carney.”

Trump also congratulated British Columbia’s premier-designate, Lorne Doerkson, ON his “Big Victory,” adding: “Conservatives are moving strong in Canada!” The post came one minute before his congratulations to Quebec’s separatist leader.

The posts come amid Trump’s trade war and repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state. St-Pierre Plamondon has criticized Trump’s tariffs and ruled out holding a Quebec independence referendum while Trump remains president.

Trump’s trade war with Canada has become an issue in the Nov. 3 midterm elections , particularly in Michigan and Maine, where Republican candidates have faced pressure over tariffs hurting local businesses. Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers has called for an end to the tariff war.

“It is highly unusual for a U.S. President to comment on Canadian provincial politics or to congratulate provincial election winners,” said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal.

Béland said neither result should be interpreted as a rejection of Carney, whose popularity has been bolstered by his response to Trump.

Nelson Wiseman, a University of Toronto political scientist, said Trump misunderstands Canada’s Conservatives, noting that Doerkson has criticized Trump’s tariffs and called him a bully.

Doerkson spoke with Carney on Tuesday, with both leaders emphasizing cooperation on economic growth and investment.

“Carney’s popularity is at a stratospheric level,” Wiseman said. “The more Trump attacks Canada and Carney, the more popular Carney becomes.”

The embassy also cited 11 Canadians charged with illegally voting in U.S. elections between 2012 and 2026, without linking the cases to the Canadian government.

Carney rejected the allegations , saying they had “no merit,” and expressed disappointment with U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra.

Béland warned that the accusations could foreshadow a “Blame Canada” narrative if Republicans suffer losses in the midterms.

“It is absurd for President Trump to comment on Canadian provincial politics while the U.S. embassy in Canada is falsely claiming that country is interfering in the U.S. midterms,” Béland said.

Rob Gillies, The Associated Press

stories.title: At least two Canadians hurt in high-speed rail crash in Spain, Carney says
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says at least two Canadians were injured in a high-speed rail crash in Spain.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Six Canadians are among the injured and a seventh remained unaccounted following a high-speed rail crash in central Spain Wednesday morning.

The deadly accident occurred just before 9 a.m. local time, when one train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks. Spanish officials reported at least 68 people killed, and another 58 were receiving treatment at local hospitals.

Global Affairs Canada spokesperson Thida Ith said Wednesday the department had confirmation six Canadians injured in the crash, and one more was still unaccounted for by Wednesday evening. Ith said Canadian officials are providing consular assistance and are in contact with local authorities to gather more information.

“Our thoughts are with their families and loved ones as well as all of those affected,” said Ith.

Earlier in the day, Prime Minister Mark Carney expressed Canada’s solidarity with victims and family members and indicated Ottawa would help as needed. Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said on social media he had reached out to his Spanish counterpart.

“I also thank the emergency responders and medical teams working around the clock to help those impacted by this tragedy,” McKinnon said.

A truck crane lifts a damaged train bogie from the wreckage of a train crash between two high-speed units around 150 km south of Madrid, Oct. 28, 2026.

Spain’s rail system operator Adif said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo. It involved two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain.

A train operated by the state-owned Renfe company struck the rear of another train operated by private company Iryo that was stopped. The collision derailed two carriages on the tail of the Iryo train and the front of the Renfe train.

Authorities said 397 passengers were in the Renfe train and 147 passengers in the Iryo train.

Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

Spain’s Transport Minister Oscar Puente said the crash was caused by what he called an “inexplicable” order from a central command centre for Spain’s trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.

Puente said at 8:30 a.m., local time, the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometres stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the Renfe train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped Iryo train at 8:53 a.m.

Puente said the train never should have been told to start moving again, since there was still a “stop signal” active on that line, and that it should at least have been told to go at a reduced speed.

Authorities were still trying to determine Wednesday how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph for that stretch of the track, Puente said.

The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yebenes, left carriages shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.

Until this year, there had been no fatal crash on Spain’s dedicated high-speed lines since the network opened in 1992. Now there have been two in just 10 months.

In January, 46 people died in southern Spain when an Iryo train jumped the track and hit an oncoming Renfe train.

“Today all of Spain is grieving,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of national mourning.

Sánchez called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in a high-speed rail system that was once a source of national pride.

“It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year,” said Sánchez, who faces a national election on Nov. 29.

With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Western chemist Elizabeth Gillies wins prestigious national research award
stories.summary: Western University chemist Elizabeth Gillies has won the 2026 Nserc John C. Polanyi Award for her pioneering work in polymer science.
stories.author: Jeff Renaud
stories.content:
Western University chemist Elizabeth Gillies has won a prestigious national research award for pioneering a new approach to polymer science, developing alternatives to traditional plastics that can remain stable until they intentionally and rapidly break down.

Gillies, Canada Research Chair in Polymeric Biomaterials, is the recipient of the 2026 NSERC John C. Polanyi Award. Created in 2006, the award recognizes an individual or team whose research conducted in Canada has led to a recent outstanding advance in the natural sciences or engineering. Gillies’ achievement marks the first time a Western researcher has received the honour.

“This award recognizes research that fundamentally changes how we understand the world,” said Penny Pexman, Western’s vice-president (research). “Elizabeth Gillies exemplifies that spirit of discovery through pioneering work in polymer science that combines scientific creativity and practical potential.”

Gillies has spent most of the past decade developing self-immolative polymers, a class of materials designed to dismantle themselves when exposed to a specific trigger, such as light, heat or a change in chemical conditions.

Elizabeth Gillies

Polymers are a broad class of materials that include the plastics we use every day. Many are designed to be durable and long-lasting – a most useful property that can also make them difficult to break down after use.

Self-immolative polymers, or SIPs, are designed to stay intact until a protective end cap is chemically removed. The reaction then travels along the chain, converting the polymer into small molecules that can be more readily broken down or recovered, rather than leaving behind long-lasting plastic waste.

“It’s basically an end-to-end mechanism that travels down the polymer backbone and converts it completely to small molecules,” said Gillies, a professor in Western’s departments of chemistry and chemical and biochemical engineering. “The advantage is you can have a material, like a plastic, that retains its properties until you want it to break down at the end of its useful life.”

The potential applications range from drug delivery, where nanoparticles or gels made from these materials could help control when and where a treatment is released, to fertilizer coatings that help nutrients reach plants more efficiently. By improving nutrient use and reducing waste, the technology could support healthier crop growth and strengthen food security.

Gillies and her collaborators have developed several polymer structures and explored their properties, including polyglyoxylates, a class of materials that can be made from commercially available starting materials.

“There are still significant challenges to overcome. In consumer products, one of the biggest is cost. Industry has developed very efficient, inexpensive ways to make conventional plastics, so we need to find applications where our materials can offer a practical advantage,” said Gillies. “In biomedical research, it’s a long process to take an innovation from proof of concept to the clinic. We’re working with academic and industry collaborators to better understand where these polymers could make a difference.”

For Gillies, the Polanyi Award also recognizes the contributions of the students and postdoctoral researchers who have advanced the work in her laboratory.

“The ideas and progress recognized with this award can also be attributed to some of my top students and postdoctoral fellows,” said Gillies. “A big part of what we do as professors is train students to do research, help them learn how to write and communicate their work and prepare them for their future careers. Our connections with companies and research groups around the world help create opportunities for them to move on to postdoctoral fellowships and jobs.”

The national award builds on an earlier milestone in Gillies’ career. In 2006, she received the provincial John C. Polanyi Prize, which recognizes outstanding researchers in the early stages of their careers at Ontario universities.

stories.title: Quebec plans to end twice-a-year time changes
stories.summary: Premier says province hasn’t yet decided whether to keep daylight time or standard time year-round
stories.author: Mathieu Paquette
stories.content:
Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says his government intends to abolish the switch between daylight and standard time.

He says the province hasn’t yet decided whether to keep daylight time or standard time year-round, but wrote on social media on Wednesday that Quebeckers will most likely set their clocks back one hour for the final time this weekend.

He said studies have found the time change is counterproductive to health and is hard for children to adjust to.

St-Pierre Plamondon said he plans to consult with experts during a series of hearings in the coming months before making a final decision on whether to stay on permanent summer or winter time. He said there will be a short parliamentary commission on the topic.

“Dear parents who have to spend several weeks managing your children’s reaction to this time change, this is likely the last year we’ll be imposing such unnecessary constraints on ourselves. We invite the public to follow our work closely,” he wrote on social media.

The previous Coalition Avenir Québec held an online consultation in 2024 that found 91 per cent of the approximately 214,000 respondents said they wanted to end the time change, and 72 per cent wanted to keep daylight time year-round.

But then-justice minister Simon Jolin-Barrette noted that the consultation had highlighted several issues, including the opinion of sleep experts and alignment with neighbouring jurisdictions.

He said in 2025 that further deliberation and consultation were necessary.

Justice Minister Marie-Claude Sarrazin said the government would follow all the necessary steps to make the change run smoothly.

“We wanted to announce our intentions at the start of the time change,” she said. “For the rest, we’ll prepare our work plans and we’ll consult with people so that things are done in an orderly way, including with our neighbours.”

St-Pierre Plamondon’s minority government could have the support of at least one opposition party to help pass any necessary legislation. Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime said he agreed with stopping the time change, but stressed the importance of collaborating with Ontario.

“I lived in the west when Saskatchewan decided to end the time change and the neighbouring provinces didn’t, and it caused all sorts of problems,” he said Wednesday in Quebec City.

“You know that the economies of Quebec and Ontario are interconnected.”

By keeping daylight time year-round, Quebeckers would enjoy a later sunset during the winter. But this would mean the sun would rise an hour later during the short winter days, which could have negative consequences, according to several experts.

The analysis published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal a few weeks ago examined multiple studies and concluded that health evidence favours moving to permanent standard time – not daylight time – in part because it better aligns with the body’s rhythm.

If Quebec were to move forward with abolishing the time change, it would follow in the footsteps of several Canadian provinces. Those include British Columbia, Alberta, and Manitoba, which ended the practice this year.

These three provinces have chosen to keep daylight time year-round, as has the Northwest Territories.

In Ontario, certain regions in the northwestern part of the province will also maintain daylight time year-round to align with Manitoba.

In 2020, Ontario passed a law to make daylight time permanent, but it has not yet taken effect. The province noted that co-ordination with its neighbours, such as Quebec and New York, was essential.

Saskatchewan has not changed its time since 1966, while the Yukon ended the practice in 2020.

stories.title: The Quebec government says it plans to end the time change
stories.summary: Montreal — Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says his government intends to abolish the time change.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Montreal — Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says his government intends to abolish the switch between daylight and standard time.

He says the province hasn’t yet decided whether to keep daylight time or standard time year-round, but wrote on social media on Wednesday that Quebecers will most likely set their clocks back one hour for the final time this weekend.

He said studies have found the time change is counterproductive to health and is hard for children to adjust to.

St-Pierre Plamondon said he plans to consult with experts during a series of hearings in the coming months before making a final decision on whether to stay on permanent summer or winter time. He said there will be a short parliamentary commission on the topic.

“Dear parents who have to spend several weeks managing your children’s reaction to this time change, this is likely the last year we’ll be imposing such unnecessary constraints on ourselves. We invite the public to follow our work closely,” he wrote on social media.

The previous Coalition Avenir Québec held an online consultation in 2024 that found 91 per cent of the approximately 214,000 respondents said they wanted to end the time change, and 72 per cent wanted to keep daylight time year-round.

But then-justice minister Simon Jolin-Barrette noted that the consultation had highlighted several issues, including the opinion of sleep experts and alignment with neighbouring jurisdictions.

He said in 2025 that further deliberation and consultation were necessary.

Justice Minister Marie-Claude Sarrazin said the government would follow all the necessary steps to make the change run smoothly.

“We wanted to announce our intentions at the start of the time change,” she said. “For the rest, we’ll prepare our work plans and we’ll consult with people so that things are done in an orderly way, including with our neighbours.”

St-Pierre Plamondon’s minority government could have the support of at least one opposition party to help pass any necessary legislation. Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime said he agreed with stopping the time change, but stressed the importance of collaborating with Ontario.

“I lived in the west when Saskatchewan decided to end the time change and the neighbouring provinces didn’t, and it caused all sorts of problems,” he said Wednesday in Quebec City.

“You know that the economies of Quebec and Ontario are interconnected.”

By keeping daylight time year-round, Quebecers would enjoy a later sunset during the winter. But this would mean the sun would rise an hour later during the short winter days, which could have negative consequences, according to several experts.

The analysis published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal a few weeks ago examined multiple studies and concluded that health evidence favours moving to permanent standard time — not daylight time — in part because it better aligns with the body’s rhythm.

If Quebec were to move forward with abolishing the time change, it would follow in the footsteps of several Canadian provinces. Those include British Columbia, Alberta, and Manitoba, which ended the practice this year.

These three provinces have chosen to keep daylight time year-round, as has the Northwest Territories.

In Ontario, certain regions in the northwestern part of the province will also maintain daylight time year-round to align with Manitoba.

In 2020, Ontario passed a law to make daylight time permanent, but it has not yet taken effect. The province noted that coordination with its neighbours, such as Quebec and New York, was essential.

Saskatchewan has not changed its time since 1966, while the Yukon ended the practice in 2020.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

Mathieu Paquette, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Alberta tables bill to prevent DEI hiring in public sector
stories.summary: If passed, legislation would prohibit public bodies from using diversity, equity and inclusion policies to make hiring decisions
stories.author: Jack Farrell
stories.content:
Alberta is looking to end public sector hiring practices aimed at diversity, equity and inclusion.

A government bill tabled Tuesday, if passed, would prohibit a number of public bodies from using DEI policies to make hiring decisions.

Premier Danielle Smith said hiring needs to be based on merit and qualifications so that everyone has a fair chance at getting jobs.

“Albertans expect public institutions to hire and promote the best-qualified people and ensure that everyone has a fair opportunity to succeed based on their skills, experience and qualifications,” Smith told reporters in Edmonton.

“These changes will help to ensure that fairness is at the heart of hiring.”

The bill covers public agencies, Crown corporations, post-secondary schools, school boards and municipalities. However, government officials said provincial employees are already hired based on merit.

The officials also said the change could apply to non-profit agencies receiving government grants, but that would be determined through future regulations.

They said there would be some exceptions to the prohibition but didn’t provide examples.

The proposed legislation would further prohibit public bodies from having mandatory DEI training for staff, except when necessary for the job. Other mandatory training would be required to be “ideologically neutral” and focus on job duties and skills.

The bill, tabled by Justice Minister Mickey Amery, specifically targets the Alberta Human Rights Act.

The government said it’s changing a section of the act that allows for policies and programs aiming to uplift those who May be disadvantaged because of their race, disability, gender or gender expression, sexual orientation, religious beliefs, age or other personal circumstance, including marital status.

Officials said hiring and promotion practices would continue to be subject to other protections or provisions under the act.

Opinion: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is targeting immigration. But what do the numbers say?

Opposition NDP member Kathleen Ganley said the NDP hasn’t heard any concerns about DEI hiring practices, leaving her to think the changes are more aimed at distracting from issues that are far bigger priorities for Albertans, like affordability and health care.

“This is a solution in want of a problem,” Ganley said.

Sandra Azocar, the president of the Alberta Union of Provincial Employees, agreed with Ganley, saying public sector employers already hire the best candidates.

Azocar, whose union represents nearly 100,000 workers that are mostly in the public sector, said she believes Smith is trying to appease the “extreme factions” within her party.

“This is pure dog-whistle politics.”

It’s not the first time Smith’s United Conservative Party government has cracked down on DEI policies.

Last year, it passed legislation prohibiting professional regulatory bodies, including the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Alberta, from making members undergo training around diversity initiatives.

That legislation also limits what behaviour regulatory bodies can police their members on. The government said at the time that it was inspired by Ontario psychologist and social media personality Jordan Peterson, who was sanctioned by his province’s professional regulator for controversial public statements.

Amery’s bill also aims to make changes to other provincial laws, including added penalties for the distribution or threat of distribution of digitally altered intimate images without consent.

While the issue is mainly a federal Criminal Code matter, Alberta has laws that allow residents to take civil court action.

The bill aims to capture other types of content, including audio recordings, livestreams and images created using artificial intelligence.

The government said those who violate the law could face fines up to $10,000, imprisonment for up to two years, or both. It also said the bill would allow the courts to give community service sentences.

Ganley said the NDP supported these change but said the government’s choice to tie the bill to ending DEI hiring practices was “inappropriate.”

stories.title: 24 Sussex restoration campaign secures $5.7M as public appeal launches
stories.summary: The Rideau Hall Foundation said Wednesday that more than 4,000 contributions have been made toward its $50-million fundraising goal.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
The campaign to restore 24 Sussex Drive has secured $5.7 million, with public donations now being accepted.

The Rideau Hall Foundation said Wednesday that more than 4,000 contributions have been made toward its $50-million fundraising goal.

RHF was tasked in June with leading a fundraising campaign to help cover the costs of restoring the derelict official residence of Canada’s prime ministers.

“As the official residence of Canada’s prime minister, 24 Sussex is part of the architecture of our democracy,” said Robert Prichard, chair of the RHF board of directors, in a news release.

“Renewing it is not simply about preserving history; it is about ensuring that our national institutions reflect the confidence and ambition of the country they represent.”

The fundraising campaign is one element of the federal plan announced by Prime Minister Mark Carney to restore 24 Sussex Drive through a national design-and-build competition.

Built in 1846, the 35-room residence has been vacant since 2015, when former prime minister Justin Trudeau chose to live at Rideau Cottage because of the building’s condition.

Inspections have found dead rodents and feces in the walls and attic, along with extensive water damage and electrical problems. Carney currently lives in Rideau Cottage, as Trudeau did.

Maintaining the vacant property is estimated to cost taxpayers approximately $150,000 annually. The National Capital Commission estimated in 2022 that restoring the residence would cost approximately $37 million. That estimate is now expected to be more than $100 million.

“There are very few opportunities for Canadians to contribute personally to a project of national significance that will still matter generations from now,” said Teresa Marques, president and CEO of RHF.

“The renewal of 24 Sussex is one of them. Whether through a leadership gift or a modest contribution, every donor is helping write the next chapter in the story of 24 Sussex.”

RHF also announced the Council for 24 Sussex group Wednesday. The group is made up of philanthropic volunteers who will use their networks to encourage contributions across Canada.

RHF said the council will grow as the campaign engages more volunteer leaders across the nation.

The winning proposal of the design-and-build competition is expected to be announced by Canada Day.

stories.title: Higher tariffs on Canadian imports would be ‘catastrophic,’ Honda exec says
stories.summary: A pending increase in U.S. tariffs on steel and auto imports from Canada starting Jan. 1 would be “catastrophic” for the industry, a Honda Motor executive said on Tuesday.
stories.author: David Shepardson and Kalea Hall
stories.content:
A pending increase in U.S. tariffs on steel and auto imports from Canada starting Jan. 1 would be “catastrophic” for the industry, Honda Motor’s head of public affairs said on Tuesday.

Automakers are closely watching talks between the U.S., Mexico and Canada, hoping the countries extend a longstanding trade deal. The three countries’ auto industries are tightly intertwined, and higher tariffs could raise costs and affect where companies such as Honda build new plants.

“We need that trilateral agreement to stay in place in order for the U.S. industry to be competitive. It’s integral to our success,” said Jennifer Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs for American Honda Motor Co, speaking at the Reuters Automotive USA conference in Detroit.

The auto industry has been grappling with tariffs since early 2025, when U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration placed varying tariff rates on imports from multiple countries , including Mexico and Canada.

“I am cautiously optimistic that cooler heads will prevail, and we will avoid that Jan. 1 doubling of the tariffs, because that really would be catastrophic just for the entire industry,” Thomas said.

The U.S. and Canada are working on a deal to ease U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel and autos, Reuters reported on Monday. Those talks are aimed at tariffs imposed under Section 232 of US trade law, including a tariff of up to 50 per cent on Canadian steel and a 25 per cent tariff on autos, with negotiators discussing potential relief from those duties.

Unlike trade deals with the EU, Japan or South Korea, the trade pact between Mexico, Canada and the U.S. has specific North American content requirements known as “rules of origin.”

In the negotiations with Mexico, the U.S. has demanded that all North American-built vehicles contain 50 per cent U.S.-specific content, a figure that would drive regional required content up to 82 per cent to qualify for U.S. benefits, sources familiar with the talks have said.

Vehicles assembled in Mexico and Canada would likely still be charged some level ⁠of tariffs, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer ​has said.

Thomas and other auto executives said that rules-of-origin requirements are not in place in other trade deals.

“Right now, North America is at an unfair disadvantage,” Thomas said.

In August, Honda said it May not build an eighth assembly plant in ​North America unless the trade deal between the three countries is extended.

“We are at capacity, and so we’re exploring all options. And at the end of the day, we’re going to continue to invest in the U.S.,” Thomas said.

“We need that trilateral agreement to stay in place in order for the U.S. industry to be competitive. It’s integral to our success,” said Jennifer Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs for American Honda Motor Co, speaking at the Reuters Automotive USA conference in Detroit.

The auto industry has been grappling with tariffs since early 2025, when U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration placed varying tariff rates on imports from multiple countries , including Mexico and Canada.
content_blocks.html: The auto industry has been grappling with tariffs since early 2025, when U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration placed varying tariff rates on imports from multiple countries, including Mexico and Canada.

content_blocks.text: “I am cautiously optimistic that cooler heads will prevail, and we will avoid that Jan. 1 doubling of the tariffs, because that really would be catastrophic just for the entire industry,” Thomas said.

content_blocks.text: The U.S. and Canada are working on a deal to ease U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel and autos, Reuters reported on Monday. Those talks are aimed at tariffs imposed under Section 232 of US trade law, including a tariff of up to 50 per cent on Canadian steel and a 25 per cent tariff on autos, with negotiators discussing potential relief from those duties.
Unlike trade deals with the EU, Japan or South Korea, the trade pact between Mexico, Canada and the U.S. has specific North American content requirements known as “rules of origin.”

In the negotiations with Mexico, the U.S. has demanded that all North American-built vehicles contain 50 per cent U.S.-specific content, a figure that would drive regional required content up to 82 per cent to qualify for U.S. benefits, sources familiar with the talks have said.
Vehicles assembled in Mexico and Canada would likely still be charged some level ⁠of tariffs, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer ​has said.
Thomas and other auto executives said that rules-of-origin requirements are not in place in other trade deals.
“Right now, North America is at an unfair disadvantage,” Thomas said.
In August, Honda said it May not build an eighth assembly plant in ​North America unless the trade deal between the three countries is extended.
“We are at capacity, and so we’re exploring all options. And at the end of the day, we’re going to continue to invest in the U.S.,” Thomas said.

stories.title: Ontario pauses some skills training funding for unemployed people
stories.summary: There has been no communication from the government about the status of the program that aims to get people off social assistance and into the work force
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
In addition to freezing Ontario Student Assistance Program payments to all private postsecondary institutions, the province has paused at least some funding through Better Jobs Ontario, which helps unemployed people get skills training.

But the government won’t explicitly say so.

There has been no public communication from the government about the status of the program that aims to get people off social assistance and into the work force, but people who were depending on the program and the institutions that were set to train them are taking note.

Reece Daniel was hoping to begin an Hvac program in London, Ont., ON Oct. 19. The government had initially scheduled a meeting for Oct. 13 to give him information about the funding agreement, but a few days before that they cancelled and said applications were under review.

The next intake for the Hvac program is in May, 2027.

“This course was something that was going to get me jumped back on my feet,” Daniel said.

“I’m still probably going to be presented with the opportunity to go to school next year, but the significant delays ... waiting for so long, putting off work for so long, it’s a little bit disappointing and frustrating.”

Pathways Employment Help Centre had been assisting Daniel in his application, and is seeing other clients experiencing the same delays and uncertainty with their Better Jobs Ontario funding decisions, the CEO said.

“Despite our agency’s repeated efforts to obtain clarification, the absence of a definitive decision prevented Reece and other clients from proceeding with their planned training as scheduled,” Ben Cecil said.

Career Colleges Ontario said the association has heard from member schools that Better Jobs Ontario funding for students at career colleges has been paused, but it has not received any formal communication from the government.

“We are concerned about any disruption to funding for students attending compliant institutions,” it wrote in a statement.

“As with Osap, we are urging the government to restore access to funding for students attending institutions where there are no identified compliance concerns. We continue to advocate for a targeted approach that allows students to access the support they need while maintaining strong accountability across the sector.”

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced earlier this month that Osap payments are paused for students at all private postsecondary institutions, after preliminary audit findings raised serious concerns about financial aid usage at some career colleges.

Trillium College has suspended classes due to the Osap pause, and wrote in a letter to students that it is a temporary measure due to the uncertainty caused by that freeze and “the separate funding interruption affecting Better Jobs Ontario-funded students at Trillium College.”

When asked recently if Better Jobs Ontario funding was also paused, Quinn’s spokesperson said little.

“Preliminary audit findings point to serious, systemic concerns about Osap usage at private postsecondary institutions,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote.

“Osap payments to students at these institutions are paused, and other streams of provincial funding to private institutions past and present are under review.”

Giacoboni refused to list those other streams of funding.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said if the government is taking action against another source of funding they should come out and say it.

“It’s happening,” he said. “They know it’s happening and I don’t know why they’re afraid to say it.”

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the government is ducking accountability.

“This government is terrified of facing the music,” she wrote in a statement.

“They won’t even do the bare minimum of explaining themselves. They’re leaving thousands of people who rely on this program to build a better future and find good jobs without any certainty or support. This is not how you protect Ontario in the face of growing job losses.”

stories.title: Three people dead following multi-vehicle crash near Windsor: OPP
stories.summary: Three people are dead following a multi-vehicle crash early Wednesday morning in a town just outside of Windsor, Ontario Provincial Police say.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Three people are dead following a multi-vehicle crash early Wednesday morning in a town just outside of Windsor.

Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) said its officers responded to the crash on County Road 22 in Lakeshore around 6:07 a.m.

The drivers of two vehicles involved in the crash were pronounced dead on scene; a passenger was taken to hospital where they were pronounced dead.

Police are assessing others for injuries. The OPP did not specify the amount of people or vehicles involved in the crash.

The cause of the crash is not known.

An investigation is underway.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Bank of Canada interest rate announcement nears as economists expect a hike
stories.summary: The Bank of Canada is expected to make an interest rate announcement Wednesday, with many economists predicting a hike for the first time in three years.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
The Bank of Canada is expected to make an interest rate announcement Wednesday, with many economists predicting a hike for the first time in three years.

The central bank is facing pressure to raise interest rates as the Iran war and other geopolitical conflicts result in higher prices for oil and gas, which is expected to lead to higher prices for goods and services beyond the gas pump.

Financial markets and a Reuters poll of economists are betting that the central bank will deliver a quarter-point hike to its policy rate, the first increase in the key lending rate since July 2023.

The floor for borrowing rates set by the Bank of Canada has been 2.25 per cent since October 2025, when rates were cut from 2.5 per cent.

Alongside the rate decision, the Bank of Canada will also release updated forecasts for inflation and economic growth.

– with a file from The Canadian Press

More to come.

stories.title: Finalists for Governor General’s Literary Awards include Miriam Toews, Hannah Moscovitch
stories.summary: The Canada Council for the Arts named 69 finalists across seven categories in English and French and winners will be announced on Nov. 12
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath
stories.content:
The Globe and Mail’s Greg Mercer is a finalist for this year’s Governor General’s Literary Awards for his non-fiction book The Lobster Trap , joining authors including Miriam Toews, Hannah Moscovitch and Kim Fu.

Toews’ memoir A Truce That Is Not Peace is one of five books up for the English-language non-fiction prize. Toews explores the question, “why do you write?” in the book while reflecting on the suicides of her sister and father. The Toronto-based writer previously won the Governor General’s fiction prize for her 2004 novel A Complicated Kindness .

The Canada Council for the Arts named 69 finalists across seven categories in English and French on Wednesday. The 14 winners, who each receive $25,00, will be announced on Nov. 12.

Moscovitch is nominated in the drama category for her play Red Like Fruit , which follows a journalist covering a high-profile domestic violence case while a sense of unease pervades her thoughts. The Halifax playwright, who is also a writer for the AMC television series, Interview with the Vampire , previously won the Governor General’s drama prize in 2021 for Sexual Misconduct of the Middle Classes .

Fu is among the five finalists for the English-language fiction prize for her novel The Valley of Vengeful Ghosts about a woman unravelling in the aftermath of her mother’s death. The Vancouver-born writer was previously a finalist for the Giller Prize in 2022 for her short story collection Lesser Known Monsters of the 21st Century .

Also nominated in the fiction category is Sharon Bala for her novel Good Guys about the dark side of philanthropy and Sara Peters for her novel Mother of God about a woman with psychic powers who returns home to see her estranged mother. Rounding out the fiction finalists is Nina Dunic for Suddenly Light and Kate Cayley for Property .

The Governor General’s Literary Awards, which celebrates homegrown literature, will also hand out honours for poetry, writing and illustration in young people’s literature, as well as French-to-English translation. There are separate French-language categories for francophone writing.
