stories.title: Ontario government announces reforms for electricity distributors with rising demand in mind
stories.summary: There are long-standing concerns about ability of local distributors to maintain existing infrastructure, let alone pay for expansions
stories.author: Matthew McClearn
stories.content:
Ontario’s government announced a slate of reforms on Tuesday intended to help the province’s several dozen electricity distributors prepare for a rapidly rising demand for power.

Stephen Lecce, Minister of Energy and Mines, said the government would introduce legislation on Tuesday afternoon in response to a series of recommendations received earlier this year from a four-member advisory group. The reforms include a new requirement that local distribution companies, or LDCs, produce 10-year plans “that include condition assessment, financing plans and work-force strategies.”

The government will also impose what it described as “a mandatory dividend stress test,” intended to ensure LDCs reinvest profits back into their grids.

“Because right now, across the board, that is not always the case,” Mr. Lecce said during a press conference in Toronto.

“Local utilities are facing aging infrastructure, rising capital requirements, work-force shortages and skyrocketing demands for connections. And so, notwithstanding very good efforts by our utilities, these challenges remain real, and they will imperil our economic growth if we don’t get it right today,” he said.

Ontario’s electricity is distributed by 58 LDCs that are mostly owned by municipalities. Many of them serve small numbers of customers, whereas other provinces are served by a single, monolithic Crown corporation such as Hydro-Québec.

Expectations of increasing demand for electricity have exacerbated long-standing concerns that many LDCs will be unable to maintain existing infrastructure, let alone pay for significant expansions. According to the Electricity Distributors Association, which represents Ontario’s LDCs, the tab for upgrading networks over the next couple of decades could amount to between $103-billion and $120-billion – an estimate the government has endorsed.

A year ago, the government convened a group called the Panel for Utility Leadership and Service Excellence, or Pulse, chaired by former Toronto Hydro Corp. president and chief executive Anthony Haines, to advise Mr. Lecce on potential reforms. Pulse’s recommendations, submitted in February and published Tuesday, warned that although LDCs have thus far managed to preserve reliability of their distribution systems, many have put off necessary capital investments for years.

Pulse warned LDCs are “increasingly misaligned with the scale, pace and complexity of growth in electricity demand now underway,” and that the pace at which Ontario can meet objectives such as building new housing, electrifying its industries and charging electric vehicles “increasingly turns on distribution system readiness.”

Pulse also found that while municipalities May, in some cases, be able to provide additional funding to LDCs, others must turn to alternative sources of capital such as pension funds and other institutional investors, or will need to merge with other utilities.

“Access to external investment, particularly from Canadian institutional investors, is likely to be a critical determinant of whether electricity distribution utilities can deliver required infrastructure on time and at reasonable cost,” its report concluded.

The government’s response to Pulse’s recommendations include imposing new governance requirements. Mr. Lecce said LDCs will be required to establish “independent, skills-based” boards of directors. Municipalities will be limited to having one member in a non-voting capacity – a departure from a status quo in which politicians occupy as much as half of LDC board seats.

Benjamin Dachis, vice-president of research at the energy think tank Clean Prosperity, said there’s strong evidence that independent directors who are not associated with municipal shareholders are more likely to promote investment by LDCs.

Teresa Sarkesian, president of the Electricity Distributors Association, expressed broad support for the reforms. She said her organization understands the government will later introduce further measures focused on removing barriers to greater private investment in LDCs.

“One of the most important things for us is to make sure that we have access to capital to properly fund the grid,” she said.

“There’s two times a year that they can implement those things: One is the fall economic statement, and one is the budget.”

Of particular interest is Pulse’s observation that when private ownership of an LDC exceeds a federally imposed threshold of 10 per cent, it’s deemed to have disposed of its assets at fair market value and faces a large departure tax. This has restricted LDCs’ access to outside investment.

Ms. Sarkesian said that while her organization supports long-term capital planning, inflation, supply chain challenges and the geopolitical environment make it difficult to forecast a decade out; five-year plans “would be more accurate and more meaningful.”

Thomas Timmins, who leads law firm Gowling Wlg’s energy practice, said the new governance and financial requirements are aimed at encouraging consolidation among the LDCs, without explicitly forcing them to do so.

The changes announced on Tuesday “put a compliance burden on the smaller utilities,” he said, “which will potentially push municipal shareholders to conclude that maintaining an independent utility is really a luxury that they can’t afford any more.”

He added: “Some of these LDCs are in financial trouble, and that is not okay. We are talking about keeping the lights and heating on – this is critical infrastructure.”

stories.title: Ontario Superior Court approves $213.5M settlement against Sun Life
stories.summary: The Ontario Superior Court of Justice has approved a $213.5 million class-action settlement against Sun Life.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto — The Ontario Superior Court of Justice has approved a $213.5 million class-action settlement against Sun Life.

A news release from law firm Kim Spencer McPhee Barristers P.C. says the action began in 2010 regarding alleged improper administration of three universal life insurance policies, including Universal Plus, Flexiplus, and OptiMet.

The policies were sold by Metropolitan Life Insurance Co. agents in Canada between 1987 and 1998.

The release says Sunlife has denied any wrongdoing, and the company did not immediately respond to a request for comment after hours.

The law firm says the settlement is the largest reported settlement in any life insurance policy dispute in Canadian history, concerning 70,000 eligible current and former Flexiplus and Universal Plus policyholders in Canada.

Eldon Fehr, representative plaintiff, says the settlement will provide significant benefits to current and former Sun Life policyholders.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Incumbent mayors, premiers losing jobs a result of Canadians not ‘getting ahead’
stories.summary: Many mayors in British Columbia and Ontario and premiers in B.C. and Quebec lost their jobs this month despite being incumbents in the race.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Cities and provinces across Canada have seen political change in recent months as frustrations over affordability and quality of life has meant incumbents being shown the door.

Multiple Ontario cities said goodbye to short and long-time mayors and councillors on Monday. A few days earlier, British Columbia ousted its NDP government and premier David Eby, following the trend of incumbent losses after several B.C. mayors were voted out of office. Those changes all came in a month that started with Quebec’s CAQ government losing every seat in the provincial election.

The back-to-back changes were a result of Canadians facing continued strain over tariffs from the U.S. administration, wavering inflation and uncertainty when affordability will get better, political experts said.

“If we think about the national mood right now in Canada … I think a lot of Canadians don’t feel like they’re getting ahead,” said Lewis Krashinsky, a political scientist and William Lyon Mackenzie King postdoctoral fellow at Harvard University. “Voters can be fickle.”

He said that when voters don’t feel like they’re getting ahead, they look for people they believe can bring new ideas.

Richard Johnston, professor emeritus of political science at the University of British Columbia, said the power of incumbency has decreased over decades. Previously, some provincial governments have served for decades such as the Progressive Conservatives in New Brunswick for 17 years, or the Alberta PCs for 43. The average length of a government now sits at about 10 years.

Incumbents have also faced multiple issues in recent months, with Johnston saying the handling of COVID-19, supply chain and inflation, and President Donald Trump’s tariffs have meant Canadians are feeling worse off.

As a result, people are pointing the finger at politicians in city hall or the provincial legislatures and punishing them for it.

“In general, this has been a decade of sort of institutional failure, I think that’s actually unfair, but that’s how voters perceive it,” Johnston said. “There’s a sense in which governments of almost any stripe seem to have dropped the ball or they’re overwhelmed by forces beyond their control.”

But Krashinsky, originally from Toronto, added that voters can choose someone new for a number of reasons including anger.

“Perhaps that’s out of a sense of anger, resentment towards a political candidate who’s been in there for so many years; perhaps it’s a sense of optimism with what the new candidate could bring in,” said Krashinsky. “Perhaps it is a sense of just needing a better option; it’s a sense of almost desperation that we’ve tried this path over and over again, and we haven’t gotten ahead.”

Long-time incumbency ended for several mayors in Ontario Oct. 26.

Gord Krantz, Canada’s longest-serving, lost his first election since becoming mayor of Milton in 1980. Further south, Sarnia’s Mike Bradley ended his 38-year run in the mayor’s seat defeated by newcomer Carrie McEachran.

It wasn’t long-time incumbents who lost either. One-term mayors in B.C. including Port Moody’s Meghan Lahti and New Westminster’s Patrick Johnstone, and Mississauga’s Carolyn Parrish and Hamilton’s Andrea Horwath in Ontario also lost.

Hamish Telford, associate political science professor at the University of the Fraser Valley in B.C., said those short-term mayors were the victims of the public disappointed in their own choices within the previous four years.

“It’s frustration with lack of progress on core issues as a generality,” he said. “People look over the past four years and say, ‘my life or my city hasn’t improved like you promised it would,’ and obviously, they come to the conclusion that the direction that the mayor set was not the right one.”

Not all incumbents are losing though, with Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow, Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown and several B.C. mayors still keeping their jobs.

Krashinsky said the reasons can range from a mixture of relatability to there not being a strong enough opposition candidate to give voters another strong choice.

“Affinity for a candidate that you know and recognize and trust someone perhaps that you’ve met,” he said. “Being able to have that personal touch that you can be established really over time I think can really help these incumbents.”

Yet Telford added even likeability won’t help if voters are losing respect for the judgment of longer-serving incumbents creating that need for change.

“The winds of change of change blow every decade in Canada and that’s what we’re seeing lately,” Telford said.

— with files from Global News’ Aaron D’Andrea and Amy Judd

stories.title: Four and a half years on, the housing correction is an Ontario and B.C. story
stories.summary: The 2023 rebound was a false bottom. Where do home prices go from here?
stories.author: Hanif Bayat
stories.content:
After the recent rise in fixed mortgage rates and the expectation that variable rates will follow, the question many home buyers and sellers are asking is whether home prices in Canada will fall further.

The national benchmark home price fell to $651,400 in September, its lowest level since February, 2021, and 22.5 per cent below the March, 2022, high. The national average home price tells a similar story: At $666,538 in September, it was lower than in February, 2021.

Four and a half years after the peak, Canada’s housing correction isn’t over. But the national number hides the real story: This is now mainly a correction in two provinces.

Ontario’s benchmark home price is $736,300, down 26.7 per cent from its peak of just over $1-million. The typical Ontario home has lost about $269,000 in value. B.C. is down 16.7 per cent from its peak, down 4.7 per cent from a year ago. Worse, both have erased the 2023 rebound, which many buyers took as a sign the bottom had passed.

Quebec and Alberta, the other two big provinces, never had a 2022 bust. Alberta peaked later, in March, 2025, and is now only 3.6 per cent below that level. Quebec set a record this April and is still up 1.1 per cent from a year ago, the only annual gain among the four big provinces. Among the six smaller provinces, all but Nova Scotia are up from a year ago.

But momentum is fading almost everywhere. In September, the benchmark fell from the previous month in every province except PEI, though part of that is seasonal.

Given recent housing market activity and rising mortgage rates , I expect Ontario and B.C. housing prices will not rise next year and will most probably fall, possibly reaching their bottom. Home prices in Alberta and Quebec May not rise either.

Not everyone agrees. Ali Salarian, the broker at RE/MAX Success Realty in Mississauga, Ont., expects things to improve once the current renewal wave passes. Owners who locked in five-year rates below 2 per cent in 2021 are now renewing at much higher rates, pushing some to sell, while those who renew next year already have rates close to today’s. “Once this listing wave clears, expect gradual growth in 2027,” he said in an interview.

He is not the only one. Desjardins senior economist Kari Norman, for example, expects Ontario’s average home price to rise 2.4 per cent in 2027 , even though she anticipates two Bank of Canada rate hikes starting in late October.

Still, the economy is soft and borrowing costs are rising. Don’t be fooled by a good spring market. Benchmark home prices tend to rise in spring and stall in the fall. This year, a January-to-May bounce was followed by four straight monthly declines. The first sign of a bottom will be when annual price declines start to narrow month after month.

Hanif Bayat, PhD, is the CEO and founder of Wowa.CA , a Canadian personal finance platform.

stories.title: Smith rejects renewed demands for Alberta health care procurement public inquiry
stories.summary: Premier made her comments after The Globe reported RCMP are investigating potential fraud and money laundering in connection with the controversy
stories.author: Carrie Tait, Tom Cardoso
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Tuesday rejected renewed demands for a public inquiry into alleged procurement irregularities in the province’s health care system after The Globe and Mail reported that the RCMP are investigating potential fraud, breach of trust and money laundering in connection with the controversy.

Ms. Smith, speaking in the legislature during its first sitting since May, said a 2025 review conducted by Raymond Wyant, a retired judge from Manitoba, adequately probed the allegations, which were lodged by Alberta Health Services former chief executive Athana Mentzelopoulos earlier that year.

The Premier has leaned on Mr. Wyant’s report when defending her government against allegations of wrongdoing tied to the procurement affair since it was released in October, 2025.

“The best way to clear the air was to have a judge-led inquiry, which is what we did,” Ms. Smith told the legislature during Question Period on Tuesday. “We gave him literally millions of pages of documents.”

Mr. Wyant did not have the power to subpoena witnesses or hear testimony under oath. Some people declined to be interviewed or to answer certain questions, and he could not compel the production of records.

Naheed Nenshi, Alberta’s New Democratic Party Leader, argued the new information reported in The Globe adds to the need for a public inquiry.

“The net is tightening around this Premier and her government,” he said.

The RCMP confirmed in early 2025 that it was investigating the province’s health care procurement practices. The Globe’s report on Tuesday, based on an Oct. 15 letter filed in court, revealed for the first time the potential crimes police are pursuing.

The procurement affair has dogged Ms. Smith since early 2025, after the government fired Ms. Mentzelopoulos as the head of the provincial health authority. The former executive alleges in court documents that the government fired her in part to shut down an investigation she ordered into inflated contracts and potential conflicts of interest in the health care system. The government, meanwhile, alleges it dismissed Ms. Mentzelopoulos because she failed at executing its strategy.

None of the allegations have been tested in court.

In September, Justice Michael Lema at the Court of King’s Bench of Alberta determined Ms. Mentzelopoulos kept records that were privileged or confidential after being fired. He ruled that she must return or destroy those records, and pay legal costs for the government and the health agency.

As part of their investigation, the RCMP seized documents from Ms. Mentzelopoulos, according to the October letter filed in court. Lawyers responsible for prosecuting potential charges stemming from the RCMP investigation want the Court of King’s Bench to provide direction around potential privileged and confidential records, the document says.

On Tuesday, Alberta Justice Minister Mickey Amery said the government will co-operate with the RCMP, but would not say whether the province would challenge the Mounties’ access to some of the same records the court ordered Ms. Mentzelopoulos to return or destroy.

“We argued that certain privileged and confidential documents should remain privileged and confidential, which is a legal right of every party involved in a civil action,” he told reporters at an unrelated press conference. “We don’t know what those documents are that the RCMP are relying on, nor can I speculate about that because we haven’t been made aware of what those documents are that they’re going to seek to rely on.

“If and when that issue arises, then we’ll have an answer for you.”

He added: “We will fully co-operate with the RCMP investigation and we’ll provide everything that we possibly can to the RCMP in supporting their investigation.”

Tom Andreopoulos, a Crown prosecutor with the Complex Prosecutions Bureau at Ontario’s Ministry of the Attorney-General, sent the Oct. 15 letter to lawyers involved in the civil dispute related to Ms. Mentzelopoulos.

“Our office is responsible for the provision of advisory support and the prosecution of any charges that May arise from the ongoing Royal Canadian Mounted Police criminal investigation into fraud, breach of trust, and money laundering arising out of procurement processes and practices at Alberta Health and Alberta Health Services,” Mr. Andreopoulos says in his letter.

The letter does not elaborate on the alleged potential offences or who is the subject of the investigation. Further, it does not specify why Ontario Crown prosecutors are involved in the RCMP’s probe in Alberta. (Provincial justice departments sometimes appoint prosecutors from other provinces when dealing with politically sensitive cases in which a potential conflict of interest May arise.)

One of Ms. Mentzelopoulos’ lawyers submitted the letter as part of a court filing disputing the costs requested by the government and Alberta Health Services in the wake of Justice Lema’s decision on privileged and confidential records.

Ms. Smith’s government had appointed Mr. Wyant, the retired judge, to examine Ms. Mentzelopoulos’ allegations. He determined Alberta Health Services did not follow its own procedure when it signed a $70-million deal for children’s medication with MHCare Medical Corp. in 2022 and that the government health ministry failed to follow its own rules regarding a private Edmonton surgical centre. MHCare denies any wrongdoing.

Mr. Wyant stressed his investigation and conclusions did not amount to clearing the government of wrongdoing.

“When I find that there was no wrongful interference by any government official in the matters concerning this report, that only means that I found no evidence of such, but I am not in a position to make a final and absolute determination,” Mr. Wyant stated.

stories.title: McEachran makes history as first female mayor of Sarnia, taking down long-time incumbent Mike Bradley
stories.summary: For the first time in 38 years, the city of Sarnia will have a new mayor.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
For the first time in 38 years, the city of Sarnia will have a new mayor.

Political newcomer Carrie McEachran soundly defeated 11-term Incumbent Mayor Mike Bradley Monday night. She also makes history as the city’s first ever female mayor.

“I’m still in shock. I’m not going to lie,” said McEachran, the day after the historic win. “I’ve gotten lots of messages from women in the community, and men that are just really inspired to see a new energy.”

McEachran, who took leave from her job as CEO of the Sarnia Lambton Chamber of Commerce, says the city needs to be open for business.

“Many businesses have looked at Sarnia over the past several years and they went elsewhere. And they went elsewhere because there’s land developed, there’s land ready for them. They’re being welcomed with open arms, rather than throwing barriers to their development. It’s, ‘What can we do to help you? What can we do to have you here in Sarnia?’”

Last year, Bradley vetoed plans for a new police headquarters, a controversial move at the time. At an estimated cost of $90 million or more, Bradley argued it would be too big a burden on taxpayers.

McEachran, who was appointed to the Sarnia Police Service Board this past April, vowed it won’t happen under her watch either.

“So, there will not be a new building in the future, for sure. As long as I’m here, there will not be,” she insisted.

McEachran won the election with 13,828 votes, almost double that of Bradley who finished second with 7,189 votes. Rounding out the results were Bill Dennis with 5,899 votes, Scott Molson with 2,207 votes, and George Stanko with 114 votes (Stanko withdrew from the race after the official deadline).

Returning councillors say the public was ripe for change.

“When the community is ready for a change, and not a change as in a cliché change, but a new direction, and new directions of optimistic opportunity, that change happens. And I’m feeling it. I felt it at the campaign trail,” said re-elected city and Lambton County Councillor Brian White.

“The thing that you’re going to find with Carrie McEachran is that she bridges both the business and the social service aspects of community life,” said re-elected city and Lambton County Councillor Adam Kilner.

Bradley could not be reached for comment Tuesday. On Monday night, he offered congratulations to the mayor-elect via a social media post.

McEachran had this to say a short time later in an interview with CTV News from her victory party; “The fact that he was the mayor here for 38 years tells me a whole lot about the respect of the community, and he’s done a great job, and I wish him all the best.”

stories.title: B.C. animal rescuer killed by drone attack in Ukraine
stories.summary: Jesse Adams, founder of RainCoast Dog Rescue Society on Vancouver Island, was evacuating animals close to the front line in the war with Russia
stories.author: Nono Shen
stories.content:
A Ukraine-based animal rescue organization says a Canadian volunteer in the war-torn country has been killed in a drone attack.

Animal Rescue Kharkiv said Jesse Adams, founder of RainCoast Dog Rescue Society on Vancouver Island, died on Sunday after the “enemy drone” struck his vehicle as it was evacuating animals from Kramatorsk, close to the front line in the war with Russia.

A separate news release from Spca International said Adams died while working to protect animals in one of the most dangerous regions in Ukraine.

It calls Adams a “hero to animals,” and says he had “endless energy, enthusiasm and compassion for making the world a kinder place.”

Animal Rescue Kharkiv said Adams was taken to hospital for emergency surgery but could not be saved.

The organization said it was an honour to work alongside Adams.

“Jesse joined our teams at Animal Rescue Kharkiv, travelling to front-line communities to save animals and help people,” it said in a social media post on Monday.

“When someone travels halfway around the world and chooses to work beside you in some of the most difficult conditions, it means more than words can say. There are hundreds of animals alive today because of him.”

In 2014, Adams co-founded the RainCoast Dog Rescue Society, a charity run by volunteers to help animals across Canada and abroad.

Canadian animal welfare groups have shared condolences.

The BC Animal Law Reform Coalition said in a statement that Adams had “selfless determination and energy” to save dogs from all corners of B.C., often in “dire circumstances.”

Northern Hope Dog Rescue Society said that Adams was their friend and “brother in rescue.”

It said Adams was the person “you could call when you needed help on a mission (who would) share the burden or simply be a shoulder to lean on when the weight of the work became too much.”

In a social media post dated Oct. 23, Adams said he was involved in an evacuation mission at a small village outside Kramatorsk in eastern Ukraine, “super close to the front line of the war.”

Adams said he was helping a family to evacuate their animals from an area that was being hit daily by drones, bombs and missiles.

He said that when they arrived and started to load cows, dogs, cats and a pig into a van, a drone hit a nearby house.

Spca International said they were fortunate to call Adams their friend and to have worked alongside him on animal rescue efforts around the world.

“There was never an animal who Jesse would refuse to save, no matter the circumstances,” their statement said. “We will never forget the hope he brought to animals and people facing their darkest moments.”

Michelle Singleton, founder of A Home for Hooves Farm Sanctuary near Duncan, B.C., said she has known Adams for at least seven years and their paths crossed again four years ago when he reached out to her about three male runner ducks that were at risk of being euthanized due to their history of aggression.

Singleton said Adams knew the ducks could be rehabilitated if they were placed in the “right situation.”

The ducks, named Kenzo, Kane and Idris, have been living at her sanctuary ever since, and anyone who meets them loves their “non-stop chattering and their unmistakable personalities.”

“He’s helped hundreds of animals and a lot of very difficult cases where the animal is incredibly sick, or they’ve been abused heavily, like he takes that on,” said Singleton.

“He had amazing relationships all over the world, but on Vancouver Island, he had a lot of really amazing relationships with different Indigenous communities,” said Singleton.

“He did everything he could to help animals in need.”

stories.title: Alberta government to end DEI public sector hiring
stories.summary: A government bill has been tabled that, if passed, would prohibit a number of public bodies from using DEI policies to make hiring decisions.
stories.author: Jack Farrell
stories.content:
Alberta is looking to end public sector hiring practices aimed at diversity, equity and inclusion.

A government bill has been tabled that, if passed, would prohibit a number of public bodies from using DEI policies to make hiring decisions.

Premier Danielle Smith says hiring needs to be based on merit and qualifications so that everyone has a fair chance at getting jobs.

The bill covers public agencies, Crown corporations, post-secondary schools, school boards and municipalities, although officials say government employees are already hired on merit.

The proposed legislation would also prohibit public bodies from having mandatory DEI training for staff except when necessary for the job.

Government officials say the new policy could also apply to non-profit agencies receiving government grants, but that would be determined through future regulations.

More coming.

Danielle Smith faces another leadership review call from UCP constituency board

What’s next for the BC NDP? Veteran MLA says party must ‘listen and learn’

stories.title: Voters send a ‘warning shot’ as many incumbents lose in fall elections
stories.summary: Election signs were still up in Mississauga, Ont. on Tuesday, the day after voters chose a first-term councillor as their next mayor. They elected Alvin Tedjo over both the incumbent, Carolyn Parrish, and her predecessor, Bonnie Crombie.
stories.author: Heather Wright
stories.content:
Toronto - Election signs were still up in Mississauga, Ont. on Tuesday, the day after voters chose a first-term councillor as their next mayor. They elected Alvin Tedjo over both the incumbent, Carolyn Parrish, and her predecessor, Bonnie Crombie.

“Sometimes we just need change, right?” said Mississauga resident Linda MacPherson. “There’s new perspectives, new ideas maybe, and some of the policies he had, I agree with.”

Mississauga was not the only place where voters wanted something new. While votes are still being tallied, at least two dozen Ontario towns and cities voted for change in Monday’s municipal elections.

In Hamilton, a city hit hard by U.S. tariffs, Keanin Loomis unseated incumbent Andrea Horwath. Voters in Windsor, another city affected by the trade war, also chose a new mayor opting for Coun. Fred Francis over incumbent Drew Dilkens. In Milton, Canada’s longest-serving politician Gord Krantz was unseated by Coun. George Minakakis. Krantz was first elected as a Milton town councillor in 1965 and had served as the town’s mayor since 1980.

“This speaks to an environment where voters are looking for solutions and they are looking for positivity and they are critically looking at all the choices that you cannot coast on your laurels,” said pollster Nik Nanos. “I think this is a bit of a warning shot. Voters are grumpy. They are worried about traffic, they are worried about safety, homelessness, cost of housing and property taxes, and you know what, if you want to hold onto your job you have got to be very proactive,” he said.

While some have called Monday’s election an “anti-incumbent wave,” many of Ontario’s large cities opted to re-elect their mayors. Ottawa Mayor Mark Sutcliffe won another mandate, as did Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown.

In Toronto, Mayor Olivia Chow won re-election decisively over challenger Brad Bradford. On Tuesday, she called for unity to address the challenges facing the city, including the cost of living, traffic, and safety. “We need to all come together, all levels of government, to deal with the existing challenges that face the people of Toronto,” Chow said.

Ontario voters are not alone in opting for change. Earlier this month, Quebec elected a Parti Québécois government after eight years of Coalition Avenir Québec rule. On Saturday, voters in British Columbia gave the Conservatives a decisive majority, removing former premier David Eby and the NDP from power.

“(Voters) are very suspicious of politicians trying to engineer their own success,” Nanos said. “I think that is definitely the case in B.C. It wasn’t just a rejection of the NDP, it was a rejection of former premier David Eby looking to call a snap election that probably wasn’t necessary.”

More Canadians will go to the polls in the next week, with Manitoba holding its municipal elections on Oct. 28, while Prince Edward Island holds its elections on Nov. 2.

stories.title: 'Hero to animals': Drone kills B.C. dog rescuer Jesse Adams in Ukraine
stories.summary: A Ukraine-based animal rescue organization says a Canadian volunteer in the war-torn country has been killed in a drone attack.
stories.author: Nono Shen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A Ukraine-based animal rescue organization says a Canadian volunteer in the war-torn country has been killed in a drone attack.

Animal Rescue Kharkiv said Jesse Adams, founder of RainCoast Dog Rescue Society on Vancouver Island, died on Sunday after the “enemy drone” struck his vehicle as it was evacuating animals from Kramatorsk, close to the front line in the war with Russia.

A separate news release from Spca International said Adams died while working to protect animals in one of the most dangerous regions in Ukraine.

It calls Adams a “hero to animals,” and says he had “endless energy, enthusiasm and compassion for making the world a kinder place.”

Animal Rescue Kharkiv said Adams was taken to hospital for emergency surgery but could not be saved.

The organization said it was an honour to work alongside Adams.

“Jesse joined our teams at Animal Rescue Kharkiv, travelling to front-line communities to save animals and help people,” it said in a social media post on Monday.

“When someone travels halfway around the world and chooses to work beside you in some of the most difficult conditions, it means more than words can say. There are hundreds of animals alive today because of him.”

In 2014, Adams co-founded the RainCoast Dog Rescue Society, a charity run by volunteers to help animals across Canada and abroad.

Canadian animal welfare groups have shared condolences.

The BC Animal Law Reform Coalition said in a statement that Adams had “selfless determination and energy” to save dogs from all corners of B.C., often in “dire circumstances.”

Northern Hope Dog Rescue Society said that Adams was their friend and “brother in rescue.”

It said Adams was the person “you could call when you needed help on a mission (who would) share the burden or simply be a shoulder to lean on when the weight of the work became too much.”

In a social media post dated Oct. 23, Adams said he was involved in an evacuation mission at a small village outside Kramatorsk in eastern Ukraine, “super close to the front line of the war.”

Adams said he was helping a family to evacuate their animals from an area that was being hit daily by drones, bombs and missiles.

He said that when they arrived and started to load cows, dogs, cats and a pig into a van, a drone hit a nearby house.

Spca International said they were fortunate to call Adams their friend and to have worked alongside him on animal rescue efforts around the world.

“There was never an animal who Jesse would refuse to save, no matter the circumstances,” their statement said. “We will never forget the hope he brought to animals and people facing their darkest moments.”

Michelle Singleton, founder of A Home for Hooves Farm Sanctuary near Duncan, B.C., said she has known Adams for at least seven years and their paths crossed again four years ago when he reached out to her about three male runner ducks that were at risk of being euthanized due to their history of aggression.

Singleton said Adams knew the ducks could be rehabilitated if they were placed in the “right situation.”

The ducks, named Kenzo, Kane and Idris, have been living at her sanctuary ever since, and anyone who meets them loves their “nonstop chattering and their unmistakable personalities.”

“He’s helped hundreds of animals and a lot of very difficult cases where the animal is incredibly sick, or they’ve been abused heavily, like he takes that on,” said Singleton.

“He had amazing relationships all over the world, but on Vancouver Island, he had a lot of really amazing relationships with different Indigenous communities,” said Singleton.

“He did everything he could to help animals in need.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

“There was never an animal who Jesse would refuse to save, no matter the circumstances,” their statement said. “We will never forget the hope he brought to animals and people facing their darkest moments.”

The ducks, named Kenzo, Kane and Idris, have been living at her sanctuary ever since, and anyone who meets them loves their “nonstop chattering and their unmistakable personalities.”

stories.title: First Nations have 'every right' to be skeptical of major projects office: Farrell
stories.summary: Ottawa - The head of the federal government's major projects office says First Nations have every right to be skeptical of her office's intentions.
stories.author: Nick Murray The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The head of the federal government’s major projects office said Tuesday First Nations have “every right” to be skeptical of her office’s intentions, elaborating on comments she made at the British Columbia Assembly of First Nations two weeks ago.

Dawn Farrell took an hour’s worth of questions from MPs on the House of Commons environment committee Tuesday.

Her committee appearance happened two weeks after she addressed the B.C. chiefs. Many of those chiefs were frustrated over what they said was a lack of consultation on whether Canada should designate the Pacific Link pipeline as a project of national interest.

Prime Minister Mark Carney designated the project — a new oil pipeline from Alberta to the southern B.C. coast — on Oct. 1.

Some chiefs said they were given just 11 working days to review and engage on the designation proposal.

Farrell told First Nations leaders on Oct. 14 that those frustrations made her feel like Canada was “never going to work,” but insisted her office was determined to try to be better.

Farrell’s choice of words generated some criticism.

On Tuesday, Farrell told MPs she was trying to convey that she knows First Nations don’t trust her office, and that it’s up to her to prove her team’s intent through their work.

“I know that the First Nations are nervous about the time frame and how much we’re trying to get done and how quickly we’re trying to do it. And I know they’re not used to that because a lot of consultations were taking years and years and a lot of projects weren’t getting done,” Farrell told MPs.

“So they have every right to be, in my mind, skeptical around what the intentions of the major projects office (is). We’re new. We’re not proven yet. We haven’t been able to show them what our intentions are, and we haven’t been able to follow through and make sure that the work that we do is as we say it’s going to be.

“So I was more expressing that, ‘I know you don’t trust us, and it’s up to me to do the work and to show you.’ And it was, of course, you know, I didn’t say it well enough and I regret that.”

The federal government initially planned to hold consultations for one month on whether to designate the pipeline as a project in the national interest under the Building Canada Act. That was extended to two months after Indigenous leaders raised concerns about the tight timeline.

A summary of those consultations posted online by the federal government says Indigenous groups decried a lack of information about the project, which they said prevented them from fully assessing its impact.

Rob Van Walleghem, general counsel and vice president of Indigenous affairs at the major projects office, said Indigenous Peoples need to have “good information” early and need to have adequate capacity to make decisions.

“Communities are not used to proponents showing up with little information. But that’s the point,” he told MPs.

“We don’t want proponents showing up in communities with plans that are so far down the road that they’re intransigent because they’ve invested too much money in developing them. We want Indigenous Peoples to be involved in the co-development of these projects.”

Cold Lake First Nations is asking the Federal Court to review the decision to list the Pacific Link pipeline as a project of national interest because they weren’t consulted over it.

The First Nation is asking the court to quash the national interest designation and to declare that Canada has a duty to consult with the community on the pipeline.

Asked on Tuesday by MPs how much confidence she had that the consultation process would hold up in court, Farrell said she was “highly confident” it would.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

— With files from Alessia Passafiume

stories.title: Danielle Smith faces another leadership review call from UCP constituency board
stories.summary: Scott Cyr riding is one of a few to recently call for a review of Smith's leadership, while others have announced their support for her.
stories.author: Jack Farrell
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is facing another call for a leadership review from one of her United Conservative Party constituency boards.

Scott Cyr, a backbencher in Smith’s caucus, says the board of his Bonnyville-Cold Lake-St. Paul constituency association passed the motion Monday.

Cyr, in a social media post Tuesday, said it passed narrowly — 10 votes to nine — in a secret ballot.

But Cyr said he doesn’t agree with the outcome and that it’s time to rally behind Smith’s leadership.

“With the 2027 provincial election approaching, I am concerned about the consequences of continued internal division within the United Conservative Party,” he wrote.

Cyr’s riding is one of a few to recently call for a review of Smith’s leadership, while others have announced their support for her. The party’s annual general meeting in Calgary is one month away.

Mitch Sylvestre, president of Cyr’s constituency association, is a prominent face in Alberta’s separatist movement.

Smith is seeking to rein in separatist elements in her party ahead of the next election, set for October 2027.

Sylvestre and others behind the independence push have set their sights on ousting Smith as party leader over her support for keeping Alberta in Canada.

Last week, three-quarters of Alberta voters in a provincewide referendum affirmed they want the province to stay in Canada rather than hold a second, binding referendum on separation.

Smith called the referendum. She said it was necessary to quell a growing debate in Alberta over its role in Confederation. Critics said there was never such a groundswell of separatist sentiment and that Smith called the vote to appease UCP separatists and keep her job.

Smith said she voted to stay in Canada.

After the referendum, she promised there wouldn’t be another separation vote while she’s premier. She said the referendum had settled the debate.

She also urged in-house separatists to find a new home, but Sylvestre has said he’s not going anywhere.

Smith was expected to face questions on the topic later Tuesday, as the legislature was to begin its fall sitting.

The UCP has also lost a legislature member. Backbencher Shane Getson announced Monday he was quitting politics completely and immediately, citing unspecified personal reasons.

Smith’s party now has 46 seats in the legislature. The NDP has 39, and there is one Progressive Tory.

Sylvestre and others behind the independence push have set their sights on ousting Smith as party leader over her support for keeping Alberta in Canada.
Last week, three-quarters of Alberta voters in a provincewide referendum affirmed they want the province to stay in Canada rather than hold a second, binding referendum on separation.

Smith called the referendum. She said it was necessary to quell a growing debate in Alberta over its role in Confederation. Critics said there was never such a groundswell of separatist sentiment and that Smith called the vote to appease UCP separatists and keep her job.
Smith said she voted to stay in Canada.
After the referendum, she promised there wouldn’t be another separation vote while she’s premier. She said the referendum had settled the debate.
She also urged in-house separatists to find a new home, but Sylvestre has said he’s not going anywhere.
Smith was expected to face questions on the topic later Tuesday, as the legislature was to begin its fall sitting.
The UCP has also lost a legislature member. Backbencher Shane Getson announced Monday he was quitting politics completely and immediately, citing unspecified personal reasons.
Smith’s party now has 46 seats in the legislature. The NDP has 39, and there is one Progressive Tory.

stories.title: Lotto ticket bought in Grey County unclaimed with 24 hours until deadline
stories.summary: Tony Bitonti has the cheque already made up, he just needs to fill in the name of the ticket holder of a $40 million LottoMax prize, that could expire if not claimed soon.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Tony Bitonti has the cheque already made up, he just needs to fill in the name of the ticket holder of a $40 million LottoMax prize, that could expire if not claimed soon.

“We’ve been waiting. Almost a year. It’s going to be a year in a little less than 24 hours that we’ve been waiting for this $40 million ticket holder to come forward,” said Bitonti, Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation’s Media Relations Coordinator.

“And what I can tell you, and this is the sad part, is that this ticket has not even been checked yet. Not been checked on our OLG app, not at our retailer.”

The $40 million ticket was bought somewhere in Grey County for the Oct. 28, 2025, draw. The winning numbers are 06, 14, 17, 19, 26, 43, 43, with bonus number 27.

“So, OLG has every piece of information about this ticket, except one critical piece of information. Exactly who the owner is, Bitonti added.

“But we know exactly where it was purchased. When it was purchased, what else it was purchased with. Was there an encore? Did they also buy a 6/49 ticket or a Pro Line ticket? We have all that information. We just need the ticket holder to come forward. And even if they’ve lost the ticket, to come forward with that information and we’ll do some due diligence, we’ll make sure that they are the rightful owner and then hopefully we can pay them $40 million.”

60 people have already claimed they have the winning ticket, but Bitonti says all the information hasn’t added up yet, so they are still searching. If the winner doesn’t come forward before midnight on Oct. 28, the $40 million goes back into the prize pool.

“Listen, $40 million is a lot of money. That’s life-changing amounts of money. And it’s not our money. It’s not Olg’s money,” Bitonti said.

“It is somebody that paid five or $10 for a ticket at a $40 million jackpot, and won the jackpot and hasn’t come forward to claim it. So where is this person? That’s the $40 million question, and I hope to fill in the name on this cheque, very soon.”

If you believe you purchased this winning Lotto MAX ticket, you can go to the OLG.CA Unclaimed Tickets page to fill in your information to start the claim or contact OLG at 1-800-387-0098.

stories.title: Halifax council puts off decision on bike network alternatives
stories.summary: Council has deferred action on alternatives to the all ages and abilities (AAA) bike network because councillors say they want to gather more feedback on the proposed plans.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Angela Capobianco
stories.content:
Halifax Regional Council has deferred action on alternatives to the all ages and abilities (AAA) bike network because councillors say they want to gather more feedback on the proposed plans.

Cycling advocates say they appreciate this step but the mayor is concerned the decision will only create more delays and increase costs.

“Those committees open the door to redesign, which opened the door to increase costs, which open the doors to delay,” said Mayor Andy Fillmore.

“Today, we had a clear path to get that section down and to help to complete the bike network. And we stepped off that path into a bit of a swirl.”

The deferral was based on a motion put forth by Coun. Sean Cleary at Tuesday’s regional council meeting.

The motion called for the two transportation committees to hear a report on alternatives to the network before council decides on a direction. Staff completed the report after Coun. Tony Mancini and Mayor Fillmore asked them to consider alternative routes to save money.

“I cannot imagine we can make an informed decision on any of these without feedback from the people who are actually going to be using it,” said Cleary.

The network would consist of protected bike lanes, multi-use pathways and local street bikeways as part of the municipality’s Integrated Mobility Plan. AAA design guidelines focus on safe infrastructure for riders of all ages, and use physical separation from motor vehicles, as well as traffic calming methods.

As of this past January, the project is expected to cost $85 million . The project was initially pegged at $25 million.

Staff have identified seven alternative routes in the report, but noted that while the alternatives May reduce costs, they likely won’t accommodate all ages and abilities.

“I have a real problem with that because the whole point of the minimum grid and expanding our protected cycling infrastructure, and other active transportation infrastructure, is to achieve a mode shift to more sustainable modes of transportation,” said Cleary.

Cyclists were in council chambers Tuesday to silently protest the report and the suggested alternatives.

“We need to get it built properly because we know if you build it improperly, they’ll use that as an argument not to improve it,” said Halifax Cycling Coalition Chair David Trueman.

Trueman adds that cyclists don’t need raised or separated lanes necessarily, but that lanes on roads with concrete dividers are sufficient.

“We don’t need the most expensive options. We just need adequate safe options,” he said.

Since work isn’t expected until 2028, reviewing the report in the committees is not expected to delay the project.

stories.title: ‘Finally, traffic relief!’ Bradley Ave. extension set to open in early November
stories.summary: Frustrated London, Ont. motorists will soon have a new way around construction and congestion in the city’s south end.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
Frustrated London, Ont. motorists will soon have a new way around construction and congestion in the city’s south end.

CTV News has learned the Bradley Avenue extension will open early next month.

Jennie Dann, director of Construction and Infrastructure, says they’re planning the opening for the week of Nov. 9.

As one passing motorist yelled, “Finally, traffic relief!”

Construction crews were seen working to meet the two-week deadline.

Everything from light standards to trees are being installed – quickly – along the stretch from White Oak Road to Wharncliffe Road.

While final touches, including resurfacing, won’t take place until spring, Dann said the span is set to reshape traffic patterns and relieve some pressure on backed-up BRT construction corridors.

“By opening up a new link like this, it’s going to adjust how people move. It can take some pressure off some of those parallel corridors. And so, it’s going to be great for traffic in the southwest,” said Dann.

It’s also great for those living in the adjacent Copperfield subdivision. For years, they have put up with traffic cutting through to get further west.

“People are driving way too fast. And you know, using the roundabouts and cutting through. It’s all the time,” said resident Dave Clark.

With the extension in place, he anticipates a safer neighbourhood.

Still, closer to the roadway, some point to a history of crashes and speeding along Bradley, just east of the new stretch.

They fear the new traffic lights will be a starting cue for street racers.

“Because once the lights turn green, it’s like, ‘Go!’” expressed Jim Matesic, the operator of White Oaks Collision.

He added, “If the speeds pick up, and once the road gets slippery, there is really nothing to stop them from losing control and coming into our building, possibly.”

The city says it will study traffic patterns, speed, and safety before the official opening in the spring. For now, the speed limit is set at 60 kilometres per hour.

Dann said the $21 million project remains on schedule and on budget, even though project costs have climbed in the decades since it was originally planned.

It’s expected 25,000 vehicles will use the span each day.

stories.title: Galloway success disappeared ‘almost overnight’ following assault claims, publisher says
stories.summary: Author’s defamation suit against his accuser, a former UBC student, is under way in Vancouver
stories.author: Brenna Owen
stories.content:
A publisher for Steven Galloway’s books has testified that the author became persona non grata in the literary community, with speaking engagements and sales potential disappearing “almost overnight,” following unproven allegations of sexual assault.

“It was extraordinary and I had not seen that before ever,” said Louise Dennys, a high-profile figure in the publishing industry who served as executive vice-president at Penguin Random House Canada and helped edit and promote Galloway’s work.

Her testimony via video conference on Tuesday came midway through the hearing of Galloway’s defamation lawsuit against his accuser, a former student at the University of British Columbia, and other defendants in a Vancouver B.C. Supreme Court.

Dennys said Galloway’s third book, The Cellist of Sarajevo , was met with “spectacular” success in Canada and internationally, and while his subsequent book, The Confabulist , didn’t initially reach those heights, the assault allegations forced the publisher to shelve the marketing campaign for its paperback run.

Galloway, the former chair of creative writing at the university in Vancouver, denies the allegations, which emerged in late 2015.

He is suing his accuser, known as A.B., whose assault claims were found unsubstantiated by a former judge, and other defendants, alleging they defamed him by publishing the unproven allegations online and elsewhere.

The court has previously heard from Galloway’s literary agent, Henry Dunow, who testified the allegations resulted in the cancellation of a $100,000 contract for a three-novel series Galloway pitched about a ventriloquist detective.

Dennys said Tuesday the publisher had signed the contract after Mary Ellen Boyd, the retired judge hired by the university to look into the allegations against Galloway, completed her probe and found the assault claims unsubstantiated.

Boyd’s report, which wasn’t made public, gave the publisher “the hope that the thing would die away completely now, because (Boyd) had indicated that there were no grounds for substantiating a rape,” Dennys said.

But the allegations didn’t cease, she said.

“We held in for two years waiting for things to pass, but in 2018, we eventually put it on hold, the (detective) series, because Steven indicated to us that he simply did not, trauma had been so great, that he certainly didn’t have the ability to write.”

Dennys said it was “one of the most heartbreaking things” she’d heard as a publisher.

Several people originally named as defendants in the lawsuit filed in 2018 have settled with Galloway and offered public apologies.

The court learned earlier this month that A.B. was no longer asserting in her defence that Galloway assaulted her, rather that she reported he had done so.

The woman, whose name is under a publication ban, is not testifying in the case, citing mental health struggles.

Galloway was fired by the university and has said the claims destroyed his career.

His lawyer, Dan Burnett, has sought to establish Galloway as a young author who was just getting started on the heels of the success of The Cellist of Sarajevo , when the allegations derailed that trajectory and destroyed his earning potential.

The case has drawn intense attention in the Canadian literary scene.

A group of authors, including Margaret Atwood, signed an open letter in November 2016 calling for an investigation into how the university handled Galloway’s case.

The court has previously heard A.B. was a former student who was older than Galloway and they had a two-year affair, which he has said ended in 2013.

A.B.’s former husband testified last week, called as a witness by Galloway’s lawyers.

Atwood has recently penned opinion articles supporting Galloway, writing in The Globe and Mail that testimony from A.B.’s ex-husband saying he was exchanging text messages with A.B. about a hockey game at the time of her alleged 2011 rape in Galloway’s office, was like the “Aha!” moment in a Sherlock Holmes novel.

stories.title: How Halifax’s famous donair fueled one man’s goal to run a marathon
stories.summary: As part of his training, David Wadden trekked to 59 locations to devour the pitas filled with spiced meat, fresh onions and tomatoes (no lettuce!) covered in a sweet sauce.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Mitchell Bailey
stories.content:
A Nova Scotia man says he recently trained for his first marathon in the most Halifax way possible: by eating dozens of donairs.

As part of his training, David Wadden trekked to 59 different locations to devour the pitas filled with spiced meat, fresh onions and tomatoes covered in a sweet sauce. Keeping with local tradition, lettuce was not on the menu.

“At the end of the day, I think it’s the donair itself that just brings everybody together,” he mused.

Wadden moved to Halifax from Cape Breton in 2018. After realizing he had little to offer in terms of donair recommendations whenever friends visited from outside the city, he embarked on a mission to strengthen his bond with Halifax’s official food.

“I decided … what if I ran or did an exercise to get to the donairs? And then the name ‘Donairathon’ came to be,” he said.

Wadden says he jogged and biked more than 800 kilometres across the city in hopes of locating the best donair, while also getting some exercise.

“Thirty-two kilometres was my longest run: 16 kilometres, eat the donair, and then 16 kilometres back,” he said.

In the process, Wadden says he became a donair connoisseur of sorts and documented his journey online.

He shares his donair reviews afterward, based on his own ranking system, which includes noting the donairs’ weight, price and size.

“ I don’t have a background in food. I don’t know if I have the best palate, but I do know that I can tell you what I’m seeing on my plate,” he said.

“So I just broke it down into a quantity category and a quality category of each ingredient in a donair and then kind of gave an overview of what I felt the donair gave me.”

The highest rating? Joann’s Pizza Land in Clayton Park.

“This donair is, it’s a milder spice, but I really like the spice blend that they have and everything that accompanies the donair meat is exactly what I like,” he said.

“It’s a perfect complement to each part.”

The restaurant’s manager, Nidhin George, says the first-place distinction has given them a boost in business.

“It was really good. It really helped us, it really helped the business,” said George. “We started getting new customers. People seemed to love the donair.”

Beyond satisfying his own curiosity and cravings, Wadden used the opportunity to help tackle food insecurity. He partnered with Feed Nova Scotia, and encourages his fans to donate to the charity through its website.

So far, he’s raised more than $2,000.

Feed Nova Scotia is even getting a bit creative with the partnership. They’re measuring donations by, what else, donairs.

“So if you donate $10, it’s like you donated a donair, $20, you donated two donairs,” said spokesperson Mandi MacDonald.

With food bank usage rising across the province, MacDonald says community-led initiatives like Wadden’s can go a long way.

“Sometimes just the smallest idea can turn into something that is so, so much bigger,” she said.

As for that marathon, Wadden successfully completed it two weeks ago in the Annapolis Valley.

“It was nice not having a backpack full of camera gear and donair rating supplies on my back. So that definitely helped my time,” he said.

“I did end up training enough, so I did finish the marathon, which was really nice.”

After the nine-month journey, Wadden says he has a newfound appreciation for donairs and the vast community of shop owners and customers that keep the city’s culture thriving.

stories.title: This Vancouver company has bagged a $3-million task order from Nasa
stories.summary: Vancouver space company EarthDaily will compare its findings to Landsat's land imaging records.
stories.author: National Post
stories.content:
A Canadian space organization has received a $3-million task order from Nasa to evaluate how its commercial satellite data can be used to complement data recorded by Landsat.

Landsat is the longest-running continuous U.S. Earth observation program, dating back to 1972, and the data it records is accessible to anyone across the world.

Vancouver-based EarthDaily, which launched in 2021, will provide Earth observation data to Nasa and the U.S. Geological Survey (Usgs), who both assist in operating Landsat.

According to an Oct. 26 press release, Nasa and Usgs scientists will assess the consistency and quality of EarthDaily’s satellite measurements and compare it to Landsat’s data.

Don Osborne, the chief executive officer of EarthDaily, told National Post that they were approached by Nasa because “they have been contemplating a next generation series of satellites called Landsat Next,” and rather than build the infrastructure themselves, they would look for commercial imagery providers to supplement the program.

He added that Nasa chose to work with the Canadian company because of its “forward-thinking” approach to Earth imaging.

“When we designed our system, one of the things that we wanted to do was to be compatible with the two major sort of gold standards for Earth imaging out there, which is Landsat in the United States and Sentinel in Europe,” said Osborne.

According to EarthDaily, its eight satellites can cover all of earth’s landmass in two days as they orbit the earth. Their satellites use multiple imaging systems to collect data across 22 spectral bands, covering the visible range, near-infrared, short-wave infrared and thermal infrared wavelengths.

The satellites operate in a similar manner to the Landsat satellites, which collect optical data and thermal-infrared data.

“If you compare an image off of our satellite with an image off of Landsat, you’ll see the same specificity,” said Osborne.

The combination of EarthDaily and Landsat data will hopefully be used in order to identify patterns and broad area changes, such as coastline changes, deforestation and glacial melting.

The pilot program will seek to determine whether commercial data products are compatible with Landsat’s long term land imaging records, and if future collaborations between government-operated systems and private organizations are possible.

“Landsat has created an extraordinary scientific record of how our planet is changing,” said Osborne in the press release. “To understand change, you first need measurements you can trust and compare over time.”

In addition to land imaging, the examination will also be used to see how commercial observations can assist in machine learning and the creation of AI observation models.

“If you have poor quality data … it could create false positives,” said Osborne. “So, the real key here is to be able to produce .. standard data which is consistent from … day to day and from year to year, and we’ve gone to great lengths to make that happen.”

This will assist in Nasa’s goal of expanding AI use in scientific research and in the analysis of complicated data sets.

The findings from the examination will be reviewed jointly by EarthDaily and the Usgs over an undetermined time period.

stories.title: Four-day retail enforcement operation in Coquitlam, B.C., leads to 31 arrests
stories.summary: Coquitlam - Thirty-one people have been arrested and more than $6,000 worth of stolen property has been recovered in a police blitz on retail theft in Coquitlam, B.C.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Coquitlam - Thirty-one people have been arrested and more than $6,000 worth of stolen property has been recovered in a police blitz on retail theft in Coquitlam, B.C.

Mounties say officers launched the enforcement operation between Sept. 14 and 17, setting off recommendations for almost three dozen charges, the seizure of two weapons and the recovery of $6,190 worth of property.

stories.title: Olivia Rodrigo turned Toronto’s Scotiabank Arena into a jamboree of lovesick girlhood
stories.summary: The 23-year-old songstress gave a performance well beyond her years, with a highly intentional setlist and note-perfect vocal stylings
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
It was a good night for Olivias in Toronto. On Monday, Olivia Chow won her bid for re-election, crushing her right-leaning challenger Brad Bradford by more than 13 percentage points.

But ask any Toronto teen, and they’ll tell you about the far sparklier Olivia who took over the city that evening: Olivia Rodrigo, whose note-perfect performance at Scotiabank Arena was a jamboree of lovesick girlhood.

Young women arrived at the venue dressed to the nines in pink lace and sequinned hot pants. On more than one occasion, I heard a school-aged girl express excitement over being allowed to swear while singing the words to Rodrigo’s punky love songs. Sugar-sweet sodas flowed plentifully alongside fruity cocktails; high-heeled shoes clogged Scotiabank’s walkways as young feet became sore from waiting in line for T-shirts.

All to say: Monday’s crowd was overwhelmingly adolescent, female and ready to scream.

You could say the same of Rodrigo, 23, who took to her flower-covered stage in a frilly babydoll dress, long ribbons flowing from her shoulders as she sang drop dead , the lead single from her recent album You Seem Pretty Sad For a Girl So in Love.

Rodrigo’s latest record is structured much like a relationship: Its tracks outline a love story from infatuated roots (“Kiss me and I might drop dead,” she croons on the infectious opener) to an inevitably brutal breakup (“Why’d I try at all?” she later laments on cigarette smoke ).

It’s a neat layout for an album, but one that doesn’t necessarily translate to a large-scale stage show. So, ON the Unraveled tour, Rodrigo instead interweaves her newest songs with her back catalogue, arranging the concert into a multirecord kaleidoscope of “seasons.” With each change in the onstage weather comes a nifty visual effect to sell the story, from that eye-catching meadow of pink-and-white wildflowers to a cathartic winter rainstorm (complete with real rain).

It’s a mature, intentional setlist that allows Rodrigo to show off her full range of songwriting, from the Disney-ish ballads of 2021’s Sour to the far edgier rock anthems of You Seem Pretty Sad For a Girl So in Love, whose influences span The Cure to The Cranberries .

After drop dead , Rodrigo transitioned into u + me = <3 , another plucky serenade to a new lover, and so american , a playful ditty from the deluxe version of the singer’s second album Guts .

Summer came in a blaze of angry songs about insecurity and the pain of the world writ large, starting with my way , about an interloper in a fragile fling. Rodrigo then turned toward politics with serena joy , a pastiche of The Handmaid’s Tale in which the singer warns obliquely that “if they do it to them, they’re gonna do it to you.” (Cue enthusiastic headbanging.)

Olivia Rodrigo’s Lilith Fair was sanctuary in turbulent times between Canada and the U.S.

By this point in Monday’s concert, the sound level in Scotiabank Arena was approaching the upper extremes of human comfort: My Apple Watch logged a high of 115 decibels during bad idea right? , Rodrigo’s tongue-in-cheek ode to an ill-advised hookup. Things got quieter – but no less passionate – during vampire and purple , two introspective songs about the symbiosis that occurs during a mismatched romance.

Fall then descended in a flurry of red confetti, the floor mostly cleared of its wildflower carpet by agile stagehands. Surrounded by dying flora, Rodrigo ratted off stupid song, maggots for brains and traitor in quick succession, occasionally taking an electric guitar to accompany herself amidst the foliage.

After a stripped-back version of begged, Rodrigo surprised fans with lacy , a new addition to the setlist, before closing the season with the oh-so-sad cigarette smoke , which saw Rodrigo stretch her voice to the upper echelons of its range, never once faltering on a high note or wail.

It’s the Unraveled tour’s winter set that’s gone the most viral on TikTok, and for good reason – the act closes with a rainy rendition of the cure , whose water effects completely melted away Rodrigo’s papery white dress to reveal a sparkly red minidress on Monday night.

The moment, executed on a small B-stage, was as thrilling for her fashion as for her voice, which continued to hold its own against an earsplitting crowd and booming band; she could have ended the concert there and no one would have felt shortchanged.

But Rodrigo kept going, returning to bright floral imagery for the most screechable songs in her canon: deja vu , all-american bitch and expectations. While Rodrigo’s own vocal health is clearly in fine shape, her Toronto audiences’ might be in trouble after Monday’s gig – the screaming during all-american bitch , in particular, seemed to shred every vocal cord in the arena. (My own included.)

Since Rodrigo’s 2022 tour to promote Sour , I’ve had my doubts about the artist’s ability to curate a setlist: Until this year, she barely had enough material to justify playing anything but her albums in full.

But with the Unraveled tour, Rodrigo has demonstrated a capacity to think deeply about how her music lands outside the studio. New live arrangements of her songs vibrate with intensity and intricate harmonies; clever long-exposure visuals make her grungiest songs look like they sound, as if experienced in a psychedelic trance.

The Unraveled setlist kills a few darlings – I was surprised not to hear get him back! or love is embarrassing , two of the centrepiece bops from Rodrigo’s last tour – but the concert ultimately emerges far greater than the sum of its songs.

On Monday night, two Olivias demonstrated that they’re blooming anew – one as a freshly sophisticated artist, one as a mayor at the start of her next term. But more importantly, both Olivias gave Toronto’s youngest women something to look up to: a decisive electoral victory, and a blossomy concert tour worthy of the rock gods who inspired it.

stories.title: Being my daughter’s sous-chef for a week was exactly what I needed
stories.summary: Watching her in her element, I was able to see the capable and resilient woman she had become
stories.author: Ann Diehl
stories.content:
First Person is a daily personal piece submitted by readers. Have a story to tell? See our guidelines at tgam.CA/essayguide .

It wasn’t the Vancouver Island getaway I had planned – or anything close to it.

My husband and I were looking forward to staying in our daughter Sarah’s new condo just before she left to work as a chef at a wilderness lodge.

Not long after we arrived, her phone rang. Sarah’s sous-chef couldn’t make the trip.

Ten guests were arriving from New York, expecting three gourmet meals a day, everything fresh and made from scratch.

“There’s no way I can do this alone,” Sarah said. “I’ll have to cancel.”

Sarah had spent years working as a professional chef around the world. Now halfway through a master’s degree and changing careers, she accepted only a few summer cooking jobs to help pay her tuition.

Knowing how important this one was, the next morning, I found myself on a boat with Sarah, surrounded by boxes and coolers stuffed with $5,000 worth of fine foods. I marvelled at the sights as we navigated the channels between the many small islands scattered along the coast.

After 90 minutes, Sarah pointed out the lodge, perched on a small hill among the trees. We were welcomed by staff who carried our supplies up to the lodge.

With guests arriving by float plane in a few hours, Sarah quickly sprang into action. We unpacked boxes, finding places for the food in the large pantry and industrial fridge and freezer. Sarah started preparing dinner and I was assigned the task of making five different salad dressings. After an hour of chopping and mixing, I proudly set the tall bottles on the counter, suggesting they needed labels.

“Don’t bother,” Sarah said, stirring a pot of crème brulee. “We don’t have time. Just taste them before you use them.”

This offended my organizational sensibilities. I spent far too long hunting for masking tape and a felt marker and carefully labelling each bottle. As I put them into the fridge, I thought it was clear that there were still a few things my daughter could learn from me.

And so began a week of chopping, peeling, mixing, stirring and scrubbing. My job was to work under the chef, carry out instructions quickly and efficiently. I was also to keep what I May have thought were good suggestions to myself.

This is not always easy when the chef is your daughter. When Sarah was young, I had been the one overseeing kitchen tasks, insisting things be done my way. Now she was looking over my shoulder, asking me to pick up the pace, make the charcuterie platter more attractive, suggesting I be extra careful when plating dessert.

After many hours on my feet and too little sleep, I sometimes couldn’t help but make a few snappish comments. Once, when Sarah told me to make another pot of rice because mine wasn’t light and fluffy enough, I found myself close to tears.

But as we settled into the daily routine, I started really watching what Sarah was doing. She could have five pots bubbling on the stove and several pans in the oven while decorating 10 plates with sauces, herbs and flowers. She knew exactly when to pull crab from a huge pot of boiling water and how long to sear fresh ling cod. She was calm, exacting and completely in charge.

Even when I burned a pan of pine nuts, she remained calm. Another test arose after I had prepared a beautiful Mediterranean salad with olives, feta, grape tomatoes and fresh herbs. I took my carefully labelled balsamic dressing from the fridge, gave the salad a generous coating and handed it to Sarah.

She popped a tomato into her mouth and frowned.

“You used the Asian dressing.”

Somehow, in my determination to label everything properly, I had mixed up the labels.

The guests were already seated. There was no time to start again. Sarah smiled, picked up the plates and carried them to the dining room. Miraculously, there were no complaints. After that, I tasted everything.

At the end of each day, guided by moonlight, Sarah and I made our way up to our little cabin in the trees. We would pour a glass of wine and talk about the day – the things that went wrong, the things that went right, the antics of the guest, sometimes laughing until we cried. Usually, after only a few sips, we crawled into bed, exhausted.

Eventually Sarah found a young sous-chef to take my place. She carried my bag down the boat and gave me a hug.

“You were great, Mom,” she said. “Are you sure you don’t want to stay?”

“I’m lucky I made it through the week,” I laughed.

As the boat pulled away, I waved at my daughter standing on the dock, amazed that she could keep up this pace for another two weeks.

I had gone to the island because I thought Sarah needed me. It turned out I needed the week, too – to step out of my familiar role as her mother. There hadn’t been any time to explore the island, swim in the bay, watch for whales. Instead, there were precious hours with my daughter, a unique opportunity to work side-by-side, to see the capable and resilient woman she had become.

Ann Diehl lives in Kamloops, B.C.

It wasn’t the Vancouver Island getaway I had planned – or anything close to it.
My husband and I were looking forward to staying in our daughter Sarah’s new condo just before she left to work as a chef at a wilderness lodge.
Not long after we arrived, her phone rang. Sarah’s sous-chef couldn’t make the trip.
Ten guests were arriving from New York, expecting three gourmet meals a day, everything fresh and made from scratch.
“There’s no way I can do this alone,” Sarah said. “I’ll have to cancel.”
Sarah had spent years working as a professional chef around the world. Now halfway through a master’s degree and changing careers, she accepted only a few summer cooking jobs to help pay her tuition.

Knowing how important this one was, the next morning, I found myself on a boat with Sarah, surrounded by boxes and coolers stuffed with $5,000 worth of fine foods. I marvelled at the sights as we navigated the channels between the many small islands scattered along the coast.
After 90 minutes, Sarah pointed out the lodge, perched on a small hill among the trees. We were welcomed by staff who carried our supplies up to the lodge.

With guests arriving by float plane in a few hours, Sarah quickly sprang into action. We unpacked boxes, finding places for the food in the large pantry and industrial fridge and freezer. Sarah started preparing dinner and I was assigned the task of making five different salad dressings. After an hour of chopping and mixing, I proudly set the tall bottles on the counter, suggesting they needed labels.
“Don’t bother,” Sarah said, stirring a pot of crème brulee. “We don’t have time. Just taste them before you use them.”

This offended my organizational sensibilities. I spent far too long hunting for masking tape and a felt marker and carefully labelling each bottle. As I put them into the fridge, I thought it was clear that there were still a few things my daughter could learn from me.

And so began a week of chopping, peeling, mixing, stirring and scrubbing. My job was to work under the chef, carry out instructions quickly and efficiently. I was also to keep what I May have thought were good suggestions to myself.

This is not always easy when the chef is your daughter. When Sarah was young, I had been the one overseeing kitchen tasks, insisting things be done my way. Now she was looking over my shoulder, asking me to pick up the pace, make the charcuterie platter more attractive, suggesting I be extra careful when plating dessert.

After many hours on my feet and too little sleep, I sometimes couldn’t help but make a few snappish comments. Once, when Sarah told me to make another pot of rice because mine wasn’t light and fluffy enough, I found myself close to tears.

Usually, after only a few sips, we crawled into bed, exhausted.

“You were great, Mom,” she said. “Are you sure you don’t want to stay?”
