stories.title: Belleville cop who prevented a Jewish massacre released from the hospital and is recovering at home
stories.summary: Constable Jeff Smith was ambushed and gravely hurt when 29-year-old Sean Ward opened fire outside Sons of Jacob Synagogue.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
“ Constable Smith and his family remain incredibly grateful for the overwhelming support shown by the community and beyond over the past several weeks. Every well wish and message of encouragement has been sincerely appreciated,” the police service said in a press release.

In an email to National Post, the police service added, “Regarding return to work question, right now, the priority is his recovery. We are encouraged by his progress and are pleased that he is able to recover surrounded by the support of family and loved ones.”

Smith, a 13-year veteran of the Belleville police force, was stationed outside Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., during a Yom Kippur service on Sept. 20. He was ambushed and gravely hurt when 29-year-old Sean Ward opened fire. Ward yelled, “you are going to die for the Jews”, presumably at Smith and his colleague Const. Michael McCurdy, who was at the scene in less than three minutes. The two officers put their lives on the line to protect approximately 25 congregants gathered inside the synagogue , none of whom were hurt as the shooting ensued.

Smith sustained critical injuries after he was shot in the head and body. He has been in the hospital since then undergoing multiple surgeries until his release Thursday. Ward sustained injuries and succumbed to them at the hospital a day after the shooting. McCurdy was not injured during the shooting.

'Right now, he is fighting': Wife of injured Belleville police officer is grateful for outpouring of support

“Jeff, we wish you strength, healing and peace as you begin this next stage of your recovery. We hope you and your family can take some comfort in knowing that thousands of Canadians continue to stand beside you,” wrote campaign organizer Derek Kreindler on Thursday. As of Friday morning, the campaign had raised $969,110.

In an email to National Post, the police service added, “Regarding return to work question, right now, the priority is his recovery. We are encouraged by his progress and are pleased that he is able to recover surrounded by the support of family and loved ones.”

Smith, a 13-year veteran of the Belleville police force, was stationed outside Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., during a Yom Kippur service on Sept. 20. He was ambushed and gravely hurt when 29-year-old Sean Ward opened fire. Ward yelled, “you are going to die for the Jews”, presumably at Smith and his colleague Const. Michael McCurdy, who was at the scene in less than three minutes. The two officers put their lives on the line to protect approximately 25 congregants gathered inside the synagogue , none of whom were hurt as the shooting ensued.

Smith sustained critical injuries after he was shot in the head and body. He has been in the hospital since then undergoing multiple surgeries until his release Thursday. Ward sustained injuries and succumbed to them at the hospital a day after the shooting. McCurdy was not injured during the shooting.

stories.title: Nearly three-quarters of Canadians support PM in seeking closer ties with Europe
stories.summary: Majorities across Canada say Carney is on the right track, though most current Conservative supporters say he is going in the wrong direction
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Almost 73 per cent of Canadians say Prime Minister Mark Carney is on the right track in seeking a closer economic and security alliance with the European Union, according to a new poll by Canada Pulse Insights , a public opinion research firm in Toronto.

Seventy-three per cent of respondents said they agree that, based on the ongoing unpredictability that has come to define Canada’s trading relationship with the United States, strengthening ties with Europe will protect Canada’s economy.

The remaining 27 per cent of respondents disagree, saying Carney is heading in the wrong direction, because closer EU ties will not be sufficient to offset the negative impact of the trade war with the U.S. That figure includes a majority of Conservative supporters who say Carney is heading in the wrong direction.

The survey findings come as the Canada–EU Summit takes place in Montreal on Oct. 29 and 30, where Carney is hosting European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa. The focus of the discussions is expected to be closer co-operation in trade, defence and security, energy, critical minerals and technology.

The poll also found majority support in every region across Canada for the Prime Minister’s approach. British Columbia leads that view at 81 per cent, followed by Atlantic Canada (79 per cent), Québec (75 per cent), Ontario (72 per cent), Saskatchewan/Manitoba (64 per cent) and Alberta (62 per cent).

Meanwhile, support rises with age and education. Among Canadians 55 and over, 83 per cent support Carney’s efforts, compared with 66 per cent of respondents 18 to 34 and 67 per cent of those aged 35 to 54.

Among university graduates, 82 per cent approve. That compares with 70 per cent of respondents with trades or college education, and 68 per cent of those with a high school diploma or less.

Support is lower among Canadians in households earning less than $50,000, at 62 per cent, compared with 75 per cent or more in higher-income households.

Men (71 per cent) and women (75 per cent) express similar views in supporting Carney.

Among supporters of the federal Liberals, 95 per cent support closer ties with Europe, as well as 86 per cent of NDP supporters and 83 per cent of Bloc Québécois supporters. A majority of undecided voters (79 per cent) also support closer ties with Europe.

However, a majority of present Conservative supporters (58 per cent) say that Carney is heading in the wrong direction, while 42 per cent say he is heading in the right direction.

There is a distinct difference between past Conservative voters and respondents who express present support for the party. Among Canadians who said they voted Conservative in April 2025, there is an even split, with 51 per cent saying Carney is on the right track and 49 per cent disagreeing.

This survey was conducted with 1,531 Canadian adults (18+) as part of a Canada Pulse Insights national omnibus survey, fielded from October 1–8, 2026. The margin of error for a comparable probability-based random sample of the same size is ±2.5 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

stories.title: Ottawa designates B.C. port expansion as project of national interest
stories.summary: Port of Vancouver plans to expand existing facility in Delta, adding capacity at the country’s largest port
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa listed a $5.9-billion West Coast port expansion on Friday as a project of national interest, the second large development to be afforded a fast-track approval process under legislation passed by the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney .

Roberts Bank Terminal 2, located in Delta, B.C., is aimed at increasing the port’s container capacity by 50 per cent and supporting up to $100-billion in annual trade, the federal government said in a statement. The expansion is led by the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority.

With the designation, the three-berth container terminal is expected to get a final investment decision by the middle of next year, the government said.

“Roberts Bank Terminal 2 will add much-needed capacity at our largest port, reduce bottlenecks and strengthen the transportation links Canadian businesses count on,” Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said in a statement.

This is the second major project to be given the coveted designation under the Building Canada Act after the Pacific Link oil pipeline , which was listed at the start of October. The pipeline project would ship one million barrels of Alberta oil a day to the same area of the port expansion south of Vancouver. It is slated to have its approval process completed by Sept. 1, 2027.

Three other developments are awaiting possible listing: the Mackenzie Valley Highway Project in the Northwest Territories, Grays Bay Road and Port Project in Nunavut and a deep nuclear waste storage project in Northwestern Ontario.

All are being evaluated by the Calgary-based Major Projects Office, which the Carney government created as a way to get more developments built to boost and diversify trade. The objective is to bolster Canadian sovereignty against U.S. President Donald Trump ’s trade war, the government has said.

The port expansion is aimed at saving $1-billion a year in shipping costs after investments in rail, logistics facilities and port modernization, the government said. It is also expected to reduce delivery times between Vancouver and Toronto by 17 per cent.

The project has already been through more than a decade of regulatory reviews. It includes a marine land mass and wharf structure, a widened causeway to add roads and rail lines, and an expanded tub basin to support shipping.

It is part of a larger Port of Vancouver Gateway Strategy that would also comprise rail infrastructure, land development for bulk terminals and environmental protections.

stories.title: How Canada's new pact with the European Union might affect you
stories.summary: Ottawa - Canada's new partnership with the European Union is meant to provide benefits to people on both continents.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Canada’s new partnership with the European Union is meant to provide benefits to people on both continents.

The two jurisdictions wrapped up a summit in Montreal on Friday with various agreements, many of which will take months or years to finalize.

Canada and the EU have signed agreements to pursue a much closer relationship. Both Prime Minister Mark Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen describe it as a step on the path to "associate membership" in the EU. (Oct. 30, 2026)

Here’s a look at some of the possible benefits for different groups.

Canada and the European Union are promising to eventually update their “youth mobility partnership” with the goal of offering young people more opportunities to go abroad.

That would build on existing university exchange programs and working-holiday programs Canada operates with multiple European countries.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU wants Canada to fully join Erasmus+, the EU’s student exchange program that offers training and study opportunities in member nations.

Canada is also hoping to become a full member of the Horizon Europe research partnership program by 2028, which would offer new funding for research and innovation projects undertaken with European peers.

Tech workers

Prime Minister Mark Carney said the pact with the EU will give Canadian researchers access to European supercomputers that can cut processing times from six months to a single day.

Canada and the EU have signed a digital trade agreement that looks to fold certain sectors into the trade agreement that has governed how goods are exchanged for a decade.

The European Commission website defines digital trade as “commerce enabled by electronic means.” It cites banks transferring data, agricultural commodity traders using e-signatures and freight companies tracking their machines through the internet.

Canada is also working on joining the EU’s “instant payment systems” to make it easier to send funds. Both jurisdictions are also exploring opening each other’s markets further to Canadian and European banks, insurers and fintech companies.

Mining firms

The European Investment Bank will seek to fund projects to mine critical raw materials in Canada, thanks to negotiations that concluded Friday.

Von der Leyen said Thursday that European “industrial demand, technology and investment” can help get such mineral projects off of the ground.

Canada has signed some sort of updated competition agreement with the EU that looks to crack down on anticompetitive actions by transatlantic businesses, though there were few details provided Friday.

The EU’s border agency is also helping its Canadian counterpart tackle migrant smuggling, human trafficking and identity fraud by exchanging information through the European Border Surveillance System.

Both jurisdictions have also agreed to launch formal discussion groups on the Arctic, foreign information manipulation and interference, climate security and transport.

A joint statement says on misinformation, both sides have agreed to move “from a reactive stance to a proactive one.”

Soldiers in Latvia

In June, Canada became the only non-European partner in the EU’s defence procurement program SAFE.

Just one project had come out of that arrangement until Friday, when Canada announced a contract worth up to $43 million to provide helmets to Latvian troops.

Montreal-based firm Galvion will produce the helmets for Latvia, which has been home to Canada’s largest foreign military presence for years. Canadian soldiers are in Latvia to prevent a Russian invasion.

As Washington pulls back support for Ukraine’s defence against Russia’s full-scale invasion, Europe has stepped up with more funding.

Carney announced Friday that Canada will join an EU loan program for Ukraine. Ottawa has pledged an initial contribution of 500 million euros, roughly C$775 million.

“We will continue to provide comprehensive political, financial, economic, energy, humanitarian, military and diplomatic support to Ukraine and its people,” says the joint statement Canada and the EU inked Friday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

stories.title: Canada still reviewing F-35 purchase after Rcaf received its first jets: minister
stories.summary: Ottawa - Defence Minister David McGuinty says the federal government's planned purchase of 88 F-35 stealth fighters remains under review, even after the military received its first two F-35s in recent days.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Defence Minister David McGuinty says the federal government’s planned purchase of 88 F-35 stealth fighters remains under review, even after the military received its first two F-35s in recent days.

McGuinty told reporters today the federal government will take all the time it needs to consider all factors, including industrial benefits and emerging autonomous air systems that can fly alongside fighter craft.

stories.title: Inquest into death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet on hold for investigation: coroner
stories.summary: Toronto - A coroner's inquest into the death of a Toronto woman who fell from a 24th-floor balcony while police where in her home has been put on hold indefinitely.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - A coroner’s inquest into the death of a Toronto woman who fell from a 24th-floor balcony while police were in her home was put on hold indefinitely Thursday just as it reached the final stretch of the proceedings.

“I know everyone has been working extremely hard during this inquest. Unfortunately, I will be adjourning the inquest until further notice,” said Dr. David Cameron, the coroner presiding over the inquest into the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet.

“The reason for this is that we have some quite unanticipated investigation that needs to be done before we can continue.”

The coroner gave no details on the nature or focus of the investigation but said jurors and the public would be informed when the inquest was ready to resume.

The inquest finished hearing evidence on Wednesday and was set to reconvene Thursday afternoon so that lawyers for about a dozen parties could make their closing remarks and suggest recommendations to the jury.

Korchinski-Paquet, a 29-year-old woman of Afro-Indigenous and Ukrainian descent, died on May 27, 2020 after police were called to the west-end apartment she shared with relatives.

Her death closely followed the police killing of George Floyd, a Black man from Minneapolis, fuelling protests as well as calls to defund the police. It was also one of several cases to draw scrutiny on how police interact with people in crisis.

One of Ontario’s police watchdogs, the Special Investigations Unit, cleared police of wrongdoing in her death, finding that Korchinski-Paquet fell while trying to move from her apartment’s balcony to the one next door. Her family disputed the findings.

The SIU did not participate in the inquest, and its investigation is outside the scope of the proceedings.

Last week, Korchinski-Paquet’s mother directed a new allegation at police as she testified about her memories of that day, throwing the inquest temporarily off course.

Claudette Beals alleged officers pushed her daughter toward the balcony, drawing concerns from several lawyers and causing the inquest to go on an extended break so they could figure out a way forward.

Two officers who were in the apartment, Const. Shane Beaudoin and then-Const. Adam Vandenbrink, had previously testified that Korchinski-Paquet was allowed into the apartment to use the bathroom, then introduced to a paramedic.

Korchinski-Paquet moved quickly to the balcony, knocking over an air conditioning unit in the process, they said. When she disappeared from view, they believed she had stepped onto the adjacent balcony, and did not realize she had fallen, the officers testified.

The inquest has focused largely on Korchinski-Paquet’s history of seizures from epilepsy as well as education and training around epilepsy and postictal delirium or psychosis, mental states that can occur after seizures and lead to uncharacteristic behaviour.

Korchinski-Paquet had experienced two seizures earlier in the day, hours before police were called over a fight involving knives. Korchinski-Paquet, her mother and her brother each called 911 and mentioned her diagnosis and seizures to the call taker, jurors heard.

The jury watched a compilation video combining the recordings of the five calls and two police microphones with CCTV footage from the hallway outside Korchinski-Paquet’s apartment and video from a police cruiser.

Korchinski-Paquet made three of the 911 calls, telling the call taker she was having difficulty breathing after being attacked by her mother and brother. She said she had lost control and thrown two bottles at them in the hallway.

She mentioned her epilepsy after being asked if anyone involved had mental health issues.

In their calls, Korchinski-Paquet’s mother and brother mentioned that she was often agitated after her seizures. Her brother, Reece Korchinski, said she assaulted him with knives after a dispute over the TV volume.

Beals testified she called 911 because she wanted police to take her daughter to Toronto’s Centre for Addiction and Mental Health.

Six police officers and two paramedics responded to the calls, the inquest heard.

Korchinski told the inquest police assumed an “aggressive” tone toward his sister, treating her like a suspect rather than a citizen. He also felt threatened by what appeared to be a shotgun in one of the officers’ hands, not knowing at the time it was a less-lethal weapon used by police, he said.

Under cross-examination Wednesday, Korchinski said that while he understood police had been called for an assault involving knives, the officers had the chance to assess the situation directly after they arrived at the scene and could see that neither he, his sister or their mother were dangerous.

The officers should have let his sister enter the apartment alone instead of going with her, he said.

“If the police never showed up that day, Regis would still be alive,” Korchinski said.

Beaudoin and Vandenbrink were the first to arrive, the inquest heard. They went up to talk to the family and debriefed each other once some of their colleagues showed up, the jury heard.

Vandenbrink told the inquest it was during that conversation that he first heard about Korchinski-Paquet’s seizures.

Both officers testified that they never stepped out onto the balcony, nor did they know at the time about postictal delirium or psychosis.

A neurologist who reviewed Korchinski-Paquet’s records after her death testified that she had previously shown symptoms in keeping with postictal delirium or postictal psychosis.

It would be “nearly impossible” to tell whether someone was acting aggressively due to delirium or psychosis after a seizure or for some other reason without knowing their medical history, Dr. Julien Hébert told the inquest.

Jurors in coroner’s inquests do not assign blame or legal responsibility, but they may make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths in the future.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

stories.title: Canada welcomes EU leaders to Montreal for talks on next steps in relationship
stories.summary: Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to welcome European Commissioner Ursula von der Leyen to Montreal today after months of pursuing closer ties with the EU.
stories.author: David Baxter The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - Prime Minister Mark Carney now says Canada is working to become an “associate member” of the European Union, after largely avoiding that term.

“We’re here because we share a common mission. We’re in the process of forging a new alliance for the future, with Canada as an associate member,” Carney said Thursday.

The prime minister on Thursday welcomed senior officials from Brussels to the two-day Canada-EU Summit in Montreal to negotiate a new partnership — though critics say the outcomes have been unclear.

“We can work on everything from AI and climate, to energy and security, you just name it,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.

She said the term “associate member” is helpful for deepening policy alignment.

“Canada cannot become a fully fledged member of the European Union because of geography. But we both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible, and this is why we are discussing the idea of Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union,” she said.

Von der Leyen first proposed associate member status for Canada in a September speech to the European Parliament. Canadian and European officials immediately downplayed that terminology, opting instead for “alliance for the future.”

Several EU member nations, including Germany, have rejected the idea of associate membership.

Some have expressed unease with Canada gaining special status while countries such as Ukraine go through arduous reforms to obtain full membership. Others fear a side deal with Canada could encourage countries to leave the EU and seek select benefits while avoiding some of the obligations of full membership.

Prime Minister Carney has said repeatedly the substance of the agreement is more important than the language used to describe it.

“This new alliance is not a marketing exercise. The name doesn’t matter,” he told reporters.

“What matters to Canadians ultimately from this new alliance is going to be affordability, it’s going to be opportunity,” he said, arguing closer economic links will lead to more purchasing power for Canadians.

Von der Leyen’s visit comes after months of Carney pursuing closer ties with the EU. He has argued Europe complements Canada’s economic strengths and shares its values.

Thursday’s agenda included a welcome dinner with elected and business leaders. Canadian and European leaders are expected to get down to talks on Friday.

In his own Thursday afternoon speech, European Council President Antonio Costa endorsed the “bold idea” of associate membership for Canada.

“Regardless of the specific term used, one thing is clear: our partnership will be the closest, deepest and most unique one possible,” he said in French.

“At our summit tomorrow, we will announce an agreement on digital trade that will complement the CETA,” he added, referring to the EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement.

“We need to strengthen labour mobility. It’s very important what we are doing with students, but we can do more with labour activity,” he said in English, pointing to how credentials are accepted in both jurisdictions.

“Mutual recognition is good. And also, to use better the digital tools to facilitate air transport on both sides of the Atlantic.”

In her Thursday speech, von der Leyen said the EU wants to work first with Canada and then with other nations to reinforce their sovereignty and interests.

“We can no longer let ourselves be shackled by the limits of the old world order,” she said, adding that nations can work strategically together instead of facing down threats alone.

“We are witnessing a deeper decay in international order. Alliances and assumptions that have enabled our prosperity and security are changing rapidly.”

She cited “choke points” in trade, where one country coerces another by manipulating supply chains. She did not name specific countries.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly told reporters Thursday that Canada’s work with the EU seeks to reduce reliance on the U.S. as Washington pursues its trade war.

“The challenge of the era is really to be capable of saving companies that otherwise will fail and will have job losses. So we’re in a hurry,” she said in French.

Von der Leyen said in her speech that a new partnership could see Canada increase its mining of critical minerals, aided by European “industrial demand, technology and investment.”

She said Canadian startups and researchers will soon be able to train their models on the EU’s supercomputers.

“Tomorrow we will finalize our agreement to bring Canada into Europe’s infrastructure for supercomputing,” she said Thursday.

Both sides are also working on joint projects in the Arctic on ocean monitoring, critical raw materials and connectivity as Russia rebuilds its military footprint in the region.

The EU “will deepen Canada’s engagement” in university student exchanges through the Erasmus+ program, von der Leyen said. Both sides are also “working to strengthen Canada’s participation” in the next phase of a scientific research program called Horizon, she added.

She said there also could be cross-Atlantic collaboration between elected officials and judiciaries.

As von der Leyen spoke, the Conservatives dismissed the summit as a “distraction” from deteriorating living standards and the trade war.

“Canadians are faced with another distraction for the next two days, of more meaningless agreements. Meanwhile, they go to food banks and struggle to pay their mortgages,” Conservative trade critic Stephanie Kusie said on Parliament Hill.

Her party colleagues argued Canada should avoid deepening ties with Europe until all EU member states ratify a decade-old trade deal with Canada and Brussels stops charging carbon tariffs on Canadian imports.

CETA was signed during the EU-Canada summit 10 years ago and has been applied provisionally since 2017.

Nine EU members have not fully ratified it. Slovenia became the latest country to ratify CETA on Sept. 29. Belgium, Bulgaria, Cyprus, France, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy and Poland are the remaining holdouts.

The Conservatives have claimed that any new deal with the EU would see Canada lose control over immigration. Federal officials have insisted repeatedly that any labour mobility agreements would be limited to specific professions or student exchanges.

The Asia-Pacific Foundation argued in a Thursday brief that Carney is focusing on European economies with far slower growth than their Asian counterparts.

“The EU — despite its many strengths — is an occasionally distracted suitor, reckoning with sluggish growth, infighting over budgets and Ukraine (and how to label Canada’s relation to the bloc), and ascendant far-right leaders,” the institute wrote in a Thursday newsletter.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

— With files from Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version said 10 EU members states had not ratified the free trade pact with Canada.

stories.title: Ontario pauses some skills training funding for unemployed people: career colleges
stories.summary: Toronto - In addition to freezing Ontario Student Assistance Program payments to all private post-secondary institutions, the province has paused at least some funding through Better Jobs Ontario, which helps unemployed people get skills training.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - In addition to freezing Ontario Student Assistance Program payments to all private post-secondary institutions, the province has paused at least some funding through Better Jobs Ontario, which helps unemployed people get skills training.

But the government won’t explicitly say so.

There has been no public communication from the government about the status of the program that aims to get people off social assistance and into the workforce, but people who were depending on the program and the institutions that were set to train them are taking note.

Reece Daniel was hoping to begin an HVAC program in London, Ont., on Oct. 19. The government had initially scheduled a meeting for Oct. 13 to give him information about the funding agreement, but a few days before that they cancelled and said applications were under review.

The next intake for the HVAC program is in May 2027.

“This course was something that was going to get me jumped back on my feet,” Daniel said.

“I’m still probably going to be presented with the opportunity to go to school next year, but the significant delays ... waiting for so long, putting off work for so long, it’s a little bit disappointing and frustrating.”

Pathways Employment Help Centre had been assisting Daniel in his application, and is seeing other clients experiencing the same delays and uncertainty with their Better Jobs Ontario funding decisions, the CEO said.

“Despite our agency’s repeated efforts to obtain clarification, the absence of a definitive decision prevented Reece and other clients from proceeding with their planned training as scheduled,” Ben Cecil said.

Career Colleges Ontario said the association has heard from member schools that Better Jobs Ontario funding for students at career colleges has been paused, but it has not received any formal communication from the government.

“We are concerned about any disruption to funding for students attending compliant institutions,” it wrote in a statement.

“As with OSAP, we are urging the government to restore access to funding for students attending institutions where there are no identified compliance concerns. We continue to advocate for a targeted approach that allows students to access the support they need while maintaining strong accountability across the sector.”

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced earlier this month that OSAP payments are paused for students at all private post-secondary institutions, after preliminary audit findings raised serious concerns about financial aid usage at some career colleges.

Trillium College has suspended classes due to the OSAP pause, and wrote in a letter to students that it is a temporary measure due to the uncertainty caused by that freeze and “the separate funding interruption affecting Better Jobs Ontario-funded students at Trillium College.”

When asked recently if Better Jobs Ontario funding was also paused, Quinn’s spokesperson said little.

“Preliminary audit findings point to serious, systemic concerns about OSAP usage at private post-secondary institutions,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote.

“OSAP payments to students at these institutions are paused, and other streams of provincial funding to private institutions past and present are under review.”

Giacoboni refused to list those other streams of funding.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said if the government is taking action against another source of funding they should come out and say it.

“It’s happening,” he said. “They know it’s happening and I don’t know why they’re afraid to say it.”

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the government is ducking accountability.

“This government is terrified of facing the music,” she wrote in a statement.

“They won’t even do the bare minimum of explaining themselves. They’re leaving thousands of people who rely on this program to build a better future and find good jobs without any certainty or support. This is not how you protect Ontario in the face of growing job losses.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

stories.title: Privacy commissioner opens investigation into Crime Stoppers data breach
stories.summary: Canada's privacy watchdog has launched an investigation into a reportedly massive Crime Stoppers data breach as police departments across the country have paused accepting tips through the platform.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Canada’s privacy watchdog has launched an investigation into a reportedly massive Crime Stoppers data breach as police departments across the country have paused accepting tips through the platform.

The office of privacy commissioner Philippe Dufresne says the probe will look into the cybersecurity incident involving Navigate360, the third-party company that manages the platform used by Crime Stoppers.

The investigation comes after CBC reported that 1.5 million tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years were exposed when Navigate360 was hacked in March.

The U.S.-based company confirmed the breach last week, saying it immediately opened its own investigation, took “mitigation measures” and “implemented additional and enhanced safeguards” with the support of another cybersecurity firm after the discovery.

Police forces across Ontario, including several in the Greater Toronto Area, temporarily paused directing public calls to Crime Stoppers following the revelation.

Beyond Ontario, at least two police departments in Manitoba, including Winnipeg, have said that they would stop taking tips through the program as they review and assess the incident.

Saskatchewan Crime Stoppers told the public over the weekend to avoid sending tips through its platform.

“The pause is temporary. We will begin accepting new tips as soon as we are confident it is safe to do so,” it said in a statement.

The privacy commissioner’s office said it has reached out to Crime Stoppers programs to offer “expertise and guidance” in response to the breach.

“The investigation will examine the security safeguards that Navigate360 had in place at the time of the breach to determine the organization’s compliance with Canada’s federal private-sector privacy law,” it said in a statement Tuesday.

The watchdog also said it has contacted Navigate360, though it didn’t say whether the company has responded.

It said its engagement “with both organizations is focused on ensuring that the necessary steps are being taken to address the breach and protect Canadians’ personal information.”

stories.title: After election victory, Chow to face budget pressure and new deal with Ontario
stories.summary: Toronto - Negotiations with the province to help relieve Toronto's budget pressures loomed over Olivia Chow's election victory, as she vowed to be the "mayor for everyone."
stories.author: Jordan Omstead The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Negotiations with the province to help relieve Toronto’s budget pressures loomed over Olivia Chow’s election victory on Tuesday, as she vowed to be the “mayor for everyone.”

Chow took her first question from reporters hours after she held off challenger Brad Bradford in Monday’s election and convinced voters to back a second term of her progressive agenda.

“There’s a firm belief that we are stronger together. And the majority of the people of Toronto spoke out so loudly, with such enthusiasm,” she said.

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow says it doesn't matter who voted for her, she'll be mayor for everyone in Toronto, and will work with the new council and other levels of government to address problems Torontonians face. (Oct. 27, 2026)

“They know that we can take better care of each other.”

Her peacemaking political style earned her approving words from Premier Doug Ford during the campaign, who stopped just short of endorsing her in the contest.

Now, Chow will likely look to summon that goodwill as she looks to negotiations with Ford on a new Toronto-Ontario fiscal deal. The city has projected a 2027 budget hole of around $1.1 billion. Transit ridership continues to lag behind pre-pandemic levels while a softening real estate market is expected to squeeze the municipal land transfer tax.

Chow inherited a $1.8 billion shortfall when she was first elected in 2023. She sought to plug the hole with two sizable property tax increases and a major deal with Ford’s government. Ontario assumed maintenance of the city’s expressways and provided $1.2 billion in operating dollars for transit and shelters, while Chow dropped the city’s opposition to the Ontario Place redevelopment.

That deal is now set to expire at the same time as Chow has campaigned on a promise to keep property taxes at or below the rate of inflation. She reiterated that tax pledge on Tuesday while highlighting that the city had secured its first credit-rating upgrade in more than two decades during her first term.

“I do know the budget very well. I just hope that there is no surprises from outside the City of Toronto, but I don’t expect any,” she said.

Asked on Tuesday how quickly she planned to hash out a new deal with the province, Chow said she had exchanged texts with the premier earlier that morning.

“And no matter which level of government, whether it’s a federal or provincial government, they want to work together and they want do the best they can for the residents of Toronto.”

Chow managed to stave off her challenger on a night where several incumbents were toppled in Ontario’s municipal elections, including Mississauga’s Carolyn Parrish, Hamilton’s Andrea Horwath and Windsor’s Drew Dilkens.

Premier Doug Ford congratulated Chow on the victory and says he will “work with anyone to drive the economy to make sure we protect communities and companies and people” from U.S. tariffs.

Chow will preside over a council with a boosted progressive bloc as she seeks to make good on other campaign promises to cap weekly transit fares, introduce free school lunches and strengthen renter protections.

The departure of rival Bradford from council heralded the political resurrection of former Liberal MP Nate Erskine-Smith, who aligned himself with Chow in his successful run in Beaches East-York after a failed pivot to provincial politics. Chiara Padovani, a tenant organizer, defeated Toronto’s longest-serving councillor Frances Nunziata in York South-Weston.

Voter turnout was around 46 per cent, the highest it’s been since 2014. Chow’s 13 percentage point victory over Bradford would mark the narrowest win by a sitting mayor since the city’s amalgamation.

The dust barely had time to settle on Monday night’s election before Chow, 69, was asked about her long-term political future. As she stood outside city hall, she brushed off a question Tuesday about whether this would be her last run for mayor.

“I’m going to spend every moment of today and the next four years working hard for the people of Toronto,” she said. “As to the future, let us take one day, one week, one month, one year at a time.”

stories.title: Quebec premier accuses Ottawa of censoring him at EU Summit
stories.summary: Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is accusing Ottawa of muzzling him at the upcoming Canada-European Union summit in Montreal.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is accusing Ottawa of muzzling him at the upcoming Canada-European Union summit in Montreal.

The federal government has assured the premier that he is invited to dinner with EU representatives, but the premier will not speak at the summit taking place Thursday and Friday.

“He was invited to the dinner and he refused,” Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters in Ottawa on Tuesday. “It’s his decision to leave the chair empty.”

But the premier wrote on social media that Ottawa is seeking to impose economic decisions on Quebec without allowing the province a seat at the negotiating table.

“The federal government would have us believe that giving the Quebec premier permission to serve shrimp cocktails at a reception constitutes an acceptable and sufficient form of influence in representing Quebec’s interests,” St-Pierre Plamondon wrote.

Federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said in Ottawa that geopolitics, including the summit, fall under federal jurisdiction.

The Parti Québécois government also says Ottawa denied Quebec’s request to host a reception on the sidelines of the summit, which was submitted by former premier Christine Fréchette in September.

A provincial government spokesperson says the EU routinely holds a forum for economic leaders during such summits, which the province could have hosted or co-hosted.

The spokesperson said that there is precedent to include Quebec at the summit, as provincial representatives participated in negotiations for the Canada-European Union Free Trade Agreement.

Marie-Claude Sarrazin, the new Quebec minister of justice and Canadian intergovernmental affairs, said the federal government’s position serves as a reminder that the province needs “to be fully in charge in our own home.”

“‘When you’re not at the table, you’re on the menu,’ Prime Minister Carney once told us,” she said. “The federal government has chosen to prevent Quebec from having a say on its own territory. This is a fundamental lack of respect toward Quebec and a denial of the role of our legislature.”

The tension around the summit comes after St-Pierre Plamondon did not participate in a meeting on Monday between the federal government, provincial premiers and First Nations.

The Quebec premier also spoke with French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday.
